dossiers.AMAT:
AMAT — Applied Materials, Inc. (Semiconductor Materials & Equipment, Information Technology)

1. Verdict

WATCH — 12–24 month horizon. This overturns the triage's ADVANCE call once a real reverse DCF is run. Applied Materials is executing extremely well (record revenue, guidance raised twice this fiscal year, net-cash balance sheet, buybacks slowed rather than chased into strength) and the stock has already fallen ~34–42% from its 30 June 2026 high. But even after that drawdown, the 10-year reverse DCF shows the market pricing in ~18–24%/year FCF growth for a decade — far above any credible through-cycle base case for a capital-equipment company, and the independent factor data agrees: AMAT's value/FCF-yield percentile is in the bottom quintile of the whole universe (19th pct). A great business, priced for more than a capital-intensive, historically cyclical franchise can plausibly deliver. Condition to upgrade: either a further material de-rating (FCF yield rising toward ~3.5%+, i.e., meaningfully lower price for the same or higher FCF) or 3–4 more quarters of evidence that AI-driven WFE demand is a structural step-change rather than a supercycle that mean-reverts.

2. Business in plain English

Applied Materials makes the machines that make chips: deposition, etch, ion implantation, chemical-mechanical planarization and inspection/metrology tools sold to foundries, memory makers and IDMs (TSMC, Samsung, Micron, Intel and others) building fabs, plus a large recurring Applied Global Services (AGS) parts/service business tied to the installed base. It is the largest wafer-fab-equipment (WFE) vendor by revenue, with leading share in several deposition/etch categories and a growing advanced-packaging business tied to AI accelerators (2.5D/3D packaging, chip-on-wafer). It makes money by selling capital equipment (lumpy, tied to customers' capex cycles) plus steadier services/parts revenue on the installed base, and its economics are fundamentally a fixed-cost manufacturing/engineering business layered on a physics roadmap — margins swing hard with fab utilisation and the industry's capex cycle, not primarily with AMAT's own execution.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Composite_qvm 0.623 (decile 7, rank 189) is driven almost entirely by momentum (fam_M 0.846, 85th pct) and respectable quality (gp/assets 66th pct, ROE 76th pct), while value is a genuine outlier weak point (fam_V 0.235, FCF/price 19th pct — bottom quintile of the entire universe) and the accruals percentile is very low (7.9th pct, a caution flag on earnings quality that likely reflects the rapid receivables/inventory build funding the revenue ramp — normal in an equipment upcycle per the sector playbook, but worth tracking). This is not durable, it is a momentum/growth read that the model's own value factor is simultaneously telling you not to buy at this price — the quant data and my fundamental reverse DCF agree, which is the strongest possible confirmation that the WATCH call, not the triage's ADVANCE, is right.

No cut identified. This is a strong, real beat-and-raise pattern — the concern in this dossier is valuation, not execution.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • FCF conversion: TTM (through Q3 FY26) operating cash flow ≈ $8.40B; TTM capex ≈ $2.77B (capex intensity ≈ 10–11% of TTM revenue, up sharply from prior years — 9-mo FY26 capex of $1.99B vs. $1.48B in the year-ago period) → TTM FCF ≈ $5.62B, FCF/NI well below 1x this year because the company is genuinely reinvesting into capacity, consistent with an investment phase rather than harvesting (a good read of the capex trend per the sector playbook, not a red flag by itself).
  • Balance sheet: cash $7.04B; total debt (current $1.20B + long-term $5.25B) = $6.44B → net cash of ≈ $0.6B — genuinely conservative, and equity has grown from $19.5B (Jul-25) to $25.6B (Jul-26) largely on retained earnings.
  • Buybacks: materially slowed — 9-mo FY26 buybacks of only $1.18B vs. $4.04B in the same 9 months of FY25 (and $4.90B for all of FY25) — even as the stock rallied 176% over the trailing year. Reading this as a positive capital-discipline signal: management did not chase its own stock at an elevated multiple, instead prioritizing cash/capacity investment.
  • Earnings-quality watch item: the low accruals percentile (7.9th) from the factor data and the Q2-vs-Q3 net-income anomaly noted in §4 both point to the same place — working-capital and below-the-line items are moving faster than the income statement's face value suggests. Not a red flag on its own in an equipment upcycle (inventory/receivables build ahead of shipments is normal), but it means near-term EPS should be read with more caution than usual.
  • China exposure: China revenue was $2.51B in Q3 FY26, 28% of total, down from 35% a year ago — a real mix shift, not (yet) an absolute collapse, as non-China (AI/leading-edge) demand is growing faster.

7. Valuation snapshot and reverse DCF

No V1 row exists for AMAT — v1_verdict set to null; this section is independent work, cross-checked against the v4 factor data (§3), which agrees on direction. Vendor NTM P/E ≈ 26–27x (peers: Lam Research, KLA typically low-to-mid 20s–30s during upcycles; ASML higher given EUV monopoly) — not obviously expensive on a simple forward-P/E basis, which is exactly the trap the sector playbook warns about: "the stock screens at 6–9x on peak earnings just as the correction begins... treat a mid-single-digit P/E on record earnings as a warning, not a valuation." AMAT's 26–27x is not in that extreme zone, but its FCF yield tells a different, much more cautious story.

10-year reverse DCF (EV ≈ $384.3B [$384.9B market cap − ~$0.6B net cash]; TTM FCF $5.62B): solving for the uniform 10-year FCF growth rate that justifies the current EV, holding terminal growth at 3–4%: - At WACC 8.5%: implied growth 17.7–19.8%/yr. - At WACC 9.0–9.5% (central estimate): implied growth 19.3–22.5%/yr. - At WACC 10.0%: implied growth 22.2–23.8%/yr.

This is robustly high across every reasonable assumption — never below ~18%/year. My evidence-based base case for a capital-equipment franchise, over a full cycle including troughs, is ~8–10%/year FCF growth: WFE spending has historically compounded mid-to-high single digits through complete cycles (with 20–40% peak-to-trough swings along the way), and even crediting a genuinely structural AI/advanced-packaging growth leg (as this dossier does for ADI's comms segment), a sustained low-20s% FCF CAGR for a full decade would be unprecedented for this industry. Implied growth is clearly above my base case → implied_vs_base = "above" → per the program's own rule, this cannot be INCLUDE or INCLUDE-SMALL.

  • Bear case (export-control impact deepens, AI-capex spending pauses/digests for 1–2 years as fabs catch up on installed capacity — a normal WFE-cycle pattern): FCF flat (0%/yr) for 3 years, multiple compresses from today's elevated ~68x EV/FCF to a mid-cycle-normalized ~27x → ~ −27%/yr 3-year annualized return.
  • Base case (capex intensity normalizes as current fab investments season, FCF growth resumes at ~9%/yr through-cycle — well below the ~20% priced in): multiple compresses toward ~37x as FCF catches up to the earnings already being recognized → ~ −11%/yr, i.e. even the "things go fine" case is a loser at today's price, which is the crux of the WATCH call.
  • Bull case (the AI-capex supercycle proves structurally durable, not just a multi-year burst): FCF growth ~16%/yr, multiple holds near current elevated levels (~65x) → ~+14%/yr.

8. Bull case

  1. Record Q3 revenue (+25% y/y) with guidance raised twice in FY26 and the full-year Semiconductor Systems growth outlook lifted from >20% to >30% — genuine, broad-based execution, not a one-quarter beat.
  2. Net-cash balance sheet and slowing buybacks into strength — capital discipline that most momentum-driven capital-equipment names lack at a cycle high.
  3. Advanced-packaging and AI-leading-edge demand may represent a genuinely new, multi-year secular layer on top of the traditional WFE cycle, not merely a repeat of past boom-bust patterns.

9. Bear case

  1. Reverse DCF shows the market pricing in ~18–24%/year FCF growth for a decade — a base rate no capital-equipment company has sustained through multiple capex cycles; even a credible "everything goes fine" base case implies a negative 3-year return at today's price.
  2. The stock already made this exact trip once: +176% over the trailing 12 months to an all-time high of $739.67 (30 Jun 2026), then −34% to −42% to the current $424–$485 range — a violent round-trip that itself signals the market has been pricing supercycle extrapolation and unwinding it in real time.
  3. A real, adjudicated compliance failure: AMAT settled with the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security for $253M on 11 Feb 2026 over past China export-control compliance issues, and the company now guides to a $600M FY26 revenue headwind from ongoing export restrictions — both a fine already paid and an active, growing drag, not a hypothetical risk.

10. Key risks & kill criteria

  1. Quarterly sequential revenue declines for two consecutive quarters (the cycle turning down from this level).
  2. China export-control revenue headwind exceeds $1B annualized (vs. the current $600M FY26 guide) without offsetting non-China demand.
  3. Gross margin falls below 46–47% (vs. current ~50%) for two consecutive quarters — a utilisation/pricing deterioration signal.
  4. A second BIS/export-control enforcement action, or a new DOJ/Commerce investigation, is disclosed.
  5. Capex/revenue stays above ~10% for four or more consecutive quarters while OCF growth stalls — over-investing into a cycle top without revenue follow-through.

11. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: ~13 Nov 2026 (Q4/FY26 results; date is a company estimate as of this snapshot, not yet formally confirmed).
  • Calendar-2026 Semiconductor Systems growth outlook (>30%, raised from >20%) will be directly tested by the Q4 print and initial FY27 commentary.
  • Any further Commerce Department/BIS action on China export controls is 8-K-reportable and would be a fast-moving catalyst in either direction.

12. Red-flag scan

  • Regulatory settlement: AMAT settled with the U.S. Commerce Department's BIS for $253M on 11 Feb 2026, resolving an inquiry into certain China customer shipments and export-control compliance. This is a material, adjudicated compliance failure, not an allegation — logged as a hard red flag even though it is now resolved.
  • Ongoing export-control drag: management guides to a $600M FY26 revenue headwind from current U.S. export restrictions preventing supply to China's memory-chip segment — an active, quantified, and (per the China revenue-share trend) plausibly growing constraint.
  • Insider selling: CEO Gary Dickerson has sold shares steadily over the past year (e.g., ~83,000 shares on 15–16 Jun 2026 at ~$590–600/share; ~78,321 shares on 29–30 Jun 2026 at low-to-mid-$700s/share — both clustered near the stock's eventual all-time high) — a consistent diversification pattern (161,321 shares sold, zero bought, over the trailing year per aggregator data) rather than a single alarming transaction, but the clustering right at the top is worth noting.
  • Earnings-quality watch: the Q2/Q3 FY26 net-income anomaly (§4) and bottom-quintile accruals factor score (§3) both warrant a closer look at the cash-flow statement and MD&A before any upgrade from WATCH.
  • No auditor change, restatement, or going-concern language identified.

1. Verdict

WATCH (12–36 month thesis horizon, revisit after Q3 2026 print on 2026-11-03). AMD's underlying business is executing an unambiguous, accelerating AI/data-center ramp (Data Center revenue +107% YoY in Q2 2026; three straight quarters of beat-and-raise; a landmark OpenAI supply/equity partnership). But the reverse DCF shows the current price already requires that acceleration to continue at a very high rate for years, the trailing GAAP P/E (160x) is not usable as a valuation anchor, and 7-of-8-quarter beat-and-raise plus a stock price up ~191% over 12 months (triage) mean consensus targets (mean $618.50) sit below the current price ($630.63) — the Street itself is not, on average, underwriting further upside from here. This matches the triage call directionally (advance, but flagged "consensus price target roughly at spot… treat as full-diligence, not automatic buy") and confirms it with primary-source numbers.

2. Business in plain English

AMD designs (and outsources manufacturing of) computer processors: CPUs for PCs and servers (EPYC, Ryzen), GPUs/AI accelerators for data centers (Instinct MI-series), embedded/gaming chips, and FPGAs (from the 2022 Xilinx acquisition). It sells to PC makers, cloud/hyperscale data-center operators, and embedded-systems customers, competing most directly with Intel in CPUs and Nvidia in AI GPUs. It makes money on chip design margins; its main current growth engine is selling AI-training/inference GPUs to hyperscalers and AI labs as a second source to Nvidia.

Reverse DCF (own construction; two-stage — 10-year explicit growth then 3% terminal, WACC 10% for higher-beta semiconductor/AI-capex-cycle exposure, consolidated basis): Using an annualized H1-2026 FCF base (~$8.25bn, chosen over the FY2025 figure of $6.7bn because the AI ramp is demonstrably already underway and a stale base would understate current earnings power) against EV of $1.019tn: solving EV = Σ FCF₀(1+g)ᵗ/(1+WACC)ᵗ (t=1..10) + terminal value at 3% gives implied 10-year FCF growth g ≈ 24–26%/yr, i.e. roughly a 6x growth in annual FCF by year 10. That is an aggressive but not obviously impossible ask given AMD's own H2 2026 guidance trajectory (Q3 2026 guide alone implies +12.7% sequential revenue growth, and management guides data-center revenue to double again in 2027) — but it requires the current hyperscaler AI-capex cycle to persist at a high rate for a full decade, well beyond the visibility any guidance track record can support. implied_vs_base: above — the price is discounting more growth than the analyst's own base case (mid-teens-to-20%% FCF CAGR moderating after 2028 as the AI-capex cycle matures and Nvidia/custom-ASIC competition intensifies).

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull (3 points): 1. OpenAI strategic partnership (announced 2025-10-06): OpenAI to deploy up to 6 GW of AMD Instinct GPUs over multiple years (1 GW in 2026), with AMD management guiding "tens of billions" of incremental revenue and >$100bn in cumulative revenue potential over four years (AMD/OpenAI press releases, ir.amd.com and openai.com, 2025-10-06). 2. Three consecutive quarters of guidance beats with the growth rate still accelerating (Q3 2026 guide of ~$13bn implies the fastest sequential growth of the last four quarters), and MI400-series (MI455X/MI430X) already being consumed by OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta per management (Q2 2026 earnings call). 3. Net-cash balance sheet (no leverage constraint) and FCF compounding quickly (H1 2026 FCF already 61% of all FY2025) give AMD real capacity to fund capacity expansion without dilution or debt stress.

Bear (3 points): 1. Reverse DCF requires ~24–26%/yr FCF growth sustained for 10 years — a high bar; if the AI-GPU capex cycle decelerates or Nvidia/hyperscaler-custom-ASIC competition compresses AMD's share/margins earlier than year 5–6, the downside to a re-rated multiple is large (46.9x NTM P/E has very little room for disappointment). 2. Analyst mean/median price targets ($618.5/$616) sit below the current price ($630.63) — a rare signal that the sell-side consensus, even after the run, is not on average underwriting further near-term upside. 3. The OpenAI warrant deal (up to 160 million AMD shares at $0.01, vesting on deployment milestones and an escalating AMD share-price target up to $600 for the final tranche) creates real dilution risk (~9-10% of shares if fully vested) and makes AMD's economics partly dependent on OpenAI's own ability to pay for and deploy the compute — OpenAI is not yet GAAP-profitable, a customer-concentration/counterparty risk this dossier flags but cannot fully quantify from AMD's own filings alone.

9. Key risks & measurable kill criteria

Any of the following would break the thesis (i.e., would move this WATCH toward REJECT): 1. Any single quarter of guided revenue growth below the prior quarter's growth rate (deceleration signal) — would break the "still-accelerating beat-and-raise" thesis this WATCH call depends on. 2. Data Center segment gross margin falls below 50% for two consecutive quarters (Q2 2026 consolidated gross margin was 53.8%; a sustained drop would signal AI-GPU pricing/competitive pressure from Nvidia or custom ASICs). 3. OpenAI deployment milestones (1 GW tranche) missed or delayed beyond 2026 — the single largest identified forward revenue driver; a delay would remove the main support for the current above-base valuation. 4. Net cash position turns negative (i.e., AMD takes on net debt) without a corresponding step-up in disclosed capacity/capex plans — would signal the AI-capex ramp is cash-flow-negative rather than self-funding. 5. Buyback pace stays at the reduced ~$220M/half-year run-rate for more than 2 more quarters combined with rising share count from OpenAI-warrant vesting — dilution without offsetting repurchase would compound the "priced above base case" risk.

dossiers.AMP:
AMP — Ameriprise Financial, Inc.

Most recent period incorporated: Q2 2026 10-Q (period ended 2026-06-30, filed 2026-08-04) and the Q2 2026 earnings release (8-K Ex-99.1, filed 2026-07-23). Checked SEC EDGAR and the company's investor-relations site for events to 2026-09-25: found and incorporated a 2026-09-03 press release on routine Q3 2026 fee-day/trading-day/tax-rate seasonality (immaterial). Q3 2026 results not yet released (confirmed next release 2026-10-29).

Basis: GAAP figures are consolidated, USD, as filed with the SEC (CIK 0000820027). "Adjusted operating earnings," "Adjusted operating EPS" and AUM/AUA figures are the company's own non-GAAP/operating definitions, labeled every time they appear.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE. Thesis horizon 12–36 months. One-sentence reason: a capital-light wealth- and asset-management franchise compounding assets under management at double-digit rates, returning the large majority of earnings to shareholders, trading at a single-digit NTM P/E with a clean red-flag scan — and the systematic valuation model (V1) independently reaches the same "fair, not demanding" conclusion this dossier reaches from primary sources.

2. Business in plain English

Ameriprise is a diversified financial-services holding company built around three businesses: Advice & Wealth Management (its largest segment — roughly 10,000+ affiliated financial advisors managing client assets for a fee, plus banking/lending products), Asset Management (Columbia Threadneedle Investments, running mutual funds/ETFs/institutional mandates), and a smaller, run-off-oriented Retirement & Protection Solutions legacy annuity/insurance book. It earns most of its money on fees tied to assets under management/administration (AUM/AUA) rather than on spread or underwriting risk — a capital-light model that requires relatively little balance-sheet capital per dollar of revenue, which is why its return on equity is structurally very high (see §6).

3. Why the model likes it — and whether that's durable

Quant context (b1_live_scores.csv, live rank 113/~1,172): strong across families — quality composite in the top decile, ROE 57th percentile of the raw factor (the b1 pct_roe is 0.568, but this compares AMP against the whole cross-sectional universe including much lower-ROE industrials/utilities; against its own asset-management peer group AMP's ROE is exceptional — see §7), earnings yield 90th percentile, FCF yield 76th percentile, momentum 93rd percentile. Durable: AUM/AUA growth of 13–19% YoY across every reported segment in Q2 2026 (§4) and four consecutive quarters of 16–22% YoY adjusted-operating-EPS growth (§5) are structural, filed facts — a genuinely growing capital-light franchise, not a one-quarter beat. Worth watching, not yet a red flag: the high ROE is partly a function of an unusually thin equity base (buybacks have shrunk shareholders' equity to ~$6.4bn against ~$4bn of TTM net income); V1's own valuation model flags that AMP's ROE would need to stay near current levels, not revert toward its 10-year median (30th percentile of own history), to fully justify the price (§7) — this is the central judgment call in this dossier.

5. Guidance track record

AMP does not issue formal quarterly or annual EPS/revenue guidance (typical for the sector); its "guidance" equivalent is quarter-ahead seasonality disclosure (fee days, trading days, mark-to-market sensitivity, tax rate) and periodic capital-return commentary. The most recent such disclosure (2026-09-03 press release, ahead of Q3 2026 earnings) is entirely routine: +92 fee days vs. 91 in Q2 2026 (~+$13m combined pretax tailwind), +64 vs. 62 trading days (~+$4m), full-year 2026 operating effective tax rate guided at 20%–22% — no negative surprise, no change in the tax-rate range from prior disclosures reviewed. Nothing in the four most recent earnings releases discloses a formal forward EPS range to raise, cut or maintain, so the "guidance track record" test from the base template does not apply mechanically here; what is trackable and has been consistently delivered is double-digit AUM growth and adjusted-EPS growth in every one of the last four quarters (§4).

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • Capital return is exceptionally high: Q2 2026 alone returned $932m to shareholders, or 91% of operating earnings (company-reported); buybacks were $2,907m in FY2025 and already $1,653m through H1 2026 (annualizing to a similar pace); dividend per share was $1.35/quarter as of the last full-year data point directly confirmed in this pass (2023; likely raised since, not independently re-verified this pass — disclosed limitation).
  • ROE: TTM net income ~$3.9–4.0bn (10-K/10-Q) against stockholders' equity of only $6.37bn (Q2 2026) → ROE ≈ 62% — genuinely exceptional, and a direct, mechanical consequence of the capital-light fee-based model plus a decade of sustained buybacks shrinking the equity base. V1's own model separately computes this as 62.0% TTM vs. a 62.0/29.998%/17.2% (80th/50th/20th percentile) 10-year-own-history distribution — i.e., today's ROE sits at roughly the 80th percentile of AMP's own trailing 10-year history, a real, sourced data point that argues for some mean-reversion risk being priced conservatively, not aggressively (§7).
  • Debt: not independently re-derived from XBRL this pass (AMP's LongTermDebtNoncurrent/LongTermDebt XBRL tags returned no recent instances in the company-facts pull — a data-availability note, not a red flag; V1's own model separately sources net debt as –$6.0bn [i.e. a net cash position at the parent-company level, per V1's D4/Yahoo cross-check] which is consistent with AMP's capital-light model and heavy cash-generative wealth-management mix). This dossier defers to V1's sourced net-debt figure rather than re-deriving a possibly-incomplete one from a partial XBRL pull.
  • Red flags: none material found. The most recent 10-Q's Legal Proceedings item (Q2 2026) contains only generic, boilerplate disclosure common to all diversified financial-services firms (regulatory inquiries, arbitration, "elevated" industry-wide regulatory activity) with no specific named material matter, no restatement, no auditor change, no going-concern language. No cash-sweep-program litigation (an issue that has affected several broker-dealer peers industry-wide) was found mentioned in the section reviewed.

7. Valuation snapshot — reconciled with V1

v4/outputs/v1_valuation_table.csv / v1_valuation.json carries a full row for AMP: verdict "fair" (score +0.071, near the neutral midpoint of the fair band), method = justified P/B [(ROE−g)/(COE−g)], current P/B 7.19x (76.8th percentile of AMP's own 177-month history) vs. peer-median P/B 2.75x (Asset Management & Custody Banks peers incl. APO/ARES/BLK/BX). V1's implied ROE priced into the current multiple is 52.4%, versus AMP's actual TTM ROE of 62.0% and its 10-year-own-history median of just 30.0% — i.e., the market is pricing AMP to partially mean-revert from today's exceptional ROE, but not all the way back to its historical median. V1's WACC (cost of equity, CAPM) is 9.87% (beta 1.13 Blume-adjusted). V1's scenarios: bear −12.7%/yr (ROE reverts to the 20th percentile, 17.2%), base +6.5%/yr (ROE holds near the 50th percentile, 30.0%), bull +67.7%/yr (ROE holds near the 80th percentile, 56.2%, compounded with 8.3%/yr share-count shrinkage).

This dossier's independent read: I largely agree with V1's "fair" verdict and treat its base case (+6.5%/yr, implied ROE mean-reverting toward the 30th-percentile historical median) as the operative base case here — it is conservative relative to the current 62% ROE run-rate, appropriately so given ROE has been on a rising secular trend for years as the business mix shifted toward capital-light fee revenue (a trend V1's flat historical-percentile framework does not fully credit, but which this dossier does not have grounds to override outright either). One reservation, flagged rather than silently accepted: V1's bull case (+67.7%/yr) compounds an 80th-percentile ROE assumption with an 8.3%/yr share-count-shrinkage assumption for three straight years — the resulting >3x price outcome (exit P/B 8.05x on top of a rising book value per share) looks like a modeling artefact of compounding two aggressive assumptions together rather than a plausible outcome, and should not be treated as a realistic upper bound; V1X's prior audit pass already reviewed this model family (no verdict-changing errors found) but did not specifically flag this compounding effect. valuation_view_vs_v1.consistent = true: this dossier's primary-source read (strong, real, but not fully "cheap" — 9.8x NTM P/E against a business capable of continuing double-digit AUM growth) matches V1's "fair" label; implied growth (V1's base case) is at or below what this dossier's evidence (§4/§6) supports as achievable, satisfying the INCLUDE eligibility rule.

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull: 1. AUM/AUA growing 13–19% across every segment (Q2 2026 YoY), a genuine structural tailwind (flows + markets), not a one-quarter pop. 2. Capital-light model returns ~90%+ of operating earnings to shareholders every quarter — one of the most shareholder-friendly capital-return policies in the S&P 500 financial sector, directly compounding per-share value via buybacks. 3. Single-digit NTM P/E (9.8x) for a business generating 62% ROE is a genuinely unusual combination even after accounting for the thin-equity-base mechanical effect.

Bear: 1. ROE sits at roughly the 80th percentile of AMP's own 10-year history — some mean reversion (already partly priced by V1's base case) is a real risk, not a remote one, if markets fall or flows reverse. 2. GAAP earnings are genuinely volatile quarter to quarter from insurance/annuity mark-to-market effects — a real legacy-block risk that a purely "Adjusted operating EPS" read can understate. 3. Continuous heavy buybacks (>$2.9bn/yr) that have driven much of the ROE/EPS story could decelerate if capital generation weakens, removing a key compounding lever.

9. Key risks & kill criteria

  1. TTM ROE falls below 40% (vs. ~62% now) for two consecutive quarters — would indicate faster-than-expected mean reversion.
  2. Total AUM+AUA growth (YoY) falls below 5% for two consecutive quarters (vs. 13–19% segment growth now).
  3. Capital returned to shareholders falls below 60% of operating earnings for two consecutive quarters (vs. ~91% in Q2 2026) — would signal a capital-return policy change.
  4. Any named, material litigation or regulatory enforcement matter (e.g. a cash-sweep-program-style industry action) is disclosed in a future 10-Q's Legal Proceedings item.
  5. Adjusted operating EPS YoY growth turns negative for any quarter (it has been +16% to +22% in each of the last four).

dossiers.AMZN:
AMZN — Amazon.com, Inc.

1. Verdict

WATCH. Horizon 12–36 months. AWS is genuinely re-accelerating (37% YoY, an 18-quarter high) with a $496bn backlog growing triple-digit — the strongest "real demand, not just capex" signal in this batch — but it is being funded by capex so large ($220bn 2026 guide) that trailing free cash flow has turned negative on one commonly used measure, leverage has risen sharply, and the model's own quality factor score is the weakest of the four names reviewed. The 25-Sep-2026 close ($249.67) implies a 10-year revenue CAGR of ~14.9% versus an evidence-based base case of ~10.9%.

2. Business in plain English

Amazon runs the largest US e-commerce marketplace (retail, third-party seller fees, advertising) and, through AWS, the largest cloud infrastructure business in the world, renting compute, storage and — increasingly — AI model access (Bedrock) and custom AI chips (Trainium) to enterprises. It makes money on razor-thin retail/logistics margins subsidized in large part by AWS's much higher-margin cloud and advertising businesses.

3. Why the model likes it — durability check

b1 composite 0.563 (decile 6, quintile 3, live_rank 218 — the model was neutral-to-mildly-positive, well outside its own top-30). The composite is carried entirely by Momentum (fam_M 0.754) and especially Earnings momentum (fam_S 0.991, the highest of any family score in this batch) — Amazon has beaten EPS estimates in all of the last 8 quarters with an average surprise of +50%. But Quality (fam_Q 0.136) is by far the weakest score of the four companies in this program, reflecting the capex-driven balance-sheet and cash-flow deterioration described in §6 below (heavy asset growth, rising leverage, and — depending on the measure — negative free cash flow are all negative inputs to the quality family). This is not an artefact: it is a real, current, disclosed condition of the business, not a modeling quirk.

4. Last two years of results (quarterly highlights, $bn GAAP)

Quarter Total revenue YoY AWS revenue AWS YoY AWS op. margin Consol. op. margin
Q2 2026 $200.6 +20% $42.2 +36.7% (fastest in 18 qtrs) 39% (+650bps YoY; +520bps ex-derivative gains) 14% (+2pp YoY)

AWS added $4.6bn of sequential revenue in Q2 2026 — about 80% more than its largest previous quarterly increase — and is now a $169bn annualized run-rate business [Investing.com transcript; TechTimes]. AWS backlog: $496bn, growing triple-digit YoY; a separate $225bn+ of Trainium revenue commitments is disclosed on top of that backlog [TechTimes, 2026-07-31; valueaddvc]. AWS AI services and custom-chip revenue each independently crossed $25bn annualized run-rate, both growing triple-digit YoY; Bedrock customer spend grew 170% QoQ in Q1 2026, with Bedrock processing more tokens that quarter than in all prior years combined [multiple sources, 2026 Q1/Q2 earnings coverage]. TTM revenue (d4): $775.7bn. NTM consensus EPS $11.13 (d4); trailing EPS $12.42.

5. Guidance track record

2026 capex guidance was raised from ~$200bn to ~$220bn at the Q2 2026 call, explicitly attributed to higher memory costs, not to weaker-than-planned demand. Management (CEO Andy Jassy) stated Amazon still won't have enough capacity to meet 2026 demand, and expects the same to be true in 2027 [Fortune, 2026-07-30] — a demand-constrained framing, which is bullish for revenue durability but confirms the capex burden will not ease soon.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet — the central issue for this name

  • Data conflict (flag per program instructions): the v4 quant snapshot (d4_live_snapshot.parquet) shows trailing FCF of +$3.2bn, while independent Q2 2026 earnings coverage reports TTM free cash flow of −$7.6bn, a 142% YoY decline from +$18.2bn a year earlier [Barchart, Investing.com, 2026-07]. The gap is very likely a definitional difference (Yahoo's FCF field vs. Amazon's own operating-cash-flow-minus-capex-and-equipment-finance-leases definition, which explicitly moved negative per the company's own slides), but it is large enough (a ~$11bn swing) that it should not be taken at face value from either source without reconciling the exact capex/lease treatment — treat AMZN's "FCF" as ambiguous pending reconciliation.
  • TTM cash capex reached $173bn, up from $107bn a year earlier; operating cash flow rose ~33% YoY over the same period — the FCF deterioration is a capex story, not an operating-cash story.
  • Long-term debt principal+interest reached $220.3bn as of 30-Jun-2026, roughly doubling within six months; Amazon has stated it will "continue evaluating funding options," i.e., more debt issuance is plausible [AlphaQuery; company disclosures].
  • Stock-based compensation: Q2 2026 $10.07bn (down 1.5% YoY — a rare instance of SBC not growing among these four names), Q1 2026 $4.03bn — treat as a real cost regardless of the recent flattening.

7. Valuation — reverse DCF (no V1 row exists for this ticker; valuation performed directly here)

10-year reverse DCF: 12.5% discount rate (higher than MSFT/GOOGL to reflect thinner margins and capex/leverage risk), 16% terminal consolidated operating margin (vs. today's 14%, allowing continued mix-shift toward AWS/advertising), 20% tax, ~10.79bn diluted shares (from market cap/price), 22x terminal P/E. The $249.67 close requires a constant 10-year revenue CAGR of ~14.9%.

My base case: AWS decelerating from 37% today toward the high-teens by year 3 as the $496bn backlog converts and the base compounds past $250bn+ annualized, blended with mid-single-digit-to-low-double-digit retail/advertising growth. Explicit path (18%/16%/13%/12%/11%/10%/9%/8%/7%/6%) gives a 10-year compound-equivalent of ~10.9% and a base-case fair value of ~$176 — ~42% below the current $249.67. implied_vs_base: above.

3-year scenario returns (IRR from $249.67; Amazon pays no dividend, so all return is price appreciation): | Scenario | Yr3 revenue | Op. margin | P/E | Yr3 price | 3-yr IRR | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Bear | $1,004.5bn | 12% | 16x | $143 | −17.0% | | Base | $1,179.7bn | 16% | 22x | $308 | +7.2% | | Bull | $1,340.4bn | 20% | 28x | $557 | +30.6% |

Of the four names, AMZN's base-case 3-year return (+7.2%) is the least unattractive on this framework — but the weak quality score and FCF ambiguity mean the margin-of-safety is genuinely lower than the headline valuation gap alone would suggest.

8. Bull case

  1. AWS's re-acceleration to an 18-quarter-high growth rate, with a $496bn backlog (growing triple-digit) plus $225bn of separate Trainium commitments, is real, dated, disclosed demand — not a hopeful extrapolation.
  2. AWS operating margin expanded 650bps YoY even while absorbing the AI capex ramp, showing the segment is not just growing but getting more profitable at the same time.
  3. Retail/advertising margin improvement (consolidated op margin +2pp YoY) provides a second, independent earnings lever besides AWS.

Bear case

  1. Quality-factor deterioration is the worst of any name in this program (fam_Q 0.136) — real, current, and driven by the same capex program that bulls point to as the growth driver, i.e., growth and quality-erosion are two sides of the same coin right now.
  2. FCF is ambiguous-to-negative on the most recent TTM data by at least one credible external measure, while long-term debt has roughly doubled in six months — a genuine, not hypothetical, capex burden.
  3. A separate FTC monopoly-power lawsuit (marketplace/pricing practices) is scheduled for a bench trial starting 9-Feb-2027 — later than earlier expected (originally Oct-2026) but a real, dated event risk to core retail-marketplace economics, distinct from and in addition to the $2.5bn Prime-enrollment settlement Amazon already paid [Bloomberg Law, MLex, 2026].

9. Key risks & kill criteria (thesis-invalidation triggers — signposts to watch)

  1. AWS revenue growth decelerates below 28% YoY for two consecutive quarters (would break the re-acceleration thesis).
  2. TTM free cash flow (reconciled, company-reported basis) remains negative for three consecutive quarters after 2026 capex guidance is met (i.e., the negative FCF print becomes structural, not a temporary supercycle).
  3. Long-term debt principal+interest exceeds $300bn without a corresponding step-up in AWS backlog.
  4. 2026 capex guidance is raised a third time beyond $220bn.
  5. FTC monopoly-power case survives Amazon's motion to dismiss and proceeds toward the Feb-2027 trial with a scope that includes structural remedies.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 2026-10-29 (per d4 snapshot). FTC v. Amazon monopoly-power bench trial: 9-Feb-2027 (quarterly status conferences precede it). No EU DMA-specific enforcement action against Amazon identified in this window beyond the general 2026 enforcement-plan framing (potential fines across Apple/Google/Meta/Amazon/Microsoft collectively exceeding €100bn, per Commission estimates, but no Amazon-specific decision dated).

11. Red-flag scan

No auditor changes, restatements or going-concern language identified. Data conflict flagged in §6 (FCF: +$3.2bn per d4 vs. −$7.6bn TTM per external Q2 2026 coverage) — resolve before using either figure as an input to portfolio-level cash-flow assumptions. Separate, closed item: Amazon paid a $2.5bn/$1.5bn-range FTC settlement over unlawful Prime enrollment/cancellation practices (dates and exact amount vary by source; treat as resolved, not a live risk). No short-seller report identified in this window.

dossiers.ANET:
Arista Networks, Inc. (ANET) — Diligence Dossier (F27, standard depth)

1. Verdict

WATCH — 12–24 month thesis horizon. Execution and moat are exceptional (accelerating growth, 45%+ non-GAAP operating margins, net-cash balance sheet, four straight quarters of beat-and-raise), but the 25 Sep 2026 close ($206.55, mkt cap ≈$260.5bn) already prices in high-teens free-cash-flow growth sustained for a full decade — above this analyst's evidence-based base case. Two customers are >40% of revenue. Re-underwrite on a pullback that brings the implied growth to ≤15%/yr, or on evidence of customer diversification.

2. Business in plain English

Arista sells high-performance networking switches and its EOS software (a single, modular network operating system across the whole product line) to hyperscale cloud, AI-cluster, enterprise campus and service-provider customers. It makes money selling hardware with high-margin embedded software/support, and increasingly selling AI-cluster "back-end" and "front-end" networking fabric to a small number of very large cloud/AI customers. Competitive position: the #2 data-center networking vendor after Cisco by most measures, with a reputation for software quality and reliability that has let it win share inside the largest hyperscalers' AI build-outs.

3. Why the model likes it / durability

Quant flags (b1_live_scores.csv): composite decile 8, quintile 4, live_rank 149/1172; Quality percentile ~50–79% across sub-factors (gp/assets 49th, ROE 60th, OCF/assets 79th), Value poor (bp 16th pct — expensive), Momentum 12-1m 82nd pct, SUE 98th pct (strong recent earnings surprises). The growth is not an artefact: revenue growth has accelerated for four consecutive quarters (27.5% → 28.9% → 35.1% → 37.7% YoY) on real unit/AI-cluster demand, confirmed in SEC filings, not a one-off comp or restatement. The valuation richness (low B/P) is real and is the central risk, not a data error.

4. Last 8 quarters (SEC 10-Q/10-K + 8-K Ex-99.1 earnings releases; GAAP unless noted)

Current guide (Q2'26 8-K, 2026-08-04): Q3'26 revenue "approximately $3.3bn", non-GAAP op margin 48–49%, non-GAAP diluted EPS $1.06–1.08. This is a genuine, accelerating beat-and-raise pattern, not a single lucky quarter.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

FCF/NI (TTM): FCF $5.16bn vs GAAP NI $4.04bn ≈ 1.28x conversion — strong, aided by growing deferred revenue (customer prepayments) rather than one-off working-capital releases. SBC/revenue (TTM) ≈ 4.2% (440.2/10,540.8) — moderate for a software-heavy hardware vendor. No debt of any kind: at 2026-06-30, cash $2,290.2m + marketable securities $11,053.1m = $13,343.3m against $0 long-term debt (10-Q balance sheet, filed with Q2'26 8-K). Net cash ≈$13.3bn (≈5% of market cap). Share count essentially flat (buybacks of $0–787m/quarter roughly offset SBC dilution; no dividend). No pending M&A of note; one small $300m acquisition (cash paid for business combinations, FY2025 10-K).

7. Valuation — reverse DCF (no V1 row exists for ANET; this analyst's own model)

No systematic V1 valuation exists for this name (v1_valuation_table.csv has no ANET row) — v1_verdict is null; this section is this dossier's own reverse DCF. - Inputs: EV = mkt cap $260.51bn − net cash $13.34bn = $247.17bn (2026-09-25 close, b1_live_scores.csv). TTM FCF $5.16bn. WACC 9.5% (rf≈4.3% + β-adjusted ERP, quality/net-cash balance sheet). Terminal growth 3.5%. - Implied 10-year FCF CAGR: ~16.9% to justify the current EV under a standard 2-stage DCF (explicit 10y + Gordon terminal). - Bear case (customer concentration bites — one hyperscaler in-sources networking silicon or pauses capex; growth decelerates to high-single-digits within 2–3 years): ≈8–10% 10y FCF CAGR. - Base case (evidence-based): ≈14–15%. Current growth (30–38% YoY) is real, but a decade of 17%+ FCF growth would be historically rare for a company already at a $10.5bn TTM revenue run-rate; AI-cluster networking capex cycles are also known to be lumpy (hyperscaler capex budgets reset annually). - Bull case (AI-fabric share gains continue beyond front-end into back-end fabric, no customer losses): ≈20–22%. - Implied (16.9%) is above base case (~14–15%) → verdict WATCH, not INCLUDE, per program discipline: a great business priced for more growth than the evidence supports. - scenario_returns_3y (annualised, this analyst's estimate, not a formal model): bear ≈ −12%/yr (growth decelerates to ~5–8%/yr, NTM multiple compresses ~42x→25x); base ≈ +10%/yr (growth ~18–20%/yr near-term normalizing, multiple ~42x→35x); bull ≈ +29%/yr (growth stays 25–30%/yr, multiple flat-to-up).

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) AI-cluster networking is a multi-year, structurally growing capex category and Arista's EOS software moat is winning share inside the largest hyperscalers; (2) net-cash balance sheet and 45%+ operating margins give enormous optionality with no leverage risk; (3) guidance has been beaten and raised for four straight quarters with growing magnitude, evidencing real demand visibility (backlog/bookings), not a one-time pull-forward. Bear: (1) two end customers were 26% and 16% of FY2025 revenue (10-K risk factors) — loss, delay or in-sourcing by either would move results materially; (2) Nvidia's Spectrum-X networking push and hyperscaler in-house silicon (e.g., custom ASIC switches at Meta/Microsoft/Amazon) are direct, well-funded competitive threats named in the company's own risk factors; (3) at the current price the market already requires ~17%/yr FCF growth for 10 years — a high bar that leaves little room for a normal cyclical air-pocket in AI capex.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Revenue from the two largest customers (26%/16% of FY2025 revenue) falls below 30% combined for two consecutive quarters without an offsetting new large customer disclosed (loss of concentration, but also loss of the visibility that supports the growth thesis) — reassess either way.
  2. YoY revenue growth decelerates below 15% for two consecutive quarters (vs. 27.5–37.7% over the last four) — the core "durable AI-networking growth" thesis is broken.
  3. Non-GAAP operating margin falls below 44% for two consecutive quarters (vs. 44.7–49.9% over the last four) — pricing power or mix eroding.
  4. Company guides below the prior quarter's actual revenue (a guidance cut in absolute terms, not just a deceleration in growth rate) — the beat-and-raise streak ends.
  5. Net cash position falls below $8bn without a value-accretive acquisition disclosed (unexplained cash burn or large buyback at a rich multiple).

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: ~2026-11-03 (estimated) based on the historical Q3 reporting cadence (Aug-4/May-5/Feb-12/Nov-4 pattern over the last five quarters); not yet confirmed by an 8-K or IR calendar entry as of 2026-09-25. No investor day announced in filings reviewed.

11. Red-flag scan

No auditor change, no material weakness, no restatement, no going-concern language found in the FY2025 10-K (filed 2026-02-17). Legal proceedings (10-K Item 3 / Note 5 Commitments and Contingencies): "provisions recorded for contingent losses... have not been significant"; no material pending litigation disclosed. Two-customer concentration (16%/26% of FY2025 revenue; two customers >10% each in each of the last three fiscal years) is confirmed directly from the 10-K and is the dossier's central red flag — carried through to kill criterion #1. No SEC/DOJ investigation found. Insider selling: not reviewed in this pass (time-boxed); flagged as a gap.

12. Data basis, recency and disclaimer

Most recent period incorporated: Q2 FY2026 (period ended 2026-06-30), 8-K filed 2026-08-04, and FY2025 10-K filed 2026-02-17. Events checked to 2026-09-25 close. GAAP figures are labelled GAAP; non-GAAP figures (as reported by the company, excluding SBC/intangible amortization/tax effects) are labelled non-GAAP throughout. This is research prepared for an internal multi-agent diligence process; it is not personal investment advice.

Research output for internal process use, not personalized investment advice.

1. Verdict: INCLUDE-SMALL — thesis horizon: 24–36 months

Aon is one of three global mega-brokers (with Marsh McLennan and, since Aon's own abandoned 2021 bid, Willis Towers Watson) — a durable, recurring-commission business with genuine scale advantages, expanding margins, and a management team that has reaffirmed the same full-year framework (mid-single-digit-or-better organic growth, 70–80bps adjusted-margin expansion, strong adjusted EPS growth, double-digit FCF growth) at every one of the last three quarterly releases without a cut. The reverse DCF below shows the market pricing in only ~4% 10-year FCF growth against a company that has delivered mid-teens FCF growth in FY2025 — a reasonably attractive entry point for the quality on offer. The specific, named reservation for INCLUDE-SMALL rather than full INCLUDE: on 2026-08-30, Aon signed a $17.0 billion, all-debt-financed agreement to acquire USI (closing expected Q4 2026), which this dossier estimates will push pro forma net debt/EBITDA from ~2.3x today toward the low-4x range at close before any synergy ramp or deleveraging, and management has explicitly said share buybacks are paused near-term to prioritize debt paydown — a real, dated change to the capital-return profile that the market may not yet have fully digested, layered on top of a first-half 2026 free-cash-flow growth deceleration (+4% YoY, versus 14–16% in FY2025) that itself deserves watching.

2. Business in plain English

Aon is a global professional-services firm operating through four segments: Commercial Risk Solutions (property & casualty insurance brokerage for corporations), Reinsurance Solutions (treaty/facultative reinsurance placement for insurers), Health Solutions (employee health & benefits brokerage/consulting) and Wealth Solutions (retirement/investment advisory, following the 2025–26 divestitures of the NFP Wealth business and Stroz Friedberg). It earns commissions and fees for advising and placing risk/insurance/benefits programs on behalf of corporate and institutional clients, competing on scale, proprietary data/analytics ("context advantage"), and global reach against Marsh McLennan and Willis Towers Watson.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Quant snapshot (b1_live_scores.csv, 2026-09-25): composite 0.163 (decile 2, live_rank 416/503 — outside the model's own top tier; AON reached this diligence batch via the triage route, per the triage note's 44.7% ROE / 14–15x forward P/E flag). Family scores: Q 0.935 (very high — pct_roe 0.962), V 0.219 (low — pct_ep 0.454, pct_fcfp 0.385, both below median; pct_leverage 0.085, i.e., in the bottom ~9% of the index on leverage, consistent with the debt-funded acquisition history discussed below), M 0.142 (weak recent momentum), S 0.138 (weak earnings-surprise score). - The Quality score is genuine and durable: 44.7% trailing ROE and the mid-single-digit-plus organic growth are recurring, commission-based economics, confirmed every quarter in the primary-source releases (§4–5), not a one-off. - The low Value score is real, not an artefact: AON trades at 14.8x adjusted NTM P/E and only a ~4.4% TTM FCF yield on EV (this dossier's own calculation, §7) — not "cheap" on an absolute basis; the triage's "44.7% ROE at only 14–15x" framing is a reasonable characterization of quality-at-a-fair-price, not of statistical cheapness. - The bottom-decile leverage percentile is the one place the model and this diligence agree most strongly: AON already carries ~$15.0bn of consolidated debt against ~$9.7bn of equity, and is about to add a fully debt-financed $17bn acquisition — this is a real, structural characteristic of AON's serial-acquirer strategy (NFP in 2024, now USI), not a data error.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

Entity scope: consolidated Aon plc, per the 10-Q's Condensed Consolidated Statement of Financial Position and Debt note (filed 2026-07-29, period 2026-06-30). - FCF conversion: FY2025 FCF $3,218M vs. GAAP net income attributable to Aon shareholders of $3,650M (approx., per FY2025 EPS × diluted shares) — a reasonably strong conversion; H1 2026 FCF $846M vs H1 2026 net income ~$1,763M reflects normal H1 seasonality (Aon's Q1 is seasonally its strongest cash quarter for commission timing) plus the divestiture/working-capital drag noted above. - SBC: not separately quantified this pass from the H1 2026 cash-flow statement — flagged as a gap; Aon's compensation-and-benefits line ($2,271M in Q2 2026, down 4% YoY on lower incentive accruals) is the relevant expense category but SBC alone was not isolated. - GAAP vs. adjusted gap: Q2 2026 GAAP EPS $2.58 vs adjusted $3.81 (a 32% gap) — driven mainly by amortization of intangibles ($174M in Q2 2026, down from $201M) and the "Accelerating Aon United" restructuring program ($96M in Q2 2026) per the company's own reconciliation; this is a normal, recurring gap for a serial acquirer and is consistently labeled in every release reviewed. - Balance sheet (2026-06-30 vs 2025-12-31): cash $1,062M (down from $1,195M) + short-term investments $205M (down sharply from $1,603M — a large planned reduction, consistent with debt paydown and buybacks); total debt (current + long-term) $14,967M (down from $15,249M) — $2,020M of this is now current, including three senior-note tranches (2.850% due May 2027, 5.125% due March 2027, 8.205% Junior Subordinated due January 2027, aggregate ~$1.72bn) reclassified to current as their maturities fell inside 12 months, which the company says it will repay from operating cash flow and cash on hand (i.e., not a distress signal, a normal maturity-ladder mechanic). Total equity $9,686M (up from $9,459M). Net debt (excluding fiduciary assets/liabilities) ≈ $13,700M; using this dossier's own TTM EBITDA estimate (~$5.9bn, cross-checked against d4_live_snapshot's y_ebitda), net debt/EBITDA ≈ 2.3x today. - Pending M&A and its financing — the dominant forward-looking item: on 2026-08-30 (after the Q2 10-Q, so not yet on the balance sheet above), Aon signed a definitive agreement to acquire USI (from KKR and other shareholders) for $17.0 billion ($16.7bn net of ~$278M of tax attributes; ~14.5x trailing synergized adjusted EBITDA), expected to close Q4 2026, to be funded entirely with new debt across a range of maturities. Aon states it expects to maintain its current Baa2/A− ratings and explicitly says it does not expect to repurchase shares in the near term, prioritizing debt repayment instead. This dossier's own pro forma estimate (purchase price ÷ disclosed multiple ⇒ USI EBITDA ≈ $1.15bn; combining with Aon's own ~$5.9bn TTM EBITDA and the announced $395M run-rate synergy target, before phase-in) implies day-one pro forma net debt/EBITDA in the low-4x range, versus 2.3x today — a real, material leverage step-up not yet reflected in the Q2 2026 balance sheet reviewed above. - Capital return: $775M returned to shareholders in Q2 2026 ($600M buybacks + $175M dividends), already exceeding the full-year "at least $1 billion" buyback objective as of Q2 — but per the USI announcement, this pace is expected to slow sharply once the deal closes.

7. Valuation snapshot and reverse DCF (no V1 row exists for AON — this dossier's own build)

At the 2026-09-25 close of $277.99 (market cap ≈ $58.97bn; EV ≈ $73.45bn, d4_live_snapshot, consistent with this dossier's own net-debt figure), trailing GAAP P/E ≈13.7x, adjusted NTM P/E ≈14.8x. TTM FCF (this dossier's own build: FY2025 FCF $3,218M − H1 2025 FCF $816M + H1 2026 FCF $846M) ≈ $3,248M, a 4.4% EV/FCF yield. Reverse DCF (two-stage, 10-year explicit FCF growth at rate g + Gordon-growth terminal value at 3.0%, WACC sensitivity shown): at WACC 8.0%, implied g ≈ +4.2%/year; at WACC 7.5%, implied g ≈ +2.9%; at WACC 8.5%, implied g ≈ +5.4%. This dossier's base case is that AON can plausibly compound FCF at a high-single-digit to low-double-digit rate over 10 years (mid-single-digit organic growth + margin expansion + bolt-on/large M&A, consistent with FY2025's 14% delivered FCF growth and the reaffirmed "double-digit FCF growth" guidance), i.e., implied growth is below this dossier's base case ("below") — a reasonably attractive entry point for the quality on offer, though the USI-driven leverage step-up and the H1 2026 FCF deceleration are real reasons for caution on the pace of that compounding over the next 1–2 years specifically (hence INCLUDE-SMALL, not INCLUDE).

8. Bull case and bear case

Bull (3 points): 1. Full-year guidance framework reaffirmed unchanged for three consecutive quarters (Jan/May/Jul 2026) — genuine forecast discipline, unlike several peers in this diligence batch. 2. Reverse DCF implies the market is pricing in only ~4% 10-year FCF growth against FY2025's delivered 14% FCF growth and a reaffirmed double-digit FCF-growth guide — a real gap between price and demonstrated execution. 3. USI (like NFP before it) extends Aon's already-strong position in the large, growing US middle-market segment, with disclosed $395M of run-rate synergies expected — a credible, not speculative, growth lever if integration goes to plan.

Bear (3 points): 1. The $17.0bn USI acquisition is entirely debt-financed; this dossier's own pro forma estimate puts net debt/EBITDA in the low-4x range at close (from 2.3x today), with buybacks explicitly paused near-term — a real, dated deterioration in balance-sheet flexibility and capital return, not yet reflected in Q2 2026 reported figures. 2. H1 2026 free cash flow grew only +4% YoY (vs. 14–16% in FY2025), attributed by the company to divestiture/working-capital effects but not yet independently verified beyond that one-line explanation — worth confirming does not represent a genuine deceleration before USI integration adds complexity. 3. AON already carries bottom-decile leverage on the model's own sector-relative measure (pct_leverage 0.085) even before USI; a fully debt-funded $17bn deal on top of that is a large bet that synergies and deleveraging execute on schedule (Q4 2026 close, multi-year synergy ramp).

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable) — what would break this thesis

dossiers.APD:
APD — Air Products and Chemicals, Inc. (NYSE: APD)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — 24–36 month horizon. Core industrial-gas franchise is executing (guidance raised three consecutive quarters), but two large green-hydrogen impairments in five quarters ($2.33B pre-tax in FQ2 FY25; up to $2.9B pre-tax in FQ3 FY26) are a real capital-allocation red flag, and leverage has roughly doubled since FY22 to fund the now-partly-written-off megaproject program. Reservation: size small until management shows one full year without a fresh write-down.

2. Business in plain English

Air Products produces and sells industrial gases (oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, argon, helium) under long-term, often take-or-pay contracts to refining, chemicals, electronics, metals and food customers, plus builds and operates large "on-site" gasification and hydrogen plants. Revenue is largely contracted and cost-pass-through (energy costs), which smooths the base business; the volatility of the last two years comes from a separate, discretionary bet on multibillion-dollar clean-hydrogen megaprojects (Louisiana blue/green hydrogen, NEOM in Saudi Arabia) that the company is now scaling back. Competitive position: one of four global industrial-gas majors (with Linde, Air Liquide, Messer) in an oligopoly with high customer switching costs (on-site plants built next to the customer's fence line).

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Quant factor scores (b1_live_scores.csv, 25 Sep 2026): quality/value composite decile 2 of 10 (i.e., statistically cheap-looking), but momentum is very weak (mom_12_1 percentile 6%) and the model's overall rank is 432/~500 — the triage flagged this as a "screen might be hiding a good business" case given the poor rank is driven almost entirely by price momentum, not by the underlying industrial-gas economics. That is partly an artefact: the stock's 12-month drawdown is a direct, rational market reaction to the impairments, not evidence the core business is broken — but the model's "cheap" P/E readings on trailing GAAP EPS are themselves distorted by the same impairments (GAAP EPS was negative in two of the last eight quarters), so neither the momentum penalty nor the naive value signal should be taken at face value.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull (3 points): 1. Core industrial-gas oligopoly economics are intact — 25.6% core operating margin even in the write-off quarter, and guidance has been raised three times this fiscal year. 2. Capex is stepping down (FY26 guide cut to ~$3.5B from $4.0B) as the failed megaprojects are abandoned, which should improve free-cash-flow conversion from here. 3. NEOM/Yara renewable-ammonia marketing deal (announced 30 Jun 2026, being finalized) shows the company can still monetize part of the green-hydrogen build-out rather than a total loss.

Bear (3 points): 1. Two impairments in five fiscal quarters (total pre-tax charges >$5B combined) is a repeated pattern, not a one-off — capital-allocation discipline on new "growth" projects is unproven going forward. 2. Debt roughly doubled in three years to fund a program that is now being partly unwound; net debt/EBITDA is estimated at ~3.7x, above historical norms for the sector. 3. Reported operating loss and negative GAAP EPS in 2 of the last 8 quarters make headline "cheap" P/E screens (on trailing GAAP earnings) unreliable — a risk this triage/model process itself is exposed to.

Amphenol Corporation (APH) — Diligence Dossier (F27, standard depth)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — 24–36 month horizon. Named reservation: total debt roughly doubled (from $6.89bn to $18.81bn between FY2024 and 2026-06-30) to fund the transformational $10.5bn CommScope (Connectivity & Cable Solutions) acquisition that closed 2026-01-09; the underlying business and execution are excellent (four consecutive quarters beating the high end of its own guidance, book-to-bill >1.2x), and estimated net debt/EBITDA (~1.4–1.5x) is manageable for an investment-grade industrial, but this is real, recently-added leverage and integration risk that argues against a full-weight position until at least two post-close quarters confirm the deal is performing to plan.

2. Business in plain English

Amphenol designs and makes electronic and fiber-optic connectors, cable assemblies, sensors and interconnect systems used inside almost every category of electronics — data centers/AI servers, telecom/IT networks, automobiles, industrial equipment, defense systems and mobile devices. It sells to a highly diversified base of OEM customers across those end markets and grows both organically and through a long, disciplined track record of bolt-on and, occasionally, large (CommScope) acquisitions, run by a famously decentralized, general-manager-owned operating model.

3. Why the model likes it / durability

b1_live_scores.csv: composite decile 4/quintile 2, live_rank 315/1172; Quality strong (gp/assets 38th but roe 67th, ocf/assets 42nd), Value mixed (bp 62nd — not particularly cheap), Momentum 32nd (below-median 12-1m), SUE 78th (strong earnings surprises). The reported "55% revenue growth" in the prior triage is partly an M&A artefact, not purely organic: management itself attributes growth to "strong organic growth... as well as contributions from the Company's acquisition program" in every one of the last four earnings releases, and FY2026 guidance explicitly separates out CommScope's now-expected $4.6bn of incremental FY2026 sales. This does not make the growth low-quality — it is real, cash-funded, disciplined M&A that the company has executed successfully for decades — but it is durable in a different sense than organic-only growth, and the diligence should not treat 55% as a clean organic run-rate.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) a 30+ year track record of successfully integrating acquisitions at scale, now applied to the largest deal in company history (CommScope), already tracking above initial expectations; (2) record backlog/book-to-bill (1.23–1.24x in the last two quarters) evidences real, broad-based end-market demand, not just M&A math; (3) highly diversified end-market exposure (IT datacom, auto, defense, broadband, industrial) reduces single-customer/single-cycle risk relative to pure AI-networking peers. Aptiv PLC (APTV) — Diligence Dossier (F34, standard depth)

1. Verdict

WATCH. Thesis horizon 12–36 months. One-sentence reason: the post-Versigent-spin "New Aptiv" is statistically cheap and has a genuinely cleaner balance sheet and a growing software/non-auto business, but it cut every headline FY2026 guidance metric just one quarter after first issuing post-spin guidance, and the market has not yet seen two clean quarters that prove the cut was a one-off.

Thesis (≤25 words): Auto electrical/software supplier just cut its first post-spinoff full-year guide; cheap and better-capitalized, but not yet proven stable.

2. Business in plain English

Aptiv designs and supplies the electrical architecture, sensors, software and computing "brains" that connect a vehicle's systems (Engineered Components: connectors, wiring, electrification hardware; Intelligent Systems: ADAS, software-defined-vehicle platforms, user experience) to automakers globally. It earns money via long-term OEM platform contracts with high switching costs (once designed into a vehicle architecture, Aptiv content is difficult to re-source mid-cycle). On April 1, 2026, Aptiv completed the spin-off of its former Electrical Distribution Systems (wiring harness) business as an independent company, Versigent (NYSE: VGNT), leaving "New Aptiv" as a more software/technology-weighted supplier of safety, connectivity and electrification systems. Competitive position: a top-tier, diversified auto-technology supplier (alongside Bosch, Continental, Denso) with particular strength in vehicle electrical/electronic architecture and a growing software/AV stack.

3. Why the model likes it / durability

Triage (Q01_triage.json, as_of 2026-09-25) scored APTV quality 3, growth 4, price_vs_growth 5, flagging "thin GAAP margin (1.1%) typical of an auto-cycle trough" and "customer concentration with OEMs pulling back EV capex" as red flags, but concluding "17% FCF yield and 7.1x NTM P/E against guided EPS more than tripling is priced for a permanently weak auto cycle... statistically too cheap... to advance without a closer look." Two things from primary sources materially update this: (a) the 17% FCF yield is stale/pre-spin — Yahoo's trailing freeCashflow figure still includes the now-divested EDS business; on the post-spin, continuing-operations guide (FCF $625–725M midpoint on a $9.48bn market cap) the real FCF yield is ~7.1%, still attractive but less than half what triage cited; (b) the pre-registered quant composite agrees the setup is weak, not strong: b1_live_scores.csv shows APTV's 12-month momentum in the 1st percentile (worst-in-market, raw) and earnings-momentum (SUE) in the 21st percentile — both consistent with a name in an unresolved cyclical air-pocket, not (yet) a name that has bottomed. The value case (fam_V pct 0.647) and quality case (fam_Q pct 0.418, helped by the deleveraged post-spin balance sheet) are real, but momentum/earnings-momentum this poor is a genuine, current fact, and it is corroborated below by an actual guidance cut in the most recent quarter — this is not merely a stale composite disagreeing with a rosier narrative.

4. Last two years of results (GAAP; source: SEC XBRL companyfacts CIK0001521332, cross-checked to 8-K earnings releases)

Important comparability caveat, disclosed rather than smoothed over: APTV's XBRL-tagged quarterly figures mix "as originally reported" (consolidated, including EDS/Versigent) and "restated for discontinued operations" (continuing-ops only) bases depending on which filing last touched that period — the underlying SEC data literally shows Q2'25 revenue at $3,199M (restated, continuing-ops only, from the 2026-08-04 10-Q) sitting next to Q3'25 revenue at $5,212M (as-originally-reported, consolidated, from the 2025-10-30 10-Q, not yet restated). This is exactly the kind of "guidance/figures compared without checking the basis" trap the program's lead audit (v3) flagged — so the table below uses only like-for-like, company-disclosed continuing-operations figures where available, and marks anything consolidated/mixed-basis clearly. | Quarter | Net sales ($M) | Basis | YoY | Adj. EDS) | — | n/a | n/a | | Q1'26 | 5,086 | Consolidated (EDS still owned Jan–Mar; spin closed Apr 1) | +5% reported / +1% adj. | 14.8% (vs 15.7% py) | $1.71 | | Q2'26 | 3,274 | First fully "New Aptiv" continuing-ops quarter | +2% (segment: EC +5%, IS flat; non-auto +12%, auto −1%) | 18.7% | $1.63 (vs $1.31 py) | On the cleanest like-for-like comparison available (Q2'25 restated $3,199M vs Q2'26 $3,274M), continuing-operations revenue grew +2.3%, matching the segment-level detail in the Q2'26 release. GAAP net income has swung enormously across this window (Q2'24 +$938M, Q1'25 −$11M, Q3'25 −$355M, Q2'26 +$248M) — these swings are dominated by multi-year separation-related items (Versigent transaction costs, debt-extinguishment charges, and other one-offs tied to the 2025–26 EDS separation process); GAAP EPS is not a usable run-rate metric for this company right now and adjusted EPS (labelled) is used for guidance comparison below.

5. Guidance track record (last four releases; "New Aptiv" continuing-ops FY2026 guide)

Release New FY2026 range Prior range Verdict
Q1'26 (2026-05-05, 8-K) — first post-spin "New Aptiv" guide Revenue $12.8–13.2bn; Adj. EBITDA $2.36–2.48bn; Adj. EPS $5.70–6.10; FCF $650–850M n/a (first post-spin guide) Initiated
Q2'26 (2026-08-04, 8-K) Revenue $12.6–12.8bn; Adj. EBITDA $2.31–2.37bn; Adj. EPS $5.60–5.80; FCF $625–725M Revenue $12.8–13.2bn; Adj. EBITDA $2.36–2.48bn; Adj. EPS $5.70–6.10; FCF $650–850M Cut on every metric
Management attributed the cut to ~$150M (China customer production-schedule changes), ~$100M (delayed launches/ramps) and ~$50M (enterprise software/services timing) — real, itemized reasons, not a vague miss, but a cut nonetheless, and it happened in the very first quarter after "New Aptiv" set its inaugural post-spin guidance. Only two data points exist on the new, post-spin basis (this is a young reporting entity), so the "last four releases" comparison the base template asks for is not yet available; this is disclosed as a genuine limitation rather than papered over.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

Free cash flow has been volatile through the separation: Q1'26 FCF was −$362M (vs +$76M in Q1'25) and Q2'26 FCF was only $12M (vs $219M a year earlier) even as adjusted EPS beat the prior-year figure — a real, current gap between adjusted-earnings optics and cash generation during the transition year, now guided to normalize to $625–725M for the full year. Balance sheet is genuinely improved post-spin: long-term debt fell from $9.25bn (Q1'26) to $5.33bn (Q2'26) after Aptiv received a $1.9bn cash dividend from Versigent at spin completion and used it (plus other cash) to redeem $1.847bn of senior notes in April 2026; cash fell in step (from $3.17bn to $761M) as that redemption occurred. Net debt ≈$4.6bn against guided FY26 adjusted EBITDA midpoint ~$2.34bn → net debt/adjusted EBITDA ≈2.0x, a comfortable, de-risked level versus the pre-spin consolidated entity. Share count has fallen from 223.8M (Q1'25) to 208.4M (Q2'26), a genuine ~7% reduction via buybacks over five quarters. Customer concentration: Aptiv's five largest customers were reported at roughly 42% of total net sales in the FY2025 10-K (secondary-source citation — the primary 10-K customer-concentration footnote was not independently re-fetched in this pass; flagged for verification), with GM, Stellantis, Ford and Volkswagen historically the largest individual names — a real, disclosed concentration risk in a soft-production auto environment.

7. Valuation snapshot & reverse DCF

Price (2026-09-25 close) $44.79; market cap ≈$9.48bn; net debt ≈$4.6bn; EV ≈$14.1bn. FY2026 P/E on the just-cut guided adjusted EPS midpoint ($5.70) ≈7.86x; FCF yield on EV (guided FCF midpoint $675M) ≈4.8% (on market cap alone, ≈7.1%) — well below the 17% Yahoo/d4 trailing figure, which is stale and still includes the divested EDS business (a data conflict disclosed here rather than carried forward). No dividend currently paid. No V1 row exists for APTV (checked v1_valuation_table.csv — no row) → v1_verdict = null; valuation view is independently derived.

Reverse DCF: EV = FCF₁×(1+g)/(WACC−g). Using FCF₁ = $675M (FY26 guide midpoint) and WACC ≈9% (cost of equity via CAPM: rf 4.2% + β1.33×ERP 5% = 10.85%; post-tax cost of debt ≈4.3%; debt weight ≈33% of EV), solving for g against EV $14.1bn gives implied perpetual FCF growth ≈4.0%/yr. My evidence-based base case is ~4–5%/yr (structural content-per-vehicle growth from software/ADAS/electrification, richening non-auto mix which grew +12% in Q2'26, offset by genuine auto-production cyclicality) — so the reverse DCF reads roughly in line, not obviously cheap, at the perpetual-growth level. The more important near-term fact is that guided FY2026 revenue growth is only ~2%, well below even this "in line" perpetual assumption — meaning the price already requires a recovery from today's just-cut guidance that has not yet shown up in the numbers, which is the central reason for a WATCH rather than an INCLUDE verdict. Bear case (further cuts, FCF flat ~$625M, P/E stays at trough ~7–8x, no re-rating): 3-yr annualized return ≈ −3%. Base case (cycle stabilizes over 12–18 months, EPS compounds ~8–9%/yr aided by buybacks, P/E re-rates modestly to 9x): ≈ +13–14%/yr. Bull case (non-auto/software mix accelerates margin expansion, re-rating to "quality auto-tech" multiples of 11–12x): ≈ +27–29%/yr.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) Non-automotive/software revenue grew +12% in Q2'26 even as automotive fell 1%, evidence "New Aptiv" is increasingly a technology-content business rather than a pure cyclical parts supplier; (2) the post-spin balance sheet is genuinely conservative (net debt/EBITDA ≈2.0x) after using $1.9bn of Versigent proceeds to redeem debt, freeing cash for buybacks that have already cut the float ~7% in five quarters; (3) at ~7.9x guided FY26 adjusted EPS, the market prices in essentially no recovery even as vehicle electrical/software content keeps rising structurally across the industry. Bear: (1) FY2026 guidance was cut on revenue, EBITDA, EPS and FCF simultaneously just one quarter after "New Aptiv" first guided — for reasons (China production schedules, delayed launches, software-timing) that are exactly the execution risk a newly separated company can least afford to demonstrate early, and the quant data's 1st-percentile momentum corroborates the market has not yet decided the cut is a one-off; (2) customer concentration is real (~42% top-5) in a soft, uneven global auto-production environment (China down, EMEA down 7% in Q1'26); (3) free cash flow has been genuinely volatile and at times negative during the separation year (Q1'26 −$362M, Q2'26 only $12M) even as adjusted EPS beat — the gap between adjusted-earnings optics and cash delivery is a current, not hypothetical, fact.

9. Key risks & measurable kill criteria

Any of the following would break the thesis; each is a specific, observable, time-bound signpost to monitor at each earnings release, not a vague worry: 1. FY2026 guidance is cut again at the Q3'26 or Q4'26 release (any further reduction to the low end of the current $12.6–12.8bn revenue / $5.60–5.80 adjusted-EPS range). 2. Non-automotive (software/AV/enterprise) segment revenue growth decelerates below 8% YoY for two consecutive quarters (from +12% in Q2'26). 3. Net debt/adjusted EBITDA rises above 3.0x (from ~2.0x post-spin) without a stated value-accretive reason. 4. Free cash flow for two consecutive quarters comes in below the low end of the then-current full-year FCF guidance range (currently $625–725M). 5. Top-5 customer concentration rises above 45% of net sales (from ~42%), or GM/Stellantis/Ford cuts North American production schedules by more than 5% for a full year.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 2026-10-29 (Q3'26, per d4 next_earnings_date). The single most important thing to watch is whether Q3'26 confirms the guidance cut was a one-off (no further reduction) and whether non-auto/software growth holds above double digits.

11. Red-flag scan

No auditor change, restatement, or going-concern language found (EY is the auditor per public filings). No SEC/DOJ investigation or short-seller report found in this cycle's search. Historical industry note: the 2012–2014 automotive wire-harness price-fixing prosecutions (Yazaki, Denso, Furukawa and others pleading guilty, >$740M in criminal fines) involved other suppliers, not Aptiv/Delphi, per the sources checked — searched specifically and found no APTV-specific antitrust matter, current or historical. Routine insider activity only (an EVP sold 3,000 shares under a pre-scheduled Rule 10b5-1 plan) — not a red flag. The customer-concentration percentage (§6) should be independently re-verified against the primary 10-K footnote in a future pass; it is cited here from a secondary source.

12. Data basis, recency and disclaimer

Most recent period incorporated: Q2 2026 10-Q and 8-K earnings release, both filed 2026-08-04. Events checked to 2026-09-25 (litigation, guidance updates, red-flag search). GAAP and adjusted figures are labelled throughout and never blended; the consolidated-vs-continuing-operations basis conflict in the XBRL data (§4) is disclosed rather than silently reconciled. This is research, not investment advice, and not a recommendation to buy or sell.
