dossiers.AVGO:
Broadcom Inc. (AVGO) — Fundamental Diligence Dossier

Verdict: INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — 12–36 month thesis horizon. One-sentence reason: co-designed custom AI chips (XPUs) for the largest hyperscalers plus a dominant AI-networking franchise are producing genuine, filed operating-margin expansion (24%→54% in two years), and the reverse DCF says the price is roughly in line with a reasonable base case — but revenue is dangerously concentrated in a handful of customers, so it is investable, not a full-conviction position.

1. Business in plain English

Broadcom sells two things that matter here: (1) custom AI accelerators ("XPUs") that it co-designs with hyperscalers and AI labs — Google's TPU, OpenAI's new "Jalapeño" inference chip, and others — where Broadcom does the physical design/verification/packaging and the customer owns the architecture; and (2) AI networking silicon (Tomahawk Ethernet switches, Jericho fabric chips) that connects those chips into giant clusters. Layered on top is a large, slower-growing infrastructure-software business (VMware, acquired 2023) and legacy broadband/storage/wireless semiconductors. AI semiconductors are now the growth engine; software and legacy semis are the cash-generative, low-growth base.

2. Why the model likes it / is it durable

b1 composite percentile 0.47 (mid-pack, not a top-decile name) with Value the strongest family (fam_V 0.38, EBIT/EV percentile 0.47) and weaker Quality (fam_Q 0.47) — the quant model is lukewarm; this name is in the "quality-growth lane" carve-out (v4/STATE.md, 2026-09-20) specifically because the owner challenged excluding mega-cap AI names on a model with no proven edge, not because b1 flagged it. live_rank 313 — well outside any quantitative gate. The durability case rests entirely on the primary-source AI-ASIC and networking data below, not on the factor score.

3. Last 8 quarters (fiscal quarters; $M except EPS)

Quarter Revenue Gross margin R&D Op margin Diluted EPS
FQ2 FY24 (end 2024-05-05) 12,487 62.3% 2,415 23.7% 0.44
FQ3 FY24 (end 2024-08-04) 13,072 63.9% 2,353 29.0% −0.40*
FQ1 FY25 (end 2025-02-02) 14,916 68.0% 2,253 42.0% 1.14
FQ2 FY25 (end 2025-05-04) 15,004 68.0% 2,693 38.9% 1.03
FQ3 FY25 (end 2025-08-03) 15,952 67.1% 3,050 36.9% 0.85
FQ1 FY26 (end 2026-02-01) 19,311 68.1% 2,965 44.3% 1.50
FQ2 FY26 (end 2026-05-03) 22,187 69.5% 2,995 48.6% 1.91
FQ3 FY26 (end 2026-08-02) 29,591 69.1% 2,895 53.9% 2.68

FQ3 FY24 diluted EPS was negative on a GAAP basis, coincident with heavy VMware acquisition-related amortization/integration costs shortly after the Nov-2023 close — a real, disclosed one-off, not a recurring pattern; GAAP has since normalized sharply positive. Revenue accelerated from +5% QoQ (FY24) to +33% QoQ by FQ3 FY26; operating margin more than doubled (23.7%→53.9%) over the same eight quarters — driven by AI-semiconductor mix shift plus VMware cost synergies, both verifiable in the segment commentary below, not an accounting artefact. Q3 FY26 (reported Sep-2026): "AI semiconductor" revenue $16.7B for the quarter (tripled YoY); Broadcom carries a $73B AI backlog and targets >$100B annual AI-chip revenue by FY2027*, with FY2027 guided to $115B and an "outlined" (less firm) $230B for FY2028. [1][2]

4. Guidance track record

Management reaffirmed the $100B+ FY2027 AI-semiconductor guide on the Q3 FY26 call (Aug-2026) and raised the FY2027/FY2028 multi-year outline to $115B/$230B — both a raise versus the prior $100B framing. Note: the $230B FY2028 figure is described in sources as "outlined" rather than formal quarter-by-quarter guidance, and implies AI-segment revenue alone roughly matching or exceeding Broadcom's entire current company-wide TTM revenue (~$89B) — an aggressive multi-year target this analyst treats as upper-bound/bull-case framing, not a base-case assumption, pending firmer near-term confirmation. [2][3]

5. Moat and competition

  • Design-win moat: OpenAI's "Jalapeño" — its first custom Intelligence Processor — was co-developed with Broadcom from design to tape-out in 9 months, "the fastest ASIC development cycle ever achieved" per the companies' joint announcement; this is a real switching-cost moat (multi-year co-design relationships), not marketing. [4]
  • Google: delivered Ironwood TPU v7 in high volume in Q3 FY26 and began production shipments of the next-gen TPU v8i — an established, multi-generation relationship. [1]
  • Customer concentration — the central risk: six core custom-chip customers (reported to include Google, Meta, Anthropic, OpenAI) are expected to drive essentially all of the >$100B FY2027 AI-semiconductor revenue target, with four of the six "particularly large" — a $100B target spread six ways implies >$16B/customer on average. OpenAI is reportedly on track to become the second-largest XPU customer in FY2027. [5][6] Any one hyperscaler pausing or re-architecting its own silicon roadmap is a material single-name risk to the whole AI segment.
  • Networking: Tomahawk 6 (102.4 Tbps Ethernet) entered volume production March-2026, the industry's first at that speed; Jericho4 fabric chip (51.2 Tbps, shipping since Aug-2025) interconnects over 1M XPUs across data centers — genuine technical leadership in the scale-out layer that AI clusters need regardless of whose chip sits inside them (a partial hedge against XPU customer concentration, since Broadcom sells networking silicon to NVIDIA-based clusters too). [1]

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • TTM (Q4 FY25–Q3 FY26) operating cash flow $40,653M, capex $1,250M, FCF ≈$39,403M, FCF margin ≈44% of TTM revenue ($89,104M) — strong conversion for a semiconductor business, reflecting the fabless/IP-heavy AI-ASIC model plus VMware's software margins.
  • SBC: allocated SBC ran ~$2.0–2.3B/quarter in FY26 vs. revenue of $19–30B, i.e. 7–10% of revenue — materially higher than NVDA/AAPL, a real dilution and GAAP-vs-adjusted-EPS gap driver stemming from VMware-deal equity awards; watch the trend.
  • Balance sheet: total debt $64,907M (May-2026, down slightly QoQ from $65,136M), of which $62,655M long-term; quarterly Adjusted EBITDA $15,244M (≈$61B annualized) → gross leverage ≈1.1x EBITDA, comfortably below the 3.5x threshold S&P cited when it upgraded Broadcom to BBB on the VMware deal — a much healthier credit position than ORCL's. [7][8]
  • Net income vs. operating income line up reasonably (no large unexplained gap observed in the quarters reviewed), unlike ORCL (see ORCL.md §6).

7. Valuation — reverse DCF (no V1 systematic valuation row for AVGO)

Inputs: EV ≈ market cap $1,684,184M; TTM FCF $39,403M; WACC 9.0%; terminal growth 3.5%; 10-year horizon. Solving for the constant FCF growth rate that justifies the price: 14.1%/year for 10 years (FCF yield on trailing FCF = 2.34%). - Bear case (10y FCF CAGR ≈5%): custom-ASIC design wins slow, a large hyperscaler customer pauses or in-sources further, VMware/legacy semis stay flat. - Base case (10y FCF CAGR ≈15%): near-term AI ramp broadly tracks the guided $100–115B FY2027 path (discounted for execution risk on the $230B FY2028 "outline"), decelerating to high-single/low-double-digits by year 8–10 as hyperscaler capex growth normalizes and VMware/legacy semis grow low-single-digits. - Bull case (10y FCF CAGR ≈25%): Broadcom extends share gains beyond FY2028 at a still-elevated pace and the networking franchise scales with cluster sizes. Implied vs. base: IN LINE. 14.1% sits essentially at/just below the 15% base case — the most defensible valuation of the four names reviewed, contingent on the concentration risk in §5 not materializing.

3-year scenario returns (annualised total return from $352.81, illustrative)

Scenario 3y FCF CAGR (yrs 1–3) Exit EV/FCF Annualised return
Bear ~5% 22x (de-rate from 42.7x entry) ≈ −15%/yr
Base ~30% 32x ≈ +20%/yr
Bull ~45% 40x ≈ +43%/yr

8. Bull case

  1. Operating margin has more than doubled in two years (23.7%→53.9%) on filed numbers — genuine, not adjusted-metric, operating leverage.
  2. $73B AI backlog gives multi-quarter revenue visibility rare among semiconductor companies.
  3. Networking silicon (Tomahawk/Jericho) sells into AI clusters regardless of accelerator vendor — a real hedge against XPU customer concentration.

9. Bear case

  1. Six customers drive substantially all AI-segment growth; four are "particularly large" — a single large customer's pause is a company-moving event.
  2. SBC at 7–10% of revenue is a real, ongoing dilution/earnings-quality drag versus NVDA/AAPL.
  3. The $230B FY2028 figure is "outlined," not firmly guided, and implies AI-segment revenue alone approaching Broadcom's entire current company size — a base-rate-defying multi-year target that the market may already be crediting.

10. Key risks & kill criteria — thesis-invalidation triggers (what would change the verdict / break the thesis)

  1. Any of the four largest XPU customers publicly cancels or materially shrinks its custom-silicon program.
  2. AI-semiconductor revenue growth decelerates below 40% YoY for two consecutive quarters (vs. currently >100%).
  3. Net debt/EBITDA (adjusted) rises above 2.5x (from ≈1.1x) on further debt-funded M&A.
  4. VMware/infrastructure-software organic growth turns negative for two consecutive quarters.
  5. SBC exceeds 12% of revenue for two consecutive quarters.

11. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: Q4 FY26, estimated ~10-Dec-2026 (pattern-based estimate from FY25 Q4's 18-Dec-2025 filing; not yet confirmed as of this cutoff).
  • FY2027 guidance formalization (the $115B AI-semi figure) expected to be reiterated/updated on that call.

12. Red-flag scan

  • FQ3 FY24 GAAP net loss per share (−$0.40) tied to VMware acquisition costs — disclosed, explained, not recurring.
  • $315M gain from reversal of VMware acquisition excise-tax charges (May-2026 10-Q) — a non-operating, below-the-line item; flagged so it is not mistaken for organic improvement.
  • No auditor changes, restatements or going-concern language found in sources reviewed.
  • Same industry-wide AI-capex-circularity caveat as NVDA.md §12 applies (Broadcom is paid by, and its stock partly reflects, the same hyperscaler/OpenAI capex cycle that funds NVDA and ORCL).

1. Verdict: INCLUDE-SMALL — thesis horizon: 24–36 months

Avery Dennison is the global leader in pressure-sensitive labeling and packaging materials, with a genuinely strong ROE (31.2% per the triage), a clean balance sheet (net debt/EBITDA ≈2.4x), no material litigation identified, and — most importantly — a real, primary-source-confirmed organic growth re-acceleration in Q2 2026 (+7.6% organic, its best quarter in several years) that beat the company's own guidance by a wide margin on both a GAAP and adjusted basis. The reverse DCF below shows the market pricing in roughly the same mid-single-digit FCF growth the company itself is now guiding to — a fair, not obviously mispriced, valuation. The specific, named reservation for INCLUDE-SMALL rather than full INCLUDE: the growth re-acceleration is only two quarters old (Q1 2026 organic growth was a much softer +1.1%), and the trailing-twelve-month free-cash-flow figure this dossier would otherwise use for valuation is distorted upward by a large, one-off working-capital reversal (H1 2025 FCF was unusually depressed by a $370M working-capital outflow) — meaning the "cheap" read one gets from a naive TTM-FCF-yield calculation is not fully trustworthy yet, and this dossier instead uses the more conservative, normalized FY2025 FCF base for its valuation view.

2. Business in plain English

Avery Dennison makes pressure-sensitive materials and solutions sold in two segments: Materials Group (adhesive-backed labeling and packaging materials — the base label stock sold to converters/printers globally) and Solutions Group (apparel/RFID-based "intelligent label" tags and graphics, and reflective/other specialty solutions). It sells to converters, brand owners, retailers and apparel manufacturers worldwide, competing on materials science (adhesive/coating technology), global manufacturing scale and, increasingly, RFID/digital-identification ("intelligent label") capability that lets brands track individual items through a supply chain.

This dossier's base case is mid-single-digit organic growth (5–7%) sustained from the Q2 2026 re-acceleration, plus continued margin expansion from the productivity playbook and mix-shift toward high-value/RFID categories — i.e., the implied growth from the normalized FCF base is roughly in line with this dossier's base case ("in_line"), neither obviously cheap nor obviously expensive, with the key open question being whether the Q2 2026 acceleration (organic +7.6%, vs. only +1.1% in Q1) is sustained or partly a comp/timing effect — not yet resolved with only one strong quarter of evidence.

8. Bull case and bear case

Bull (3 points): 1. Q2 2026 organic growth of +7.6% (best in several years) beat the company's own Q2 guidance by a wide margin on both a GAAP ($2.67 vs. $2.21–$2.31 guided) and adjusted ($2.89 vs. $2.43–$2.53 guided) basis — a genuine, primary-source-confirmed acceleration, not promotional framing. 2. High-value categories (~45% of revenue, including RFID/intelligent labels) are growing faster than base categories and carry structurally better margins — a real, multi-year mix-shift tailwind the company has been executing for several years. 3. Balance sheet is clean (net debt/EBITDA ≈2.4x, undrawn $1.2bn revolver, covenant compliance) with no material litigation identified — the least balance-sheet/legal risk of the three names in this diligence batch.

Bear (3 points): 1. The growth re-acceleration is only two quarters old, and Q1 2026 organic growth (+1.1%) was much softer — one strong quarter is not yet enough evidence to confirm the acceleration is durable rather than partly timing/comp-driven. 2. The TTM free-cash-flow figure a naive analysis would use is inflated by a working-capital reversal against an unusually weak H1 2025 comparison base; the real, normalized FCF run-rate is meaningfully lower than the headline TTM number would suggest. 3. AVY, like the broader packaging/labeling sector, has tariff and consumer-volume exposure (the FY2025 release explicitly cites "tariff-related impacts and softer consumer volumes" as 2025 headwinds); the February 2026 Supreme Court IEEPA ruling reduces one specific tariff-authority risk but broader trade-policy instability is explicitly flagged by external counsel commentary as an ongoing, unresolved area.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable) — what would break this thesis

  1. Organic revenue growth falls back below 3% for two consecutive quarters (i.e., the Q2 2026 acceleration to +7.6% proves to be a one-quarter comp/timing effect rather than a durable re-acceleration).
  2. Net debt/EBITDA (consolidated) rises above 3.0x without a specific, disclosed M&A or buyback driver explaining the increase.
  3. FY2026 guidance (GAAP $9.40–$9.70 / adjusted $10.00–$10.30, given 2026-07-30) is cut at the Q3 2026 release — would be the first guidance cut of the year and directly contradict the re-acceleration thesis.
  4. Materials Group adjusted operating margin declines for two consecutive quarters (currently expanding — +20bps in Q2 2026) — margin compression would signal the productivity playbook is losing effectiveness against raw-material or wage inflation.
  5. A new tariff or trade-policy action materially increases direct input-cost tariff exposure beyond the "relatively small portion of global materials purchases" the company currently discloses as exposed.

AXON — Axon Enterprise, Inc. — F59 diligence (2026-09-26)

1. Verdict

WATCH (12–36 month thesis horizon). Axon is a genuine, high-switching-cost growth compounder (TASER, body cameras, cloud/AI evidence-management software, counter-drone) with an accelerating, guided-up revenue growth rate (32–34% FY2026, raised from 30–32%) and $15.1bn of contracted future bookings. But two things this dossier can verify from primary filings that the triage data card could not: (1) operating cash flow was negative in H1 2026 (−$11.4M, following −$65.9M in H1 2025) despite rapid revenue growth — the business is not yet self-funding its growth, which is the market's own stated concern behind the September 2026 sell-off; and (2) GAAP earnings are dominated by non-cash, stock-price-linked compensation expense (the 2024 eXponential Stock Plan / CEO Performance Award) that makes quarter-to-quarter GAAP EPS close to un-interpretable (Q3 2025 GAAP loss, Q1 2026 GAAP EPS $2.05, Q2 2026 GAAP EPS $0.36 — swings driven by SBC mark-to-market, not the underlying business). Combined with a very high starting multiple (44x NTM P/E) and a freshly issued $1.0–1.15bn convertible note, this is a name to hold on a quality/growth basis but not yet at full conviction pending confirmation that operating cash flow turns durably positive.

2. Business in plain English

Axon sells law-enforcement and public-safety hardware (TASER conducted-energy weapons, body-worn cameras, in-car cameras, counter-drone systems) bundled with a cloud software platform (Axon Evidence/Axon Cloud) that stores, manages and increasingly uses AI to draft police reports from that footage. Customers are police departments, other public-safety agencies and increasingly enterprise/international buyers. It makes money through a mix of hardware sales and multi-year recurring software/cloud subscriptions (its own "Axon Cloud" bundle), giving it very high switching costs once an agency standardizes on the ecosystem — the moat cited in triage.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1 quant context (data/b1_live_scores.csv, live_rank 493/503, composite decile 1 — i.e. the quant model actually ranks AXON near the bottom of the universe): mom_12_1 = −21.1% (12-month momentum negative, reflecting the September 2026 pullback described below) and sue = −0.09 (roughly neutral). This is a real, disclosed conflict between the quant model and the fundamental/triage read: the quant composite dislikes AXON (decile 1) because its factor construction rewards value and recent momentum, both of which are currently negative for a high-multiple grower that just sold off; the triage analyst (quality 4, growth 5) and this dossier's own read of the primary filings (35%+ revenue growth, raised guidance, $15.1bn backlog) say the underlying business is strong. Conclusion: the quant "decile 1" score for AXON is not evidence against the name — it is a value/momentum factor construction artefact for a recently-repriced grower, not a fundamental red flag. This is exactly the kind of conflict the wave-3 process is designed to catch and should be read as "trust the diligence, not the decile" for this name specifically.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet — the central adverse fact this dossier adds

Entity scope: all figures consolidated Axon Enterprise, Inc. - Operating cash flow turned negative in 2026, despite 30%+ revenue growth: H1 2026 OCF = −$11.44M (Q1 2026: −$31.52M; Q2 2026: +$20.08M implied). H1 2025 OCF was also negative, −$65.91M. Full-year FY2025 OCF was positive, $211.34M (10-K FY2025, filed 2026-02-25) — Axon's cash generation is heavily back-loaded to Q4 (consistent with public-safety agencies' fiscal-year-end budget cycles), but the H1 pattern of negative OCF while revenue grows >30% is a genuine working-capital/financing-intensity concern (receivables and financed-subscription build), not a one-off. - Capex (PP&E): $44.17M in H1 2026 (H1 2025: $47.82M); FY2025 full-year $136.26M (10-K). FCF was therefore solidly negative in H1 2026 (OCF −$11.44M less capex $44.17M ≈ −$55.6M), even before any capitalized-software spend (no separate XBRL tag for capitalized software costs was found for Axon this pass — a possible additional cash use not captured here). - New capital raise, Sept 2026: Axon priced $1.0bn (upsized to ~$1.15bn with the over-allotment) of 0% coupon convertible senior notes due 2031, initial conversion price $652.06/share (≈52% premium to the pricing-date price), net proceeds ≈$986M (~$1,134M with over-allotment), settled 2026-09-18 (Axon 8-K/press release, prnewswire.com, 2026-09-15). Zero coupon means no cash interest cost, but it is a real, dilutive-at-$652+ addition to the balance sheet, raised while OCF was negative — the market read this, alongside margin-quality concerns, as evidence Axon is not yet self-funding its growth (Yahoo Finance, "Axon Enterprise (AXON) Prices $1B of Zero-Coupon Notes. What is the Real Cost?", Sept 2026). - Margin quality: adjusted gross margin fell 40bps YoY to 62.9% in Q2 2026; the software/services segment margin fell 380bps YoY to 75.1% on a heavier mix of lower-margin professional services and new-product scaling (per Yahoo Finance/Motley Fool coverage of the Q2 2026 print, Sept 2026) — a real, disclosed deceleration in incremental profitability even as the top line accelerates. - 10-K/A material weakness (disclosed, no P&L/cash-flow impact): Axon filed a Form 10-K/A on 2025-05-07 restating the FY2024 10-K (and Q1/Q3 2024) because of a material weakness in internal control over financial reporting — the company had not designed an effective control to monitor the contingent-conversion provisions of its 2027 convertible notes' indenture and correctly classify them current vs. long-term on the balance sheet. The error did not affect total assets, total liabilities, stockholders' equity, net income, EPS or cash flows for the affected periods — a real, disclosed control deficiency, but a narrow balance-sheet-classification one, not an earnings-quality problem (SEC EDGAR 10-K/A, accession 0001069183-25-000075, filed 2025-05-07).

Reverse DCF (own construction; two-stage — 10-year explicit growth then 3% terminal, WACC 10.5% for a smaller-cap, high-multiple grower with negative near-term FCF, consolidated basis): Because trailing/H1 2026 FCF is negative, a standard reverse DCF off current FCF is not computable; instead this dossier reverse-solves off FY2025's positive full-year FCF (OCF $211.34M − capex $136.26M = $75.08M) as the last clean annual base, grown at consensus-implied near-term rates (FY1 EPS growth 37.6% used as a proxy for FY2026-27 FCF growth given SBC/NI are not comparable) tapering to 3% terminal. Solving EV ($37.31bn) = Σ FCF₀(1+g)ᵗ/(1+WACC)ᵗ + terminal value implies 10-year FCF growth needs to average roughly 30%+/yr — i.e. Axon's FCF would need to compound from ~$75M (FY2025) to roughly $1.0–1.1bn by year 10, a >13x increase. Given revenue is already guided to grow 32–34% in FY2026 alone, this is not obviously unreasonable if the negative-OCF pattern reverses toward FY2025-style full-year cash conversion — but it is a demanding, multi-year bar, and the FY2025 FCF base is small and volatile (a single bad working-capital quarter would materially move the required growth rate). implied_vs_base: above — the price requires sustained hyper-growth in cash profitability, not just revenue, for a decade; the analyst's base case (revenue growth moderating from ~33% toward high-teens by year 5–7 as the law-enforcement TAM matures, with FCF margin normalizing toward 15–20% of revenue as SBC dilutes and working capital stabilizes) implies a lower path than the reverse DCF requires.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull (3 points): 1. Two consecutive guidance raises in 2026 (to 32–34% FY2026 revenue growth) backed by $15.1bn of contracted future bookings — real, disclosed forward revenue visibility, not just a momentum story. 2. High switching costs once an agency standardizes on the TASER/body-camera/cloud-evidence ecosystem, plus expansion into counter-drone and connected-devices — a genuine moat triage correctly identified. 3. The September 2026 sell-off (>20% in a month) has repriced the stock well below Street targets (mean $706 vs spot $430) even as fundamentals (revenue growth, backlog) kept improving — if the OCF/margin concerns prove transitory, there is a real re-rating opportunity.

Bear (3 points): 1. Operating cash flow was negative in H1 2026 (−$11.4M) and FCF was solidly negative (≈−$55.6M) despite >30% revenue growth — the business is not yet self-funding, and the company just raised $1.0–1.15bn in convertible debt to bridge that gap. 2. GAAP earnings are dominated by large, volatile, stock-price-linked SBC (2024 eXponential Stock Plan/CEO Performance Award) — a genuine earnings-quality problem that makes quarter-to-quarter GAAP results nearly uninterpretable and could keep surprising in either direction as the stock price moves. 3. Adjusted gross margin and software/services margin both declined YoY in Q2 2026 (−40bps and −380bps respectively) even as revenue accelerated — a real signal that incremental growth is currently lower-margin (professional services mix, new-product scaling), which if it continues would undercut the reverse DCF's need for FCF margin expansion.

9. Key risks & measurable kill criteria

Any of the following would break the thesis (i.e., would move this WATCH toward REJECT): 1. Full-year (or two consecutive quarters') operating cash flow remains negative beyond the normal H1 seasonal pattern — i.e., FY2026 OCF prints below FY2025's $211.3M — would confirm the business is structurally consuming cash to grow, not temporarily. 2. Software/services segment margin declines for two more consecutive quarters (already down 380bps YoY in Q2 2026) — would confirm a durable mix-driven margin problem rather than one quarter of professional-services noise. 3. Revenue growth decelerates below 25% YoY for two consecutive quarters — would break the "still-accelerating, guidance-raising" thesis this WATCH depends on. 4. A third consecutive year of eXponential Stock Plan/CEO Performance Award SBC exceeding ~8% of revenue — would confirm the GAAP/non-GAAP gap is structural, not a one-time mega-grant working through the system. 5. Any further debt or equity capital raise within 12 months of the Sept 2026 convertible note — would confirm the company cannot fund its growth from operations even with the new $1.0–1.15bn cushion.

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • FY2026 guidance likely to be reiterated or refined at Q3 2026; watch specifically for any comment on operating cash flow/FCF conversion, given this is now the market's stated top concern.

AZO — AutoZone, Inc. (NYSE: AZO)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — 24–36 month horizon. Durable, well-run auto-parts retailer compounding revenue at ~7–8%/yr with a share-buyback engine that has driven negative book equity; core economics are intact (adjusted debt/EBITDAR flat at 2.5x), but this fiscal year's EPS growth decelerated sharply from AutoZone's historical mid-teens pace to roughly mid-single-digits on gross-margin deleverage, and the negative-equity balance sheet leaves no cushion if a recession hits used-car-age-driven demand at the same time debt service needs cash. Reservation: size small given the leverage structure and the deceleration in per-share earnings growth versus AutoZone's own history.

2. Business in plain English

AutoZone sells automotive replacement parts, accessories and maintenance items to DIY (do-it-yourself) retail customers and, increasingly, to commercial repair shops (DIFM, "do it for me") through a dense US/Mexico/Brazil store network with same-day/overnight parts delivery. It makes money on retail gross margin (~52–53%) funded by scale purchasing and a network of distribution centers, and has for decades redeployed nearly all free cash flow into share buybacks rather than dividends, which has pushed reported book equity negative. Competitive position: one of three dominant national auto-parts chains (with O'Reilly and Advance), with store density and commercial-delivery speed as the moat.

Triage/model context: the quant model ranked AZO 479 of ~500 (very poor rank, largely because momentum has been -30% over the past year and the model has almost no coverage of the "financial" quality family for AZO, given the negative book equity makes standard ROE/leverage ratios undefined). Triage overrode the poor rank specifically because the weak momentum reads like "a screen hiding a good business" rather than a deteriorating one. Having now checked the primary filings: partially confirmed, partially not. The business is genuinely durable (steady 7–8% revenue growth, stable ~2.5x adjusted leverage), but the triage's stated reason — "guided EPS growth of 34%" — does not match what I can verify from the filings: AutoZone does not issue EPS guidance at all, and trailing GAAP diluted EPS growth this fiscal year was roughly mid-single digits (Q4 FY26 EPS +15% YoY was the strongest print, aided by buybacks, but full-year EPS growth was closer to +5–6%). Eight straight quarters (all shown here) of positive domestic same-store sales (+1.6% to +4.8%), with commercial (DIFM) growth outpacing DIY — a structurally growing, repair-not-replace category. 2. Adjusted leverage flat at 2.5x while still funding both elevated growth capex and buybacks — the balance sheet is not visibly deteriorating despite negative book equity. 3. Tariff-refund and buyback authorization increases ($1.6B remaining vs $632M a year ago) suggest management sees capital-return capacity ahead.

Bear (3 points): 1. Reported EPS growth decelerated hard from AutoZone's historical mid-teens pace to ~5.5% for FY2026, driven by opex deleverage ("investments to support growth initiatives") outrunning gross-margin gains in three of four quarters. 2. Negative stockholders' equity of $(2.78B) means there is no equity cushion; if a downturn hits (used-car-age cycle turning, as triage flagged) at the same time as elevated capex, the buyback engine that has driven per-share value for 20+ years could have to pause. 3. A meaningful share of this year's reported gross-margin improvement (LIFO swing + tariff refunds) is non-recurring — underlying margin trend is closer to flat-to-down, which the reported headline numbers can obscure.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Domestic same-store sales turn negative for two consecutive fiscal quarters (from +1.6% to +4.8% now).
  2. Adjusted debt/EBITDAR rises above 3.0x (from 2.5x now).
  3. Full-year diluted EPS growth (ex-LIFO/ex-tariff one-offs) is negative for a full fiscal year.
  4. Share-repurchase spend falls below $1.5B over a trailing four quarters (from a pace of ~$427–540M/quarter now, i.e., an implicit signal management is preserving cash for stress) without a stated capex-driven reason.
  5. A second consecutive year of gross-margin deleverage (ex the identified one-off items).

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: Q1 FY27 — estimated early December 2026 (historical pattern: 9-Dec-2025 for Q1 FY26, 2024 release similarly early December; not yet confirmed by an IR calendar posting as of 26-Sep-2026 — treat as an estimate).
  • AGM/proxy voting typically mid-December (5.07 8-K filed 19-Dec-2025 last cycle).
  • Watch International segment reporting for constant-currency same-store sales — the FX-driven "10.7%" headline in Q4 FY26 should not be read as organic strength.

11. Red-flag scan

  • Negative stockholders' equity — a structural feature of AutoZone's buyback policy for many years, not a new distress signal, but it does remove any equity buffer; flagged as the primary balance-sheet risk, consistent with the triage note.
  • Used-car-age cycle risk flagged by triage (demand sensitivity if consumers replace rather than repair vehicles) — not independently verified against a primary source in this pass; flagged as an open item.
  • No auditor change, restatement, going-concern language, or SEC/DOJ investigation identified in the reviewed 8-Ks/10-Qs; a full 10-K risk-factor diff and Form 4 insider-trading pattern review were not completed in this standard-depth pass — flagged as a coverage gap.

dossiers.BAC:
BAC — Bank of America Corporation (NYSE: BAC)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — 24–36 month horizon. Second-largest US bank, delivering accelerating YoY EPS growth (+18% Q4-25 → +25% Q1-26 → +34% Q2-26) on higher net interest income, improving efficiency and low, falling credit costs, all while returning ~$8B/quarter to shareholders. Reservation, and the reason this is not a full-weight INCLUDE: price/book is at a 15-year-plus high (94th own-history percentile) and credit costs are unusually low in the cycle — the systematic valuation model (V1) independently flags the stock as "excessive." I partly disagree with V1's magnitude (see §7) but not its direction, so size is capped at half weight pending either a pullback in P/B or further evidence the current ROE level is durable through a full credit cycle.

2. Business in plain English

Bank of America is the second-largest US bank by assets, with four main businesses: Consumer Banking (deposits, cards, small-business lending — #1 in US consumer deposits), Global Wealth & Investment Management (Merrill, Private Bank), Global Banking (corporate/commercial lending and investment banking) and Global Markets (sales & trading). It makes money on the spread between what it pays depositors and earns on loans/securities (net interest income, ~50% of revenue) plus fees (wealth management, trading, investment banking). Competitive position: one of four "too big to fail" US universal banks (with JPMorgan, Citi, Wells Fargo), with the largest low-cost deposit base as its structural advantage.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1_live_scores.csv (25 Sep 2026): live_rank 19/~500, composite decile 10 (top decile), quality (fam_Q) and value (fam_V) factor scores both strong. This ranks BAC as one of the most attractive names in the whole triage batch. Cross-checking against the primary filings, the strong quant read is substantially confirmed by real operating momentum, not just a cheap multiple: NII, revenue and EPS have all been growing and accelerating YoY for at least three straight quarters (see §4), and the efficiency ratio has improved from 63% (2Q25) to 59% (2Q26). The one place the quant read and the systematic valuation model disagree with each other is P/B: BAC's P/B is at a 15-year-plus high (V1: 94.35th own-history percentile) even though the b1 value factor score treats it as statistically cheap versus the market on other measures (P/E, FCF yield) — a genuine internal tension addressed in §7.

4. Last quarters — results table (GAAP, consolidated; all $ figures in US dollars, billions unless per-share)

Source for every cell in this table: BAC 8-K Ex-99.1 earnings press releases, as filed with SEC EDGAR (accession numbers and URLs in §Sources below; one release per quarter shown).

FY2025 full-year net income: $30.5B (company-stated headline). Sequential (QoQ) growth in 2Q26 was boosted by Global Markets (sales & trading revenue +33% YoY, 17th consecutive quarter of YoY growth) and GWIM (asset-management fees +19% YoY on higher market valuations) alongside the core NII tailwind — i.e., growth is broad-based across segments, not a single-line artefact.

5. Guidance track record

Banks generally do not give point EPS guidance; BAC instead frames forward NII/expense expectations qualitatively on earnings calls (not fully captured in the Ex-99.1 press releases reviewed here — a coverage gap, flagged). Each of the four reviewed releases described NII as growing YoY (+9% in 1Q26 and 2Q26, +10% in 4Q25) "driven by higher loan and deposit balances and fixed-rate asset repricing, partially offset by the impact of lower interest rates" — a consistent narrative across quarters, not a reversal. No formal raise/cut table is applicable in the addendum sense.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet (bank-appropriate metrics)

  • CET1 (Standardized): 11.2% at 2Q26, down from 11.6% a year earlier — capital ratio has been drawn down modestly to fund $8.0B of shareholder returns in 2Q26 alone (buybacks + dividends), while still "well above the regulatory minimum" (company's words).
  • Credit quality: net charge-off ratio improved steadily from 0.58% (3Q25) to 0.47% (2Q26); nonperforming loans ratio ~0.47–0.52% and provisions have been trending down or flat — credit costs are benign, arguably unusually so for this point in a rate cycle (a risk noted in §8/§9, not a red flag on its own).
  • ROE: return on average common shareholders' equity improved from ~11.0% (implied, 4Q25) to 12.0% (1Q26) to 12.7% (2Q26) — an accelerating trend, not a static number.
  • GAAP vs adjusted: figures above are GAAP except NII (FTE) and efficiency ratio, which are standard fully-taxable-equivalent bank convention, clearly labelled by the company; no aggressive non-GAAP adjustment identified.
  • No pending M&A or major litigation disclosed in the reviewed press releases.

7. Valuation — V1 reconciliation (required)

V1 systematic valuation (outputs/v1_valuation.json, v1_valuation_table.csv), method = justified P/B = (ROE−g)/(COE−g): - Price used: $56.70 (25-Sep-2026). P/B: 1.374x, at the 94.35th percentile of its own 15-year (177-month) history — i.e., BAC has rarely been this expensive on book value. - COE 9.58% (beta 1.06, rf 5.17%, ERP 4.14%); implied ROE priced in: 12.03%; delivered TTM ROE: 11.18%; historical (15-yr) ROE 20th/50th/80th percentile: 4.25% / 7.96% / 10.33%. - Scenarios: bear −16.4%/yr (ROE reverts to 15-yr 20th pctile 4.25%), base −1.9%/yr (ROE reverts to 15-yr median 7.96%), bull +11.7%/yr (ROE holds near 15-yr 80th pctile 10.33%). - V1 verdict: "excessive" (score −0.67), driven mainly by the P/B percentile term and the negative base-case return vs. the 9.58% hurdle rate; sanity check: base 3-yr value ($53.56/sh incl. dividends) sits below the Street's 12-month low target ($62).

Do I agree? Partly. I agree with the direction — P/B at a 15-year-plus high is a real and fair caution, and I would not call this stock cheap. I disagree with the magnitude of V1's base case, because its base-case ROE assumption (7.96%, the 15-year median) is anchored heavily to the 2011–2021 near-zero-rate decade, when the whole US bank sector's ROE was structurally depressed — not obviously the right "base" for the next 3 years given the primary-source evidence in §4 that BAC's own ROE has been rising, not falling, for at least three consecutive quarters (11.0% → 12.0% → 12.7%). If I instead assume ROE holds near its current ~12% run-rate as the base case, the same P/B formula implies a fair P/B of roughly (0.12−0.03)/(0.0958−0.03) ≈ 1.37x — almost exactly today's multiple — which would put the base-case return closer to the dividend yield plus modest per-share book-value growth (roughly low-single-digits, still below the 9.58% cost-of-equity hurdle, but nowhere near V1's −1.9%). Reconciliation: both readings agree BAC is fully priced, not undervalued — the disagreement is only about how far above fair value it sits, and I lean less negative than V1 because the ROE trend is the opposite of what V1's mean-reversion assumption implies. - v1_verdict: "excessive"; v1_base_3y: −0.0188 (−1.9%/yr); dossier_view: "full"; consistent: false (I agree on direction/richness, disagree on the size of the gap); reconciliation as above. - Implied vs. my own base case: using my adjusted ~12% ROE base case against the ~12.03% ROE the market is implicitly paying for, implied is "in_line" — not clearly cheap, which is why this is INCLUDE-SMALL rather than a full-weight INCLUDE, and not clearly overpriced enough on fundamentals alone to be a REJECT (V1's harsher framing would push toward WATCH/REJECT; I land one notch more constructive given the accelerating ROE evidence).

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull (3 points): 1. EPS growth has accelerated for three straight quarters (+18% → +25% → +34% YoY) on broad-based segment strength (Global Markets' 17th consecutive quarter of YoY sales & trading growth; GWIM AUM +17%), not a single one-off item. 2. Efficiency ratio improving (63%→59% YoY) and net charge-offs falling (0.58%→0.47%) simultaneously — operating leverage and credit quality are moving the same direction. 3. CET1 of 11.2%, still comfortably above requirement, supports continued large capital returns (~$8B/quarter) even as the ratio normalizes down from a post-stress-test peak.

Bear (3 points): 1. P/B at a 15-year-plus high (94th percentile) — even V1's own bull case (+11.7%/yr) requires ROE to sustain near a 15-year 80th-percentile level; this is priced for continued strength, not a business trading at a margin of safety. 2. Credit costs (0.47% net charge-off ratio) are low in absolute and historical terms; a turn in consumer or commercial credit (which the model has no way to time) would hit both NCOs and CET1 simultaneously. 3. Much of the recent NII acceleration is explicitly attributed to "fixed-rate asset repricing" (i.e., a one-time structural tailwind from replacing low-yielding legacy securities/loans) — once that repricing cycle completes, NII growth should mechanically decelerate even without a rate cut.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Net charge-off ratio rises above 0.65% for two consecutive quarters (vs. 0.47% now).
  2. CET1 (Standardized) falls below 10.5% (vs. 11.2% now) without a clearly stated, temporary reason.
  3. YoY EPS growth turns negative for any quarter (from the current +18%/+25%/+34% accelerating trend) absent a one-off/non-repeating item.
  4. NII growth decelerates to flat-or-negative YoY for two consecutive quarters (from +9–10% now), signalling the fixed-rate-asset-repricing tailwind has fully played out.
  5. P/B rises further into a new multi-year high (>1.45x) without a corresponding rise in delivered ROE above ~12.5%, widening the gap V1 already flags.

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: Q3 2026 — estimated mid-October 2026 (historical pattern: 15-Oct-2025 for 3Q25, 14-Jan/14-Apr/14-Jul-2026 for the three most recent quarters; not yet confirmed by an IR calendar posting as of 26-Sep-2026 — treat as an estimate, likely ~14-Oct-2026).
  • Federal Reserve rate-path decisions remain the single largest swing factor for NII given BAC's asset-sensitive balance sheet (explicitly cited each quarter as a partial offset).
  • Annual CCAR/stress-test results (typically released by the Fed each June) drive next year's buyback/dividend capacity — none due before the next earnings date.

11. Red-flag scan

  • No auditor change, restatement, or going-concern language identified in the reviewed press releases.
  • No SEC/DOJ investigation or material litigation disclosed in the documents reviewed (a full 10-K/10-Q litigation-note read was not completed in this standard-depth pass — flagged as a coverage gap).
  • A data conflict already logged by V1 itself: D3 TTM revenue ($121.1B) vs. Yahoo TTM revenue ($113.9B) differ by 5.9%, and the D3 figure implies an implausible >100% EBIT margin — V1 substituted the Yahoo TTM revenue figure for its reverse-DCF; I did not independently resolve this vendor discrepancy but flag it as inherited, not re-verified.
  • Form 4 insider-selling pattern was not reviewed in this pass — flagged as a coverage gap.

dossiers.BBY:
Best Buy Co., Inc. (NYSE: BBY, CIK 0000764478)

Recency: most recent reported period incorporated: Q2 FY27 (13 weeks ended 2026-08-01), published 2026-08-27 (8-K earnings release) / 10-Q filed 2026-09-04; checked for events to 2026-09-25. Also incorporates the FY26 10-K (fiscal year ended 2026-01-31, filed 2026-03-18) and 8-K/press-release history back to Q3 FY25 (November 2024).

Reporting basis: consolidated, USD millions unless stated. Fiscal year ends the Saturday closest to January 31 (FY26 = year ended 2026-01-31).

1. Verdict line

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). BBY is a genuine, primary-sourced turnaround — comparable sales have gone from -6.8% (FY24) to +0.5% (FY26) to +4.1% (Q2 FY27), and guidance has been raised twice this year — but a scenario-weighted DCF (run via valuation.py) puts fair value at ~$86/share against a $90.51 price, the CEO and CFO are both departing within the same six months, and the market is already pricing in slightly negative long-run FCF growth, leaving little margin of safety for a concentrated position. Thesis horizon: 12–24 months (through the CEO/CFO transition and FY27 guidance delivery).

2. Business in plain English

Best Buy is the largest specialty consumer-electronics retailer in North America, selling computing devices, mobile phones, consumer electronics, appliances, gaming and entertainment products through ~1,068 stores (926 Domestic, 142 Canada) and e-commerce (bestbuy.com / bestbuy.ca), plus services (Geek Squad support/installation, memberships, Best Buy Health) (10-K filed 2026-03-18, Item 1). It makes money on product gross margin (~22-24%), high-margin services/membership and, increasingly, two capital-light "profit streams" it is scaling — Best Buy Marketplace (third-party seller commissions) and Best Buy Ads (retail media) (10-K, Item 7). Competitively it sits between mass-market generalists (Walmart, Amazon, Costco) that also sell electronics at thin margins and it competes on staffed expertise, in-home delivery/installation, and vendor partnerships (Apple, Samsung) that de-prioritize pure price competition.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

The pre-registered QVM model gives BBY Quality 0.753, Value 0.866, Momentum 0.65 (composite 0.756, the lowest of the three retail names under review). Momentum is well-supported: four consecutive comp-sales beats and two guidance raises in the last four earnings releases (Section 5) are real, dated, primary-sourced events, not noise. Value is directionally real — NTM P/E (~12.8-14.0x depending on source/date; see Section 7), FCF yield 9.3%, EV/EBITDA 8.3x are all below BBY's own 10-year average (P/E ~14.35x, EV/EBITDA ~7.4x median per MacroTrends/GuruFocus, cross-check only) — but the model's own reverse-DCF (Section 7) shows the market is pricing in negative trailing FCF growth, i.e. the "cheapness" is compensation for real, disclosed risk, not free money.

Quality is the one to interrogate, and the orchestrator's hypothesis is partly correct. The very low leverage input (0.073) is genuinely structural, not a shrinking-asset artefact: funded net debt is trivial and has been for years — BBY has actually run a net cash position excluding leases every year in this sample (net debt ex-leases is negative $1,086M at Q2 FY27: $1,169M gross debt less $2,255M cash), and gross debt has been flat at $1.14-1.17B since FY24 (10-K, Note 8; 8-K balance sheets). That part of Quality is durable.

But the gross-profit/assets (0.594) and other asset-efficiency inputs are partly an artefact, for two documented reasons, not one: 1. Non-cash impairments have shrunk the denominator. Best Buy Health (the healthcare/aging-in-place unit built around the Current Health and Lively/GreatCall acquisitions) took a $475M goodwill impairment in Q4 FY25 and another $171M goodwill/intangible impairment in Q3 FY26 — $646M cumulative in two years, explicitly tied to "downward revisions in the long-term financial projections for Best Buy Health" and "pressures in the Medicaid and Medicare Advantage markets" (8-K filed 2025-03-04; 10-K filed 2026-03-18, Item 7 & Note 3). Goodwill fell from $1,383M (FY24) to $790M (FY26/TTM) on write-offs, not monetization. 2. The store fleet is genuinely shrinking and undercapitalized. ratios.py flags, as a MEDIUM-severity quality warning, that capex has run below depreciation in all four periods sampled (0.81x-0.89x) — net PP&E fell from $2,260M (FY24) to $1,986M (FY26). Total store count fell from 1,125 (FY24) to 1,068 (FY26), and management guided 10-15 further closures in FY27 (Retail Dive, Feb-2026 earnings call coverage) while planning only ~+4 net Best Buy-banner stores.

Net: the underlying retail operation is genuinely improving (ROIC ex-goodwill 21.9%→28.9% FY24→TTM per ratios.py, comp sales inflecting positive, adjusted operating margin expanding), which is durable. But part of the asset-efficiency half of the Quality score is flattered by writing off a failed diversification bet and running the store base leaner rather than by compounding capital at a high rate — a meaningfully different, less repeatable story than the headline score suggests.

8. Bull case and bear case

Bull case: 1. Comp sales have inflected from -6.8% (FY24) to +4.1% (Q2 FY27, the strongest quarter in the 8-quarter window), with broad-based category strength (computing +6.8%, home theater +5.6% in Q2 FY27) and guidance raised twice this fiscal year on the strength of it (Section 5). 2. Two new, capital-light profit streams — Best Buy Marketplace (US launch, FY26) and Best Buy Ads — are explicitly cited as the primary driver of the domestic gross-margin improvement in three of the last four quarters, and management (incoming CEO Jason Bonfig) has made expanding them a named FY27 priority. 3. Balance sheet is genuinely conservative: net cash position ex-leases, an undrawn $1.25B revolver through 2030, interest coverage of 38x EBIT/interest (TTM, ratios.py), and a 4.2% dividend yield backed by ~57-64% payout — a shareholder-yield floor while the turnaround plays out.

Bear case: 1. Leadership discontinuity at the worst possible time. CEO Corie Barry (7 years in the role) departs 2026-10-31 and CFO Matt Bilunas departs 2026-07-31 with an external CFO search still ongoing as of the 2026-09-25 cutoff — both transitions land inside the next two quarters, with a new, first-time CEO (Jason Bonfig) and possibly a new external CFO simultaneously executing a strategy pivot (Marketplace/Ads/Retail-media) neither has run before. 2. Two years of impairments from the same failed bet. $646M cumulative Best Buy Health goodwill/intangible write-offs (FY25 + FY26) plus a near-total wind-down of the Yardbird store format (21 stores → 2, per the FY26 10-K store table) show a real, recent history of value-destructive diversification — a portfolio manager should ask what Marketplace/Ads/Best Buy Health-next-act risk looks like under new leadership. 3. Margin and revenue exposed to two live, quantifiable external cost shocks: (a) IEEPA tariffs were ruled unauthorized by the Supreme Court (2026-02-20) and BBY has booked $75M of refunds (Q2+Q3 FY27) that will not repeat, while the government has "initiated further actions under existing trade authorities" that could reimpose tariffs under different legal cover (10-Q filed 2026-09-04); (b) a DRAM/NAND ("memory") cost spike is pushing computing ASPs up mid-teens% with unit volumes down high-single-digits in Q2 FY27 (Q2 FY27 earnings call, 2026-08-27) — i.e., a meaningful share of the headline comp-sales beat is price/mix from a memory shortage passing through to consumers, not pure volume strength.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (thesis-invalidation triggers)

  1. Comp sales turn negative for two consecutive quarters (baseline: Q2 FY27 +4.1% enterprise; FY27 guidance assumes 1.9-3.0% for the year) — would signal the recovery was a comp-driven sugar high, not durable share gain.
  2. CFO hire is delayed past Q3 FY27 earnings (expected ~late Nov 2026) or is an internal/interim appointment without prior public-company CFO experience — the company itself said it "expects to name a successor with previous CFO experience" (8-K filed 2026-06-22); failure to do so raises succession-planning-quality concerns during a CEO transition.
  3. Gross margin down >150bps YoY in any quarter once the ~$75M of one-off IEEPA tariff refunds fully laps (by Q4 FY27) — would show the tariff/memory cost pressure is structural, not transitory.
  4. Another Best Buy Health-scale impairment or a third consecutive year of goodwill write-offs from the same unit — would confirm the capital-allocation risk flagged in Section 8 is systemic, not resolved.
  5. Lease-adjusted leverage (net debt + operating leases)/(EBITDA+rent) rises above ~1.5x (baseline 0.53x TTM) — would indicate the conservative balance sheet BBY is relying on as a floor is eroding, e.g. from a large debt-funded buyback restart or a sustained FCF decline.

BKNG — Booking Holdings Inc. — Fundamental Diligence Dossier

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — 24–36 month horizon. The world's largest online travel agent is statistically as cheap versus its own history as it has ever been, operating income has grown in every comparable quarter for four years, and leverage on a cash-flow basis is very low. I agree with V1's directional "attractive" call. Named reservation: V1's +39.3%/yr "base case" is not a credible base case — it depends on the NTM P/E more than doubling (13.8x→30.1x), an assumption management's own guidance does not support — so size this as attractive-but-not-39%/yr-attractive, and be aware of two unresolved items: a rapidly deepening negative-equity/rising-debt position, and a live EU regulatory/litigation overhang.

2. Business in plain English

Booking Holdings is an online travel agent (Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, Kayak, OpenTable) that connects travelers with hotels, alternative accommodations, rental cars and flights, earning a commission (agency model) or a margin on room revenue it collects and remits (merchant model — now ~73% of gross bookings, +4pts YoY). It makes money on the volume of "room nights" booked and the take rate per booking, funded by heavy performance-marketing spend to acquire direct and paid traffic. Its competitive position is the largest global OTA by gross bookings, competing chiefly with Expedia, Airbnb, and direct hotel-chain booking channels, with Booking.com itself now designated an EU "gatekeeper" platform.

Note on share count/EPS: Booking Holdings executed a 25-for-1 forward stock split effective April 2, 2026 (record date 2026-03-06; traded split-adjusted from 2026-04-06). All EPS and share-count figures below are presented on a split-adjusted basis for comparability; pre-split GAAP releases (e.g., Q2 2025's originally-reported $27.43 EPS) are divided by 25 throughout ($27.43⁄25=$1.10, matching the figure below).

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

B1 ranks BKNG #63 (composite 87.3rd percentile) on strong Value (earnings yield 87.3rd percentile, book/price 78.6th, EBIT/EV 91.6th) and reasonable Quality, with weak recent Momentum (50.6th percentile, unremarkable) and weak Earnings-momentum/SUE (11.3rd percentile — the SUE-based earnings-momentum factor is actually a negative contributor, worth noting since it cuts against the "attractive" quant read). The value read is durable, not an artefact: it is confirmed independently in this review — Q2 2026 room nights +5%, gross bookings +9% reported, operating income growth positive in every comparable quarter since 2022 (Q1: $450M→$791M→$1,062M→$1,271M; Q3: $3,103M→$3,179M→$3,483M) — this is a genuinely cheap multiple on a genuinely still-growing business, not a statistical illusion.

Total debt $20,180M (+9.2% YoY); cash $17,214M (includes merchant/customer funds in transit — not all "excess" cash); net debt ≈$2,966M, matching V1 exactly. TTM EBITDA ≈$9.86bn (V1) → net debt/EBITDA ≈0.30x — very low leverage on a cash-flow basis despite the alarming-looking equity headline.
  • Buybacks have accelerated sharply: H1 2026 buybacks $7,758M vs. H1 2025 $3,668M (+111.5% YoY), funded by ~$2.975bn of new debt raised in H1 2026 plus strong OCF. $14.5bn of authorization remains. Quarterly dividend $0.42/share declared for Q3 2026 (dividend only initiated in 2024).

7. Valuation snapshot — reconciliation with V1 (task explicitly asks to scrutinise this)

V1 verdict: attractive (score +0.993 — among the highest in the entire ~500-name universe). NTM P/E 13.8x — 1.1st percentile of its own ~14.75-year history (essentially the cheapest it has ever traded) and roughly in line with a peer median of 13.1x (peer set ABNB, CCL, EXPE, HLT and others — note CCL is a cruise operator with a very different capital/risk profile; peer comparability is imperfect). Implied 10-year growth from the current price is only +2.3% (i.e. the price itself does not require much growth), but V1's bear/base/bull 3-year annualised returns are +11.3% / +39.3% / +86.4% — even the bear case is positive, reflecting how cheap the starting point is. I do not accept V1's +39.3%/yr figure as a credible "base case." Decomposing the scenario: revenue growth assumed 16.8%/yr, and the NTM P/E exit multiple assumed to expand from 13.8x to 30.1x — more than doubling — by year 3. That multiple-expansion assumption, not fundamentals, is doing most of the work: management's own FY2026 guidance (high-single-digit bookings/room-nights/revenue, low-to-mid-teens adjusted EPS growth) implies something like 10–15%/yr EPS growth with a flat multiple, not 39%/yr. The model's base-case fair value ($443.57) is 47% above the single highest Wall Street 12-month price target ($301) — a useful sanity check that the "base" is really more like this model's bull case. My view: the stock is genuinely, statistically cheap (1.1st percentile of own history is a real, checkable signal) and the business is executing (bookings/room-nights growth, raised guidance, very low cash leverage) — I agree with "attractive" as a direction. But I would treat V1's 39.3%/yr as the upside case, and underwrite a realistic base case closer to high-teens-to-low-20s%/yr (management's own EPS growth guidance plus a partial, not total, re-rating), which is still an attractive risk/reward but materially different position-sizing math than 39%/yr compounded for three years. dossier_view: attractive but base case overstated; consistent with V1: no — I am explicitly flagging the exit-multiple assumption (13.8x→30.1x) as the V1 input I believe is too aggressive to call "base," with the primary-source support being management's own low-to-mid-teens adjusted-EPS guidance and the Street's own $301 high target.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: 1. 13.8x NTM P/E is at roughly the 1st percentile of BKNG's own trading history; Q2 2026 room nights +5%, gross bookings +9% reported (+8% cc), FY2026 guidance just raised to high-single-digit growth plus low-to-mid-teens adjusted EPS growth. 2. Net debt/EBITDA ≈0.3x despite deeply negative book equity — ample capacity funding a rapidly growing capital-return program (H1 2026 buybacks +112% YoY, $14.5bn authorization remaining) that mechanically compresses share count. 3. Operating income has grown in every comparable quarter for four years — the core marketplace economics are intact regardless of GAAP net-income noise below the operating line.

Bear: 1. V1's +39.3%/yr "base case" requires the NTM multiple to more than double (13.8x→30.1x) — management's own guidance does not support anything close to that without a multiple re-rating; the base-case fair value already exceeds the Street's highest 12-month target by 47%. 2. Shareholders' equity is deeply and rapidly more negative (−$10.78bn, −$4.67bn in the last four quarters) funded partly by fresh debt (+$2.975bn raised in H1 2026 alone, total debt +9.2% YoY) — low leverage today, but a capital-markets-dependent model. 3. GAAP net income fell sharply in Q1 2025 (−57%) and Q2 2025 (−41%) for reasons not fully isolated in this review, making 2026's headline GAAP growth rates partly a base-effect artefact; separately, the EU Digital Markets Act "gatekeeper" obligations (parity-clause restrictions) took effect November 2024 and remain a live overhang — the European Parliament in April 2026 pressed the Commission to open a formal non-compliance investigation, Italy's AGCM opened its own April 2026 consumer-protection inquiry, and a hotel-industry class action (potentially up to ~18,000 European hotels) is seeking billions in damages for 2004–2024 parity-clause conduct.

9. Key risks & measurable kill criteria

  1. Room-night or gross-bookings growth falls below 3% YoY for two consecutive quarters (currently +5% / +9%).
  2. Net debt/EBITDA rises above 1.5x (currently ≈0.30x).
  3. FY2026 guidance (high-single-digit volume/bookings/revenue, low-to-mid-teens adjusted EPS growth) is cut.
  4. The European Commission opens a formal DMA non-compliance proceeding against Booking.com, or the EU hotel class action produces a disclosed material damages award/settlement.
  5. Quarterly buyback spend falls by more than 50% quarter-over-quarter without a stated capital-return-policy reason — a signal management itself sees less value at the prevailing price.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: ~late October/early November 2026 (estimated from cadence: 2025-10-28, 2024-10-30, 2023-11-02; not yet officially confirmed). Watch for: European Commission DMA enforcement decisions; progress/disclosure on the European hotel-industry class action; quarterly dividend declarations ($0.42/share declared for Q3 2026).

11. Red-flag scan

  • EU regulatory: Booking.com designated a DMA "gatekeeper" (May 13, 2024; compliance required from Nov 14, 2024). As of April 2026, the European Parliament has pushed for a formal Commission non-compliance investigation over continued use of parity clauses; Italy's AGCM opened a related consumer-protection probe the same month. No fine has been levied as of this review, but DMA non-compliance findings can carry fines up to 10% of global annual turnover.
  • Litigation: Texas Attorney General "junk fees" settlement, $9.5M, August 2025 (immaterial in size, notable for the deceptive-pricing theme). Separately, a European hotel-industry class action (10,000+ hotels filed, potentially representing up to ~18,000) seeks damages for 2004–2024 use of parity clauses; no accrual size could be confirmed in this pass.
  • Insider transactions: Multiple Form 4 sales by the EVP/General Counsel, CFO, CHRO and two directors in Jul–Sep 2026, all appear to be routine Rule 10b5-1 pre-scheduled sales of modest size relative to holdings — not read as an adverse signal, but noted for completeness.
  • No 8-K Item 4.01/4.02 (auditor change/restatement) found in the submissions history reviewed.
  • Unresolved: the Q1–Q2 2025 GAAP net-income air-pocket described in §6 — recommend the audit/valuation team confirm the specific driver before relying on 2026 GAAP EPS growth-rate comparisons.

dossiers.BLK:
BlackRock, Inc. (BLK) — Diligence Dossier (F22, standard depth)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Thesis horizon 24–36 months (per this dossier's own §7 reverse DCF and §4 quarterly filings, not a data-provider figure). One-sentence reason: the world's largest, most durable asset-management franchise is compounding fee earnings at a rate the current price does not fully require, but roughly 30% of headline growth is acquisition-driven (GIP/HPS/Preqin, per §3/Q2-26 8-K) and GAAP EPS has been distorted by non-cash contingent-consideration marks (§4, Q1-26 10-Q), so full weight is not warranted until organic, adjusted growth is cleanly separable for another 2–4 quarters.

Thesis (≤25 words): As of the 2026-09-25 close, the world's #1 asset manager (iShares, Aladdin, and newly acquired private-markets platforms per Q2-26 8-K) growing AUM 20%+ a year (§4), priced at a market-average multiple (§7).

2. Business in plain English

Per its Q2 2026 10-Q (period ended 2026-06-30) and 8-K earnings release, BlackRock manages $15.3tn of client assets (index funds/ETFs via iShares, active strategies, and now private markets) for a fee, plus licenses its Aladdin risk-management/data platform to other institutions. It earns a percentage of assets under management (AUM), so revenue scales with markets and net client inflows; it does not take principal risk on client money. Competitive position (as characterized in the FY2025 10-K and Q2-26 8-K, filed 2026-02-25 and 2026-07-15 respectively): #1 global AUM, #1 ETF platform (iShares), and a quasi-operating-system moat in Aladdin used by hundreds of institutions including some competitors.

3. Why the model likes it / durability

b1 factor data (v4/data/b1_live_scores.csv, as_of 2026-09-25): Quality 5, Growth 4, price_vs_growth 4; factor composite driven by quality (gp/assets, ROE, low accruals) and growth (54% forward EPS growth cited in v4/outputs/Q04_triage.json). Partly an artefact: a large chunk of both the AUM growth (22% YoY per the Q2-26 8-K, filed 2026-07-15) and the EPS growth is inorganic — the GIP (infrastructure), HPS (private credit) and Preqin (data) acquisitions closed through 2024–2025 and are still being integrated and amortized (Q1-26 intangible amortization $277m). Underlying organic base-fee growth is durable (Aladdin technology services +13–15% YoY per the Q1-26/Q2-26 8-Ks) but slower than the headline.

No V1 row exists for BLK (v1_valuation_table.csv — 93 rows, BLK/BX/EG absent) → v1_verdict = null, no reconciliation possible; this dossier's valuation view is independently derived.

Reverse DCF: solving a 10-year explicit-growth + Gordon-terminal model (r = 10.5% cost of equity [rf 4.2% + beta ~1.3 × 5% ERP], terminal growth 3.5%) for the growth rate that reproduces the current price from NTM adjusted EPS ($62.15) gives implied 10-year EPS growth ≈ 6.7% p.a. (mid-single-digit organic base-fee growth + operating leverage + buybacks + full run-rate contribution from HPS/GIP/Preqin), i.e. above the implied rate → valuation view = cheap-to-fair, not demanding. Bear case 3% (fee compression, weak markets, messy integration); bull case 13% (AI-driven Aladdin/data adoption, private-markets scaling faster than modeled).

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) Aladdin + data (Preqin) creates a recurring, high-margin technology-services annuity growing mid-teens; (2) private-markets AUM (GIP infra, HPS credit) scales into a $600bn+ fee pool with higher yields than traditional index products; (3) buybacks ($550m/quarter) plus a 22% AUM growth rate compound EPS even if markets are flat. Bear: (1) organic (ex-M&A) base-fee growth is genuinely mid-single-digit and the market is paying up for a growth rate propped up by acquisitions; (2) integration of three large deals (GIP, HPS, Preqin) in 18 months raises execution risk, visible in intangible-amortization drag and lumpy GAAP EPS; (3) index-fund antitrust/ESG political risk (see §11) could force costly structural changes to the core iShares business.

9. Key risks & measurable kill criteria

  1. Organic base-fee (ex-acquisition) net flow growth below 3% for two consecutive quarters.
  2. Adjusted operating margin falls below 42% for two consecutive quarters (Q1-26 was 44.5%, Q2-26 was 45.9%).
  3. Net outflows (negative total net flows) in any single quarter.
  4. A further negative fair-value mark or impairment on GIP/HPS/Preqin contingent consideration/goodwill exceeding $500m in a quarter.
  5. Adverse final ruling or consent decree in the 13-state-AG antitrust (coal) suit or the LifePath ERISA litigation that restricts index-voting or fee practices.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 2026-10-14 (Q3-26, per d4 next_earnings_date). Integration updates on HPS/GIP/Preqin expected on that call; continued Fed rate path affects fixed-income AUM/flows.

No auditor change, restatement, or going-concern language found. Litigation: (a) 13 state Attorneys General (E.D. Texas) allege BlackRock, State Street and Vanguard conspired via common index-fund ownership to suppress coal-industry output — an antitrust theory novel to asset managers, unresolved; (b) ERISA class actions on BlackRock's LifePath target-date funds have survived motions to dismiss and are in discovery; (c) a securities class action against BlackRock TCP Capital Corp (a separate, externally-managed BDC, ticker TCPC) alleges NAV overstatement — BLK is the external manager, not a named defendant in the excerpts found, so direct P&L exposure to BLK looks limited but reputational risk exists. 1. Verdict: INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — thesis horizon 12–36 months

A genuinely improving, well-diversified growth portfolio and a deleveraging balance sheet are real, but the "statistically cheap" framing overstates the case: BMS's own 10-Q attributes a $1.4bn H1-2026 operating-cash-flow decline directly to the Eliquis Medicare price cut even as headline Eliquis revenue keeps growing, FY2025 non-GAAP EPS actually missed the company's own most-recently-reissued guidance range once a fourth-quarter M&A charge landed, and a reverse-DCF shows the current price already assumes roughly flat-to-declining free cash flow in perpetuity — i.e., the market is pricing this as a melting-ice-cube income stock, not an undiscovered bargain. Own it for the covered, growing dividend and multi-year LOE-defense optionality; do not size it as a high-conviction compounder.

2. Business in plain English

Bristol-Myers Squibb is a global biopharmaceutical company that discovers, develops and sells prescription medicines, mainly in oncology, hematology, cardiovascular disease, immunology and neuroscience, to patients via physicians, hospitals, pharmacies and payers (Medicare/Medicaid, commercial insurers, and international health systems). It earns money by selling patent-protected branded drugs at a large gross margin (~71% GAAP) while losing that margin rapidly once patents/exclusivity expire and generics enter. Its historically dominant products — the anticoagulant Eliquis and the multiple-myeloma drug Revlimid — are both now past peak and in structural decline (Revlimid) or newly subject to U.S. government price-setting (Eliquis), while a second wave of newer drugs (Opdivo/Opdivo Qvantig, Breyanzi, Reblozyl, Camzyos, Opdualag, Cobenfy, Krazati) is scaling to replace that lost revenue. Competitive position: top-5 global oncology/immunology franchise with real depth (not a single-product story), but facing the same IRA Medicare price-negotiation and patent-cliff dynamics as every large-cap innovator.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Quant snapshot (d4_live_snapshot.parquet, 2026-09-25): composite 0.842 (rank 9/503); Q 0.791, V 0.860, M 0.876 (sector-relative percentiles). - V (0.860, "statistically cheap"): confirmed directionally — trailing P/E ≈13.9x and NTM P/E ≈9.4-9.6x are well below the ~17.8x healthcare-sector average forward P/E (general market context, Sept 2026) and below the sector playbook's own 10–16x "core EPS" range for developed-market innovator pharma. But valuation.py's reverse-DCF on TTM FCF ($11.44bn) at a 7.5% WACC shows the current EV already implies ≈‑0.3% FCF growth for 10 years fading to 1% — the market is not underpricing growth, it is pricing BMS as a flat-to-shrinking cash cow. Cheap-on-a-ratio and cheap-on-a-DCF are different claims; only the first is clearly true here. - Q (0.791) — the ROE question the brief flagged: TTM ROE (computed via ratios.py) is 43.3% (FY2025 36.7%), close to the prelim snapshot's 41.6%. DuPont (3-step) shows this is not primarily a margin or efficiency story: net margin 13.2%→17.9% and asset turnover ~0.53x→0.55x are both unremarkable; the equity multiplier is 5.25x–4.36x (average assets ÷ average equity) and the tool's own 5-step DuPont flags "largest move: interest/tax burden, financing-driven" as the dominant swing factor. Mechanically, BMS's tangible book value is negative in every period tested (avg tangible equity −$19.6bn TTM; tangible BVPS −$8.21) — goodwill ($21.7bn) plus acquired intangibles ($17.4–23.3bn) exceed total equity, a direct legacy of debt/stock-funded M&A (Celgene 2019, then Karuna/RayzeBio/Mirati in 2024) that also produced a $43.6bn treasury-stock balance shrinking the equity base. Current-period buybacks are zero (PaymentsForRepurchaseOfCommonStock = $0 every quarter, FY2024–FY2026 YTD, per XBRL) — so the high ROE is not being freshly manufactured by today's capital allocation; it is a structural artefact of a thin/negative tangible-equity base plus a real (but partly base-effect) margin recovery as the 2024 mega-impairment year rolls off. Verdict: durable-ish margin recovery, but the headline ROE is substantially a leverage/intangible-base artefact, not "genuine capital efficiency." - M (0.876) — "beat the bar" check: BMS beat consensus EPS 8-for-8 over the last 8 quarters per the prelim snapshot (not independently re-verified this session; FMP analyst/earningsTranscript tools were plan-gated). What is independently verifiable from primary filings: the company's own full-year guidance was raised three times in the last four releases but the FY2025 actual non-GAAP EPS of $6.15 still landed below the most recently reissued guidance range of $6.40–$6.60 (see §5) — i.e., against its own bar, not just the analyst bar, 2025 was a miss. This supports the brief's suspicion that the external analyst bar has been set lower than the company's own internal bar. - Beta sanity-check: the snapshot's beta of 0.227 looks too low even for defensive pharma (large-cap pharma historically trades closer to 0.4–0.7); not independently recomputed this session (no price-history tool in scope), but flagged as a data-quality item for the quant team, not confirmed.

The FY2025 miss is the key finding here, and it was previously easy to miss: BMS raised FY2025 EPS guidance in October 2025 to $6.40–$6.60 (already inclusive of a stated $(0.80)/share Acquired-IPRD-and-licensing net impact), then reported actual FY2025 non-GAAP EPS of $6.15 — below that range — once a $1.4bn Q4 IPR&D charge from the Orbital Therapeutics acquisition (explicitly excluded from guidance when it was set, since the deal was only "expected to close in Q4 2025" as of the October release) hit. BMS's guidance methodology structurally excludes any future/unidentified M&A or licensing charge — which means a "raise" can still be followed by a miss if a deal closes late in the year, exactly the failure pattern this program was asked to check for.   • OCF/FCF — the clearest adverse fact in this file: FY2025 OCF $14.156bn vs FY2024 $15.190bn (−6.8%, 10-K MD&A: "higher GTN [gross-to-net] payments"). TTM FCF is $11.44bn vs a prior-TTM $14.58bn (−21.5%). This is BMS's own quantification that the Eliquis IRA Medicare price cut (see below) is landing at the cash-flow line even while headline Eliquis revenue is still growing — a real tension the market does not appear to be pricing separately from the revenue growth.
  • Eliquis IRA Maximum Fair Price (verified against CMS's primary published price list): effective 2026-01-01, CMS's negotiated Medicare Part D price is $231/30-day supply vs a 2023 list price of $521 (a 56% discount) (CMS, "Negotiated Prices for Initial Price Applicability Year 2026," Aug 2024). Despite this, reported Eliquis WW revenue grew +16% YoY (Q1'26) and +22% YoY (Q2'26), and FY2026 Eliquis growth guidance was raised from 10–15% to 20–25%. BMS's press releases attribute this only to generic "demand" and do not publish a volume/price bridge. Both things are simultaneously true and both are primary-sourced: revenue is growing, and BMS's own 10-Q says the Eliquis price cut is the primary driver of a $1.4bn cash-flow decline. This is a watch item, not a resolved question — gross-to-net/rebate accounting can lag, and a reader relying only on the revenue line would miss the cash-flow deterioration entirely.
  • GAAP vs. non-GAAP gap and its drivers: the gap is large and volatile — driven mainly by (i) Amortization of acquired intangibles ($3.3bn FY25, $8.9bn FY24 — declining as Revlimid-related intangibles fully amortize) and (ii) Acquired IPR&D charges, which BMS's non-GAAP explicitly does NOT exclude ("GAAP and non-GAAP EPS include the impacts of Acquired IPRD charges and licensing income," repeated in every release) — a genuine mitigant vs. peers who strip M&A charges from non-GAAP entirely. Other specified items (restructuring, litigation/settlement charges, contingent-consideration fair-value marks, priority-review-voucher purchases) are smaller and disclosed line-by-line in each release's Specified Items schedule.
  • SBC: $553M FY2025 / ~$562M annualized (H1'26 ×2) ≈ 1.1–1.2% of revenue — low, not a dilution concern.
  • Restructuring/impairment quantification (angle 6): 2023 Restructuring Plan — total expected charges ~$2.5bn through 2027, of which $1.8bn incurred to date (through Q2 2026 10-Q, Note 6); separately, a ~$2.0bn cost-savings target by end-2027 is stated but no cumulative realized-savings figure is disclosed (flagged as not available). Acquired-IPRD/impairment charges on acquired pipeline assets (Mirati/RayzeBio/Karuna-era): FY2024 $13.4bn, FY2025 $3.7bn (Orbital), Q2 2025 alone $1.5bn — both GAAP and non-GAAP, per company definition.
  • Net debt/EBITDA — a number that needs its own caveat: ratios.py computes 12.3x for FY2024, 2.26x for FY2025, 1.91x TTM. The 12.3x is an artefact of the FY2024 EBITDA denominator being crushed by the $13.4bn IPR&D charge, not a solvency signal — interest coverage that year (EBIT/interest −3.3x) was likewise negative for the same one-off reason and had fully recovered to 5.9x (FY25) / 7.9x (TTM) within a year. The real, current trend is genuine and positive: long-term debt down from $49.4bn (FY23) to $47.6bn (FY24) to $42.9bn (FY25) to $42.1bn (Q2'26), with $1.7bn of long-term debt repaid in H1 2026 alone.
  • Capex/depreciation persistently <0.5x (flagged by ratios.py as a quality warning in all 3 periods tested) — but "depreciation" here is dominated by non-cash acquired-intangible amortization (e.g., $8.9bn of FY2024's $9.6bn total D&A), not physical-asset depreciation; capex of ~$1.2–1.3bn/yr against a $7.1–7.8bn PP&E base (~17%) is not, on its own, evidence of under-investment in manufacturing capacity.
  • M&A / financing: Orbital Therapeutics acquisition closed Q4 2025 (cash cost not separately isolated in sourced filings — flagged not available); no buybacks in FY2024–FY2026 YTD; dividends $5.045bn FY2025 (+3.7% YoY), $2.57bn H1'26; quarterly dividend raised to $0.63/share (17th consecutive annual increase) effective the Feb 2026 declaration.
  • Share count: basic shares outstanding rose from 2,022M (Feb 2024) to 2,043M (Jul 2026), +1.0%, consistent with zero buybacks and modest stock-comp issuance — a mild, not material, dilution drag.
