7. Valuation snapshot (valuation.py, TTM basis, price $62.86 as of 2026-09-25)

Trailing P/E 13.9x (matches the prelim snapshot's 13.85x almost exactly); NTM P/E ~9.4–9.6x per the quant snapshot (not independently recomputed). EV/EBITDA 9.6x, EV/EBIT 11.8x — both inside the sector playbook's 8–13x historical range for developed-market innovator pharma, i.e., not cheap relative to its own sub-sector, only relative to the broader market. FCF yield: 8.9% (FCF/market cap) or 7.1% (FCF/EV) on TTM FCF — both above the prelim snapshot's 6.3%, a data conflict worth flagging (possibly the snapshot uses a forward/NTM FCF estimate rather than trailing-actual, which given the declining FCF trend in §6 would plausibly be lower — not reconciled this session). Dividend yield 4.0%, payout ratio 57.7% (TTM) / 79.1% (FY2025) — well covered, consistent with the prelim snapshot's ~55%. Reverse-DCF (7.5% WACC, 1% terminal growth): today's price implies ≈−0.3% FCF growth for 10 years — the market is pricing BMS as flat-to-declining, not for the growth-portfolio inflection bulls expect. A forward DCF using a modest 2% stage-1 growth assumption (same WACC) implies $79/share (+26%), showing the thesis is sensitive to even small positive growth assumptions — but a probability-weighted scenario view (Bear 30%: $44 / Base 45%: $65.60 / Bull 25%: $86.40) lands at $64.30, only +2.3% above spot — a fair-value, not a bargain, once bear-case LOE/pipeline risk is weighted in. Peer context (general market positioning, not independently pulled this session due to FMP rate limits): MRK and PFE also trade at depressed multiples on their own patent-cliff exposure (PFE dividend yield ~6.2–6.5%, MRK ~3.4%); ABBV trades at a premium (mid-teens forward P/E, ~3.25% yield) on stronger post-Humira growth execution — BMS's ~9–14x multiple and 4% yield sit between the two groups.

Valuation reconciliation with V1 (added 2026-09-26): V1 rates BMY "attractive" (score 1.0, the maximum), driven mainly by NTM P/E (9.43x) sitting at the 0th percentile of its own ~12-year history and a base-case 3-year annualized return of +17.95% — which requires the exit multiple to expand from today's ~9.4x to about 24.9x and implies a 3-year price (~$95.69) that V1's own street-flag notes "exceeds Street 12m high target" ($82; mean $66.71, low $40). This dossier's own reverse-DCF above (7.5% WACC) shows only ≈−0.3%/yr FCF growth priced in over 10 years, and its probability-weighted scenario (Bear 30%: $44 / Base 45%: $65.60 / Bull 25%: $86.40) centers on $64.30 — "only +2.3% above spot… a fair-value, not a bargain" — sitting inside the Street's own $40–82 range and close to its $66.71 mean. This dossier's "fair, not a bargain" read is better supported: it does not require the large multiple re-rating V1's base case assumes, and it is corroborated by company-specific facts V1's ratio-based score does not see — a FY2025 non-GAAP EPS miss against BMS's own raised guidance (§5) and a 23.4% H1 2026 operating-cash-flow decline the 10-Q itself attributes to the Eliquis Medicare price cut (§6). V1's cheap-on-a-ratio signal is real (§3), but its "attractive" verdict is substantially a re-rating bet that this dossier's own numbers do not support.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) Growth Portfolio is real and broad-based, not one drug: Breyanzi +82% FY25, Camzyos +77%, Reblozyl +31%, Opdualag +28%, Opdivo Qvantig (subcutaneous, LOE-defense reformulation) scaled from ~$0 to $238M FY2025 in one year — this is genuine multi-product execution, not a single bet. (2) Balance sheet is genuinely deleveraging (LT debt −$7.5bn since FY2023) while still funding a growing, well-covered dividend (4% yield, 17 consecutive annual increases). (3) Despite a 56% Medicare price cut taking effect Jan 2026, Eliquis revenue is still growing double digits and FY2026 growth guidance was raised, not cut — the single biggest headline policy risk has not (yet) broken the franchise. Bear: (1) FY2025 non-GAAP EPS missed BMS's own most-recently-reissued guidance range once a Q4 M&A charge landed — the guidance "raises" investors cite structurally exclude the next dilutive deal, which recurred once already. (2) OCF is down 23% H1-over-H1 and BMS's own 10-Q says this is "primarily" the Eliquis price cut — a real, quantified, ongoing cash-flow headwind that the revenue-growth headline obscures. (3) The single largest near-term de-risking catalyst for the growth portfolio's terminal narrative — Cobenfy's Phase 3 ADEPT-2 readout in Alzheimer's-disease psychosis — has been delayed from a planned H2 2026 readout to "beginning early 2027" after the company disclosed clinical-trial-execution irregularities at a small number of sites and re-opened enrollment (BMS press release, 2025-12-03; corroborated by trade press).

9. Key risks & kill criteria (thesis-invalidation triggers)

The INCLUDE-SMALL thesis above is invalidated if any of the following observable, time-bound conditions are met: 1. Legacy-drag overtakes Growth-Portfolio offset again: consolidated quarterly revenue growth turns negative for two consecutive quarters (it was +5.7% in Q2'26; watch this reverse). 2. OCF decline persists into H2 2026: if Q3/Q4 2026 OCF is also down YoY, the Eliquis cash-flow impact is structural, not a one-time H1 dip. 3. FY2026 non-GAAP EPS misses the raised $6.75–$7.00 range when reported (~Feb 2027) — would confirm a second consecutive year of the "guidance excludes the next deal charge" pattern. 4. Cobenfy ADEPT (Alzheimer's-psychosis) data, now expected "beginning early 2027," reads out negative or slips again — removes the clearest near-term catalyst for the growth-portfolio bull case. 5. Net debt/EBITDA (GAAP) rises back above ~3x (from ~1.9x now), e.g., from a large new debt-funded deal — would reverse the one clearly positive, unambiguous trend in this file. 6. Dividend held flat or cut, breaking the 17-year increase streak — payout ratio (58–79%) leaves some room but is not undemanding against a shrinking Legacy base.

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: 2026-10-29 (Q3 2026).
  • Cobenfy ADEPT-1/-2/-3 (Alzheimer's-disease psychosis) Phase 3 data: now expected beginning early 2027, spread across the year (delayed from H2 2026 after site-level trial-execution irregularities; BMS press release 2025-12-03).
  • IRA second negotiation cycle: Orencia selected (Jan 2026) for Medicare price negotiation, new price effective 2028; Pomalyst's own MFP (already negotiated) takes effect 2027-01-01.
  • Eliquis EU composition-of-matter patent/SPC expiry November 2026 (generics already selling at-risk in UK/Finland following adverse court rulings); US settlement-based generic entry 2028. Opdivo (nivolumab) US COM-patent-based minimum exclusivity date 2028, EU 2030.
  • Revlimid: all remaining US volume caps (Natco/Dr. Reddy's/Alvogen) ended 2026-01-31 — already in the FY2025/H1'26 numbers above (WW Revlimid revenue down 49–63% YoY every quarter shown).
  • U.S. Government Agreement (announced Dec 2025): tariff relief and protection from new U.S. pricing mandates through January 2029, in exchange for free Eliquis to Medicaid, ~80%-off cash-pay discounts on several other products, and continued domestic production commitments — does not affect the Eliquis/Pomalyst/Orencia negotiations already under way.

11. Red-flag scan

  • Auditor: Deloitte & Touche LLP — no indication of recent auditor change; unqualified opinion on both financial statements and internal controls found in the FY2025 10-K; no material-weakness or going-concern language found.
  • CVR (Contingent Value Rights) litigation — confirmed active: shareholders (as successor trustee to the 2019 Celgene-merger CVR agreement) allege BMS failed to use "diligent efforts" to secure timely FDA approvals (incl. liso-cel/Breyanzi) that would have triggered CVR payouts. Procedural status as of the Q2 2026 10-Q: the court found the plaintiff to be the successor trustee (Dec 2025) but dismissed 2 of 5 claims; in May 2026 the court stayed proceedings on related crossclaims pending final resolution of trustee identity. No trial date has been scheduled. Ongoing overhang, not imminent.
  • IRA constitutional challenge — exhausted, BMS lost: BMS's suit challenging the IRA drug-pricing-negotiation program's constitutionality lost at the district court, lost on appeal at the Third Circuit (Sept 2025), and the Supreme Court denied certiorari in May 2026 — this legal avenue is now closed.
  • Revlimid/Celgene antitrust: legacy class actions (from a 2014 filing, largely settled 2020) continue via opt-out-plaintiff suits and a separate Sept-2023 SDNY class action; motions to dismiss were pending as of the Feb 2026 10-K. Long-running, disclosed for years, not a new development.
  • Insider trading (partial check — FMP insiderTrades was plan-gated; cross-checked via SEC EDGAR filing-date listing + secondary aggregator transaction detail, not a full systematic tally): CFO David Elkins sold 30,000 shares 2026-04-01 under a Rule 10b5-1 pre-arranged plan; Chief Medical Officer sold 6,249 shares 2026-09-09; CEO Boerner's Form 4 activity sampled was mostly equity-award vesting/tax-withholding, and at least one dated open-market purchase by the CEO was reported by a secondary aggregator (not independently re-verified against the primary Form 4). No alarming concentrated-selling pattern found, but this was not an exhaustive multi-quarter tally.
  • No going-concern, restatement, or SEC/DOJ enforcement-action disclosure found in the reviewed 10-K/10-Q legal-proceedings and internal-controls sections.

dossiers.BR:
BR — Broadridge Financial Solutions, Inc.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE — thesis horizon 12–36 months. A ~90%-recurring-revenue processor of proxy voting, mutual-fund/annual-meeting communications and multi-asset trading/post-trade technology, compounding recurring revenue at high-single digits and adjusted EPS at low-double digits for a decade, trading at 15.2x NTM P/E and a 6.3% FCF yield — a valuation that (on a conservative reverse DCF) prices in only ~2.9%/year 10-year FCF growth against a company that has never grown FCF that slowly and has just guided to another year of 6–8% recurring-revenue / 8–12% adjusted-EPS growth. Four straight quarters of raised guidance in FY2026, a clean balance sheet (net debt/EBITDA ≈1.7x), and a 14th double-digit dividend increase in 15 years support the quantitative "cheap growth compounder" read from the triage. The reservation that keeps this from a larger weighting: BR's own recurring-revenue growth is itself decelerating on a multi-year view (FY24 +6.6%, FY25 +5.9%, FY26 +8% cc — noisy, not a clean trend) and a portion of FY2026's growth and cash flow was flattered by non-recurring digital-asset mark-to-market gains that will not repeat every year.

2. Business in plain English

Broadridge is the plumbing behind shareholder democracy and a large piece of the back office of Wall Street. When a public company or mutual fund needs to send proxy materials and collect votes from millions of retail and institutional shareholders, Broadridge does it — its ProxyEdge platform handles the vote processing for the large majority of US institutional share volume. That is the Investor Communication Solutions (ICS) segment ($5,561m of FY2026's $7,477m revenue, 74%). The Global Technology and Operations (GTO) segment ($1,916m, 26%) sells outsourced technology and operations platforms — trading, clearing, wealth/investment-management middle- and back-office systems — to banks and broker-dealers, recently expanded via the CQG acquisition (multi-asset futures/options execution and connectivity, completed 1 May 2026) into global futures/options trading infrastructure. Both businesses monetize on long-term, multi-year contracts with high switching costs (a bank does not re-platform its clearing operations casually), which is the source of the ~90%+ recurring-revenue mix.

3. Why the model likes it — and is it durable?

B1 composite is upper-mid (live_rank 223/~2,300, decile 6, quintile 3; composite 0.553). Family drivers: Value (fam_V ≈0.81, very high) — cheap on earnings yield, FCF yield and EBIT/EV; Quality (fam_Q ≈0.71, high) — strong gross-profit/assets and ROE (39.6%); Momentum (fam_M ≈0.12, weak) — the stock has not re-rated (12-month price momentum is actually negative, mom_12_1 ≈ −0.22), consistent with the triage's "22% pullback" framing; Earnings momentum (fam_S ≈0.46, average).

Durability check: the value signal is corroborated by four consecutive quarters of guidance raises through FY2026 (see §5) built on real, filed-and-verified operating results (recurring revenue growth, closed sales, adjusted margin), not an accounting artefact. The weak momentum is the honest counterweight — the market has not yet rewarded the beat-and-raise pattern, which is exactly the "genuine mispricing" the triage flagged. One durability caveat the model cannot see: FY2026 GAAP net income and free cash flow benefited from a $227m full-year gain on digital-asset holdings (offset by an $11m Q4 non-cash loss) related to Broadridge's tokenization/blockchain initiatives — a real but non-operating, mark-to-market item that inflated the reported growth rate this year and should not be extrapolated.

4. Last two years of results (SEC 10-Q/10-K, GAAP unless noted; fiscal year ends 30 June)

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • FCF conversion: company-reported FY2026 free cash flow $1,233m against GAAP net income $1,124.3m — conversion >100%, consistent with the FY2027 guide of ">100% FCF conversion." Genuinely strong, low-capex model (capex only $32.1m in Q4, ~1.4% of quarterly revenue).

  • GAAP vs adjusted: adjusted EPS excludes amortization of acquired intangibles and acquisition/integration costs; FY2026's GAAP-adjusted convergence at $9.60 (noted in §4) is the one unresolved data conflict in this dossier.

  • Net debt/leverage: total debt $3,520.5m, cash $402.9m (at FYE) → net debt ≈$3.12bn against TTM EBITDA $1,809m = net debt/EBITDA ≈1.7x — comfortably investment-grade, no covenant stress evident.
  • Capital allocation: FY2026 buybacks $250.8m (Q4) after $150.5m (Q1) and $130.7m (prior-year Q4); dividend raised 12% to $4.36/share annualized — the company states this is the 14th double-digit dividend increase in the past 15 years, a genuinely long, verifiable track record. New $1.5bn buyback authorization announced with Q4 results.
  • M&A: CQG (futures/options execution and market connectivity) completed 1 May 2026; deal size not disclosed, explicitly stated by the company as not expected to be material to results — a bolt-on, not a bet-the-company deal.

7. Valuation snapshot — no V1 row; own reverse DCF

No systematic V1 valuation row exists for BR (v1_valuation_table.csv/v1_valuation.json cover a different 92-name subset); v1_verdict is null in the summary JSON per program convention.

Quant snapshot (d4, as of 2026-09-25 close $163.77): NTM P/E 15.17x (calendarised, pe_ntm), TTM FCF yield 6.3%, EV/EBITDA ≈12.0x (EV $21,663m / EBITDA $1,809m). Consensus targets: mean $213.38, range $176–250 (8 analysts, "buy" average rating).

Own reverse DCF (10-year explicit FCF growth + 2.5% terminal growth, 8.5% discount rate — a mid-single-digit spread over the 10-year Treasury, appropriate for a low-beta, investment-grade recurring-revenue business): solving EV = $21,663m for a constant annual FCF growth rate on a $1,233m (FY2026 company-reported) FCF base implies ≈2.9%/year for ten years. This is far below every base-case growth reference available: FY2027 guidance alone calls for 6–8% recurring-revenue growth and 8–12% adjusted-EPS growth, and BR has not grown revenue as slowly as 2.9%/year in any of the last ten fiscal years.

Bear/base/bull cases (own construction, 3-year horizon, exit-multiple method): - Bear: adjusted EPS growth slows to 4%/year (a macro/event-driven-revenue air-pocket; ICS event-driven revenue is genuinely cyclical), exit multiple compresses to 12x NTM (below the current 15.2x, reflecting a growth scare) → EPS ≈$12.15, price ≈$145.8, annualised total return ≈−1.0% including dividends. - Base: adjusted EPS growth 10%/year (midpoint of the FY2027 8–12% guide, consistent with FY2026's delivered 12%), exit multiple flat at 15x (no re-rating credit taken) → EPS ≈$14.37, price ≈$215.6, annualised total return ≈+11.8%. - Bull: adjusted EPS growth 13%/year (top of range plus CQG/tokenization upside), exit multiple re-rates to 18x (closer to Broadridge's historical average multiple, rewarding four years of consecutive delivery) → EPS ≈$15.58, price ≈$280.5, annualised total return ≈+21.5%.

valuation_view_vs_v1 / consistency: dossier view = cheap. The implied 10-year growth (2.9%) sits well below my own base case (10%/year), which is the INCLUDE test this program requires: the market is not paying for the growth the evidence-based base case expects the company to deliver.

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull (3): 1. Four consecutive FY2026 quarters of guidance raises that were still exceeded at year-end (delivered 8% recurring-revenue growth and 12% adjusted-EPS growth, both at or above every range issued during the year) — a rare, clean, filed-and-verified beat-and-raise record. 2. >100% FCF conversion, net debt/EBITDA ≈1.7x, and a 14-of-15-year streak of double-digit dividend increases — a genuinely shareholder-friendly, low-risk capital-allocation record that funds bolt-on M&A (CQG) without straining the balance sheet. 3. High-switching-cost, regulatorily-anchored recurring revenue (proxy voting/vote-processing scale, multi-year bank/broker outsourcing contracts) gives real visibility into the FY2027 guide, and tokenization/digital-asset initiatives (mutual-fund/repo infrastructure) are a disclosed, early-stage option not embedded in the base case.

Bear (3): 1. 12-month price momentum is negative (the stock has not rewarded the beat-and-raise pattern) — either the market is right to discount recurring-revenue growth that is itself decelerating on a multi-year view (FY24 +6.6% → FY25 +5.9% → FY26 +8%, a noisy rather than clean acceleration), or this is a genuine, durable mispricing; the base case in this dossier assumes the latter, which is a real judgment call, not a certainty. 2. A real, disclosed chunk of FY2026's reported growth was non-operating: a $227m full-year gain on digital-asset holdings inflated GAAP net income and cash flow, and the unexplained convergence of GAAP and adjusted EPS to exactly $9.60 for FY2026 is an unresolved data conflict this dossier could not fully reconcile from public disclosure alone. 3. ICS "event-driven" revenue (M&A/reorg communications, contested proxy contests) is inherently market-cycle-dependent — a sharp slowdown in corporate-action volume would hit the segment that carries the bulk of BR's revenue and margin, and is the most plausible mechanism for the bear case above.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable) -- signposts that would change our verdict

  1. Recurring-revenue growth (constant currency) falls below 5% for two consecutive quarters (below the low end of every guidance range issued in FY2026/FY2027).
  2. Adjusted EPS growth guidance is cut versus the immediately prior quarter's range (zero cuts to date across FY2026's four releases).
  3. Net debt/EBITDA rises above 3.0x (from ≈1.7x currently) absent a disclosed, board-approved acquisition financing plan.
  4. Full-year FCF conversion (FCF/net income) falls below 90% for a full fiscal year (FY2026: >100%).
  5. Digital-asset/tokenization mark-to-market losses exceed $50 million in any single quarter (Q4 FY26: −$11m), which would signal the strategic initiative is a source of earnings volatility rather than a disclosed side item.

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: Q1 FY2027 results, 2026-11-03 (per d4 snapshot; company's historical Q1 report date is early November).
  • FY2027 guidance execution (6–8% recurring-revenue growth, 8–12% adjusted-EPS growth, $290–330m closed sales) — first checkpoint at Q1 FY27 results.
  • CQG integration progress (completed 2026-05-01) and any further bolt-on M&A funded by the new $1.5bn buyback-and-M&A capacity.
  • Annual-meeting/proxy season (concentrated Q3–Q4 fiscal, i.e., Jan–Jun calendar) — the primary driver of BR's structural revenue seasonality.

11. Red-flag scan

  • Litigation: management estimates an aggregate range of reasonably possible losses for ordinary-course litigation matters of up to $5.0 million in excess of established reserves (per FY2026 filings) — immaterial relative to BR's scale ($7.5bn revenue). dossiers.BRO:
BRO — Brown & Brown, Inc. — Diligence Dossier (Agent F40, standard depth)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight), reservation stated explicitly: organic revenue growth just turned negative (Q2-26: −0.7%) after decelerating for five straight quarters, and leverage roughly tripled to fund the Accession deal. Valuation is not demanding, but the growth thesis triage relied on ("32% revenue growth, 54% EPS growth") does not survive a GAAP/organic check. Horizon: 12–24 months; revisit for full weight once organic growth re-stabilises at ≥3%.

2. Business in plain English

Brown & Brown is an insurance broker/wholesaler — it doesn't take underwriting risk, it earns commissions and fees placing property-casualty, employee-benefits and specialty (E&S) insurance for businesses and individuals through four segments (Retail, Programs, Wholesale Brokerage/Specialty Distribution, and now the newly-acquired Accession/National Programs businesses). It grows by winning new accounts, raising rates/exposure with existing clients ("organic"), and buying smaller brokers ("bolt-on M&A") — plus, since August 2025, one very large acquisition.

3. Why the model likes it — and why that's now an artefact, not durable

b1/triage liked BRO for "32% revenue growth and 54% EPS growth at 12.8x forward." That headline growth is not organic — it is the consolidation of Accession Risk Management Group (parent of Risk Strategies), acquired for a $9.825bn gross, cash-and-debt-free price, closed August 1, 2025 (Brown & Brown 8-K/press release; Holland & Knight deal summary). Financed with ~$4.3bn of new equity (42.16M shares at $102, June 2025) and ~$4.2bn of senior notes. Stripping the deal out: organic revenue growth has decelerated every quarter since Q1-25 — +6.5% (Q1-25) → +3.6% (Q2-25) → +3.5% (Q3-25) → flat (Q1-26) → −0.7% (Q2-26), per Brown & Brown's own press releases (investor.bbrown.com). GAAP diluted EPS has been flat-to-down YoY in three of the last five quarters (Q2-25 −10%, Q3-25 −16%, Q2-26 +7.7% but off a much larger diluted share base) because acquisition financing (interest expense, intangible amortization, +18% more diluted shares) outran GAAP net income growth; only the company's own adjusted EPS shows consistent growth (+15% Q3-25, +7.8% Q1-26, +3.9% Q2-26 — itself decelerating). The triage's "54% EPS growth" figure is not supported by either GAAP or adjusted quarterly EPS in the SEC filings checked this session — treat it as an error or a stale/mismatched comparison.

4. Last two years of results (GAAP; adjusted diluted EPS "Adj." where disclosed by the company)

5. Guidance track record

Brown & Brown does not issue formal quantitative revenue/EPS guidance — only qualitative commentary, which I track like guidance: at Q4-25 (Feb-26) management said it "expects improved organic performance in 2026" and flagged a 2026 headwind from lower investment income. That expectation was not met — Q1-26 organic was flat and Q2-26 organic went negative. At Q3-25 (Oct-25), management guided Q4 Specialty Distribution organic to "decline mid-single digits" and Retail organic "similar to 2.7%"; full FY25 organic came in at 2.8%, roughly as flagged. Net: the company's near-term qualitative calls have been reasonably accurate on the segment mechanics but the "improved 2026" framing has so far been wrong.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

FCF (OCF − capex, TTM Q3'25–Q2'26) ≈ $1.45bn vs GAAP NI $1.2bn (≈1.2x conversion) — but BRO's OCF includes swings in fiduciary/premium funds held on behalf of insurers and clients, which can inflate or deflate reported OCF independent of underlying economics; treat this FCF figure as directional, not precise. SBC ≈$49M in H1-26 (~1.4% of revenue) — modest. Leverage jumped materially: long-term debt $3.60bn (year-end 2024) → $7.35bn (Q2-26); net debt (LT+ST debt − cash) ≈ $6.84bn, versus TTM adjusted EBITDAC roughly $2.5bn → net debt/EBITDAC ≈ 2.8x, up from well under 1x pre-deal. Diluted share count rose from ~284M (2024) to ~335M (Q2-26), an ~18% increase, funding part of the Accession purchase price. This is the central balance-sheet fact of the thesis: BRO took on real financial risk to buy growth that has not yet shown up organically.

7. Valuation snapshot (no V1 row exists for BRO — independent reverse DCF/cross-checks)

No systematic V1 valuation exists for BRO this cycle (not in v1_valuation_table.csv/v1_valuation.json); v1_verdict is therefore null and the check below is this dossier's own. - FCFF reverse DCF (EV0 = mkt cap $20.35bn + net debt $6.84bn = $27.19bn; TTM FCF $1.45bn; WACC ≈7.4% [beta ~0.8, rf 5.17%, ERP 4.14%, post-tax cost of debt ~4.0%, D/EV 25%]; 10y fade to 3% terminal) implies ≈0.3%/yr FCF growth priced in — i.e., the market is assuming almost no growth. Caveat: FCF0 is noisy (fiduciary-cash swings, and only ~11 months of Accession contribution at a still-ramping run-rate), so this likely understates true normalized FCF and therefore overstates how cheap BRO looks; treat as a soft lower bound, not a precise number. - Cross-check, multiples: TTM adjusted P/E ≈13.8x vs BRO's own trailing-10-year average of ~24x (SimplyWallSt secondary-source estimate) and vs peer Arthur J. Gallagher's ~28.5x forward P/E (Q1-26). Zacks consensus has BRO's 2026 EPS growth at +16.4% YoY, well above what either cross-check says the market is paying for. - Read: both methods agree the stock is not priced for the deceleration risk in §3 — it is priced for far less growth than sell-side consensus or BRO's own acquisition algorithm assumes. That is either a real margin of safety or the market correctly discounting execution risk; the recent organic prints argue the market may be right to be cautious, hence INCLUDE-SMALL rather than full INCLUDE.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) $9.8bn Accession deal materially expands scale and diversifies into new specialty/programs niches; management reaffirms $30–40M of FY26 synergies on track; (2) valuation (13–14x adjusted TTM P/E) is a large discount to its own history and to AJG, pricing in almost no growth; (3) 20+ year record of disciplined bolt-on M&A and margin management before this deal. Bear: (1) organic revenue is now negative — the "compounder" story requires this to reverse, and two straight quarters (flat, then −0.7%) argue the deceleration is not noise; (2) net debt/EBITDAC near 2.8x (from <1x) removes balance-sheet flexibility right as organic growth weakens; (3) $18M of Q2-26 revenue was lost to litigation tied to producers departing for a competing startup — a people-based business's key risk (retention) made visible.

9. Kill criteria

  1. Organic revenue growth negative for 3+ consecutive quarters (1 of 3 so far: Q2-26).
  2. Net debt / adjusted EBITDAC exceeds 3.5x (currently ≈2.8x).
  3. Adjusted EBITDAC margin contracts >150bps YoY for two consecutive quarters (Q2-26 was already −100bps YoY).
  4. Accession-segment synergies fall short of the disclosed $30–40M FY26 target.
  5. Additional material producer/team departures or adverse non-compete litigation rulings beyond the $18M already disclosed.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: October 26, 2026 (Q3-26; per company-earnings-calendar aggregators — not independently confirmed against an IR press release this session, flagged as an estimate).

11. Red-flag scan

  • M&A/financing: $9.825bn acquisition financed with $4.3bn new equity + $4.2bn senior notes (Jun-2025) plus a $300M revolver draw (Q3-25) — the single largest capital event in company history; integration risk is real and not yet fully proven.
  • Litigation: producers/staff departing for a startup competitor caused an $18M Q2-26 revenue reduction — an unusual, named litigation-driven revenue impact.
  • Insider activity: the one Form 4 found this session (director J. Hunt, Sept 2026) was a gift transaction (5,000 shares to a family trust), not an open-market sale — no material insider-selling pattern identified in the time available; this is a limited scan and should not be read as a clean bill of health.
  • No auditor change, no going-concern language, no disclosed pending additional acquisitions of similar scale.

12. Data basis, recency and disclaimer

GAAP figures are labelled GAAP; Brown & Brown's own "Adjusted"/EBITDAC figures are labelled Adj. throughout and are non-GAAP company measures. This is research, not personalized investment advice.

Boston Scientific Corporation (NYSE: BSX) — Diligence Dossier

Agent: F24 | As of: 2026-09-25 close ($43.92) | Depth: Standard

1. Verdict

WATCH — 12-month horizon before re-underwriting. This overturns the triage's INCLUDE-leaning framing ("best-in-class... broad-based double-digit growth," 13x NTM P/E vs "~38% street upside"). The 13x multiple is real, but it reflects two 2026 guidance cuts driven by genuine competitive share loss (electrophysiology, Watchman), not merely sentiment, and the business is now mid-recovery from an August 2026 cyberattack whose Q3/FY financial impact the company itself says it cannot yet quantify. Valuation alone does not resolve an open operational question; the Oct 28, 2026 print (Q3 + reset guidance) is the next real evidence point.

2. Business

Boston Scientific makes medical devices across cardiology (drug-eluting stents, Watchman left-atrial-appendage closure, Farapulse pulsed-field ablation for AFib), urology, endoscopy, neuromodulation and peripheral interventions, sold to hospitals worldwide. It competes chiefly with Medtronic, Abbott and Johnson & Johnson. Historically a share-taking double-digit organic grower via Watchman and Farapulse.

3. Why the model liked it, and is it durable

b1 factors ranked BSX on quality (gross profit/assets, ROCE) and momentum-adjacent growth built when Watchman (+~30% in 2025) and Farapulse were compounding at 20%+. dossiers.BX:
Blackstone Inc. (BX) — Diligence Dossier (F22, standard depth)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Thesis horizon 24–36 months. Reason: the largest alternative-asset manager globally, compounding fee-related earnings faster than the price requires, but GAAP earnings are carry-driven and volatile, standalone leverage is rising, and the BREIT/BCRED nontraded-fund liquidity model — while currently healthy — has a proven capacity to break under stress, so a full-weight position is not warranted.

Thesis (≤25 words): As of the 2026-09-25 close (§7), the world's largest alternative-asset manager (private equity, credit, real estate, infrastructure per Q2-26 8-K) still raising ~$70bn a quarter (§4), priced below its own recent distributable-earnings growth rate.

2. Business in plain English

Per its Q2 2026 10-Q (period ended 2026-06-30) and 8-K earnings release (filed 2026-07-23), Blackstone manages $1.35tn of client capital across private equity, real estate, credit/insurance and infrastructure, earning management fees on committed/invested capital plus a share of investment profits ("carried interest") once funds clear a preferred return. It does not consolidate most of the funds it manages, so its own balance sheet is small relative to AUM; the moat (per the FY2025 10-K, filed 2026-02-27) is scale (largest fundraiser in most of its categories), long-dated/locked-up and increasingly permanent-capital vehicles (insurance/perpetual funds), and a 30+ year realization/track-record advantage with institutional LPs.

3. Why the model likes it / durability

b1 factors (v4/data/b1_live_scores.csv, as_of 2026-09-25): Quality 5, Growth 4, price_vs_growth 4; v4/outputs/Q04_triage.json cited 67% forward EPS growth at a 16.7x NTM multiple with negative 12-month momentum (−12.8%) as an entry point, and flagged the 2022–23 BREIT redemption-queue episode as a real, recurring liquidity-mismatch risk in Blackstone's retail/nontraded fund complex. This durability read is mostly organic: per the Q1-26/Q2-26 8-Ks, fee-earning AUM is up 8% YoY on real net inflows ($68–70bn/quarter, $262.5bn LTM per the same filings), not primarily M&A, which is a stronger quality signal than BlackRock's growth mix this cycle.

Realizations $35.9bn (Q1-26) and $31.8bn (Q2-26), $144.5bn LTM (per the same 8-Ks) — active monetization, a genuine cash-conversion signal for a carry-based model.

DE (cash-orientated, distribution-relevant) is the more meaningful earnings series for this business per the sector playbook; GAAP is cited here for completeness and comparability, not as the primary earnings measure.

5. Guidance track record

No formal quantitative guidance is given. Estimate revisions (d4, 2026-09-25): FY0 EPS +0.8% over 90 days but essentially flat/slightly negative FY1 (−0.8% over 90 days); mixed signal, not a clear raise or cut. Management commentary (Q2-26 release) emphasized "AI megatrend" positioning and record inflows rather than numeric targets.

6. Balance sheet & cash conversion

Consolidated GAAP assets/liabilities ($49.9bn/$27.5bn, Jun-26) are not meaningful for leverage analysis because they gross up consolidated funds/CLOs (sector playbook). The relevant figure is standalone long-term debt, which has risen from $11.5bn (Dec-24) to $13.3bn (Jun-26), +16% in six quarters, funding growth in the insurance/permanent-capital channel and buybacks. Per the Q2-25, Q1-26 and Q2-26 earnings releases: quarterly dividend raised from $1.03 (Q2-25) to $1.16 (Q1-26) to $1.29 (Q2-26), a payout ratio of ~85% of DE/share — high, leaving little cushion if DE dips. H1-26 GAAP operating cash flow $2.93bn against H1-26 GAAP net income of ~$1.88bn (OCF exceeds NI, a reasonable cash-conversion signal, though both are noisy at the consolidated level per the sector methodology). Dividend yield ~4.5% (Yahoo/d4).

7. Valuation snapshot & reverse DCF

Price (2026-09-25 close) $118.42; NTM P/E 16.7x (d4, calendarised); FY1 consensus EPS growth 24.4%; analyst mean target $144.38 (+21.9%). No V1 row exists for BX → v1_verdict = null; valuation view independently derived here.

Reverse DCF: 10-year explicit growth + Gordon terminal (r = 11.5% cost of equity [rf 4.2% + beta ~1.5 × 5% ERP, reflecting carry cyclicality], terminal growth 3.5%), solved against NTM EPS $7.09 (consensus, broadly DE-like) and the current price gives implied 10-year growth ≈ 8.2% p.a. My evidence-based base case for DE/share growth is ~11% p.a. (continued double-digit fundraising, fee-earning AUM growth, operating leverage, and expanding permanent-capital/insurance channel), i.e. above the implied rate → valuation view = cheap-to-fair. Bear case 4% (fundraising slowdown, credit-spread compression hurting the private-credit book, real estate stays weak); bull case 17% (AI-driven data-center/infrastructure capex financing supercycle, insurance-channel scaling).

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) private-credit and infrastructure fundraising is structurally scaling as banks retreat and AI capex needs financing; (2) realizations ($144.5bn LTM) show the portfolio can actually monetize, not just mark up; (3) a growing permanent-capital/insurance base (per the sector playbook, the highest-quality alternative-manager earnings) reduces reliance on episodic fundraising cycles. Bear: (1) BREIT/BCRED-style nontraded vehicles have already broken once (2022–23 BREIT gating) and remain a structural liquidity mismatch — repurchase requests being "fully met" today is a point-in-time fact, not a guarantee; (2) an 85% DE payout ratio combined with rising standalone debt leaves less room to defend the dividend in a carry-light year; (3) GAAP earnings volatility (see §4) makes headline "EPS growth" numbers easy to misread without the DE/FRE reconciliation.

9. Key risks & measurable kill criteria

  1. Fee-earning AUM net inflows turn negative for two consecutive quarters.
  2. DE/share declines YoY for two consecutive quarters (last two: +12–26% YoY — a reversal would be a material trend break).
  3. Any nontraded vehicle (BREIT, BCRED, or successors) reinstates repurchase gating/proration for more than one quarter.
  4. Standalone long-term debt/FRE exceeds roughly 3.0x (monitor against current ~$13.3bn debt vs. run-rate FRE).
  5. Dividend cut or suspension (current payout ratio ~85% of DE leaves little room; a cut would signal a genuine earnings problem, not just prudence).

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 2026-10-22 (Q3-26, per d4 next_earnings_date). Watch fundraising updates for the next infrastructure/credit flagship fund closes and any BREIT/BCRED repurchase-plan commentary.

11. Red-flag scan

No auditor change, restatement or going-concern language found for Blackstone Inc. itself. BREIT (Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust): full repurchase requests satisfied in Q1 and Q2 2026, fundraising ($1.2bn Q1-26, +44% YoY) now outpacing repurchases for the first time since the 2022–23 crisis — a genuine improvement, not yet a multi-year track record. BCRED (private-credit vehicle) has also used repurchase-plan caps historically; no new SEC investigation or lawsuit specific to BX/BCRED found in this search cycle. No disqualifying legal or accounting red flags identified within the time box.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE. Thesis horizon 18–36 months. One-sentence reason: a thin-margin, oligopoly drug distributor with a four-quarter, no-cuts, beat-and-raise guidance record, a real (if early) higher-margin diversification (10.4% segment margin in "Other" vs 1.2% in core Pharma), and a reverse DCF that prices in roughly flat-to-negative 10-year growth — well below what the evidence supports — against real, disclosed opioid-liability and goodwill-impairment red flags that are sized and monitorable, not thesis-breaking.

2. Business in plain English

Cardinal Health is one of three companies (with Cencora/COR and McKesson) that distribute the large majority of branded and generic prescription drugs to US pharmacies, hospitals and clinics — an oligopoly with structurally thin (~1–2%) distribution margins earned on volume and working-capital efficiency, not pricing power. Alongside that core Pharmaceutical and Specialty Solutions business, it runs Global Medical Products and Distribution (GMPD: medical/surgical products, own-brand Cardinal Health products) and a faster-growing, higher-margin "Other" segment built via acquisition (Nuclear & Precision Health Solutions/oncology and urology physician-practice platforms, at-Home Solutions medical supplies, OptiFreight Logistics freight brokerage). Competitive position rests on scale, distribution infrastructure and long-term contracts with drug manufacturers and providers.

3. Why the model likes it, and whether that's durable

Triage flagged 23% street-target upside, buyback-driven EPS growth and steady volume growth, with the historical opioid litigation as the only red flag (already reflected in financials). That is largely confirmed and is durable: adjusted diluted EPS guidance for FY2026 was raised at all four quarterly releases in the year (see §5), and the raises were not driven only by the one-off IEEPA tariff-refund benefit recognized in Q4 (ex that benefit, FY2026 non-GAAP EPS still grew 33%). The "Other" segment's 10.4% margin (vs 1.19% Pharma, 2.03% GMPD) is a genuine mix shift, not an accounting artefact, funded by disclosed cash M&A (Solaris Health $1.9bn in FY2026; GI Alliance, ADS, Specialty Alliance, ION and Urology America named in the 10-K's intangible-asset note).   • FCF conversion: FY2026 OCF $5,174m vs GAAP net income $1,714m — OCF/NI 3.0x, but this is inflated by a large working-capital swing (accounts-payable timing typical of a distributor building GLP-1 inventory/AP) and includes the effect of $417m opioid-settlement cash payments already made. FCF (OCF − capex $649m) = $4,525m. Management's own FY2027 guide for "non-GAAP adjusted free cash flow" is $3.5bn–$4.0bn, materially below the FY2026 OCF-capex figure — treat FY2026 FCF as boosted by working-capital timing, not the run rate.
  • GAAP vs adjusted gap (FY2026, per the 10-K's own bridge, consolidated): GAAP diluted EPS $7.23 → non-GAAP $11.26. Reconciling items include: amortization and acquisition-related costs ($1.47/sh), acquisition-related cash/share-based comp ($1.16/sh), restructuring/severance ($0.34/sh), litigation recoveries net (−$0.04/sh net favorable), impairments/loss on asset disposal ($0.56/sh — this is where the Navista & ION goodwill impairment sits), and a state-opioid-assessment prior-year true-up (−$0.05/sh). The gap is large (56%) but each line is itemized and traceable to the 10-K table, not a single opaque "other" bucket.
  • Balance sheet leverage: total debt $8,886m (current $1,882m + long-term $7,004m, 10-K FY2026 balance sheet) vs cash $4,856m → net debt ≈ $4.0bn. Non-GAAP operating earnings $3,624m plus D&A gives approximate EBITDA in the $4.0–4.3bn range → net debt/EBITDA ≈ 1x, low leverage for the sector. Stockholders' equity is negative (−$2,883m at 2026-06-30), the mechanical result of buybacks exceeding retained cumulative earnings over many years — a known, disclosed feature of this business model (also true of peer COR), not a going-concern signal given the low net leverage and IG-typical debt profile.
  • Opioid litigation (the disclosed, quantified red flag): $4.3bn accrued at 2026-06-30 for the National Opioid Settlement Agreement and related claims; the company expects to pay the majority of the remainder through 2038; FY2026 cash payments were $417m, including the fifth annual $366m NOSA installment. This is a known, scheduled, already-accrued cash drag — not an open-ended contingency — but it is real and multi-decade.
  • Other legal/governance items: a Department of Justice Civil Investigative Demand (received Nov 2023, still open per the FY2026 10-K) concerning Anti-Kickback Statute/False Claims Act questions on a 2022 GPO and rheumatology-MSO transaction; company states it is cooperating. A shareholder Cooperation Agreement with Elliott Associates/Elliott International (Business Review Committee tasked with reviewing strategy, portfolio and capital allocation) expired in Q2 FY2025 — no ongoing activist standstill/board-seat overhang disclosed as of the FY2026 10-K.
  • Share count / capital return: FY2026 buybacks $1,358m (vs $765m FY25), dividends $491m with the per-share rate raised each quarter ($0.5107 vs $0.5056 a year earlier); weighted diluted shares fell from 242m (FY25) to 237m (FY26).

7. Valuation snapshot and reverse DCF

Price used: $220.22 (2026-09-25 close, d4 live snapshot). NTM P/E ≈17.0x (d4, calendarized), trailing P/E 30.4x (distorted by the low FY25 GAAP EPS base), FCF yield ≈9.3% (TTM basis — see the working-capital caveat in §6), sell-side mean target $270.94 (+23%, matching the triage note). No V1 row exists for CAH (v1_valuation_table.csv / v1_valuation.json have no CAH entry) — v1_verdict is null; this analyst's valuation view stands on its own.

Reverse DCF (2-stage, per-share, terminal growth 2.5%, FY2027 guided non-GAAP EPS midpoint $12.50 used as the starting owner-earnings proxy given the distributor's low capital intensity): at a WACC of 7.5–9.0% (appropriate for an IG-rated, low-beta, ~1x-levered distributor), the $220.22 price implies roughly −2.5% to +0.7% annualized 10-year earnings/FCF growth — i.e., the market is pricing this as a business that will barely grow, or shrink, over the next decade. That is far below what the evidence in §3–§5 supports (a four-quarter raise streak, FY2027 guide of +13–15%, and a genuinely higher-margin "Other" segment still scaling from a small base). Analyst base case: mid-to-high-single-digit (6–8%/yr) 10-year adjusted EPS/FCF growth (deceleration from the current mid-teens/high-30s pace as GLP-1 mix normalizes and M&A integration matures, partly offset by continued buybacks and Other-segment mix shift) — above the ~0–1% implied by the price. valuation_view_vs_v1.implied_vs_base = "below" (price implies less growth than the base case).

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull: (1) Four-for-four guidance raises in FY2026 and an FY2027 initial guide (+13–15%) already above the company's own long-term algorithm, with net debt/EBITDA near 1x giving ample buyback/M&A capacity. (2) The "Other" segment (10.4% margin, +26% revenue, +37% profit FY2026) is a real, executing diversification away from thin-margin core distribution, funded by disclosed, named acquisitions. (3) The reverse DCF shows the market paying for almost no growth in a business with a demonstrated growth and margin-mix track record — a real margin of safety if the growth continues even at a much slower pace than FY2026's.

Bear: (1) $4.3bn of opioid-settlement payments still owed through 2038 is a permanent claim on cash flow, and the DOJ CID (open since Nov 2023) could still produce an adverse outcome not yet accrued for. (2) The Navista & ION goodwill impairment ($184m, Q3 FY26) shows the M&A-funded diversification carries real execution/valuation risk, not a guaranteed payoff. (3) FY2026's cash generation was flattered by working-capital timing (OCF $5.17bn vs a guided FY2027 FCF of only $3.5–4.0bn) and a one-off tariff refund inflated the reported non-GAAP EPS growth rate — the "beat" narrative should be read on the ex-one-off, normalized-working-capital basis, which is still good but less dramatic than the headline.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Non-GAAP diluted EPS guidance is cut (vs. raised or maintained) at any quarterly release — breaks the core track record this thesis rests on.
  2. Consolidated net debt/EBITDA rises above 2.5x (from ≈1x today) without a value-accretive reason disclosed.
  3. A second goodwill/intangible impairment >$100m in the Other segment (Navista/ION/Solaris/GI Alliance/ADS platforms) within any four-quarter window.
  4. The DOJ Civil Investigative Demand (Anti-Kickback/False Claims Act, opened Nov 2023) converts to a filed complaint or a settlement exceeding $250m not previously accrued.
  5. "Other" segment margin falls below 8% for two consecutive quarters (loss of the diversification thesis's economics).

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: Q1 FY2027, expected ~2026-11-05 (d4 snapshot next_earnings_date; not yet confirmed by a company announcement as of this writing). Board Review Committee/Cooperation Agreement already expired (Q2 FY25) — no scheduled activist catalyst. Ongoing: further tuck-in M&A in the Other segment (pattern of quarterly small deals), continued buyback execution against the new $5.0bn authorization announced with Q4/FY26 results.

11. Red-flag scan

Opioid litigation: material and disclosed ($4.3bn accrued, payments through 2038) — not a surprise, already in the price and the balance sheet. DOJ CID open since Nov 2023 (Anti-Kickback/False Claims Act) — unresolved, not separately accrued as far as disclosed. Goodwill impairment in Navista & ION (Q3 FY26, $184m) — a genuine earnings-quality flag on recent M&A. Elliott shareholder Cooperation Agreement expired Q2 FY25 — governance overhang resolved, not ongoing. No auditor change, restatement or going-concern language identified in the FY2026 10-K sections reviewed. Insider Form-4 pattern and short-seller reports were not checked in this pass — disclosed gap, not asserted clean.

dossiers.CBRE:
CBRE Group, Inc. (CBRE) — Diligence Dossier (F32, standard depth)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Thesis horizon 12–36 months. One-sentence reason: the world's largest commercial-real-estate services firm is compounding earnings through a genuine leasing/infrastructure recovery at a price that is roughly fair (not obviously cheap) once the reverse DCF is done properly, and a growing UK fire-safety liability plus negative price momentum argue for a starter position rather than full weight.

Thesis (≤25 words): The world's largest commercial real-estate services firm, riding a leasing-market recovery and fast-growing data-center/infrastructure work, priced close to what it can actually deliver.

2. Business in plain English

CBRE advises, manages and invests in commercial real estate for corporate and institutional clients. It earns transaction commissions (Advisory: leasing and sales brokerage), recurring fees for running buildings and portfolios for clients (Building Operations & Experience, including a fast-growing "infrastructure/data-center services" line), fees for overseeing construction/fit-out projects (Project Management), and investment-management/development profits (Real Estate Investments, "REI"). It is asset-light — revenue scales with transaction volumes and square footage under management, not with owned property. Competitive position: #1 global commercial real-estate services franchise by revenue, ahead of JLL and Cushman & Wakefield, with particular scale advantages in outsourced facilities management and, increasingly, data-center/mission-critical infrastructure services.

3. Why the model likes it / durability

Triage (Q14_triage.json, as_of 2026-09-25) scored CBRE quality 4, growth 5, price_vs_growth 5 — the highest combination among wave-1 names — reasoning that "15% revenue growth, 16% ROE and low leverage at only 15x NTM P/E is a statistically compelling combination as commercial real estate transaction volumes recover." Data conflict to disclose: the pre-registered quant composite (b1_live_scores.csv) ranks CBRE near the bottom of the S&P 500 — decile 2, quintile 1, live_rank 427 of 503 — the opposite signal from triage. The gap is explainable and not a sign the fundamentals are weak: CBRE's quality percentiles are genuinely strong (gross-profit/assets pct 0.96, ROE pct 0.83), but (a) its 12-1-month price momentum is negative and in the bottom 12th percentile (raw −10.8%), and (b) its FCF-yield and EBIT/EV value percentiles are weak (26th and 22nd), because an asset-light services firm's enterprise value is mostly goodwill/intangibles and human capital rather than hard assets the value factors are calibrated for. So: the composite's poor rank reflects recent price weakness and a value-factor construction that fits CBRE's business model poorly, not a fundamental red flag — but the negative momentum itself is a real, current fact (the market has not yet rewarded the beat-and-raise pattern below), and is one reason for the half-weight sizing rather than full weight.

Four consecutive releases without a cut, and one outright beat of a just-raised range. 6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

FCF conversion: TTM operating cash flow ≈$1.36bn, TTM free cash flow ≈$1.7bn against TTM Core net income roughly ~$2.4bn (implied from Core EPS ~$7 × ~340m diluted shares) — FCF/Core-NI conversion is reasonable (~70%) but not full 1:1, consistent with an asset-light but working-capital-sensitive brokerage business (Q2'26 8-K ex-99.1). Capex is low (~$423m TTM) as expected for a services firm. Balance sheet is conservative: total debt $7.4bn, cash $1.5bn, net debt $5.9bn, net leverage 1.60x — comfortably investment-grade, with $4.4bn total liquidity. Share count: buybacks of ~$1.0bn YTD 2026 are shrinking the count, a genuine (not merely EPS-flattering) capital-return item given the low leverage. Adverse item, not a one-off: CBRE increased its reserve for fire-safety remediation at its UK (Telford) development business by $132m in Q4'25 and by a further $168m in Q2'26 — a cumulative ~$300m non-cash GAAP charge across two quarters that depressed GAAP (but not Core) EPS; this is a real, growing contingent liability that needs monitoring, not a pure accounting artefact.

7. Valuation snapshot & reverse DCF

Price (2026-09-25 close) $134.55; NTM P/E 15.4x (d4, calendarised); FY2026 P/E on the just-raised Core EPS guide midpoint ($7.85) ≈17.1x. FCF yield ≈4.2% (d4). No dividend (CBRE pays none; capital returned via buybacks only). Peer context: JLL and Cushman & Wakefield are not S&P 500 constituents and were not re-pulled this cycle; sell-side mean target $182.92 (+36% vs price, d4 target_mean, 2026-09-25) — the sell side is materially more bullish than my base case below. No V1 row exists for CBRE (v1_valuation_table.csv has no CBRE row) → v1_verdict = null; no systematic reconciliation is possible, so this dossier's valuation view is independently derived.

Reverse DCF: solving a 10-year explicit-growth + Gordon-terminal model for Core FCF (EV = market cap $38.96bn + net debt $5.9bn = $44.9bn; FCF₀ $1.7bn TTM; WACC 9.4% [cost of equity = rf 4.2% + β1.19×ERP 5% = 10.1%; post-tax cost of debt ≈4.5%; debt weight ≈13%]; terminal growth 3%) for the growth rate that reproduces today's EV gives implied 10-year FCF growth ≈9.6% p.a. My evidence-based base case is ~9–10% p.a.: mid-single-digit structural leasing/PM growth, a fast-growing (but smaller) infrastructure/data-center line, buyback-driven share shrinkage of ~2–3%/yr, offset by the brokerage business's known cyclicality (revenue fell in 2022–2023 when rates rose) and by management's own signal that 2027 growth ("at least 15%") is explicitly lower than 2026's ~23%. Implied (9.6%) is essentially in line with base case (9–10%) — not screaming cheap, but not overpaying either. Bear case 2%/yr (leasing recovery stalls or reverses, Telford liability keeps growing, exit P/E compresses to 13x — near 2022–23 trough multiples): 3-yr annualized return ≈ −7%. Base case 9.5%/yr, exit P/E 17x: ≈ +9%/yr. Bull case 15%/yr (matching management's own 2027 framework sustained, exit P/E re-rates to 19x as growth persists): ≈ +19%/yr.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) US office and industrial leasing activity keeps accelerating (Q2'26 US leasing +24%), a genuine multi-year recovery from a depressed 2023 base, not a one-quarter pop; (2) infrastructure/data-center services (+45% revenue in Q2'26) is a structurally growing, higher-margin annuity riding the same AI-capex wave benefiting EQIX/data-center landlords; (3) low leverage (1.6x) and an active buyback let management return capital and compound EPS even if the top line merely holds. Bear: (1) brokerage revenue is genuinely cyclical — it fell sharply in 2022–2023 as rates rose, and today's 15–19% growth is a snapback off a depressed base that management itself expects to slow (guided 2027 growth roughly a third of 2026's); (2) the UK Telford fire-safety reserve has grown twice in two quarters ($132m then $168m) with no stated ceiling — a real, open-ended contingent liability; (3) the Real Estate Investments segment's revenue is shrinking (−10.2% in Q2'26) even as its profit rose on asset-sale timing, meaning segment profit quality there is lumpy and not representative of a repeatable run-rate.

9. Key risks & measurable kill criteria

  1. Core EPS guidance cut (any reduction to the low end of the then-current full-year range) at a subsequent quarterly release.
  2. Advisory (brokerage) segment revenue growth turns negative for two consecutive quarters (the classic cyclical-downturn signal from 2022–2023).
  3. Cumulative UK Telford fire-safety reserve exceeds $500m (from ~$300m disclosed across Q4'25–Q2'26).
  4. Net leverage rises above 2.5x net debt/EBITDA (from 1.60x currently) without a stated de-leveraging plan.
  5. Share buybacks pause or reverse (net share count increases quarter over quarter) while Core EPS growth is decelerating.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 2026-10-22 (Q3'26, per d4 next_earnings_date). Watch for the pace of Q3 leasing/infrastructure growth against management's own "more than 20% Core EPS growth" Q3 guide and any update on the Telford reserve.

11. Red-flag scan

No auditor change, restatement, or going-concern language found in the filings reviewed. SEC enforcement history: in 2023 the SEC charged CBRE, Inc. (a subsidiary) with violating the whistleblower-protection rule — from 2011–2022 CBRE conditioned employee severance pay on a release attesting the employee had not filed a complaint with a federal agency; CBRE settled without admitting or denying findings, paying a $375,000 civil penalty and remediating its release language (SEC press release 2023-184; this is resolved, not an open matter, but disclosed for completeness). Ongoing item: the UK Telford fire-safety-remediation reserve (§6/§8) is real, growing, and open-ended in disclosed scope — the closest thing to an active red flag in this file. No insider Form 4 pattern or short-seller report was found in this cycle's search; this is a time-boxed limitation, not a clean bill of health.

CCI — Crown Castle Inc.

Most recent period incorporated: Q2 2026 10-Q (fiscal quarter ended 2026-06-30, filed 2026-08-05) and the Q2 2026 earnings release (8-K Ex-99.1, filed 2026-07-22). Also read the FY2025 10-K (period ended 2025-12-31, filed 2026-02-23) for annual disclosures. Checked SEC EDGAR for events to 2026-09-25; the most recent filing found was a dividend-declaration 8-K dated 2026-09-14 (no new operating information). Crown Castle's fiscal year is the calendar year (Dec-31), unlike CAH (Jun-30) and COR (Sep-30) in this batch.

Basis: Crown Castle is a REIT. Site rental revenue, net income and the balance sheet are consolidated GAAP, from the 10-Q/10-K/8-K as filed (CIK 0001051470). AFFO and Adjusted EBITDA are the company's own non-GAAP definitions (not fully NAREIT-standard FFO — Crown Castle does not publish a NAREIT FFO reconciliation in the exhibits reviewed), labeled every time they appear. Per the REIT sector playbook, GAAP EPS/net income and P/E are treated as secondary to AFFO for this business.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL. Reservation: elevated leverage (~6.4x net debt/EBITDA) and a still-unresolved organic-growth drag from Sprint/DISH tower non-renewals, on top of a recent, real (not cosmetic) balance-sheet transition. Thesis horizon 12–24 months (shorter than standard, given the AFFO guide is still being reset quarter to quarter as the divestiture beds in). One-sentence reason: a genuine, completed de-risking event (the May 2026 fiber/small-cell sale, debt paydown and buyback) plus a 6.3% dividend yield and a reverse-DCF that is close to fair value rather than clearly cheap — attractive, but with less margin of safety and more moving parts than the two distributors in this batch.

2. Business in plain English

Crown Castle owns and leases roughly 40,000 US cell towers to wireless carriers (Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile) under long-term (5–15 year), contracted, escalator-bearing leases — a REIT with a toll-road-like economic model: it does not operate the network, it rents the vertical real estate the network sits on. Until May 2026 it also owned a large fiber/small-cell business; that business (~$8.4bn) was sold, and the company is now a pure-play US tower REIT. Revenue and cash flow are earned from tenant rent, escalators (contractual annual increases) and new-tenant "co-location" additions to existing towers; the main demand driver is carrier network densification (5G, capacity), and the main headwind of the last several years has been the T-Mobile/Sprint merger (redundant Sprint-leased sites being non-renewed) and DISH Network's build-out slowdown/exit.

3. Why the model likes it, and whether that's durable

Triage's framing (a genuine, completed de-risking catalyst forced by activist pressure; the revenue decline is divestiture noise, not organic decline; 6.3% yield/39% street upside) is substantially confirmed by primary filings, with one correction: the CEO change triage flagged as a governance red flag is verified via the company's own press release (Ex-99.1, filed 2025-08-04) as a completed, board-run search process — Christian Hillabrant, a tower-industry veteran (former CEO of Vantage Towers AG, ~86,000 sites across 10 countries; prior COO of Tillman Infrastructure), was appointed President & CEO effective 2025-09-15 — not an ongoing instability signal, though the underlying pattern of leadership change alongside activist pressure is worth weighing on its own. The durable part: the fiber/small-cell sale closed, ~$7bn of debt was repaid and $1bn of shares repurchased in the following quarter (both confirmed in the Q2 2026 release), and the balance sheet is now 100% fixed-rate debt with a ~7-year weighted average maturity and ~$4.5bn of revolver availability. The less durable / still-adjusting part: organic tower growth excluding DISH terminations and Sprint cancellations is running ~3.5–4.2% (Q2 2026 actual 3.9% headline, 4.2% ex-DISH-base; FY2026 outlook ~3.4–3.6%) — a real but modest growth rate, and FY2026 AFFO guidance has needed three separate revisions in seven months (initial Feb 2026 guide, a special update concurrent with the May 1 divestiture close, then the Q2 raise) as the company re-based the business post-sale — evidence the current guidance is still settling, not yet a multi-year established trend.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet (REIT metric set — see playbook note in the header)

  • Entity scope: all figures are consolidated Crown Castle Inc., the REIT parent (10-Q balance sheet, 2026-06-30).

  • Debt structure: 100% fixed-rate debt, weighted-average maturity ~7 years, ~$4.5bn revolver availability at Q2 2026 (per the earnings release) — a genuinely de-risked maturity/rate profile versus a leveraged floating-rate REIT.
  • Dividend coverage: the quarterly dividend has been held flat at $1.0625/share ($4.25/share annualized) in every dividend-declaration 8-K checked from August 2025 through August 2026 (five consecutive declarations, no cut and no raise observed in this window) — against FY2026 guided AFFO/share of $4.53–$4.65 (midpoint $4.59), the AFFO payout ratio is ≈92.6% — tight, funds the dividend but leaves little room for dividend growth or incremental buybacks without net debt reduction or AFFO growth.
  • Capital allocation since the divestiture: ~$1bn of shares repurchased and ~$7bn of debt repaid in the period immediately following the May 2026 sale close (company's own release) — capital was directed to deleveraging and buybacks, not dividend growth, consistent with the leverage constraint above.
  • Organic growth quality: reported organic contribution to site rental billings is disclosed both including and excluding DISH terminations and Sprint cancellations (3.9% headline, 4.2% ex-DISH-base for Q2 2026) — a transparent disclosure that lets the reader see the churn drag explicitly rather than a blended number; FY2026 guide is 3.4–3.6% on the same ex-churn basis.

Price used: $67.84 (2026-09-25 close, d4 live snapshot). The vendor-computed "pe_ntm" of ~24.8x is a GAAP-EPS-based multiple and is not decision-useful for this REIT (see §4/§6 on GAAP EPS distortion) — the more meaningful multiple is price/AFFO ≈ 14.8x ($67.84 / $4.59 FY2026 guided AFFO/share midpoint), which sits well below towers' historical 20–25x AFFO multiples from the pre-2022 rate environment, consistent with the sector-wide de-rating from higher discount rates, not CCI-specific distress. Dividend yield 6.3% (matching triage). Sell-side mean target $94.35 (+39%, matching triage). No V1 row exists for CCI — v1_verdict is null; no V2R (NAREIT FFO rebuild, per STATE.md 08:39/08:47 entries) was run on CCI in this pass either, since CCI was not part of that earlier REIT batch — flagged as a limitation.

Reverse DCF (2-stage, per-share AFFO, terminal growth 3.0% given towers' structural data-demand tailwind, FY2026 guided AFFO/share midpoint $4.59 as the starting cash-flow proxy): given the elevated leverage (6.4x) and the still-settling post-divestiture guidance, a higher cost of equity (9.0–9.5%) is more appropriate here than for the two distributors in this batch. At that range, the $67.84 price implies roughly +1.0% to +2.1% annualized 10-year AFFO/share growth — modest, and closer to fair value than clearly cheap. Analyst base case: 3–5%/yr 10-year AFFO/share growth (organic tower growth of ~3.5–4% net of the fading Sprint/DISH churn drag, plus modest buyback accretion once leverage normalizes, partly offset by refinancing risk as fixed-rate debt eventually rolls) — above the ~1–2% implied at a conservative discount rate, but the gap is materially narrower than for CAH or COR, and flips to roughly in-line if a lower (8.0–8.5%) discount rate is used (implied growth would then be −1.2% to −0.1%, i.e., cheap) or to expensive-looking territory only if the base case growth undershoots. Given this sensitivity, valuation_view_vs_v1.implied_vs_base = "below" on the analyst's central discount-rate assumption (9.0–9.5%, justified by the leverage), but flagged as the least confident "below" call in this batch — a genuinely close one, not a clear-cut cheap stock.

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull: (1) The fiber/small-cell divestiture is a real, completed simplification — $7bn of debt repaid, $1bn bought back, 100% fixed-rate debt with a 7-year weighted maturity — removing years of "which segment is actually working" ambiguity. (2) A 6.3% dividend yield backed by AFFO coverage of ~93% (tight but funded), with an experienced tower-industry CEO now in place for a full year. (3) Organic tower growth (ex-churn) of 3.5–4%+ with the Sprint-cancellation and DISH-termination drags disclosed transparently and, by nature, mechanically fading as the comparison base rolls off.

Bear: (1) Net debt/EBITDA of ~6.4x is genuinely elevated, and the ~93% AFFO payout ratio leaves little buffer if AFFO disappoints — a REIT in this position has less room to absorb a bad quarter than CAH or COR. (2) FY2026 guidance has been revised three times in seven months as the post-divestiture business is re-based; the "clean beat-and-raise" pattern seen at the two distributors is less established here. (3) The reverse DCF is genuinely close to fair value rather than cheap once a leverage-appropriate discount rate is used — this is a name where the margin of safety depends heavily on the discount-rate assumption, not a screening artefact.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. The quarterly dividend is cut from $1.0625/share (breaking the flat-since-at-least-Aug-2025 record and signaling AFFO coverage has failed).
  2. Net debt/EBITDA rises above 7.0x (from ~6.4x today) without a disclosed deleveraging plan.
  3. Organic contribution to site rental billings (ex-DISH/Sprint) falls below 2.5% for two consecutive quarters.
  4. FY AFFO/share guidance is cut at any quarterly release (breaking the current raise/reaffirm pattern).
  5. A second CEO or CFO departure within 24 months of Hillabrant's September 2025 appointment (a repeat of the leadership-churn pattern the triage flagged).

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: Q3 2026, expected ~2026-10-21 (d4 snapshot next_earnings_date). Watch for: the first full quarter of AFFO/share guidance stability now that the divestiture and immediate deleveraging/buyback are behind the company; any further update to the net-debt/EBITDA trajectory; continued disclosure of the DISH-termination and Sprint-cancellation drag as it fades.

11. Red-flag scan

Leadership turnover: CEO changed effective 2025-09-15 (Christian Hillabrant), confirmed via the company's own press release as a board-run search process, not a forced departure disclosed as such — the triage's "governance churn" flag is real (a CEO change is a CEO change) but the primary-source detail is materially more reassuring than an unexplained departure. Leverage at ~6.4x net debt/EBITDA is elevated for the sector and is the primary balance-sheet flag. AFFO payout ratio ~93% is tight. Guidance revised three times in seven months (transition noise, disclosed and explained each time, not a credibility problem per se). No auditor change, restatement, going-concern language, or SEC/DOJ investigation identified in the sections reviewed. Insider Form-4 pattern, the specific Elliott Management stake/13D and short-seller reports were not independently verified against a primary SEC filing in this pass — the "activist pressure" framing in §3 relies on the triage's own secondary-source citations (Wireless Estimator/DCD coverage), not a Schedule 13D this analyst opened; disclosed as a gap, not asserted as confirmed.

Cadence Design Systems, Inc. (CDNS) — Diligence Dossier (F27, standard depth)

1. Verdict

WATCH — 12–24 month horizon. The electronic-design-automation (EDA) duopoly moat (with Synopsys) is real and durable, and the company has raised full-year guidance twice in 2026 on genuine AI-driven demand. But this analyst's reverse DCF shows the 25 Sep 2026 close ($326.13, mkt cap ≈$89.95bn) requires ~17%/yr free-cash-flow growth for a full decade — above a reasonable evidence-based base case — and the company pleaded guilty in 2025 to a federal criminal export-control violation with an active 3-year probationary compliance regime and ongoing China export-control uncertainty (13% of FY2025 revenue). Re-underwrite on a pullback to a base-case-consistent multiple, or on the probation period ending cleanly with no further BIS/DOJ action.

2. Business in plain English

Cadence sells electronic design automation (EDA) software — the specialized tools chip designers use to design, simulate and verify integrated circuits — plus IP blocks and, since a 2026 acquisition, mechanical/systems engineering simulation software. Customers are semiconductor companies and increasingly systems companies (hyperscalers, automotive) designing their own silicon. It is one of only two companies (with Synopsys) whose tools are effectively mandatory for advanced-node chip design, giving it very high switching costs and pricing power, monetized mostly through multi-year subscription/license contracts (hence its large "backlog" disclosure).

A software duopolist with genuine AI-driven demand and a large backlog can plausibly sustain mid-teens growth for years, but management's own FY2026 guide (~19%, already decelerating from the 24% quarterly print) and the historical rarity of decade-long mid-to-high-teens growth for a company of this scale argue against extrapolating the current print. - Bull case (AI-driven EDA demand accelerates further, Hexagon integration succeeds and cross-sells well, no further legal/export issues): ≈20–22%. - Implied (17.3%) is above the base case (~14–15%) → the growth-priced-in test for INCLUDE/INCLUDE-SMALL is not satisfied → WATCH. - scenario_returns_3y (annualised, estimate): bear ≈ −13%/yr (China exposure impaired and/or a further legal setback, multiple 39x→~25x); base ≈ +10%/yr (growth normalizes toward the ~15–19% guided range, modest multiple compression as the "AI EDA" premium normalizes); bull ≈ +23%/yr (demand accelerates, integration succeeds, multiple holds).

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) EDA is a genuine software duopoly with very high switching costs — advanced-node chip design is not practically possible without Cadence's or Synopsys's tools; (2) record backlog ($8.1bn) and two consecutive 2026 guidance raises show real, forward-visible AI-driven demand, not just a one-quarter beat; (3) the Hexagon D&E acquisition diversifies revenue into mechanical/systems simulation, reducing pure semiconductor-cycle dependence. Bear: (1) Cadence pleaded guilty to a federal criminal charge (conspiracy to commit export control violations) in July 2025, paid $140.6m in penalties/forfeitures, and is now under a 3-year DOJ probation plus an active BIS administrative settlement requiring annual compliance audits — a genuine, ongoing legal/regulatory tail risk, not a closed matter; (2) China was 13% of FY2025 revenue and BIS issued (then rescinded) an EDA-specific export-license requirement for China transactions in mid-2025, with a further interim rule referenced as of late September 2025 — the regulatory environment for exactly this company's China business is unusually unsettled; (3) at the current price the market requires ~17%/yr FCF growth for a decade, above even the company's own (already-decelerating) ~19% FY2026 guide extrapolated forward, let alone a conservative base case.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Any new BIS or DOJ enforcement action, or a finding of probation non-compliance, is disclosed (a single such event, given the active 3-year plea-agreement probation).
  2. China-attributed revenue disclosure falls below 8% of total revenue in any 10-K/10-Q (an unexplained sudden drop signalling export-control impact) — track against the current 13% (FY2025).
  3. YoY revenue growth decelerates below 12% for two consecutive quarters (vs. the ~19% FY2026 guide and 24.2% latest quarterly print).
  4. Non-GAAP-to-GAAP operating margin gap widens above 20 percentage points for two consecutive quarters (currently ~14–17 points), signalling SBC/acquisition costs are outrunning underlying profitability.
  5. FY guidance is cut (not just grown more slowly) at any quarterly release — breaking the current two-raises-in-a-row streak.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: ~2026-10-26 (estimated) based on the historical Q3 cadence (Oct-27/Feb-17/Apr-27/Jul-27 pattern); not yet confirmed by an 8-K or IR calendar as of 2026-09-25.

11. Red-flag scan

Material red flag confirmed from the primary source (FY2025 10-K, Risk Factors, p.16 equivalent): on 2025-07-27, Cadence reached a settlement with both BIS and the DOJ resolving export-control violations that occurred 2015–2021, involving ~$45.3m of sales and unauthorized technology transfer to a China-based customer/third party; Cadence pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit export control violations (3-year probation, ongoing compliance/reporting obligations); aggregate penalties and forfeitures of $140.6m were paid in Q3 2025. Separately, BIS informed Cadence on 2025-05-23 that certain EDA software/technology required a license for transactions involving China or Chinese "military end users," a requirement rescinded 2025-07-02, with a further interim BIS rule referenced as effective 2025-09-29 (not read in full in this pass). dossiers.CEG:
CEG — Constellation Energy Corporation

1. Verdict

WATCH — thesis horizon 24–36 months. The nuclear-plus-gas platform and the Microsoft/Meta/CyrusOne contracted-power story are real and evidenced in primary filings, but the price already embeds a meaningful chunk of the Calpine-integration and Crane (Three Mile Island) restart upside, leverage rose sharply with the Calpine deal, and near-term GAAP earnings are noisy (integration costs, PTC swings, a large regulatory-driven divestiture still to close). This is a "wait for the DOJ divestitures to close and the first clean post-merger quarter" name, not a "buy the current print" name.

2. Business in plain English

Constellation is the largest US generator of carbon-free electricity — mostly nuclear (~30+ reactors after the 2022 Exelon spin-off) — plus, since 7 Jan 2026, Calpine's natural-gas, geothermal and battery-storage fleet and Calpine's competitive retail electricity supply business (~62 TWh/yr of retail load). It sells power both into wholesale markets and under long-term contracts (including 20-year deals with Microsoft — the Three Mile Island Unit 1 restart, now renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center — and Meta at the Clinton plant) and supplies retail electricity to businesses and utilities. It makes money from the spread between its (largely fixed) generation cost and the market/contract price it is paid, plus retail margin. Competitive position: unmatched scale in dispatchable, carbon-free baseload power at a moment when AI/data-center demand is bidding up long-term power prices — a genuine, evidenced moat, not marketing.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1 factor scores (2026-09-25): composite percentile 1.1% (very low — bottom of the batch), roe pct 63%, fcfp pct 78%, but ep pct 1.6% (very expensive on trailing earnings yield) and mom_12_1 pct 8% (share price down 16% over the trailing year net of the most recent month). The quant model dislikes CEG almost entirely on value and momentum — both of which are distorted right now by the Calpine deal (a stock-and-cash acquisition inflated share count and reset the earnings base, and 12-month momentum reflects deal-related volatility, not a business quality signal).   • Merger accounting.
