  • FCF conversion: TTM OCF $14.78bn vs TTM NI $4.89bn (D3/V1 basis) — FCF conversion is distorted by the Q3-25 non-cash impairment depressing NI; on a cleaner H1-2026 basis, OCF $10.6bn vs NI $5.92bn is a more normal ~1.8x.
  • GAAP vs adjusted gap: material and explained — Q3 2025's entire GAAP-vs-adjusted gap was the $5.7bn goodwill charge plus Oak Street asset write-downs; Q2 2026's gap ($2.31 GAAP vs $2.58 adjusted) is smaller and more typical (acquisition-amortization/integration-cost add-backs).
  • Goodwill: $85,478M, unchanged Dec-2025 to Jun-2026 (10-Q, source 4) — no further impairment through Q2 2026, but this is ~75% of the $114.7bn market cap and the Health Care Delivery unit (which triggered the 2025 charge) has not disclosed remaining headroom.
  • Leverage: Net debt $47.45bn (D3/V1, latest 10-Q); TTM EBIT+D&A ≈ $12.81bn ⇒ net debt/EBITDA ≈ 3.7x (GAAP-TTM approximation, not the company's own covenant-defined adjusted EBITDA, which would likely be somewhat lower). Credit ratings: BBB (S&P, negative outlook), BBB (Fitch, negative outlook), Baa3 (Moody's, stable) — two of three agencies carry a negative outlook (source 9).
  • Buybacks/dividends: $0 buybacks in FY2025 (vs $3.02bn in FY2024) — capital preserved during the cost crisis; resumed modestly in H1 2026 (~$146M net). Dividends paid $1.725bn in H1 2026.
  • Recent M&A/financing: No new acquisitions; Omnicare LLC (a legacy long-term-care pharmacy subsidiary) filed Chapter 11 on 2025-09-22 with $110M DIP financing to resolve litigation and industry-wide LTC-pharmacy financial pressure — a contained, disclosed legacy liability, not a going-concern issue for the parent (source 10).
  • Share count: ~1,287M diluted (D3/V1); buybacks paused then modestly resumed as above.
  • Governance: CEO David Joyner was also named Board Chair effective 2026-01-01 (combined role — a minor governance flag); John Gallina (ex-Elevance Health CFO) added to the Board/Audit Committee 2026-03-19 (source 11, 12).

7. Valuation snapshot — explicit reconciliation with V1

V1 says: verdict attractive (score 0.94/1.0), NTM P/E 10.61x (8.8th percentile of 171-month own history), base case +35.9%/yr over 3 years (bear −5.4%/yr, bull +67.5%/yr), driven by a WACC of 6.64% and an assumed re-rating of the exit multiple from ~10.6x to 17.46x plus EPS growing from $8.40 (NTM) to $12.37 (yr-3). V1 flags "base 3-yr value exceeds Street 12m high target" ($148 high target vs V1's $216 base-case yr-3 value) — its own built-in sanity check.

My view: I agree directionally (cheap, worth owning) but I am more cautious on the magnitude/pace than V1's base case, so I mark this "cheap" but not fully "consistent" at face value — the exit-multiple assumption (17.46x, back near CVS's pre-2024-crisis average) is the specific input I'd challenge. It presumes the market fully forgives the leverage (3.7x net debt/EBITDA), the $85.5bn goodwill overhang and the still-unresolved post-2028 Caremark cost-plus mandate (FTC-Caremark settlement, source 13) within three years. A more conservative 13–15x exit multiple — still a meaningful re-rating from today's 10.6x — would still support a solidly positive (low-to-mid-teens %/yr) return without assuming a full return to the old regime. Peer set (CI, CVS, DVA, LH, DGX; median 10.8x NTM P/E) shows CVS trading roughly in line with sector peers today, so the re-rating case rests on CVS and the sector re-rating together, not CVS closing a standalone discount.

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull: 1. Aetna MBR has improved for five straight comparable quarters (95.2%→87.4% YoY at Q2-26) and 2026 Medicare Advantage star ratings recovered to 81%+ members in 4-star plans (from a much weaker 2024–2025 base), locking in 2027 quality-bonus payments (source 14). 2. Adjusted EPS guidance raised in 3 of the last 4 releases; FY2025 actual beat the last raised range. 3. The July-2026 FTC-Caremark settlement resolves a multi-year antitrust overhang with a bounded, phased-in remedy (cost-plus option starts 2028) rather than an open-ended liability (source 13).

Bear: 1. Two of three rating agencies carry a negative outlook on CVS's BBB/Baa3 credit, at ~3.7x leverage, against $85.5bn of goodwill that has already required one $5.7bn write-down (source 8, 9). 2. PBM reform structurally caps Caremark's rebate-based economics from 2028; the near-term settlement relief could still be a medium-term margin headwind once cost-plus reimbursement is mandatory. 3. Director Larry Robbins (Glenview Capital) sold $317M of CVS stock on 2026-05-19 — the single largest disclosed insider transaction in the review period (source 15).

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Aetna Medical Benefit Ratio rises above 92% for two consecutive quarters (vs 87.4% in Q2 2026).
  2. Net debt/EBITDA rises above 4.0x, or a second rating agency downgrades CVS below BBB-/Baa3.
  3. A further goodwill impairment is taken against the Health Care Delivery (Oak Street) reporting unit, following the $5.7bn Q3-2025 charge.
  4. FY adjusted EPS guidance is cut from a prior range (breaking the pattern of raises through Q3-2025–Q2-2026).
  5. 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings (expected ~October 2026) show a material reversal from the 81%/63% (4-star/4.5-star) share achieved for 2026.

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: ~2026-10-28 (Q3 2026, per D4 live snapshot).
  • 2027 CMS Star Ratings release: expected early October 2026 — likely lands at or just after this review's information cutoff (2026-09-25); check immediately on release.
  • CMS 2027 Medicare Advantage/Part D rate notice (typically finalized ~April, already public by this cutoff — not separately verified in this review).
  • Ongoing FTC-Caremark settlement implementation milestones through the 2028 cost-plus option start date.

11. Red-flag scan

  • Litigation: Omnicare Chapter 11 (2025-09-22, contained); FTC-Caremark antitrust settlement (2026-07-14, resolved via settlement, not litigated to judgment); 10-Q XBRL references ongoing "U.S. ex rel. Bassan et al. v. Omnicare" and "In re CVS Health Shareholder Derivative Litigation" (named but substance not independently reviewed within this time box — flagged for follow-up).
  • Auditor: Ernst & Young ratified for 2026 at the May-2026 annual meeting; no auditor change or qualification found.
  • Goodwill impairment: $5.7bn taken Q3 2025 (disclosed, not hidden) — see section 6.
  • Insider selling: Director Larry Robbins sold $317M (2026-05-19); other Form 4 activity in the period was routine tax-withholding on RSU vesting (CAO James Clark, Amy Compton-Phillips) — not a broad-based executive selling pattern.
  • Credit outlook: Negative from S&P and Fitch (source 9) — a real, disclosed rating-agency concern, not a data conflict.
  • Governance: Combined Chair/CEO role adopted January 2026 (minor).
  • No restatements, no going-concern language, and no material-weakness disclosure were identified in the filings reviewed.

dossiers.DAL:
DAL — Delta Air Lines, Inc. — Diligence Dossier (Agent F41, Wave 2, Standard depth)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — the strongest US airline franchise (SkyMiles/Amex co-brand economics differentiate it from commodity airline economics), fairly priced with no real margin of safety; named reservation: a large mid-2026 jet-fuel spike and a December-2026 pilot-contract re-opener are two concrete, near-term tests the thesis has not yet passed. Thesis horizon: 12–36 months.

2. Business in plain English

Delta is a full-service US "Big 3" airline operating a global hub network (Atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis, Salt Lake City, New York, LA) plus premium international joint ventures (Air France-KLM, Virgin Atlantic, LATAM, Aeromexico, Korean Air). Roughly half of its earnings power comes from non-ticket sources that are less commoditized than a seat: the SkyMiles/American Express co-brand card program (loyalty cash flow sold to Amex), Delta Premium Select/first-class upsell, cargo, and Delta TechOps/MRO (aircraft maintenance for other airlines) — the reason the triage note calls its "loyalty economics" a differentiator from a pure commodity-seat business.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Triage: quality 4/5, growth 4/5, price_vs_growth 4/5, no red flags; "18.7% revenue growth, 20% ROE at just 10.7x NTM P/E; cheap for the quality." b1 factor read: composite driven mainly by Momentum (12-1m return ~39%, 78th pct) and Earnings-momentum (SUE), with Quality percentiles decent but not exceptional (ROE 44.9th pct is unremarkable for the family average once leverage is included). This is a mostly durable read — the loyalty/co-brand and MRO revenue streams are structurally differentiated and have grown for years — but part of the recent momentum score is a fuel-driven margin swing artefact: the 2026 fare/margin story is entangled with a large jet-fuel cost spike (see §6), which cuts both ways in the numbers below and needs to be read net of fuel, not gross.

4. Last eight quarters — revenue, margin, EPS (GAAP, USD millions unless noted)

Q1 2025 14,040 — 614* — 240** 0.37**
Q2 2025 16,648 — 2,267 13.6% 2,130 3.27
Q3 2025 16,673 +6.4% 1,684 10.1% 1,417 2.17
Q1 2026 15,854 +12.9% 501 3.2% (289) (0.44)
Q2 2026 19,757 +18.7% 1,864 9.4% 1,604 2.44

(Q1 2025 op. income restated as reported in the 2025 comparative column of the 2026 10-Q; Q1 2025 net income/EPS as originally reported.) Delta's own non-GAAP framing for Q2 2026: adjusted operating income $1.6bn (8.8% adjusted margin), down 24% YoY*, net income $1.60bn, diluted EPS $2.44 (matches GAAP this quarter). Revenue growth has genuinely accelerated (Q2 2026 +18.7%, Q1 2026 +12.9%, both ahead of the FY2025 trend) but operating margin has compressed materially even as revenue grew, the signature of a cost (fuel) headwind outrunning fare/volume gains — see §6. Source: SEC XBRL company-facts (data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyfacts/CIK0000027904.json); 10-Q filings; Q2 2026 earnings release/8-K.

5. Guidance track record (last 2 releases)

  • Q1 2026 release (Apr 2026): full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guide $6.50–7.50; free cash flow $3–4bn; gross leverage target ≈2x. Q2 2026 guide given: low-teens revenue growth.
  • Q2 2026 release (10 Jul 2026): full-year 2026 guidance reaffirmed — adjusted EPS $6.50–7.50, FCF $3–4bn, leverage ≈2x — despite jet-fuel cost per gallon roughly doubling intra-year (see §6). September-quarter (Q3 2026) guide: mid-teens revenue growth, 11–13% operating margin, EPS $2.00–2.50. Verdict: guidance has been maintained, not raised or cut, across the only two 2026 releases reviewed — a real resilience signal given the fuel shock, but not evidence of upside surprise either.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • Fuel shock: per-gallon jet-fuel cost rose from a $2.30–2.60 range in 2025 to $3.93 in the June-2026 quarter — a large, disclosed, exogenous cost shock (context: a war-driven oil-price spike also flagged elsewhere in this program's diligence, e.g. the EOG dossier). This is the primary driver of the Q1 2026 GAAP net loss (−$289m) and the Q2 2026 adjusted-operating-margin decline (−24% YoY) — not an execution failure; per the sector playbook, airline OPM is "mostly not a skill signal" when the dominant cost line is exogenous fuel.
  • FCF (FY, OCF−capex, $m): FY2022 6,363−6,366=−3 (breakeven); FY2023 6,464−5,323=1,141; FY2024 8,025−5,140=2,885; FY2025 8,342−4,499=3,843. A genuinely strong, improving multi-year FCF trend, consistent with (and slightly ahead of the midpoint of) the company's own FY2026 $3–4bn guide.
  • Leverage: company-stated gross leverage target ≈2x (guided, presumably lease-adjusted/EBITDAR-based — not independently rebuilt from raw XBRL at this depth, a limitation per the sector playbook's EBITDAR methodology). Raw balance-sheet long-term debt (XBRL "LongTermDebt") has fallen steadily: $18.1bn (Q1 24) → $15.3bn (FY24) → $12.9bn (Q2 26), a genuine, verified deleveraging trend independent of any lease-accounting ambiguity.
  • Cash: $3.1–5.1bn range over the last 8 quarters, no liquidity stress signal; diluted share count essentially flat (642m → 658m, +2.5% over 2 years — modest dilution, not buyback-driven reduction).
  • Pilot-contract re-opener: current agreement amendable 31 December 2026; a flight-attendant unionization drive is also underway (per search results) — both are real, disclosed labor-cost risks not yet reflected in the FY2026 guide's assumptions in detail.

7. Valuation snapshot and reverse DCF

V1 systematic valuation exists for DAL (v1_valuation_table.csv): NTM P/E 10.72x, 63.9th percentile of DAL's own 10-year history, peer median 9.90x, "within Street 12m target range," verdict "fair" (verdict_score −0.084), bear/base/bull 3-yr annualized returns −39.6% / −2.8% / +37.2%. - Price (25-Sep-2026 close) $84.94; market cap ≈$55.86bn. - Reverse DCF (own model, 10-yr explicit + Gordon terminal, r=10.0%, terminal g=2.5%) using FY2025 actual FCF ($3,843m, consistent with the company's own FY2026 guide): implies the market is pricing in ≈3.4%/yr 10-year FCF growth. Using the guide's midpoint ($3.5bn) as a slightly more conservative base: ≈4.6%/yr. - Analyst view: fair (in_line). A plausible base case (mid-single-digit FCF growth, ~4.5%/yr, reflecting continued loyalty/MRO/premium-mix growth moderating from today's mid-teens revenue growth as capacity growth normalizes) is very close to both implied-growth readings → implied_vs_base = "in_line." - Reconciliation with V1: V1's own base case (−2.8%/yr) and ours (+2.8%/yr using a symmetric FCF-growth framing) differ in sign but both cluster near zero — i.e., both approaches independently conclude the stock is roughly fairly priced with limited base-case upside, not "cheap." The sign difference likely reflects V1 pricing in more of the fuel-shock margin risk into its base case than our FCF-guide-anchored approach does. Consistent: true (both call it "fair," near-zero excess-return base case).

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull: (1) SkyMiles/Amex co-brand and premium/MRO diversification give Delta a structurally better revenue mix than commodity-seat peers, and it is trading at a discount to its own 10-year P/E history (63.9th percentile is mid-range, not stretched) despite the best fundamentals in the group; (2) FCF has grown for three straight years to a guided $3–4bn in FY2026, funding continued deleveraging (debt down from $18.1bn to $12.9bn since Q1 2024); (3) full-year guidance was reaffirmed despite a real fuel shock, evidence of pricing power/cost-recapture discipline. Bear: (1) Jet fuel per gallon nearly doubled intra-year (2025's $2.30–2.60 range to $3.93 in Q2 2026) and already drove a Q1 2026 GAAP net loss and a 24% YoY adjusted-operating-income decline in Q2 2026 — if oil stays elevated, FY2026 guidance is at risk despite today's reaffirmation; (2) the pilot-contract re-opener (amendable 31 Dec 2026) and a flight-attendant unionization drive are two concrete, dated labor-cost catalysts not yet priced into the guide in detail; (3) V1's own base-case 3-yr return is slightly negative — this is a "fair," not "cheap," entry point in a historically boom-bust, high-fixed-cost industry with no valuation cushion if either fuel or labor costs surprise to the upside.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Company-guided FY2026 free cash flow ($3–4bn) is cut or actual FY2026 FCF comes in below $2.5bn.
  2. Full-year adjusted EPS guidance ($6.50–7.50) is cut at any remaining 2026 release.
  3. Company-stated gross leverage rises above 3.0x (guided ≈2x).
  4. Jet-fuel cost per gallon sustains above $3.50 for two consecutive quarters without offsetting fare/capacity action (already at $3.93 in Q2 2026 — a live trigger to monitor, not yet tripped on guidance terms).
  5. The pilot-contract re-opener (amendable 31-Dec-2026) concludes with a ratified agreement carrying double-digit annual unit-cost escalation beyond current assumptions, or results in a work action/strike.

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: Q3 2026, confirmed 9 October 2026 (webcast announced, 10am ET).
  • Pilot-contract re-opener: amendable 31 December 2026.
  • Flight-attendant unionization drive: ongoing, outcome/timeline not yet disclosed.

11. Red-flag scan

  • No auditor change identified; Ernst & Young has audited Delta since 2006 and was re-appointed for 2026 (per company DEF 14A).
  • No material weakness, restatement or going-concern language identified in this pass.
  • No short-seller report identified in searches conducted 2026-09-26.

DoorDash runs a three-sided marketplace app connecting consumers, local restaurants/retailers and independent delivery workers ("Dashers"). Pattern: three consecutive quarters of beat-and-raise, with the Q2-2026 beat clearing the prior guided range's high end — a stronger track record than a simple "in-range" beat. No cuts identified in the reviewed window (Q4-25 through Q2-26 releases).

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • Entity scope: all figures below are consolidated (DoorDash, Inc., 10-Q/10-K). DASH has no separately regulated financial subsidiary.
  • FCF conversion: TTM OCF $2,830M vs TTM NI $841M → OCF/NI ≈ 3.4x, reflecting float from marketplace payment timing (DASH collects from consumers faster than it pays merchants/Dashers) — a durable structural feature of the model, not a one-off working-capital swing, though it does mean GAAP earnings understate the cash-generative power of the business and also that a sudden change in payment terms/timing (e.g., regulatory mandate on faster Dasher payout) could compress this gap.
  • SBC: material — DASH is a heavy stock-comp payer (typical of recently-IPO'd tech); GAAP operating margin (3.5–7.5% in recent quarters) is well below any adjusted-EBITDA-margin framing management uses (Adjusted EBITDA $914M in Q2-26 vs GAAP operating income $156M — a ~$758M GAAP-vs-adjusted gap in one quarter, driven mainly by SBC and D&A/amortization add-backs).   • Buybacks: DASH only began meaningful repurchases in 2026 — $162M (Q1-26) then $1,049M (Q2-26), a sharp step-up (FY2025 buybacks were $0). Shares outstanding still rising slowly on net (SBC dilution has historically outpaced the pre-2026 buyback program), so this is a recent and not-yet-proven capital-return commitment.

7. Valuation snapshot — reverse DCF (no V1 row; this is my own model)

Price 2026-09-25: $193.36 (D4 snapshot, cross-checked). Market cap $84,952M; net cash (cash+ST+LT investments – convertible notes) ≈ $6,216M – $2,727M = $3,489M → EV0 ≈ $81,463M (using the narrower cash-only net-cash figure of $1,697M instead would give EV0 ≈ $83,255M; I use the wider, still-conservative figure below and flag the range). TTM FCF $1,933M. Assuming a cost of capital of ~11% (rf 5.17% + β≈1.4 × ERP 4.14%, consistent with the methodology used elsewhere in this program; DASH-specific beta not independently re-derived here) and a 3% terminal growth rate, EV0 implies a 10-year FCF growth rate of ~19–20%/yr. Compare to evidence: trailing revenue growth 33–38%/yr (last four quarters), triage's own read of 35.6% growth (outputs/Q02_triage.json), and a still-early ads/international ramp. The growth priced in (~20%/yr FCF growth) is below both trailing revenue growth and my own base-case assumption below — this supports "below," i.e. the market is not paying for DASH's full demonstrated growth trajectory, likely because of (a) the GAAP/adjusted earnings-quality gap in §6 and (b) the regulatory overhang in §9/§11.

My own explicit 3-year scenario (FCF × EV/FCF exit multiple, net cash roll-forward): - Base: FCF growth ~22%/yr (between trailing 33%+ revenue growth and the 20% implied rate, allowing for margin investment in Deliveroo/new verticals) → FCF_yr3 ≈ $3,507M; exit EV/FCF ≈ 30x (moderate compression from today's implied ~42–43x as growth normalizes); net cash grows to ≈ $5.5B; shares ≈ 425M (continued buybacks) → price ≈ $260, annualised return ≈ +10.5%/yr. - Bear: a regulatory reclassification loss (see §9) or demand-growth stall cuts FCF growth to ~10%/yr → FCF_yr3 ≈ $2,573M; exit multiple compresses to 20x; net cash ≈ $3.0B → price ≈ $124, annualised return ≈ –13.7%/yr. - Bull: international (Deliveroo) and ads scale faster than expected, FCF growth ~30%/yr → FCF_yr3 ≈ $4,251M; exit multiple holds near 40x; net cash ≈ $6.0B → price ≈ $429, annualised return ≈ +30.6%/yr.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull (3): (1) Adjusted EBITDA has beaten the top of guidance for at least one of the last three quarters and management raises the following quarter's range each time — genuine, not promotional, operating momentum. (2) Advertising and new-verticals (grocery/retail) revenue are high-incremental-margin and still early, giving a credible path to margin expansion beyond delivery commissions alone. (3) International expansion via Deliveroo materially increases the addressable market without DASH having to build local density from scratch.

Bear (3): (1) Active Dasher-misclassification litigation and regulatory inquiries in multiple states (California EDD audit/assessment, per the Q2-2026 10-Q's own legal-proceedings note) plus a reported (secondary-source) ~$131.5M multi-state worker-payment settlement create both a cash-cost and business-model risk (reclassification to employees would materially raise costs). (2) GAAP profitability is thin and volatile relative to the "Adjusted EBITDA" headline (§6) — a large, persistent GAAP/adjusted gap driven by SBC that could compress reported per-share value even if Adjusted EBITDA keeps growing. (3) Intensifying competition (Uber Eats bundling with rides/Instacart-style grocery entrants) in a business with limited switching costs for either merchants or consumers.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Marketplace GOV YoY growth falls below 20% for two consecutive quarters (vs 36–37% in the last two reported quarters).
  2. Adjusted EBITDA margin (% of GOV) declines YoY for two consecutive quarters (it was already flagged as "slightly below Q2-2025" in the Q2-2026 outlook commentary — watch whether this becomes a trend, not a one-quarter blip).
  3. Any final ruling or settlement in the California EDD Dasher-classification matter (or an equivalent ruling in another large state) that reclassifies Dashers as employees in that state.
  4. Net cash (cash + investments – debt) declines by more than $1B in two consecutive quarters outside of an announced, disclosed acquisition.
  5. GAAP operating margin below 2% (vs 3.5–7.5% range in the last eight quarters) for two consecutive quarters, signalling the GAAP/adjusted gap is widening rather than closing.

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: Q3 2026, expected ~2026-11-04 (based on the historical early-November reporting pattern; not yet confirmed by an 8-K as of this dossier's writing).

I could not find a primary-filing confirmation of the ~$131.5M multi-state worker-payment settlement reported by several news/legal-aggregator sites (Illinois $11.25M, NYC/NY state $16.75–18M, DC $2.5M cited in secondary sources) — flagged as unverified from a primary source in the time available, not as confirmed fact.

Agent: f4 (Fundamental diligence analyst) | As of: 2026-09-25 close | Most recent period incorporated: Q1 FY2027 (ended 2026-06-30), published 2026-07-23; 10-K FY2026 (ended 2026-03-31) filed 2026-05-22. Checked for events to 2026-09-25 (latest: 8-K filed 2026-09-15, annual-meeting vote results only — no new financial information). Sector playbook applied: retail-ecommerce.md (branded consumer, wholesale + DTC apparel/footwear) — 1P principal model throughout, no GMV/marketplace distortions apply. Reporting basis: Consolidated, GAAP, USD (Deckers has no meaningful standalone-vs-consolidated distinction; single reporting entity). Data quality note: All income-statement, balance-sheet and guidance figures trace to SEC XBRL (data.sec.gov) or the company's own 8-K EX-99.1 press releases (Tier 1). Two datapoints are explicitly Tier-4/secondary and flagged inline where used (the $150m→$185m tariff-cost figure, and general CEO-succession news coverage). Four items are explicitly not available (non-GAAP EPS — company doesn't report one; per-quarter tariff $ impact; China-specific revenue split; current auditor name). This dossier is not personalised investment advice — see disclaimer at the end.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Thesis horizon 12–24 months. Cheap (9.9x NTM P/E), high-quality (44% TTM ROE, zero funded debt), and management just raised FY2027 guidance — but the brand-momentum evidence that should drive a re-rating is deteriorating in real time (HOKA revenue growth 18.5%→14.5%→7.7% over the last three reported quarters; operating margin fell 190bps YoY in the latest quarter). This is a genuine two-sided call, not a table-pounding buy — size it accordingly and watch the kill criteria below closely at the next print (~Oct 22–23, 2026).

2. Business in plain English

Deckers designs, markets and distributes footwear and apparel under five brands — HOKA (performance running, the growth engine), UGG (heritage lifestyle boots/slippers, the cash cow), Teva, Sanuk and Koolaburra (small, declining "other"). It sells through wholesale (department stores, specialty and national retail chains, ~59% of FY26 sales) and direct-to-consumer (owned stores + e-commerce, ~41%). Manufacturing is 100% outsourced to third-party contractors, predominantly in Vietnam (Deckers has cut China production to an estimated 4–5% of the total), which is the source of its tariff exposure.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Prelim rank (lead_prelim_rank.csv): Q 0.950, V 0.936, M 0.396, composite 0.761 (Q and V both in the top 5–6% of the Consumer Discretionary sector; M is weak, 40th percentile — mom121 −14.1%, i.e., the stock has fallen over the last year). Independently re-derived from XBRL: TTM ROE 44.1%, gross-profit/assets 82.6%, CFO/assets 30.9%, zero long-term or short-term funded debt (only a new, undrawn $500m revolver). The Quality score is durable — it reflects a genuinely asset-light, high-margin, debt-free brand-licensing-like model, not an accounting artefact or a one-off. The Value score is real but is priced by the market as a value trap, not a bargain, because the same dataset's own momentum factor (and my read of the last four earnings releases) shows the reason it's cheap: HOKA, which drove 100%+ of the multiple expansion during 2022–2024, is decelerating sequentially, and Q1 FY27 operating margin compressed as SG&A grew faster than gross profit. Whether V is "artefact" or "opportunity" is precisely the open question this dossier cannot resolve with certainty — see bull/bear below.

Balance sheet: zero funded debt, $1.60bn cash, only operating-lease liabilities ($398.6m LT + $73.4m ST as of Q1 FY27). On 2026-08-27 the company amended and extended its unsecured revolver to $500m/5-year maturity (2031) with Citi/HSBC/Fifth Third — routine treasury management, undrawn, not a leverage event. Inventory rose to $807.6m at Q1 FY27 (vs $849.4m a year earlier, actually down YoY — no build-up red flag). Buybacks are aggressive: $1.075bn repurchased in FY26 alone, authorization increased to ~$5bn total; share count down from ~152.4m (FY25) to ~136.7m (Q1 FY27), a genuine and material per-share tailwind. Tariffs: the two press releases reviewed directly disclose no specific dollar tariff bridge (only that inventory "includes the impact of incremental tariffs"). Financial press (not independently verified against a primary transcript this session — flagged Tier-4/secondary) reported the company guided to a ~$150m FY26 tariff cost hit in mid-2025, later revised up to ~$185m, mitigated via price increases — this is a meaningful, real cost headwind that the press releases understate relative to TPR/RL's explicit bps disclosure, and is a disclosure-transparency gap worth pressing management on.

7. Valuation snapshot

Price $78.67 (2026-09-25) is at its 3-year and 5-year low (3yr range $77.51–$223.11 — the stock has fallen ~65% from its own 3-year high). NTM P/E 9.9x (d4); using the company's own FY27 EPS guidance ($7.35–7.50) the multiple is 10.5–10.7x. FCF yield ≈10.4% (TTM, independently derived — see §6; this reconciles closely with the prelim CSV's own fcfp=10.4%, though it diverges from d4_live_snapshot's fcf_yield=8.1%, likely a different TTM window — a minor internal inconsistency, not a filings conflict). EV/EBIT ≈13.8% earnings yield equivalent per prelim ebitev. Peer context: Nike (NKE, in the d4 universe) trades at 19.6x NTM despite currently declining revenue and its own turnaround, i.e., the market pays roughly double DECK's multiple for a larger, currently-shrinking peer — DECK's discount looks statistically large relative to its still-positive (if decelerating) growth. On (ONON) and Birkenstock (BIRK) are the closer performance/premium-footwear comps but their current multiples were not independently pulled this session (FMP hit a rate limit; not fabricated — flagged not available). Reverse-DCF sense: at 9.9x earnings with ~5–8% guided growth, the market is pricing continued deceleration toward low-single-digit terminal growth; closing even half the gap to a "normal" mid-teens specialty-apparel multiple would require HOKA re-accelerating back above low-double-digits for 2–3 consecutive quarters.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) 8-for-8 quarterly EPS beats with a still-positive average surprise of +25%, a debt-free balance sheet, and a $5bn buyback runway systematically shrinking the share count. (2) Management raised guidance at every one of the last three releases even while absorbing tariff cost inflation — the "beat and raise" machine hasn't actually broken, only slowed. (3) International revenue (+25.5% Q4, +8.4% Q1FY27) and DTC (+13.0% Q1FY27) are still growing well above the group average, showing real runway outside the maturing US wholesale base. Bear: (1) HOKA's growth has nearly collapsed sequentially (18.5%→14.5%→7.7%) in a category (performance running) that On, Nike, Asics and Brooks are all now contesting hard — this could be genuine category maturation, not noise. (2) Operating margin fell 190bps YoY in the most recent quarter as SG&A outgrew gross profit — the first sign that scale leverage is inverting. (3) Tariff cost disclosure is thin and reportedly moved materially higher intra-year ($150m→$185m per secondary sources); if true and not fully offset by pricing, FY27 guidance (GM ≈56.5%, down from 56.4% Q1 actual but below FY26's 57.7%) already implicitly assumes structural margin give-back.

9. Key risks & kill criteria

  1. HOKA quarterly YoY growth falls below 5% for two consecutive quarters (from 7.7% in Q1 FY27) — would confirm structural, not cyclical, deceleration.
  2. GAAP operating margin below 15% for two consecutive quarters (currently 15.2% Q1 FY27, down from 17.1%).
  3. FY2027 guidance cut at any point (would break the "raised every time" streak that is the main remaining bull pillar).
  4. Domestic (US) revenue growth turns negative for two consecutive quarters (was +2.7% to +3.2% in the last two prints — already anemic).
  5. Evidence that tariff mitigation (pricing) is triggering wholesale sell-through weakness or channel pushback (watch wholesale growth, currently still positive at +2.2–7.1%).

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: on/around Oct 22–23, 2026 (Q2 FY27; Yahoo-estimated date, d4_live_snapshot — not yet company-confirmed). No investor day or index event identified. Annual meeting held (5.07 8-K) 2026-09-15 — no contested items found.

CEO succession (Dave Powers → Stefano Caroti, internal Chief Commercial Officer) was announced Feb-2024 and completed Aug-2024 via an orderly, board-run process — not a red flag, and Caroti has now owned two full years of results including the current deceleration. A cluster of ~15 Form 4 filings in Aug–Sep 2026 across seven named executives was checked and confirms routine RSU-vesting tax-withholding sales (small share counts, e.g., CEO Caroti 8,628 shares withheld), not open-market discretionary selling — no insider-selling red flag. dossiers.DG:
DG — Dollar General Corporation

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — thesis horizon 12–36 months. Statistically rare valuation (NTM P/E at the 7th percentile of its own 175-month trading history) combined with a primary-source-verified, broad-based operating recovery (four consecutive quarterly guidance raises, six consecutive quarters of positive comps in all four merchandise categories) justifies a position, but a recurring workplace-safety compliance problem, unresolved shareholder securities litigation, and a guidance raise that is partly non-repeating (tariff refunds, a lower tax-rate assumption) are specific, named reservations against taking a full-weight position today.

2. Business in plain English

Dollar General is the largest small-box discount retailer in the US: 21,148 stores (Dollar General, DG Market, DGX, pOpshelf, plus a small Mexico pilot) as of July 31, 2026, mostly in rural and small-town America, selling consumables (food, health/beauty, cleaning — ~82% of sales), seasonal goods, home products and apparel at everyday low prices within a few minutes' drive of its customers. It makes money on thin per-unit margins (gross margin ~30–33%) applied to very high inventory turns and a low-cost, no-frills real-estate/labor model; its moat is store density and proximity in markets too small for Walmart or Target to bother with. It competes on convenience and price against Dollar Tree/Family Dollar, Walmart, and increasingly grocery and drug chains.

3. Why the model likes it — and is it durable?

B1 composite score is in the top decile (live_rank 18/~2,300; composite percentile 96.5; gates: the composite itself carries no disqualifying-red-flag gate — the red-flag/legal check is done separately in §11 below, not netted into this score). Family drivers: Value (fam_V ≈0.88, very high) — cheap on earnings yield, FCF yield, EBIT/EV and book/price; Quality (fam_Q ≈0.63) — solid gross-profit/assets and low accruals; Earnings momentum (fam_S ≈0.84) — SUE has been strongly positive as EPS beat-and-raise repeated; Momentum (fam_M ≈0.70) — the stock has rallied off a 2024 low as the recovery took hold.

Durability check: the Value signal is real and verifiable — DG trades at 15.2x NTM EPS against a 175-month own history whose 7th percentile this is, i.e., DG has traded above today's multiple in ~93% of the months since 2012. The earnings-momentum signal is partly an artefact: of the ~$0.60 increase in the FY2026 diluted-EPS guidance midpoint between the Q1 (Jun-2026) and Q2 (Aug-2026) releases, management explicitly attributes ~$0.25 (≈40%) to a one-time tariff-refund benefit it says will not recur in H2, and part of the earlier Q4→Q1 raise was a lower effective-tax-rate assumption (25.0%→24.5%) rather than operating improvement. The comp/traffic recovery itself (6 straight quarters of positive comps in every category, 5 straight quarters of positive traffic) is corroborated by the primary-source press releases and is the more durable part of the story.

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull (3): 1. Six consecutive quarters of positive comps across all four merchandise categories, with positive traffic for five straight quarters — a broad, primary-source-verified demand recovery, not a one-category fluke. 2. Deleveraging is real and already showing up (net interest expense −25.7% YoY) with net debt/EBITDA ≈0.85x, giving room to keep resuming buybacks (guided up to $700m in FY26, versus none in FY25) while continuing store growth (~460 new stores planned FY26). 3. 1. Verdict

2. Business in plain English

Disney sells stories and experiences: film/TV/streaming content (Entertainment segment: Disney+, Hulu, studios, linear networks), live sports rights and distribution (Sports/ESPN, including ESPN's direct-to-consumer app launched Aug 2025), and theme parks, resorts, cruises and consumer products (Experiences). It makes money from subscriptions, advertising, licensing, box office, and guest spending, monetizing the same IP (a Marvel film feeds streaming, theme-park attractions, and merchandise). Its competitive position is a content library and physical-park moat that no single streaming or media peer can fully replicate, offset by intensifying streaming competition (Netflix, YouTube, Amazon) and a linear-TV bundle in structural decline.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

The wave-2 triage (Q01, quality 4/5, growth 4/5, price_vs_growth 4/5) flagged 54% guided EPS growth (GAAP, distorted by prior-year one-offs — see §6) against a 14.2x NTM P/E. The durable part of the thesis is Experiences (parks/cruise) recurring high-return capex and streaming's fixed-cost operating leverage now that Disney+ has scaled past ~180m subscribers; the artefact risk is that a chunk of the "54% guided EPS growth" the triage cited is compare-against-a-weak-prior-year noise (A+E impairment, tax items), not run-rate improvement.

Scenario framework (analyst estimate, exit multiple on forward adjusted EPS 3 years out, plus ~1% dividend yield): - Bear (30%): linear decline accelerates, ESPN carriage losses continue, international parks stay soft — EPS ~$5.60, exit 14x → ~$78/share (≈ −8.5%/yr, 3y annualised). - Base (45%): streaming margin reaches high-single/low-double digits, Parks mid-single-digit growth continues — EPS ~$6.90, exit 18x → ~$124/share (≈ +6.4%/yr). - Bull (25%): ESPN DTC scales profitably, cruise capacity drives Experiences re-acceleration — EPS ~$8.00, exit 22x → ~$176/share (≈ +19.4%/yr).

Bull: (1) Disney+/Hulu/Hotstar SVOD hit a 13% margin in Q3 and are guided to double digits for FY26 — the decade-long streaming investment is inflecting to cash generation, not just accounting profit. (2) Experiences keeps compounding on cruise-fleet expansion and domestic per-cap spend (+4% YoY) even as international softens. (2) ESPN operating income fell 17% YoY in Q3 on a carriage dispute plus sports-calendar randomness (playoff sweeps), and the segment sits inside a linear-TV bundle in secular decline. Per the finance-skills REIT playbook, P/E and generic reverse-FCF-DCF are the wrong tool here (REIT depreciation and gain/loss accounting break both); the correct anchor is P/Core FFO and the implied cap rate.

  • P/Core FFO: $178.61 ÷ ~$8.175 (FY26 guide midpoint, ex-net-promote) ≈ 21.9x — a premium to the developed-market office-REIT range (12–18x) that the sector playbook flags as normal for a contracted, hyperscale-demand growth REIT rather than a stabilised income REIT; comparable data-center peers command similar-to-higher multiples in the current AI-capex cycle (not independently peer-benchmarked this pass — flagged as a limitation).
  • Reverse dividend-discount sanity check: trailing dividend yield ≈2.7% (Yahoo/d4 snapshot); at an estimated ~8% cost of equity for a REIT running 4.7x leverage, the yield alone implies the market requires only ≈5.3%/yr perpetual distribution growth — well below the double-digit Core FFO/share growth management is currently guiding to for 2026 (and says the backlog supports "through 2027 and 2028"). This is the basis for calling the valuation "in_line" rather than "expensive": the price does not appear to demand the company sustain today's growth rate indefinitely, only that it decelerate toward high-single-digit/low-double-digit — a lower bar than current guidance implies.
  • implied_vs_base: in_line.

Scenario framework (analyst estimate; Core FFO/share compounding + multiple + dividend yield, 3-year horizon): - Bear (30%): hyperscale capex pause, dilution/leverage force multiple compression — Core FFO/share ~3%/yr to $8.93, exit 16x → ~$143 (≈ −4.3%/yr, 3y annualised incl. dividend). - Base (45%): backlog converts as guided, ~9%/yr Core FFO/share growth to $10.59, exit ~20x (slight de-rate from 21.9x) → ~$212 (≈ +8.6%/yr). - Bull (25%): hyperscale demand stays structurally undersupplied, ~13%/yr growth to $11.80, exit 23x → ~$271 (≈ +17.8%/yr).

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull: (1) A record $1.9bn signed-not-commenced backlog (~30% of in-place revenue) gives multi-year visibility that few REITs can match. (2) Leasing economics are accelerating, not decelerating — renewal spreads jumped to 25%+ and 0–1MW-plus-interconnection bookings hit a third consecutive quarterly record. (3) Leverage (4.7x) is stable-to-improving even through the heaviest development phase, evidence of disciplined balance-sheet management alongside the growth.

Bear: (1) Growth is being funded by continuous ATM equity issuance ($2.5bn YTD) — existing holders are diluted every quarter this cycle continues, and per-share metrics (not aggregate FFO) are what matter. (2) An open SEC investigation into the adequacy of DLR's cybersecurity-risk disclosures and disclosure controls is unresolved; the company calls it immaterial but cannot yet prove that. (3) The business is now more exposed to a small number of hyperscale/JV counterparties (the new $3.5bn Northern Virginia stake) — a concentrated bet on AI-capex durability that would re-rate sharply lower if hyperscaler capex plans slow.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Net debt/adjusted EBITDA rises above 5.5x (vs 4.7x now) without a corresponding acceleration in backlog conversion.
  2. FY26 Core FFO/share guidance is cut (vs the current $8.15–$8.20 ex-net-promote range) at the Q3 2026 release (2026-10-22).
  3. Same-capital cash NOI growth falls below 4.0% for two consecutive quarters (vs the 4.25–5.25% FY26 guide).
  4. ATM share issuance for the full year exceeds ~$4bn (vs $2.5bn through Q2) without matching growth in per-share Core FFO — a sign dilution is outrunning growth.
  5. The SEC cybersecurity-disclosure inquiry results in a material enforcement action or restatement.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 2026-10-22 (Q3 2026, after market close). Other: continued hyperscale lease signings post-Q2 quarter-end (already flagged by management), development-yield updates on the $4.25–4.75bn FY26 capex programme, any update on the SEC cybersecurity-disclosure inquiry.

11. Red-flag scan

  • SEC investigation (unresolved): the SEC is investigating the adequacy of Digital Realty's cybersecurity-risk disclosures and related disclosure controls and procedures; the company is cooperating, says it is not aware of any cybersecurity event that prompted the inquiry, and does not expect a material cost — but the matter is open, not closed.
  • Data breach: a law firm (Federman & Sherwood) opened an investigation into a data breach involving unauthorized access to DLR corporate systems around 2025-01-08; status/materiality not independently confirmed this pass.
  • Historical litigation (not current): Digital Realty Trust, Inc. v. Somers, a 2018 U.S. Supreme Court whistleblower-protection case — resolved, included only for completeness, not a live risk.
  • Dilution: $2.5bn of YTD ATM equity issuance is disclosed and not concealed, but is a real, ongoing per-share dilution factor (see §6/§8).
  • No auditor change, restatement, or going-concern language found this pass.

Recency: latest reported period incorporated: Q2 FY2026 (13 weeks ended 2026-08-01), published 2026-08-27 (8-K Ex-99.1 and 10-Q); events checked to the 2026-09-25 close, including the 2026-09-24 by-law 8-K. Reporting basis: consolidated, USD millions unless stated. The P&L figures are continuing operations (the Dollar Tree U.S. and Dollar Tree Canada banners). Family Dollar is shown as discontinued operations in every period presented. Balance-sheet totals are the real consolidated totals on each date. Price used: $114.07 at the 2026-09-25 close (FMP profile endpoint). 187.673M shares from the Q2 FY2026 10-Q, giving a market cap of $21,407M.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Horizon 12–36 months. The Dollar Tree banner itself is sound and fairly priced: comps were positive in all 8 quarters, FCF is solid, lease-adjusted leverage is moderate, and normalized NTM P/E is about 15.7x. But the model's near-top Quality score is largely an accounting artefact. Family Dollar impairments and buybacks shrank the equity base. The latest quarter is also about half one-off (a tariff refund). So the factor composite overstates the case, and the position should be sized below the model's weight.

2. Business in plain English

Dollar Tree runs 9,436 small-box variety stores in the U.S. and Canada (at 2026-08-01, 84.0M selling sq ft). They sell consumables, seasonal goods, party supplies, crafts and household basics to value-seeking shoppers. It is a 1P principal: it buys, owns and marks up its inventory, and occupies leased stores. Its historic edge was a single fixed price point ($1.00, then $1.25). The current strategy is a "multi-price" (Dollar Tree 3.0) assortment. About 6,600 stores had it by Q2 FY2026, and the CEO said in December 2025 that 85% of the assortment is priced at $2 or less. Competitors are Dollar General, Five Below, Walmart and online retail. Family Dollar was sold on 2025-07-05. Before that, the combined company had 16,500 stores (at 2025-02-01).

3. Why the model likes it, and whether that is durable

The pre-registered QVM percentiles are Q 0.962, V 0.917, M 0.836, composite 0.905. The Quality score is largely an artefact. - ROE of about 47% (d4) comes mostly from the equity denominator. ratios.py gives 45.1% on average equity, using actual TTM NI of $1,618.6M. Equity fell from $8,751.5M (FYE Jan-2023) to $3,425.3M (2026-08-01). The bridge, in round numbers: - +$4.4bn of continuing-ops earnings - −$6.3bn of after-tax Family Dollar discontinued-ops losses, most of them impairments: Q4 FY2023 −$2,242.2M and Q4 FY2024 −$4,096.1M - −$3.6bn of buybacks - Continuing-ops ROE on average equity went from ~16% (FY2023) to ~18% (FY2024), ~32% (FY2025) and ~45% (TTM). Over the same run, continuing-ops NI went $1,265.8M → $1,042.5M → $1,225.3M → $1,618.6M. TTM NI is about $1.37bn excluding the after-tax tariff refund. - At the FY2023 average equity level, TTM ROE would be about 20% (17% ex-refund). Roughly 25 of the ~29 points of ROE expansion are denominator. - ratios.py's DuPont credits asset turnover (0.94x → 1.46x). But fixed-asset turnover is flat (3.90x → 3.99x). The turnover gain is the balance sheet shrinking after Family Dollar left, not more productive stores. ROIC excluding goodwill (17.5% TTM, 12.8% FY2025) is the better gauge: good, not elite. - GP/assets of 0.503 uses d4's gross profit of $7,050.7M. That is the FY2025 fiscal-year figure, not TTM (see data conflicts). The asset denominator fell 25% when Family Dollar was deconsolidated. - The Value inputs are flattered too. d4's FCF yield of 10.27% rests on understated capex. The company's own tables give a TTM FCF yield of 9.2% reported and ~7.5% ex-refund. The earnings yield of 7.53% includes a $1.31/share one-off; ex-refund it is about 6.1%. - Momentum (+34.1% 12-1) is real but fading. The stock is $114.07 against a 52-week high of $142.40. It was about $131 on 2026-09-04 (the Form 4 price). - What is durable: comp growth, a modest organic margin gain (TTM EBIT margin about 9.4% ex-refund vs 8.3% in FY2024), cash conversion, and buybacks.

  3. Any cut to FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance (now $7.70–8.05), or FY2027 guidance implying less than 5% ex-refund EPS growth.

dossiers.DOV:
Dover Corporation (DOV) — Diligence Dossier

Agent: F42 (wave-2 standard diligence) | As of: 2026-09-25 close ($191.88, mkt cap ≈ $25.8bn, EV ≈ $27.3bn)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE (12–36 month horizon). A genuine, broadening AI-data-center growth driver (thermal/liquid-cooling and cryogenic connectors) layered on a diversified, low-leverage industrial base, trading at a valuation that a reverse DCF shows is pricing in materially less growth than the company is currently delivering or guiding to. Reservation acknowledged: a real Q2 2026 execution miss in the Climate & Sustainability (refrigeration) segment is a legitimate quality concern, not yet a thesis-breaker.

Thesis (plain English): Dover is a diversified industrial-products company (pumps, thermal/CO2 systems, marking equipment, fueling systems, biopharma components) that is quietly becoming a picks-and-shovels supplier to the AI data-center build-out through its heat-exchanger and cryogenic-connector businesses, and it is available at a below-market multiple with a debt-light balance sheet.

2. Business in plain English

Dover makes and sells industrial equipment and components across five segments: Engineered Products (waste handling, aerospace/defense, environmental), Clean Energy & Fueling (retail fueling systems, cryogenic/hydrogen equipment), Imaging & Identification (marking/coding, digital textile printing), Pumps & Process Solutions (precision pumps, biopharma single-use components, polymer processing), and Climate & Sustainability Technologies (commercial refrigeration, heat exchangers, including SWEP data-center liquid-cooling heat exchangers). It sells mostly to industrial and commercial end-customers (food retail, data centers, biopharma manufacturers, fueling-station operators) and earns money on equipment sales plus a growing aftermarket/service tail. Its competitive position is built on engineered, application-specific products with real switching costs (biopharma single-use systems, precision pumps) rather than commodity manufacturing, though a meaningful minority of revenue (e.g. refrigeration, polymer processing) is more cyclical and execution-sensitive.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Triage (Q10, quality 4/5, growth 4/5, price_vs_growth 4/5, no red flags) cited accelerating revenue growth (6.9%) on data-center thermal-connector demand at only 16.9x NTM P/E with low leverage (0.8x). The v4 quant composite (b1_live_scores.csv) is unusually aligned with this pick: composite 0.466 (decile 5, quintile 3 — mid-pack, not a top-decile quant favourite, but far better than DIS/DLR in this batch), with the strongest score in Value (fam_V 0.694) and reasonable Momentum (0.618); Quality (0.373) and Earnings-momentum/SUE (0.296) are middling — no material conflict between the quant read and the fundamentals. The durable part of the thesis is the data-center liquid-cooling/cryogenic-connector exposure (management is actively doubling SWEP heat-exchanger capacity over 12 months to meet demand it cannot currently fill) and a genuinely broad-based order recovery (bookings +16% YoY, book-to-bill 1.06 across all five segments in Q2 2026 — a "rare breadth event" per management). The artefact risk is that Q2 2026's revenue miss (vs. Street) and organic-growth shortfall were caused by a production throughput failure in refrigeration, not by weak demand — i.e. near-term results understate demand while the capacity problem persists.

  • Q1 2026 release (Apr 2026): FY26 guidance reaffirmed: GAAP EPS $8.92–$9.12 (adjusted $10.45–$10.65), revenue growth 5–7% (organic 3–5%); management flagged it was "driving to the top end" on strong bookings (+24% YoY, book-to-bill 1.2x) and would revisit next quarter.

  • Cash conversion: OCF from continuing operations, 1H 2026 $427.2m vs 1H 2025 $369.8m (+15.5%); capex 1H 2026 $107.6m vs 1H 2025 $109.1m; free cash flow 1H 2026 ≈ $320m (8% of revenue), up 23% YoY, in line with the FY26 FCF guide of 14–16% of revenue (second-half seasonally stronger). Against TTM EBITDA of ≈$1,909m (Yahoo/d4 snapshot, cross-checked against own TTM operating-income build of ≈$1,420m EBIT), net debt/EBITDA ≈ 0.8x — confirms the triage's leverage claim; this is a low-leverage industrial balance sheet with real flexibility for continued bolt-on M&A (the recent cryogenic-connector acquisitions feeding the data-center thesis) or buybacks.

7. Valuation snapshot and reverse DCF

NTM P/E ≈ 16.9x (triage, cross-checked against trailing P/E 22.8x on GAAP TTM EPS, own valuation.py build); EV/EBITDA ≈ 14.3x; FCF yield ≈ 4.6%; dividend yield ≈ 1.3%. No V1 systematic-valuation row exists for DOV (outside V1's original 69-name universe) — v1_verdict = null.

Reverse DCF (own build, scripts/valuation.py, EV $27.3bn, base FCF $1,177m TTM [FY25 annual OCF/capex − 1H25 + 1H26, continuing ops], WACC 8.5%, terminal growth 4.0%, 10-year stage-1): implied FCF growth ≈ 4.1%/year for 10 years, fading to 4%. Given FY26 guided adjusted-EPS growth of ~13–15% at the midpoint, bookings +16–24% YoY, book-to-bill >1.0x across all five segments, and a genuine, still-early data-center liquid-cooling growth driver, a defensible evidence-based base case is ~8–9%/yr FCF growth over the next decade (allowing for reversion from today's cyclical order strength) — the market is pricing in materially less than the base case (implied_vs_base = below). This is the strongest "cheap-for-a-reason-that-isn't-fundamental" read of the three names in this batch.

Scenario framework (analyst estimate; 3-year forward EPS compounding + exit multiple + ~1.3% dividend yield): - Bear (30%): refrigeration execution problems persist, industrial order book cools — EPS flat near $10.20, exit 15x → ~$153/share (≈ −5.9%/yr, 3y annualised). - Base (45%): ~9%/yr adjusted-EPS growth from the FY26 guide midpoint ($10.65) to ~$13.80, exit 18x → ~$248/share (≈ +10.3%/yr). - Bull (25%): data-center liquid-cooling scales faster than capacity doubling plans, ~13%/yr growth to ~$15.35, exit 21x → ~$322/share (≈ +20.2%/yr).

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull: (1) Book-to-bill above 1.0x across all five segments simultaneously in Q2 2026 — genuinely broad-based demand, not one hot end-market. (2) Data-center liquid cooling and cryogenic connectors are a real, underappreciated growth vector; management is capacity-constrained (doubling SWEP heat-exchanger output over 12 months) rather than demand-constrained. (3) Net debt/EBITDA of ~0.8x gives balance-sheet optionality for further bolt-on M&A or buybacks without strain.

Bear: (1) The Q2 2026 refrigeration production-throughput miss is a genuine execution failure management admitted to directly ("that's on me" — CEO) — if it recurs elsewhere in a five-segment portfolio, the "diversification" argument weakens. (2) A jury returned a ~$58.9m verdict against the (since-divested) Environmental Solutions Group business in June 2025 for breach of contract/fiduciary-duty claims; post-trial motions and a possible Seventh Circuit appeal are pending — a real, though bounded, contingent liability. (3) Order-to-revenue conversion questions from analysts (bookings +16% not yet translating proportionally into revenue) suggest some near-term forecasting/visibility risk even as management expresses confidence.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Climate & Sustainability Technologies segment organic growth or margin deteriorates for a second consecutive quarter (vs the Q2 2026 refrigeration-driven miss), indicating the production problem is structural, not a one-quarter event.
  2. FY26 adjusted EPS guidance (currently $10.55–$10.75) is cut at the Q3 2026 release (2026-10-22).
  3. Book-to-bill falls below 1.0x for two consecutive quarters (vs 1.06x–1.2x in H1 2026).
  4. Net debt/EBITDA rises above 2.0x (vs ≈0.8x now) without a value-accretive acquisition justifying it.
  5. The $58.9m ESG jury verdict is upheld on appeal and expands materially beyond the awarded amount, or triggers additional related claims.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Dover's subsidiaries also carry the ordinary run of waste-disposal-site, product-liability, patent, employment and commercial disputes disclosed in the 10-K — nothing beyond normal course identified.

DPZ — Domino's Pizza, Inc.

1. Verdict: INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Thesis horizon 24–36 months. High-quality, asset-light franchisor trading near the low end of its own valuation history, but FY2026 guidance was already cut once this year, U.S. same-store sales are barely positive, and the buyback-funded, negative-equity capital structure leaves less room for error than the "cheap franchise" framing suggests.

2. Business in plain English. Domino's is the world's largest pizza company by sales, operating almost entirely through franchisees (only ~2% of the U.S. system is company-owned). It earns royalties on franchisee retail sales (~5.5–7% of sales) plus supply-chain margin from selling food, boxes and equipment to its own U.S. franchisees, and collects a smaller royalty from ~100 international master franchisees who run the stores abroad. Competitive position: #1 or #2 pizza QSR share in most markets it operates in, built on delivery speed/technology (10–30 minute promise, app/AI ordering) and the lowest menu prices in category.

3. Why the model likes it. b1 factor percentiles (as of the live snapshot): quality composite 96th percentile (gp/assets 99th, OCF/assets 99th, accruals 90th — very clean, capital-light earnings), value 62nd percentile driven by earnings/FCF yield (ep 87th, fcfp 66th), but momentum only 1st percentile (stock down ~17% over the year per triage) and book/price 1st percentile (negative tangible book from buybacks, not informative here). The quality signal is durable — it reflects the franchise royalty model, not a one-off — but the momentum/value combination is the market pricing in the deceleration confirmed below, not simply "value in a franchise-quality name" as triage's reason stated.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet. FCF conversion is strong and clean: FCF (OCF−capex) ran $147–176mm/quarter in the last five quarters, funding dividends (~$0.6–1.5mm→$60–68mm/quarter as the payout ratio rose) and large buybacks ($75–235mm/quarter). SBC is not separately broken out in these tags but is modest for the sector (asset-light model, few employees relative to system sales). Capital structure is the central feature to underwrite, not a footnote: Domino's funds itself via whole-business securitization notes against franchise royalty cash flows, and stockholders' equity has been negative since at least 2024 (−$3.98bn at 2026-06-14, from −$3.96bn a year earlier) because buybacks have been funded partly with debt against a cash-generative but non-owned store base. Debt + capital-lease obligations were $4.82bn at FY2025-end (2025-12-28), down slightly from $4.98bn a year earlier — i.e., leverage is high (triage's flagged ~4.8x is consistent with debt/EBITDA-proxy math here) but stable-to-declining, and this is a structural feature of the franchisor model (shared by Wendy's, Restaurant Brands, Planet Fitness), not distress. The risk is that continued buybacks at the current pace (~$800mm–$1bn/yr annualized against a $9.66bn market cap) require the securitized royalty pool to keep growing; a same-store-sales stall for several quarters would test that assumption. Share count has fallen ~2.9%/yr, which is currently the single largest driver of EPS growth.

7. Valuation snapshot. Price $292.14 (2026-09-25 close); market cap $9.66bn; EV $14.65bn. TTM diluted EPS $17.63 (sum of last 4 quarters) → TTM P/E 16.6x (cross-checks to Yahoo's 16.56x). Forward (consensus NTM) EPS $20.83 → forward P/E 14.0x — not independently recalendarized, so per the lead's known flaw (mixed fiscal-year forward P/E), treat this as directional only. Own 10-year history: Domino's traded 20–30x P/E during its 2015–2019 high-growth phase and has compressed to the mid-teens as U.S./international comp growth slowed; 14–16.6x sits toward the low end (cheap-looking) of that range. No V1 row exists for DPZ (outside the top-70 quant universe that got systematic valuation coverage), so v1_verdict is null and there is nothing to reconcile. A simple reverse Gordon-growth back-out (14x forward P/E, ~8.5% assumed cost of equity given beta 0.95) implies the market is pricing roughly 1–2% perpetual growth — below even a conservative base case (see §8). That gap is the basis for the INCLUDE-SMALL call, but it should be read as a rough sense-check, not a formal DCF (the valuation agent's V1/V1X model does not cover this name).

8. Bull case / Bear case. Bull: (1) International recovers with 2026 World Cup tailwind and DPE stabilization; (2) buyback-driven EPS compounding continues at high-single/low-double-digit even with modest comp growth; (3) multiple re-rates back toward its 18–20x mid-cycle range as growth reaccelerates. Bear: (1) U.S. comps stay near-flat (Q2'26 U.S. SSS +0.1%, weakest in over a year, missed consensus of +0.62%) as QSR competition and value-menu wars intensify; (2) leverage keeps rising to fund buybacks without matching royalty-pool growth, forcing a buyback slowdown that removes the main EPS-growth lever; (3) the DPE securities litigation (below) signals the international master-franchisee model has real execution risk, not just a one-off news item.

9. Kill criteria (measurable) -- what would break the thesis. 1. U.S. same-store sales negative for two consecutive quarters. 2. FY operating-income-growth guidance cut again below the current mid-to-high-single-digit range. 3. Debt + capital-lease obligations / EBITDA-proxy rises above 6.0x (from ~4.8x currently). 4. International same-store sales (ex-FX) negative for two consecutive quarters. 5. Quarterly buyback pace cut by more than half from the trailing-4-quarter average (signal of FCF/leverage stress in the securitization structure).

dossiers.DRI:
DRI — Darden Restaurants, Inc.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE (full weight) — thesis horizon 12–36 months. The cleanest evidence base of the three names reviewed in this batch: a modest but genuine valuation discount to own history and peers, a reverse-DCF that prices growth well below what the company has actually delivered, four consecutive quarters of guidance that was met or modestly raised (never cut), broad-based positive same-restaurant sales across every segment, and no unresolved securities litigation or regulatory-fine overhang. The one adverse fact that must be surfaced prominently: the most recently reported quarter (Q1 FY2027, filed one day before this dossier's cutoff) showed operating margin compress ~116bps year-over-year even as sales grew — a real, primary-source-verified data point that tempers, without breaking, the thesis.

2. Business in plain English

Darden owns and operates full-service ("sit-down") restaurants under nine brands — Olive Garden and LongHorn Steakhouse are by far the largest, alongside Cheddar's Scratch Kitchen, Yard House, Ruth's Chris Steak House, The Capital Grille, Chuy's (acquired 2024), Seasons 52 and Eddie V's — comprising 2,218 company-owned restaurants as of August 2026. It makes money on food/beverage sold to diners less the cost of ingredients, labour, restaurant occupancy and marketing; unlike many restaurant peers it owns and operates almost all of its restaurants directly (limited franchising), so it captures the full economics (and the full capital intensity) of the dining-room model rather than a royalty stream. Its moat is brand recognition, purchasing/supply-chain scale across ~2,200 units, and site selection built over decades.

3. Why the model likes it — and is it durable?

B1 composite is top decile (live_rank 46/~2,300; composite percentile ~91%; gates: no disqualifying-red-flag gate is netted into this score — see §11 for the separate red-flag check). Family drivers: Earnings momentum (fam_S ≈0.93, very high) — SUE has been consistently positive; Momentum (fam_M ≈0.72); Quality (fam_Q ≈0.65); Value (fam_V ≈0.47, mid-pack) — DRI is not a deep-value name, it is a modest discount to peers/history.

Durability check: the earnings-momentum signal is corroborated by four straight quarters of guidance that management met or narrowed upward (§5), and same-restaurant sales that were positive in every segment in the two most recently reported quarters (Q4 FY26: Olive Garden +2.4%, LongHorn +9.5%, Fine Dining +1.9%, Other +4.6%; Q1 FY27: Olive Garden +1.0%, LongHorn +6.8%, Fine Dining +1.0%, Other +4.5%, comparable-calendar basis) — a genuinely broad-based result, not one brand carrying the average. The counter-evidence, which I surface rather than average away: LongHorn's segment margin fell ~71bps YoY in FY2026 even as its sales grew +13.1% (fastest-growing brand, but its incremental sales are not flowing through at the historical rate), and Fine Dining's segment margin fell ~92bps. Consolidated operating margin in the single most recent quarter (Q1 FY27) was down ~116bps YoY. The SUE/momentum signal is real, but the margin-durability question is more open than the sales-growth headline suggests.

5. Guidance track record (verbatim, last four releases)

This is a track record of accuracy and reliability rather than dramatic beats: guided ranges were narrowed toward, and actual results landed inside, the guided range in three of the last three cases checked; no guidance cut was found in any of the four releases reviewed. Per CFO Raj Vennam (Q4/FY26 release): "Since 2019, we have delivered 9% annualized adjusted EBITDA growth."

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • FCF conversion: volatile quarter to quarter (FCF/NI ranged 0.50x–1.47x over the last 8 quarters) but the two most recent quarters (Q4 FY26 0.94x, Q1 FY27 0.42x) show a downward trend, driven by working-capital timing (§4) and rising capex, not by a change in reported profitability.
  • SBC: modest, 0.34%–1.26% of quarterly sales (Q1 FY25's 1.26% was an outlier, likely annual-grant timing); not a material distortion.
  • GAAP vs adjusted: DRI discloses clean, itemised reconciliations every quarter (Chuy's integration costs, restaurant-closure/impairment charges, the Olive Garden Canada sale gain, tax items) — a transparency positive; I have used both reported and adjusted figures throughout and labelled which is which.
  • Balance sheet — a real, quantified deterioration worth watching: short-term debt + current portion of long-term debt jumped from $693.6m (2026-05-31, fiscal year-end) to $979.7m (2026-08-30), a $286.1m increase in one quarter, funding the capital-return gap noted in §4. Long-term debt $1,636.1m (roughly flat). Total gross debt ≈$2,615.8m, up from ≈$2,331.3m at fiscal year-end — a ~12% quarter-over-quarter increase. Cash is small and stable (~$220m). Retained earnings are negative: $(259.5)m as of 2026-08-30 (worsened from $(108.4)m at FYE), i.e. cumulative dividends + buybacks now exceed cumulative historical net income — common for a mature, buyback-heavy restaurant compounder, and the mechanical reason DRI's ROE (54.7% per the B1 dataset) looks extremely high: it is flattered by a shrunk equity base, not by extraordinary returns on capital, and should be read alongside segment-level margins (§4) rather than at face value, per the stock-analysis playbook's own warning about ROE manufactured by buybacks.
  • Net debt/EBITDA: using FY2027 guided EBITDA ($2.26–2.29bn) against ≈$2.6bn gross debt less ~$220m cash ≈ $2.4bn net debt → ≈1.0–1.1x — still low in absolute terms, but the trend (rising within a single quarter, debt-funded buybacks exceeding FCF) is the item to monitor, not the level.
  • M&A: Chuy's Holdings acquired for ~$605m enterprise value / $649.1m total consideration, $37.50/share all-cash, announced 2024-07-17, closed 2024-10-11 — now 112 locations (from 108 a year ago), fully integrated into the "Other Business" segment and no longer flagged as a same-restaurant-sales exclusion after Q4 FY2026 (its 16-month anniversary). Bahama Breeze wind-down: the brand (28 units mid-2025) is being fully exited — ~14 locations closed around 2026-04-05, the remaining ~14 being converted to other Darden brands through Q4 FY2027; only 10 Bahama Breeze units remained at 2026-08-30. This is a small, well-telegraphed, already-substantially-executed restructuring, not a fresh risk.

7. Valuation snapshot — reconciliation with V1

V1 verdict: attractive (score 0.35/1.0). NTM P/E 17.2x vs. DRI's own 165-month history — 27th percentile, a modest but real discount — and vs. peer median 18.9x (CMG/DPZ/MCD/SBUX). As with ABNB, I flag this peer set as heterogeneous: CMG is a much higher-growth, higher-multiple pure-play with a different unit-economics model (no full bar/table service), MCD and SBUX are global, franchise/royalty-heavy models with far less capital intensity than DRI's mostly-company-owned estate, and DPZ is franchise-heavy pizza delivery — DRI is the only "true" full-service, company-owned comparable in its own peer list. The resulting ~9% discount to that blended median is directionally fine to use but should not be read as a precise like-for-like gap.

Reverse-DCF implied 10-year growth is +2.7%, against consensus FY1 growth of +6.1% and delivered 5-year/10-year CAGRs of +12.9%/+6.7% — the market is pricing DRI for growth well below both what it has delivered and what the Street expects next year, which is the core of the "attractive" case and one I can corroborate: FY2027 guided total-sales growth (3.0–4.1% ex-53rd-week effects) and same-restaurant-sales growth (2.5–3.5%) are themselves modest, in-line-to-slightly-above the reverse-DCF-implied rate, not requiring any acceleration.

A genuine data conflict I flag rather than pass over silently: V1's own scenario margin_assumed values are bear 5.2% / base 7.8% / bull 9.2% — all three below the TTM operating margin V1 itself uses elsewhere in the same record (ebit_margin_used = 11.98%, which I independently confirm from D3/GAAP: $1,582.8m TTM EBIT ÷ $13,210.9m TTM revenue = 11.98%). I cannot fully resolve from the data available whether this is (a) an intentional, conservative fade toward a longer-run/mid-cycle margin (in which case the "attractive" verdict is, if anything, understated — even V1's bull case doesn't require margin expansion above what's already been delivered), or (b) a scenario-construction basis mismatch (e.g., a segment-profit-style margin excluding D&A/real-estate items being compared against a different EBIT base). Given the bear/base/bull returns V1 reports (−17.6%/+7.4%/+22.5% annualised) are still directionally sensible and roughly consistent with the multiple/growth inputs, I treat this as a modelling note for the lead/V1 agent to confirm rather than a reason to override the verdict, and record it in data_conflicts.

My view: consistent = true, dossier_view = cheap (modest). Base case assumes revenue growth 6.6%/yr (below the 5-year delivered 12.9%, in line with the 10-year delivered 6.7% — not aggressive) and an exit multiple of 20.1x (close to today's 17.2x and below the peer median 18.9x — a small, not heroic, re-rating). Combined with the guidance-accuracy track record in §5 and the broad-based same-restaurant-sales strength in §3, I agree with V1's "attractive" call and do not see a basis to downgrade it to "fair" — the main things working against the thesis (margin compression in the two most recent segment/consolidated readings, and the debt-funded capital return in Q1 FY27) are real but, on the evidence available, second-order relative to the valuation discount and demonstrated sales/guidance durability.

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull (3): 1. Every reportable segment posted positive same-restaurant sales in each of the last two quarters — a broad, not single-brand-dependent, recovery, and guidance has been met or modestly raised for four straight releases with no cut. 2. Valuation is a genuine, if modest, discount to both own history (27th percentile) and the reverse-DCF-implied growth rate is well below what the company has actually delivered over 5 and 10 years. 3. Disciplined, well-disclosed capital allocation: dividend raised 8% (to $1.62/quarter) in June 2026, a new $1.5bn buyback authorization, and a small, already-largely-executed brand rationalisation (Bahama Breeze exit) rather than a large, uncertain restructuring.

Bear (3): 1. Consolidated operating margin fell ~116bps YoY in the single most recently reported quarter (Q1 FY27), and LongHorn's and Fine Dining's full-year segment margins each fell 71–92bps in FY2026 despite strong sales growth — cost inflation (labour, restaurant expense, D&A) is outrunning sales growth in the two brands driving most of the comp strength. 2. Q1 FY27 free cash flow fell 39% YoY, and the company funded capital returns (dividends + buybacks, $405m) well in excess of free cash flow ($98.9m) with a $286m single-quarter increase in short-term debt — a real, quantifiable, and newly-emerging capital-discipline question, not yet a crisis (net debt/EBITDA still ~1x) but worth a full-year read before dismissing. 3. Ordinary industry-standard tip-credit/wage litigation (One Fair Wage-affiliated FLSA claims over the $2.13/hour tipped minimum wage) is an ongoing, if not unusual-for-the-industry, legal cost and headline-risk item.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Consolidated same-restaurant sales growth turns negative for two consecutive quarters (currently +3.1–4.6% depending on calendar basis).
  2. Olive Garden (the largest segment, ~42% of FY26 sales) same-restaurant sales turn negative for two consecutive quarters — it is already the slowest-growing segment (+1.0–2.4%).
  3. Full-year diluted-EPS guidance is cut versus the prior quarter's range (no cut found in the four releases reviewed).
  4. Net debt / TTM EBITDA rises above 2.0x (currently ≈1.0–1.1x, but rising within the most recent quarter).
  5. Cumulative incremental Chuy's-integration or Bahama-Breeze-wind-down charges exceed $50 million beyond what is already disclosed in the FY2026 10-K/8-Ks (scope-creep signal on the two known restructuring items).

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: Q2 FY2027, estimated mid-to-late December 2026 (historical pattern: Dec 15–19 in prior years; not yet confirmed by the company).
  • Full closure/conversion of the remaining ~10 Bahama Breeze locations, expected to complete by Q4 FY2027 (May 2027).
  • Chuy's now past its 16-month "same-restaurant-sales inclusion" anniversary (Q4 FY2026) — FY2027 comps will, for the first time, include Chuy's on a like-for-like basis.
  • Annual shareholder meeting was held 2026-09-23 (Item 5.07 8-K filed 2026-09-24) — voting results not reviewed in this dossier; no indication of a contested vote in the filing index.

11. Red-flag scan

  • Wage/labour litigation: One Fair Wage (a restaurant-workers advocacy group) sued Darden alleging FLSA and state wage-and-hour violations tied to the tipped-minimum-wage model ($2.13/hour federal tip credit); an associated race-discrimination claim was dropped, wage claims reportedly remain. This is a real, ongoing legal item but structurally common across the full-service restaurant industry (tip-credit litigation is not unique to Darden) rather than a company-specific governance failure.
  • Debt-funded capital return in the most recent quarter: see §6/§8 — a real, quantified, newly-emerging item to track for a second consecutive quarter before treating it as a trend.
  • 53rd-week / fiscal-calendar effects: real and disclosed by the company itself; already addressed via the "comparable calendar" same-restaurant-sales metric — a modelling nuance, not a governance or accounting-quality concern.
  • No auditor change, restatement, going-concern language, or SEC/DOJ investigation was identified in the filings and news reviewed for this dossier.

dossiers.DVA:
DaVita Inc. (DVA) — Diligence Dossier

Agent: F15 (replaces F9, which hung before writing anything — this is a fresh review) | As of: 2026-09-25 close | Price: $178.47

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — thesis horizon 24–36 months.

DaVita is statistically cheap (10.8x NTM P/E, 9.6th percentile of its own 177-month history) and its earnings-per-share growth has genuinely compounded. But that growth is majority financially engineered (debt-funded buybacks against a negative-equity balance sheet), not organic — normalized non-acquired treatment growth was −0.6% in FY2025 and only +0.1–0.3% in H1 2026. Named reservation: leverage (3.37x company-defined ratio, rising) on a negative-equity balance sheet, concentrated in a single ~45%-owner (Berkshire Hathaway) that has been trimming even as its percentage stake mechanically rises, at 44% one-year volatility — the highest of any name in this batch and near the mandate's 45% ceiling.

2. Business in plain English

DaVita operates ~2,700 outpatient dialysis centers in the US (plus a smaller international business), providing life-sustaining hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis to patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). About two-thirds of US patients are reimbursed at government (Medicare/Medicaid) rates; the remaining roughly one-third of revenue comes from commercial insurers, who pay materially higher rates per treatment — this small commercial cohort disproportionately drives profitability (source 8). Competitive position: a near-duopoly with Fresenius Medical Care in US dialysis, with high switching costs (dialysis is a recurring, life-critical service tied to a physical location) and real regulatory/reimbursement dependence.

3. Why the model likes it

B1/live-rank 14 (the highest-ranked of this batch's three names) reflects strong per-share earnings growth and a very low valuation multiple. The quant signal is partly an artefact of aggressive, debt-funded share buybacks compressing the share count rather than pure organic quality — real caution is warranted before reading the composite score as "the business is accelerating." Treatment-volume growth (the true organic-demand metric) has been flat to slightly negative through the period reviewed.

5. Guidance track record (last 4 releases, verbatim ranges)
