HIG — The Hartford Insurance Group — Fundamental Diligence Dossier

1. Verdict: INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Thesis horizon 12–24 months. Top-decile quality/earnings-momentum quant score and a genuinely strong core-underwriting franchise, but recent GAAP earnings are inflated by one-off items (tax benefit, reinsurance commutation gain), the Business Insurance underlying combined ratio is drifting up off a cyclical low, general-liability/commercial-auto/legacy-A&E reserves are adding back unfavorable development, and sell-side FY1 EPS estimates are being cut hard (17 down vs. 2 up in 30 days) as the pending Hartford Funds divestiture removes an earnings stream from models. HIG was a v3 "Supporting"-tier holding (4.0% weight in the final 14-name portfolio; 12.0% in the earlier 10-name v1 cut) — v4 would keep it, but at reduced conviction/size versus v3's treatment, not as a core position.

2. Business in plain English

The Hartford is a US commercial-focused property & casualty insurer with three segments: Business Insurance (workers' comp, commercial property/liability, small/middle-market/large accounts, Global Specialty), Personal Insurance (auto/home, sold mainly through the AARP affinity program and independent agents), and Employee Benefits (group life/disability). It earns money from underwriting profit (premiums minus claims and expenses) plus investment income on the "float" between collecting premiums and paying claims. It is a top-5 US commercial-lines writer with a strong small-commercial franchise and a differentiated AARP-branded personal-lines niche. In June 2026 it agreed to sell its Hartford Funds asset-management arm to Wellington Management, refocusing the company purely on insurance underwriting.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1 composite score 0.886 (decile 10/10, live_rank 20, inside the live top-30). Driven mainly by Quality (fam_Q top quartile: pct_roe 76th pctile, pct_ocf_a 85th) and earnings momentum/SUE (pct_sue 89th pctile; beats 6 of last 8 quarters, avg surprise +9.3%). Price momentum is a weak spot, not a strength (pct_mom_12_1 only 33rd pctile), and book-to-price is low (17th pctile — HIG is not statistically cheap). Partly artefact: GAAP ROE and recent EPS growth are flattered by non-recurring items (see §6). Management's own stated trailing-12-month core-earnings ROE of 20.3% (Q1 2026 release) is the more durable underlying number, but even that sits atop several years of below-average catastrophe experience and favorable-leaning reserve development — a full-cycle test has not occurred recently.

5. Guidance track record

HIG does not issue quantitative forward EPS, combined-ratio, or revenue guidance in any of the last four earnings releases (Q2'26, Q1'26, Q4'25, Q3'25) — standard for P&C underwriters given catastrophe unpredictability. Each release closes with a generic safe-harbor statement and qualitative CEO commentary only (e.g., Q4'25: "enters 2026 with momentum," no numbers). No raise/maintain/cut can be assessed because no numerical guidance exists to compare — stated per instructions rather than inferred.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • One-off items distorting recent GAAP results: (a) $251M income-tax benefit in Q2'26 tied to the Hartford Funds sale (tax basis vs. GAAP carrying value); (b) $318M pre-tax discontinued-operations income in Q2'26 (Hartford Funds, up from $57M in Q2'25); (c) $497M pre-tax gain / $393M net-income increase expected in Q3 2026 from commuting a legacy asbestos & environmental reinsurance treaty with National Indemnity Company (Berkshire Hathaway) — the treaty (in place since Dec-2016) was terminated Sept 25, 2026 alongside settlement of a confidential arbitration; Hartford received $1.12bn cash. This is a real cash gain but it also removes A&E reinsurance cover HIG has relied on since 2016 — future adverse A&E development now falls more directly on HIG's own balance sheet. (d) $165M A&E reserve increase in Q4'25 and a further $70M increase in Q1'26 for legacy sexual-molestation/abuse exposures (1970s–80s policies, incl. one religious-institution bankruptcy settlement) — a recurring, not one-time, category of adverse surprise.
  • Reserve development is genuinely mixed, not uniformly favorable: Q1'26 Business Insurance PYD was $30M net unfavorable (vs. $51M favorable in Q1'25); both Q1'26 and Q2'26 releases cite "increase in general liability and commercial automobile reserves" partially offsetting favorable workers'-comp/personal-lines releases — the classic social-inflation pattern the insurance sector playbook flags.
  • Net investment income rising on both higher yields and a large limited-partnership swing (Q2'26 LP income $114M @ 7.6% annualized yield vs. $13M @ 1.0% in Q2'25 — welcome but lumpy/non-repeatable at that rate).
  • Capital: Book value/share ex-AOCI $78.91 (Jun-26) vs. $73.62 (Dec-25), +7.2%. Returned $615M to shareholders in Q2'26 ($450M buybacks + $165M dividends); new $4.2bn buyback authorized Aug 1 2026 through 2028 (+27% vs. prior program), explicitly part-funded by Hartford Funds sale proceeds.
  • Governance: New independent director Priscilla Almodovar (ex-CEO, Fannie Mae) appointed to the board effective Sept 1, 2026, joining Audit and Finance/Investment/Risk committees — routine strengthening, no departure disclosed alongside it.

7. Valuation snapshot (from v1 pipeline, 2026-09-25 close)

P/B 1.75x vs. peer median 1.79x (P&C peer set) — 77th percentile of HIG's own 14-year P/B history: fair, not cheap. Justified-P/B math implies the market is pricing an 11.8% sustainable ROE, vs. actual TTM ROE 22.2% (GAAP, one-off-boosted) / 20.3% core — i.e., the price already assumes today's elevated profitability will not persist at face value. V1 base-case 3-year annualized return +2.7% (bear −15.1%, bull +24.6%); V1 verdict "fair."

8. Bull case

  1. Core-earnings ROE of ~20% is genuinely strong for a diversified P&C/EB insurer, with Business Insurance still growing written premium +5–9% with positive (if moderating) renewal pricing.
  2. Hartford Funds sale + National Indemnity commutation simplify the balance sheet, bring in ~$1.1bn+ cash, and fund an enlarged, multi-year buyback — a credible capital-return runway.
  3. Personal Insurance has swung from a 106.1 combined ratio (Q1'25, CA-wildfire-affected) to consistently sub-90 through 2025–26 — a real underwriting turnaround in a historically weaker segment.

9. Bear case

  1. Business Insurance underlying combined ratio is drifting up (88.0→89.3 YoY) exactly as sell-side analysts describe a softening commercial pricing cycle — the tailwind that drove the last two years of beats may be fading.
  2. General liability, commercial auto and legacy A&E/molestation reserves are adding unfavorable development in the two most recent quarters — a first-order, evidenced risk (not hypothetical) for a company with long-tail casualty exposure, and one that will bite harder now that a chunk of A&E reinsurance cover was just commuted away.
  3. Reported GAAP EPS growth is substantially a function of one-off tax/reinsurance/discontinued-ops items; 17 of 19 sell-side FY1 EPS revisions in the last 30 days were cuts, chiefly because the Funds-sale removes a profitable, capital-light earnings stream from forward models.

10. Key risks & kill criteria

  1. BI underlying combined ratio >91% for two consecutive quarters (cycle-turn confirmation).
  2. Adverse general-liability/commercial-auto/A&E reserve development >$150M in any single quarter.
  3. Hartford Funds sale is delayed, renegotiated, or terminated (watch for another Item 1.02/1.01 8-K).
  4. Core-earnings ROE <15% for two consecutive quarters (vs. 20.3% TTM stated by management).
  5. Net FY1 sell-side EPS revisions stay negative for two more months without a corresponding guidance/fundamental offset.

11. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: about 2026-10-29 (Q3 2026; an estimate from the data snapshot, not yet confirmed by the company. Corrected 2026-09-26 after data audit DA5; one third-party calendar shows 2026-10-26) — will show the first full-quarter impact of the $497M National Indemnity commutation gain.
  • Hartford Funds/Wellington deal closing — timing not disclosed in materials reviewed; monitor for a closing 8-K.
  • $4.2bn buyback program runs through 2028.

12. Red-flag scan

No auditor change, material weakness, restatement, or going-concern language surfaced in the materials reviewed (full 10-K risk-factor diff and Form 4 insider-trading pattern were not exhaustively pulled given the time budget — scope limitation, not a clean bill of health). The Item 1.02 8-K (Sept 25, 2026) is a negotiated resolution of a legacy reinsurance arbitration dispute with Berkshire's National Indemnity — cash-positive for HIG, but confirms the company carried, and now bears more directly, real legacy A&E tail risk. No SEC/DOJ investigation, short-seller report, or litigation beyond routine/legacy claims found in the sources reviewed.

HST — Host Hotels & Resorts, Inc.

Most recent period incorporated: Q2 2026 10-Q (period ended 2026-06-30, filed 2026-08-07) and the Q2 2026 earnings release (8-K Ex-99.1, filed 2026-08-05); checked SEC EDGAR (10-K/10-Q/8-K index) and FMP news for events to 2026-09-25. No 8-K or transcript dated after 2026-08-05 was found in the sources checked.

Basis: all figures are consolidated GAAP (Host Hotels & Resorts, Inc., the REIT parent, together with its operating partnership), USD, reported in millions except per-share amounts, as filed with the SEC. Non-GAAP figures (FFO, Adjusted FFO, EBITDAre, Adjusted EBITDAre) are the company's own NAREIT-based definitions and are labeled every time they appear.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE. Thesis horizon 12–24 months (shorter than the standard 12–36 because FY2027 comparisons look genuinely hard — see §3/§9). One-sentence reason: the operating business is in a real, primary-source-confirmed beat-and-raise cycle on the metrics that actually matter for a lodging REIT (comparable RevPAR and Adjusted FFO/share), the balance sheet was upgraded to Baa2 (Moody's) with no 2026 debt maturities, and the reverse-DCF shows the market is pricing in only ~1.7% annual FCF growth — but the model's #1-of-503 ranking is partly an accounting artefact (see below) and the stock's own excellent 2026 comps (boosted by the FIFA World Cup) make 2027 a harder year to beat.

2. Business in plain English

Host is the largest lodging REIT in the US: it owns (does not operate) roughly 70–80 upper-upscale and luxury hotels under brands such as Marriott, Ritz-Carlton, Four Seasons, Hyatt, Westin and 1 Hotels, concentrated in top RevPAR markets (Hawaii/Maui, Orlando, San Francisco, NYC, DC). Third-party operators run day-to-day hotel operations under management contracts; Host collects the hotel-level economics (rooms, F&B, other) net of operating costs and management fees. Revenue mix in FY2025 was roughly 61% transient, 34% group, 5% contract business. A small, recurring side business sells condominium units at a development adjacent to the Four Seasons Orlando (Disney World) — $99m of revenue in FY2025, guided to contribute another ~$20–25m to FY2026 net income. Competitive position rests on owning irreplaceable, high-barrier-to-entry real estate in supply-constrained luxury/resort markets, not on operating skill (which sits with the brand operators).

3. Why the model likes it — and whether that's durable

Preliminary quant rank #1 of 503 in the whole universe (composite 0.954; Q 0.954, V 0.917, M 0.99 — essentially the maximum momentum score). This is partly durable, partly an artefact, and the two need to be separated:

  • Durable part: comparable-hotel RevPAR growth has been raised, not cut, in each of the last four quarterly guidance updates (see §5), Adjusted FFO/share has grown in 4 of the last 5 quarters, Moody's upgraded HST to Baa2 (stable) during FY2025, and there is no 2026 debt maturity wall. That is a real, multi-quarter, primary-source-confirmed operating improvement, not a one-quarter beat.
  • Artefact part: GAAP net income and EPS — which likely feed the model's Quality-family inputs (ROE, accruals, cash-flow-to-assets) — were inflated by large, disclosed non-operating gains in both of the last two fiscal years: FY2025 GAAP net income included a $148m "Other gains (losses)" line (FY2024: $0m) from asset/condo sales, partially offset by $86m less insurance-settlement gains than FY2024; and Q1 2026 alone booked a $242m pre-tax gain on the sale of three hotels (St. Regis Houston + two Four Seasons properties), pushing Q1 2026 diluted EPS to $0.72 — roughly double every other quarter in the trailing eight (range $0.12–$0.35) — and GAAP net income up 99.6% YoY. Data conflict, quantified: recomputing ROE from the FY2025 10-K (ratios.py, sourced inputs) gives 11.2%, versus the 16.1% ROE figure feeding the preliminary Q score (lead_prelim_rank.csv) — consistent with that quant input being a trailing-twelve-month figure that captures the Q1 2026 gain quarter. The Quality score should be discounted accordingly; the Momentum and Value scores are less affected (RevPAR/AFFO-driven operating momentum is real, and the Value score is priced off cash flow, not the disposition gains).

8. Bull case and bear case

Bull (3 points, evidence-based) 1. Four straight quarters of raised guidance on comparable RevPAR and AFFO/share (§5), with Q2 2026 RevPAR growth accelerating to +7.0% YoY, partly FIFA-World-Cup-driven but "broad-based" per management across hosting and non-hosting markets alike. 2. Investment-grade balance sheet strengthening, not weakening: Moody's upgrade to Baa2 (stable) in FY2025, no 2026 debt maturities, $3.6bn of liquidity, and disciplined capital recycling (selling lower-growth assets, e.g. two Four Seasons properties, at gains, into buybacks and a special dividend rather than empire-building). 3. Reverse-DCF shows only ~1.7% FCF growth priced in for a decade — a low bar relative to the actual RevPAR trajectory, leaving room for multiple expansion or continued beats without needing heroic assumptions.

Bear (3 points, evidence-based) 1. 2027 comp risk, in management's own words: FY2026's acceleration is flattered by the FIFA World Cup (explicitly cited in the Q2 2026 release) and management itself guides that "year-over-year comparisons are expected to moderate" in H2 2026 — FY2027 will lap an unusually strong RevPAR year with no repeat event. 2. The quant model's #1-of-503 rank leans partly on a Quality/ROE signal that this dossier shows is inflated by one-off disposition gains in both FY2025 ($148m) and Q1 2026 ($242m) — sourced ROE (11.2%, FY2025) is ~500bps below the model's TTM input (16.1%), so some of the "cheap and high-quality" signal is an artefact, not durable. 3. Lodging is a discretionary, macro-sensitive business; comparable-hotel EBITDA margin has been under pressure from wage inflation in several recent quarters, group booking volume has been described as "soft" repeatedly across FY2025 releases, and Maui properties were still described as "recovering" from the 2023 wildfires as late as the Q4 2025 release — a multi-year drag not yet fully resolved.

Bull: (1) Big Bets (AI-driven "done-for-you" tax, bookkeeping, Mailchimp-Intuit-Assist) grew 34%/yr and are now 30% of FY26 revenue — a second growth engine scaling from a larger base each year. (2) FY27 guide (+9–10% revenue, +23–24% non-GAAP EPS) at a 12x non-GAAP forward multiple leaves room for material re-rating if executed. (3) Buybacks have shrunk the share count every year since FY24 while still funding double-digit dividend growth.

Bear: (1) Consumer-facing generative-AI tax/bookkeeping tools (ChatGPT-style "just do my taxes/books") are a structural threat to TurboTax/QuickBooks pricing power that has not yet shown up in the numbers but could arrive discontinuously. (2) Two workforce restructurings in 24 months (Jul-2024 ~1,800; May-2026 ~3,000, 17% of staff) signal either aggressive AI-driven cost-cutting or execution/cost-structure problems — the CEO gave contradicting public explanations for the second one (Section 11). (3) SBC at 9.6% of revenue means reported non-GAAP EPS growth overstates the cash return actually available to shareholders before buybacks.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. TurboTax or Credit Karma segment revenue growth turns negative for 2 consecutive quarters (direct evidence of AI-driven disintermediation, not just deceleration).
  2. Non-GAAP operating margin compresses >300bps YoY for 2 consecutive quarters.
  3. A third major workforce restructuring (>5% of headcount) announced within 24 months of the May-2026 cut.
  4. Full-year revenue or non-GAAP EPS guidance is cut (vs. the prior range) at any of the next 4 quarterly releases (it has never happened in the last 4 — this would be a first).
  5. Net debt/EBITDA rises above 1.5x via debt-funded M&A (currently ≈0.4x).

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next scheduled release: Q1 FY27 earnings, estimated ~19-Nov-2026 (Q1 FY26 was reported 20-Nov-2025; date not yet confirmed by the company — flagged as an estimate). FY27 guidance (already issued 25-Aug-26) will be updated/reiterated at that release — first read on whether the AI-disruption risk is showing up in TurboTax/ Credit Karma growth. Quarterly dividend record dates follow the normal Nov/Feb/May/Aug cadence.

11. Red-flag scan

  • Workforce restructuring, May 2026: Intuit announced ~3,000 job cuts (17% of ~18,200 employees) alongside Q3 FY26 earnings, with $300–340M of restructuring charges (largely in Q4 FY26). This is the second major cut in two years (July 2024: ~1,800, ~10%). CEO Sasan Goodarzi told employees the goal was a "leaner, more focused" organization but told CNBC's Jim Cramer "none of it had to do with AI" — an inconsistency with the company's own AI-platform narrative to investors, worth discounting management commentary on execution going forward (source 5, 6).
  • FTC consent order (since Jan-2024, ongoing): Intuit is permanently barred from advertising TurboTax as "free" unless it discloses the ~1/3 qualification rate; company also chose not to renew participation in the IRS Free File Program for the 2026 season, a reputational/political exposure given renewed public attention on free-filing access (source 7, 8). No new fine in FY26; compliance risk is ongoing, not escalating.
  • No auditor change, restatement, going-concern language, or SEC/DOJ investigation found in the FY26 10-K or recent 8-Ks reviewed.
  • No unusual insider-selling pattern identified within the standard-depth time box (not exhaustively checked — disclosed limitation).

dossiers.ISRG:
ISRG — Intuitive Surgical, Inc. — Diligence Dossier (Agent F53, wave 3)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — the global leader in robotic-assisted surgery, with a large recurring instrument/accessory revenue base and genuine procedure-volume growth, but priced at a rich absolute multiple with two real, evidenced risks the triage did not surface: an active antitrust appeal over instrument-repair tying, and a disclosed ~30% 2026 drawdown tied to Medtronic's Hugo launch. Half weight given the lack of valuation cushion and unresolved litigation. Horizon: 24–36 months.

2. Business in plain English

Intuitive makes the da Vinci surgical robot (and the Ion bronchoscopy platform) and sells it to hospitals, then earns recurring revenue from the single-use/limited-use instruments ("EndoWrists") and service contracts consumed in every procedure. Surgeons use it for urology, gynecology, general surgery and increasingly thoracic/bronchoscopic procedures. Moat: a large (and growing) installed base of systems creates a switching-cost and training moat; instruments and service are ~80% of revenue and recur with every procedure regardless of system sales.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1_live_scores.csv: pct_roe 0.587, pct_ocf_a 0.833 — solidly good but not extreme (ROE is lower than a typical "quality 5" name because ISRG carries a very large cash/investments balance that dilutes ROE). Value percentiles are low (pct_ep 0.080, pct_fcfp 0.079) — correctly flags an expensive stock. Momentum (mom_12_1 percentile 0.13) and SUE (0.077) are weak — the stock has lagged over the past year and recent earnings surprises have been unremarkable-to-negative, consistent with the ~30% 2026 drawdown discussed below. This is a case where the "quality" score is durable (real moat, real recurring revenue) but the model's own momentum/earnings-surprise signals already reflect real, disclosed bad news — not an artefact.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • FCF conversion: FY2025 OCF $3,030.5M − capex (PaymentsToAcquireProductiveAssets) $539.8M = FCF ≈ $2,490.7M vs GAAP NI $2,856.0M → FCF/NI ≈ 87%. TTM (Q3'25–Q2'26): OCF ≈ $3,706.4M, capex ≈ $483.8M, FCF ≈ $3,222.6M vs TTM NI ≈ $3,138.8M → FCF/NI ≈ 103%.

  • Balance sheet (consolidated, 10-Q Q2 2026): cash $2,760.4M (note: d4's vendor "totalCash" of $5.2B includes short-term marketable-securities investments beyond the strict cash line — a data-conflict worth flagging, resolved in ISRG's favor either way since it carries no long-term debt — LongTermDebt/LongTermDebtNoncurrent tags are absent from XBRL, consistent with a debt-free balance sheet). Stockholders' equity $18,168.4M.
  • Share count: 358.4M (Apr 2025) → 353.3M (Jul 2026), down ~1.4% — modest buybacks, mostly offsetting SBC dilution rather than aggressively shrinking the count.
  • M&A: none material; the company continues to invest in R&D (Ion, da Vinci 5) organically.

7. Valuation snapshot & reverse DCF

Price $405.18 (25 Sep 2026 close). This is well off a 2026 high — third-party coverage (Motley Fool, TIKR, July 2026) describes an ISRG decline of roughly 30% during 2026, attributed to the Medtronic Hugo competitive launch and guidance/procedure-growth deceleration concerns — consistent with the weak b1 momentum/SUE percentiles above. NTM P/E ≈ 34.5x (on consensus adjusted forward EPS), TTM GAAP P/E ≈ 46.5x — a large GAAP-vs-adjusted gap driven by SBC. No V1 row exists for ISRG → v1_verdict = null. Reverse DCF (10-yr FCF growth + terminal 3.5%, WACC 8.5%, EV $136.05B, TTM FCF $3.223B base): implied 10-yr FCF growth ≈ 12.6% (range 9.5–15.3% across WACC 7.5–9.5%/terminal 3–4%). My base case: procedure growth guided at 13.5–15.5% for 2026 but explicitly decelerating from 18% (2025) as the installed base matures and China/international capital spending stays soft; a reasonable 10-year average, allowing for continued deceleration plus margin/buyback contribution to EPS, is ≈11–13%/yr. implied_vs_base = in_line (implied sits within, not clearly above, my base range) — but this is a thin, judgment-call reconciliation, not a comfortable margin of safety, which is why the verdict is INCLUDE-SMALL rather than INCLUDE.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) da Vinci 5 system placements grew ~37% YoY in Q2 2026 (246 vs. 180 units) — an active upgrade cycle that raises the recurring-instrument base; (2) Ion (bronchoscopy) procedure growth of +36% YoY shows a second, earlier-stage growth leg; (3) debt-free balance sheet with a large net-cash position gives full strategic flexibility. Bear: (1) an antitrust jury found evidence of tying/exclusive dealing in the EndoWrist repair market (Rebotix Repair v. Intuitive, N.D. Cal.; summary judgment for Intuitive denied, case settled shortly before trial in 2025); a related case, Restore Robotics Repairs LLC v. Intuitive Surgical, was on appeal at the 11th Circuit as of a December 2025 filing — an adverse appellate outcome could force ISRG to open its high-margin instrument-repair/service market, which the triage's "no red flags" call missed entirely; (2) Medtronic's Hugo and J&J's Ottava are now real, launched competitors, not theoretical ones, and the stock has already re-rated down ~30% in 2026 partly on this; (3) management itself is guiding a sharp deceleration in procedure growth (18%→13-15%) and flagged China-specific capital-spending headwinds.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Worldwide da Vinci procedure growth < 10% YoY for two consecutive quarters (vs. guided 13.5–15.5% for FY2026).
  2. An adverse or unfavorable-settlement outcome in the Restore Robotics 11th Circuit appeal that opens the EndoWrist repair/service market to third parties.
  3. Full-year gross-margin guidance cut below the current 67–68% (non-GAAP) range.
  4. Two consecutive quarters of da Vinci system placement growth (units) turning negative YoY (a leading indicator ahead of the recurring-revenue base).
  5. Net debt/leverage — not applicable today (debt-free); this kill criterion is instead framed as: a debt-funded acquisition or buyback program that takes net cash negative would remove the balance-sheet cushion and should trigger a full re-review.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 2026-10-20 (Q3 2026, per d4_live_snapshot).

Intuitive Surgical Inc., 11th Circuit docket 25-14202 (appeal filed per Justia docket, referenced Dec 2025) — antitrust tying/exclusive-dealing claims over EndoWrist repair, following a related case (Rebotix Repair) in which a federal judge denied summary judgment, finding a jury could conclude Intuitive engaged in tying/exclusive dealing to maintain monopoly power; that case settled in 2025. This dossier opened and read the actual case dockets/rulings cited (FindLaw, MLex, Justia), not a news summary alone, per the wave-3 mandatory requirement.

dossiers.JBHT:
J.B. Hunt Transport Services (JBHT) — Diligence Dossier

Recency gate: Most recent period incorporated: Q2 FY2026 (quarter ended 2026-06-30, 10-Q filed 2026-07-24; earnings released 2026-07-15). Checked for events to 2026-09-25 close. Data-quality note: SEC EDGAR's Archives document server was in a maintenance outage for part of this research session; XBRL structured data (data.sec.gov) and the FY2025 10-K full text were both obtained once it came back up. All figures below are GAAP unless marked "(non-GAAP)"; JBHT discloses very few non-GAAP adjustments (mainly "revenue excluding fuel surcharge," used for volume/mix commentary, with no formal reconciliation table published).

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Thesis horizon: 12–24 months. JBHT is a genuinely high-quality, low-leverage, non-union logistics franchise showing real evidence of a freight-cycle inflection (Q2 FY26 revenue +19% YoY, intermodal operating income +58%), but the stock's 31x trailing / ~24x NTM P/E already prices a durable recovery that is one quarter old, management itself declined to extrapolate ("careful in ensuring Intermodal is the correct long-term answer" rather than chasing volume — CFO/COO on the Q2'26 call), and two of five segments (Final Mile, Truckload) are shrinking or losing money. Half-weight reflects strong conviction on business quality, low conviction on the entry price.

2. Business in plain English

J.B. Hunt is a US surface-transportation and logistics company operating through five segments: Intermodal (JBI — the largest, moving freight in containers via rail plus company-owned drayage trucks), Dedicated Contract Services (DCS — trucks and drivers committed to a single customer's network), Integrated Capacity Solutions (ICS — an asset-light freight brokerage matching shippers with third-party carriers), Final Mile Services (big-and-bulky home delivery), and Truckload (JBT — traditional over-the-road trucking). It makes money by charging shippers (retailers, manufacturers, e-commerce companies) for capacity and network reliability, competing on service and price against rail-owned intermodal competitors, other asset-based truckers, and brokers.

3. Why the model likes it

From the preliminary quant screen (lead_prelim_rank.csv, families Q/V/M; official point-in-time scores not yet live): JBHT ranks #12 of ~500 S&P names, prelim composite 0.814, driven by top-decile Quality (0.968) and top-decile Momentum (0.978), with only middling Value (0.495 — it is not cheap). The Quality score is durable and evidenced independently here: ROE ~16–19%, ROIC ~13.5–15%, net debt/EBITDA ~1.0x, zero unionized labor, strong buybacks funded from internally generated cash (see §6). The Momentum score is largely an artefact of one quarter — FY2025 segment revenue was essentially flat (Intermodal +0.3%, DCS -0.6%, Final Mile -9.5%) and the acceleration is entirely a 2026 phenomenon (Q1'26 revenue +4.6% YoY, Q2'26 +19.4% YoY) tied to a specific, checkable cause: industry-wide truckload capacity tightening plus "road-to-rail" conversion, not a structural re-rating of the whole business. Whether this is durable is precisely the open question this dossier flags as the central risk.

Acceleration is real but narrow and recent. FY2025 (the full prior year, per source [2] segment footnote) was essentially flat to down — this is not a multi-quarter trend yet, it is one strong quarter (Q2'26) following one modest one (Q1'26). Segment detail for Q2'26 (per the Q2'26 earnings release, source [4]): Intermodal revenue +22% (load volume +10%, i.e. real volume growth, not just price/fuel), operating income +58%; Dedicated +9% revenue; ICS (brokerage) +49% revenue and flipped from a loss to a small profit; Final Mile -6% revenue (management disclosed a deliberate $90M revenue headwind from "disciplined account management" — i.e., walking away from unprofitable volume, per the Q2'26 call, source [5]); Truckload +35% revenue but an operating loss (source [4]), as purchased-transportation cost inflation outpaced the segment's own rate increases. Adverse fact, not softened: operating cash flow was down year-over-year in H1'26 ($723.3M vs $806.2M in H1'25, per source [3] XBRL) despite higher earnings — consistent with working-capital consumption (receivables) from the volume surge; FCF was still up YoY only because capex fell even faster (H1'26 capex $144.9M vs H1'25 $399.1M, a 64% cut, source [4]).

5. Guidance track record

JBHT does not issue formal quantitative revenue or EPS guidance — consistent across all of the last four releases (Q3'25, Q4'25/FY25, Q1'26, Q2'26 earnings calls) — so there is no "raised/maintained/cut vs. prior range" table to build for the headline numbers, and no prior report should have claimed otherwise. The one quantified, trackable guidance item is the effective tax rate: full-year 2026 guidance was narrowed on the Q2'26 call to 24.0%–24.5%, versus an effective rate of ~25.4% realized in Q2'26 itself and ~24.8% for FY2025 — a modest tightening, not a raise or cut of substance. Beyond that, management gives only qualitative color: on Q2'26 it guided to demand "remain[ing] strong" through H2 2026 and a peak season "similar" in timing/shape to 2025, explicitly declining to quantify the intermodal volume outlook when pressed by analysts (Evercore's Jon Chappell asked directly whether June's growth rate could hold; management would not commit to a number).

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

FCF conversion: FY2025 FCF/NI = 947.6/598.3 = 158% (capex well below D&A in a low-investment year); TTM-through-Q2'26 conversion is even higher given the capex pullback — but see the OCF-decline point in §4, which is the more important quality signal than the FCF/NI ratio in isolation. SBC: not separately broken out in the sources reviewed here — flagged as a gap; recommend the valuation/quant team pull ShareBasedCompensation from XBRL directly. GAAP vs. adjusted: minimal gap — JBHT does not report a separate adjusted EPS; the only routinely-cited non-GAAP figure is "revenue excluding fuel surcharge" for volume/mix analysis. Leverage: gross debt $1,227.7M (current maturities + long-term), cash just $4.2M (JBHT runs a deliberately lean cash balance and sweeps excess cash to debt paydown and buybacks — confirmed by the CFO's Q2'26 comment that consolidated debt fell to $1.15B at 2026-06-30 from $1.72B a year earlier); net debt/EBITDA ≈ 1.0x on FY2025 EBITDA, improving toward ~0.7–1.0x on the TTM run-rate — comfortable, and interest coverage is very strong (EBIT/interest ≈ 13x on FY2025 interest expense of $75.2M). Debt composition: senior notes issued March 2019 and March 2025 plus a revolving credit facility (exact coupons/maturities not extracted from the excerpt reviewed — recommend a follow-up XBRL pull of the debt footnote if precision is required for the credit view). M&A: none identified in 2025–2026. Share count: buybacks are substantial and ongoing — $1B authorization (Aug 2024) plus a further $1B (effective Oct 2025); $968M remaining after Q4'25 (843k shares at avg. $166.02); $791M remaining after Q2'26 (392k shares at avg. ~$250/share — notably above today's $225.46, i.e. some recent buybacks were done at a higher price than today's, a minor capital-allocation-timing demerit, not a red flag). Dividend: modest (0.78% trailing yield, 25% payout ratio), well covered, room to grow.

7. Valuation snapshot

NTM P/E (calendarized) 24.1x; trailing P/E 31.4x (via valuation.py EV bridge: EV $22.39B on TTM EBITDA $1.67B → EV/EBITDA 13.4x, EV/EBIT 23.4x); FCF yield 4.3–4.5%. Against its own history, JBHT has historically traded in a wide range (high-single-digit to mid-20s trailing P/E, richest at earnings troughs and cheapest at peaks — a cyclical inversion the sector playbook explicitly warns about), so today's multiple sits at the rich end even before judging the recovery's durability. Against peers, JBHT is actually the cheapest of the large-cap truckers on forward P/E — Old Dominion Freight Line ~35–39x forward, Knight-Swift ~34–36x forward, versus JBHT's ~24–30x depending on source — but "cheapest of an expensive peer group" is not the same as cheap. Reverse-DCF (via valuation.py, WACC 8.5%, terminal growth 3%): the current EV already implies ~6% per-year FCF growth for a full decade — a plausible but non-trivial hurdle for a historically cyclical trucker whose FY2025 revenue was flat. A probability-weighted bear/base/bull scenario (bear $5.50 EPS/16x, base $7.20/22x, bull $8.50/27x) centers on $155/share, ~31% below the current price — i.e. the market is already underwriting meaningfully more than this dossier's base case.

Valuation reconciliation with V1 (added 2026-09-26): V1 rates JBHT "fair" (score −0.03, essentially neutral), with a base-case 3-year annualized return of +6.4% — implying a price near $266 in three years versus $225.46 spot — and notes this stays inside the Street's 12-month target range ($182–370, so no internal street-flag caution is raised). This dossier's own probability-weighted bear/base/bull scenario above centers on $155/share, about 31% below the current price, and §3/§7 state plainly that the stock's 31.4x trailing / 24.1x NTM P/E already "prices a durable recovery that is one quarter old" and that "the market is already underwriting meaningfully more than this dossier's base case." The two are not reconcilable as a rounding difference: V1 sees modest further upside, this dossier sees material downside risk to fair value. This dossier's more cautious reading is better supported, because it rests on current, concrete facts a trailing-multiple model does not see: the freight-cycle inflection is one quarter old and management itself declined to extrapolate it (§3/§9); two of five segments (Truckload, Final Mile) are shrinking or unprofitable (§4/§9); and H1 FY26 operating cash flow fell year-over-year despite higher earnings (§4/§9). V1's own-history percentile (36.7%, on NTM P/E) is not itself a red flag, so the two models are not flatly contradictory on every input — but on the bottom-line valuation call, the dossier's downside-weighted scenario is the better-evidenced one, consistent with this dossier's smaller, INCLUDE-SMALL sizing.

8. Bull case

  1. Verified, real freight-cycle inflection, not just a comp effect: Q2'26 intermodal load volume +10% (units, not just price) alongside operating leverage (JBI operating income +58% on +22% segment revenue), and management cites industry-wide capacity tightening (safety enforcement, driver-market tightness) as the structural driver — a classic late-cycle-to-recovery signal for a bellwether name.
  2. Balance sheet and capital discipline are genuinely excellent: net debt/EBITDA ~1x, zero union exposure, debt down ~$570M YoY, and $135M of structural cost already removed with "additional runway" cited by management — this is a company that used the freight downturn to get leaner, not just survive it.
  3. Record dedicated-fleet sales pipeline ("record level in terms of number of trucks," per DCS president, exceeding COVID-era peaks) and record "mini-bid" frequency across the network suggest share-of-wallet gains are still to come through 2027, independent of the broader freight cycle.

9. Bear case

  1. One good quarter does not confirm a cycle turn, and management itself would not commit to extrapolating June's growth rate — the stock has already re-rated as if it has. A reversion of intermodal pricing/volume in H2'26 (management flagged rail-service "moderation" as volumes accelerated, a potential constraint) would be a straightforward disappointment against a 24x NTM multiple.
  2. Two of five segments are structurally weak right now: Truckload is losing money on purchased-transportation inflation despite 35% revenue growth (a genuine earnings-quality flag — growth funded by higher-cost outsourced capacity, not owned assets), and Final Mile revenue is shrinking by management's own choice. A "sum of the parts" investor would not pay a premium multiple for either.
  3. OCF fell year-over-year in H1'26 even as earnings rose — working-capital consumption from the volume surge is a real, current adverse fact, not a hypothetical risk, and the FCF improvement it's paired with was capex-driven (capex -64% YoY) rather than earnings-driven; capex cannot fall indefinitely if volume growth is to be sustained.

10. Key risks & kill criteria

These are the specific, observable, time-bound conditions that would invalidate the INCLUDE-SMALL thesis above: - Intermodal revenue growth (ex-fuel) decelerates back below ~5% YoY for two consecutive quarters — the core recovery thesis fails. - Truckload (JBT) segment operating losses persist for more than two more quarters without a clear path to breakeven from pricing actions. - Net debt/EBITDA rises above 2.0x (would indicate the buyback/capex-cut strategy has outrun cash generation). - OCF conversion (OCF/NI) stays below 1.0x for two consecutive quarters, signaling the working-capital drag is structural rather than transitory. - Any loss of the "record" DCS sales pipeline translating to signed, revenue-generating fleet growth within the stated 12–18 month cycle.

11. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 2026-10-15 (Q3 2026, per company snapshot data; confirm closer to date). 2027 intermodal bid season commentary (management flagged growing optimism into it) is the next major qualitative catalyst, likely discussed on the Q3'26 and Q4'26 calls. No investor day identified in the filings reviewed.

12. Red-flag scan

Auditor: PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP; no auditor change identified. Material weakness / going concern: none identified in the sources reviewed (the FY2025 10-K's legal-proceedings section is boilerplate — "will not have a material adverse effect" — with no named material litigation). Restatements: none found. Investigations: none found in the sources reviewed. Related-party transactions: none disclosed in the FY2025 10-K excerpt reviewed, notably including no disclosed dealings with Hunt-family-affiliated entities despite the family's large stake. Insider ownership/selling: insider ownership is unusually high at 20.4% (per d4_live_snapshot.parquet) — plausibly Hunt-family-related given the company's history (founder Johnnie Bryan Hunt; co-founder Johnelle Hunt remains associated with the company) — this was not independently itemized to a specific Form 4 pattern in this session; flagged for the audit team to verify concentration and any recent large sales. Leadership: clean, telegraphed succession — Shelley Simpson became CEO/President effective 2024-07-01 (nominated to the board April 2024) after nearly 30 years at the company; John N. Roberts III (outgoing CEO) became executive chairman; former chairman Kirk Thompson and director Wayne Garrison moved to advisory ("Honorary Founding Director") roles. New independent directors added recently include Pat Ottensmeyer (former CEO, Kansas City Southern Railroad — directly relevant to the intermodal/rail relationship). No governance red flags identified. Short-seller reports: none identified in this session's research.

Data-quality note for the lead (D3/B1 pipeline)

lead_prelim_rank.csv's rev field for JBHT ($7.1896B) is wrong — verified FY2025 GAAP revenue (10-K, filed 2026-02-24) is $11,999.096M, and TTM-through-Q2'26 is ~$12,701M ($4.4–5.5B, or 43–57%, understated). dossiers.KLAC:
KLA Corporation (KLAC) — Diligence Dossier (Agent F28, standard depth)

1. Verdict

WATCH — not now, on valuation discipline, not business quality. KLA is the best-moat business of the three names in this batch, and the triage's quality/growth scores (5/5) are well supported by primary data. But the reverse DCF shows the price already assumes a growth rate this industry has never sustained for a full decade, even in this AI-capex supercycle. A great business priced for more than it can plausibly deliver is a WATCH under this program's own pre-committed rule, not an INCLUDE. Horizon if it re-rates or grows into the multiple: 24–48 months.

2. Business in plain English

KLA makes process-control and yield-management equipment (inspection and metrology tools) that semiconductor fabs use to find defects during manufacturing. It holds the leading share in this sub-segment of semicap equipment — every advanced logic and memory fab, and increasingly every advanced-packaging line, needs its tools regardless of which chipmaker wins the underlying race, which gives it a toll-booth-like position on the entire industry's capital spending rather than exposure to any single customer's success.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1_live_scores.csv: composite 0.46 (live_rank 270/503 — a lower composite than FSLR/GEN because KLA scores weakly on the Value family at today's price, which is exactly the tension this dossier resolves). Triage (Q12_triage.json) called it the "best moat in semicap," citing a 33x NTM P/E as fair for 15% revenue and 83% EPS growth. Verified: the growth numbers are real and accelerating — Q1 FY26 revenue +13.0% YoY, Q2 +7.2%, Q3 +11.5%, Q4 FY26 +15.2% YoY (all SEC XBRL, cross- checked against earnings releases), and FY2026 GAAP net income grew to $4.83bn (FY2025: $4.06bn, FY2024: $2.76bn) — a genuine acceleration, not a one-quarter blip. China revenue concentration has been falling, not rising, as a risk (29.8% of FY2026 revenue vs 33.3% FY2025 and 42.8% FY2024, per the FY2026 10-K), which reduces (does not eliminate) the export-control tail risk. What needs adjustment: the "33x NTM P/E is fair for 83% EPS growth" framing understates how much growth is already priced in over a full decade, not just next year — see §7. It is durable near-term, not an artefact, but the multiple is pricing perpetuity-level assumptions onto a single strong year.

  • Cash conversion — data conflict corrected: FY2026 (annual) operating cash flow = $4,143.1m (SEC XBRL, 10-K); FY2026 capex = $375.9m. Primary-sourced TTM FCF ≈ $3,767.1m. This is the largest and most consequential data conflict found in this dossier, since FCF yield feeds directly into the V-family quant score; the true FCF yield is ~1.5% of EV, not the lower figure a naive read of d4 would produce (though still low either way, given the size of KLA's EV — this is a low-FCF-yield, high-multiple name regardless of which figure is used).
  • Balance sheet: cash $1.650bn + marketable securities $3.253bn = $4.90bn liquid assets; long-term debt $5.887bn; net debt ≈ $1.25bn — trivial relative to $245bn market cap. Investment-grade-quality balance sheet.

7. Valuation snapshot and reverse DCF

Price 25-Sep-2026 close: $187.92 (post-split). Market cap $245.24bn. EV (net debt $1.25bn) ≈ $246.49bn. Trailing P/E 50.8x (elevated by the lower-margin early part of FY2026 still sitting in the trailing window); NTM P/E per d4's headline (reliable) field ≈ 28.0–32.7x depending on the exact forward-EPS vintage used. Trailing P/FCF on the corrected FCF figure = 65.4x; FCF yield 1.5%.

Reverse DCF (WACC 10.0%, terminal growth 3.5%, 10-year horizon, base FCF = corrected TTM $3,767.1m, EV anchor $246.49bn): implied stage-1 FCF growth ≈ 22.5% per year for 10 years. This is the key finding of this dossier: sustaining ~22–23% compound FCF growth for a full decade would require KLA's FCF to grow roughly 8x by 2036, in an industry that is structurally cyclical (semicap equipment order books historically swing with the 3–5 year memory/logic capex cycle). An evidence-based base case of roughly +12–14%/yr over 10 years (front-loaded high-teens-to-20% growth through the current AI-capex upcycle for 2–3 years, fading to high-single-digit growth as the cycle normalises and China-related headwinds persist) is well below the ~22.5%/yr the market is paying for. Implied vs base: above (expensive) — this is the reason for the WATCH verdict despite best-in-class business quality. No V1 systematic valuation exists for this name yet.

Scenario table (post-split GAAP EPS basis, 3-year horizon, dividend yield ~0.4%/yr added): | Scenario | Prob. | 3y-forward EPS | Exit P/E | Value/share | 3y annualised total return | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Bear | 30% | $5.00 | 20x | $100 | ~-19.5%/yr | | Base | 45% | $7.50 | 25x | $187.50 | ~+0.4%/yr | | Bull | 25% | $9.50 | 30x | $285 | ~+15.3%/yr |

Bear reflects a semicap-cycle downturn (memory/logic capex digestion after the current AI build-out) compounded with a tighter China export-control regime; base assumes the current growth trajectory moderates to a sustainable mid-teens rate and the multiple normalises from its currently elevated trailing level; bull assumes the AI capex cycle extends without a digestion phase.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) Structurally the best-positioned company in semicap equipment — process control/inspection is needed regardless of which chipmaker or foundry wins the AI race, and KLA's share in this sub-segment is the highest in the industry (triage assessment, consistent with the accelerating, broad-based revenue growth seen across all four FY2026 quarters). (2) China revenue concentration is falling (42.8%→33.3%→29.8% over three fiscal years) even as absolute China revenue held roughly flat — the mix is diversifying away from the single largest geopolitical risk. (3) Fortress balance sheet (net debt ~$1.25bn against $245bn market cap) and a 17-year dividend-growth streak fund growth and buybacks simultaneously.

Bear: (1) The reverse DCF shows the market pricing ~22.5%/yr FCF growth for a decade — a bar this cyclical industry has not cleared over any historical 10-year window, including the most recent AI-driven upswing (KLA's own 3-year revenue CAGR into FY2026 is well under half that rate). (2) Export-control risk to China is not resolved, only reduced in relative weight — the FY2026 10-K explicitly attributes flat China revenue to export-control restrictions offsetting legacy-node capex, meaning further tightening could still cut absolute dollars, not just share. (3) Trailing P/FCF of ~65x (corrected figure) means the stock is priced overwhelmingly on the next several years' growth, not today's cash generation — a classic setup for a sharp de-rating if the semicap cycle turns even briefly.

9. Key risks & kill criteria

  1. Quarterly revenue YoY growth below 5% for two consecutive quarters (a classic early semicap-cycle-turn signal; currently accelerating at 7–15%).
  2. GAAP diluted EPS guidance cut at any subsequent release (currently 2-for-2 met/beaten in this pass's sample).
  3. China revenue share or absolute dollars fall further in a way the company attributes explicitly to new export restrictions (as opposed to the already-disclosed, gradually diversifying trend).
  4. Net debt/EBITDA (currently trivial) rises above 1.0x without a value-accretive reason disclosed (would signal a large, possibly dilutive, capital-allocation shift).
  5. Trailing P/FCF (corrected basis) stays above 50x for more than two quarters after revenue growth decelerates below 10% YoY — the combination that would confirm the market has not yet re-rated the stock down to the base case.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 28-Oct-2026 (Q1 FY2027, quarter ended 30-Sep-2026; company guided revenue $4.0bn ±$200m, GAAP diluted EPS $1.14 ±$0.10 at the Q4 FY26 release). No investor day identified in the sources reviewed.

dossiers.LDOS:
LDOS — Leidos Holdings, Inc.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — thesis horizon 12–36 months. A diversified US federal-government IT/defense/intel/health/civil contractor with a $48.7bn backlog, a clean four-quarter beat-and-raise FY2026, and a genuinely cheap valuation (9.8x NTM P/E, 7.4% FCF yield — a reverse DCF implies only ~3.6%/year 10-year FCF growth against guided ~7% FY2026 EPS growth even before crediting further M&A). The named reservation: leverage jumped from ≈2.0x to ≈2.45x net debt/EBITDA after a debt-funded $2.4bn acquisition (ENTRUST, closed 30 March 2026) that meaningfully changes the company's risk profile, and the triage's own flagged red flag — US federal budget/DOGE-era spending-cut policy risk to contract awards — is real, ongoing, and only partially tested so far (Leidos has weathered DOGE cancellations better than peers, but a 93-person WARN-notice layoff tied to a CBP contract change in March 2026 shows the risk is not merely theoretical). Half-weight reflects genuine business quality and a real margin of safety, offset by event-driven leverage and policy risk that a full-weight holding should not carry.

2. Business in plain English

Leidos is one of the largest US government IT-services and defense-technology contractors, organized into four reporting segments: Intelligence & Digital ($1,499m of Q2 2026 revenue, the largest segment — intelligence-community IT, cyber, digital modernization), Health ($1,086m — health IT and managed health services, including large VA/DHA contracts), Homeland ($1,018m — border/security/aviation screening technology, including TSA-related work), and Defense ($955m — defense systems, sensors, and the Dynetics missile-defense/hypersonics business). It earns money almost entirely from multi-year US federal government contracts (cost-plus, fixed-price, and time-and-materials mixes), competing on cleared personnel, incumbency, and technical differentiation rather than on price alone. The March 2026 acquisition of ENTRUST Solutions Group (energy-infrastructure engineering, ~3,100 professionals) is a deliberate diversification move — it roughly doubles Leidos' presence in electric-grid and natural-gas engineering, a non-federal, utility-customer revenue stream that reduces (modestly, at this scale) the company's near-total dependence on US government appropriations.

3. Why the model likes it — and is it durable?

B1 composite is below the program median (live_rank 359/~2,300, decile 3, quintile 2; composite 0.277) — LDOS is not a broad quant favorite; it is here because of the triage's independent quality+growth+price-vs-growth screen. Family drivers: Value (fam_V ≈0.99, essentially the highest percentile in the program) — cheap on earnings yield, FCF yield and EBIT/EV; Quality (fam_Q ≈0.47, average); Momentum (fam_M ≈0.08, weak) and Earnings momentum (fam_S ≈0.15, weak) — the stock has not re-rated and recent EPS surprises have been unremarkable, consistent with a name the market is treating as a low-growth "value trap" candidate rather than rewarding for its guidance beats.

Durability check: the guidance beats are real and filed (see §5) — four straight raises through FY2026, with FY2026 book-to-bill running 1.1–1.3x and funded backlog up sequentially. But a meaningful share of the FY2026 guidance raise (the +$500m revenue step-up between the initial February guide and the May Q1 guide) is explicitly attributed by management to the ENTRUST acquisition closing, not organic acceleration — organic growth in Q2 2026 was 4% against 7% total reported growth. The cheap valuation is durable relative to the current, verified profile (double-digit-percent free cash flow yield, growing backlog); whether the growth rate underlying it is durable depends materially on federal-budget/appropriations outcomes that are outside the company's control.

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull (3): 1. Four consecutive quarters of guidance raises in FY2026 (revenue and non-GAAP EPS both raised at Q1 and Q2), a 1.1–1.3x book-to-bill and $48.7bn total backlog ($10.2bn funded) — real, filed evidence of demand, not merely a cheap multiple. 2. NTM P/E of 9.8x and a 7.4% FCF yield are genuinely inexpensive for a company guiding to high-single-digit EPS growth — the reverse DCF implies the market is pricing in almost no growth. 3. The ENTRUST acquisition is a disclosed, deliberate diversification into non-federal, utility-customer revenue (energy-grid engineering) that — if integration goes to plan — reduces Leidos' near-total dependence on US federal appropriations over time, a structural de-risking the market has not yet given credit for.

Bear (3): 1. The triage's own flagged red flag is real and only partially tested: US federal budget/DOGE-era spending-cut policy risk to contract awards and backlog conversion. Leidos has weathered DOGE cancellations better than named peers (Accenture Federal, Deloitte Federal, IBM all lost more in disclosed cancellations), but the March 2026 WARN notice (93 jobs, Ashburn VA, tied to a CBP contract change) is a concrete, dated instance of the risk materializing at a small scale — a larger recompete loss or a prolonged government shutdown (a risk explicitly flagged by analysts per Federal News Network reporting) remains a live, unhedged exposure. 2. A DOJ/SEC investigation stemming from a 2021 internal FCPA-related inquiry (international operations, third-party representatives) remains only partially resolved: the DOJ closed its investigation with no further action in December 2024, but the SEC investigation was still open as of the most recent 10-K reviewed in this search — an unresolved legal overhang, low in probability of material impact but not yet formally closed.

  1. FY revenue or non-GAAP EPS guidance is cut versus the immediately prior quarter's guidance (zero cuts across the last four releases; four consecutive raises).
  2. Net debt/EBITDA rises above 3.0x (from ≈2.45x currently) without a disclosed deleveraging plan.

  4. A single contract recompete loss, cancellation, or government-shutdown-driven revenue disruption exceeding $300 million of annualized revenue is disclosed (calibrated as roughly 1.5x the scale of the March-2026 Ashburn WARN-notice event).
  5. The SEC's FCPA-related investigation (open since 2021) results in a formal enforcement action, fine, or admission of wrongdoing (currently: DOJ closed with no action Dec-2024; SEC status not confirmed closed as of the most recent 10-K reviewed).

dossiers.LIN:
LIN — Linde plc — Diligence Dossier (Agent F53, wave 3)

1. Verdict

WATCH — the world's largest industrial-gas company, an genuine oligopoly (with Air Liquide, Air Products) with a record, largely contracted project backlog and a real, evidenced string of guidance raises. But the reverse DCF implies growth above Linde's own guided long-term earnings algorithm, and the current elevated-capex phase (funding that backlog) is temporarily depressing free cash flow, making today's price look even more demanding on an FCF basis. A great business, priced for more than its own guidance says it will deliver — the addendum's own standard for WATCH, not INCLUDE. Horizon: revisit if the multiple de-rates or backlog conversion accelerates growth above the current guided range.

2. Business in plain English

Linde produces and distributes industrial and medical gases (oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, argon, CO2, specialty gases) via on-site plants built next to large customers (steel, chemicals, refining, electronics/semiconductor fabs, healthcare), pipeline networks and bulk/cylinder delivery. On-site contracts are typically 15–20 year take-or-pay agreements passing through energy costs — very low volume/price risk once built. Moat: capital intensity, pipeline network density and long-term contracts make it nearly impossible for a new entrant to replicate a regional gas network; Linde, Air Liquide and Air Products effectively split the global on-site/merchant market.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) record $11B project backlog (record $8.1B sale-of-gas backlog) is largely contracted/take-or-pay, de-risking multi-year growth visibility; (2) three consecutive guidance raises show real execution momentum into a historically defensive, oligopolistic business; (3) electronics/semiconductor and clean-hydrogen end-markets provide a genuine secular growth optionality layer on top of the base industrial-gas business (data-center/AI-driven electricity and gas demand is a plausible tailwind, though not confirmed in Linde's own Q2 2026 release, which discussed "electronics" strength generically without naming AI/hyperscaler demand specifically — flagged as an unconfirmed narrative some investors use). 9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Net debt/EBITDA > 2.25x (vs. 1.67x today) without a disclosed, value-accretive reason (e.g., large M&A).
  2. Full-year adjusted-EPS guidance cut (vs. the immediately preceding range) — would break the three-quarter raise streak that is central to the bull case.
  3. Project backlog shrinks (vs. the current $11B) for two consecutive quarterly disclosures — a leading indicator that contracted future growth is not being replenished.
  4. Underlying/organic sales growth < 2% for two consecutive quarters (Q2 2026 was +4% organic — a decline back toward flat would signal industrial-cycle weakness).
  5. GAAP net income growth negative for two consecutive quarters beyond what is explained by disclosed purchase-accounting/restructuring items.

dossiers.LRCX:
LRCX — Lam Research Corporation (diligence agent F29, standard depth)

1. Verdict

WATCH (12–36 month thesis horizon). Lam is a genuinely excellent, share-gaining wafer-fab-equipment (WFE) franchise riding a real AI/leading-edge/HBM-packaging capex wave with record margins — but at $315.21 (25-Sep-2026 close) the stock is priced, on V4's own systematic reverse DCF, for sustained growth roughly 2.5–4x its own trailing history, and the triage's "override to advance" rationale (net-cash balance sheet, ~8% required growth) does not match V1's own math. I side with V1's "excessive" verdict, not the triage override.

2. Business in plain English

Lam Research makes wafer-fab-equipment — principally etch and deposition tools — used by memory and logic chipmakers to build semiconductors. It is one of a handful of companies (with Applied Materials, KLA, Tokyo Electron, ASML) that customers have no real alternative to for advanced nodes and, increasingly, HBM/advanced-packaging manufacturing steps. Roughly a quarter of revenue still comes from China, a share that has been shrinking under US export controls.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1 quant (v4/data/b1_live_scores.csv, 2026-09-25): composite 0.906 (decile 10, but live_rank 47 — outside the top-30 momentum/earnings tier that MU sits in), driven again mostly by momentum (fam_M 0.983, mom_12_1 +126%) and earnings-surprise (fam_S 0.942, SUE 3.55); fam_V is very low (0.021 — the model sees LRCX as expensive on every value metric, which is the correct read given a NTM P/E of 31.4x). This is a real, filing-verified upcycle (record revenue, record non-GAAP operating margin 38.4% in FQ4'26), but the WFE sub-sector is the most cyclically amplified link in the chain (sector playbook: "a 15% cut in foundry capex can mean a 30%+ decline in tool orders, and the reverse on the way up") — the current growth rate is a cycle peak, not a new trend line, even though the underlying AI-capex driver is real for several more years.

I could not independently verify FY26 Q1/Q2 guidance-vs-actual from public sources in the time available for this pass; the two verified data points both show consistent beats-and-raises, but the forward guide itself is the number the reverse DCF in §7 has to be tested against.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • FCF conversion: TTM (to FY2026 year-end, per V1/D3) OCF $5.86B, capex $0.97B, FCF $4.89B, TTM NI $7.27B → FCF/NI ≈ 67%. SBC $386M TTM ≈ 1.7% of TTM revenue ($23.23B) — modest.
  • Balance sheet: long-term debt $3.72B (essentially flat for two years, per SEC 10-Q LongTermDebtNoncurrent), current portion negligible ($0.15M as of 2026-06-28); cash $5.58B (2026-06-28). Net cash of roughly −$1.86B per V1. Buybacks running ~$975–1,000M/quarter (largest in the two-year window); dividends ~$292M/quarter, both funded comfortably by FCF.
  • Sector-appropriate lens: capex/D&A for the TTM period is roughly 2.2x ($966M capex vs $442M D&A per V1/D3), i.e. genuinely investing rather than harvesting — a normal, healthy signal at this point in the cycle, not a red flag.
  • GAAP vs non-GAAP: the FQ4 FY26 figures quoted from the press release (52.0% GM, 38.4% op margin, $1.82 EPS) are non-GAAP; I was not able to pull the matching GAAP figures from XBRL in the time available since the FY2026 10-K (filed 2026-08-07) was not parsed to the line level for this pass. This is a genuine gap in this dossier's coverage — flagged, not glossed over.

7. Valuation — reconciling with V1

V1 (outputs/v1_valuation.json, priced 2026-09-25): verdict "excessive" (score −0.881), reverse-DCF FCFF, WACC 11.8%. NTM P/E 31.4x, at the 80th percentile of its own 177-month (14.75-year) history — i.e., this is one of the more expensive points in Lam's own trading history, not a discount. V1's implied 10-year FCFF growth is 48.5%/yr, against a historical 5-year CAGR of only 9.7% and 10-year CAGR of 14.7%, and even the sell-side's own next-fiscal-year consensus growth is 18.1% — a fraction of the 48.5%/yr implied. V1's base case (20.3% assumed growth, 20.4x exit multiple) still produces a 3-year annualised return of −20.2%, its bull case (28.1% growth) only reaches +2.4%/yr, and its street-flag again notes the base case sits below the Street's own 12-month low target ($290 vs $315.21 spot). My reconciliation: the triage's "override to advance" argument (net-cash balance sheet and "net-cash-implied required growth of ~8%") looks like it referenced a different, easier hurdle than V1's actual reverse-DCF framework — the ~8% figure resembles a bond-like "growth needed to cover the multiple via earnings yield alone" heuristic, not the 10-year FCFF-growth-at-WACC reverse DCF V1 (and this dossier) actually solve for. On the harder, filing-grounded test, implied growth (48.5%/yr) is well ABOVE any defensible base case (my own base case: high-teens to low-20s%/yr, i.e., roughly consensus-to-slightly-above, allowing 2–3 more years of AI/HBM-driven WFE strength before the capex cycle normalises). valuation_view_vs_v1.implied_vs_base = "above".

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) Genuinely record, company-verified non-GAAP operating margin (38.4% FQ4'26) and gross margin (52.0%) from pricing actions, mix and efficiency, not just volume. (2) HBM/advanced-packaging and leading-edge etch/deposition steps are structurally gaining share of the WFE dollar as chipmakers add process steps — a real, multi-year tailwind, not merely a spending-cycle peak. (3) China revenue mix has fallen from 43% to 26% of sales in three quarters, and the company says Taiwan (27%) and Korea (20%) demand "more than offsets" the loss — i.e., the China de-risking that many feared is already mostly priced through the P&L rather than a future shock. Bear: (1) WFE is the most amplified link in the semiconductor value chain; the forward guide implies the largest single-quarter sequential jump (+20.5%) in the two-year data reviewed — a hard bar to clear twice in a row. (2) A Shanghai-based, state-backed Chinese toolmaker has begun shipping homegrown immersion DUV lithography systems (5 units in 2026, 20 planned for 2027) to SMIC/CXMT/Hua Hong, and the pending US MATCH Act would tighten export controls further — a two-sided China risk (less addressable China revenue, and slowly emerging Chinese-equipment competition at the margin) that is not fully reflected in a 31.4x, 80th-percentile multiple. (3) V1's own reverse DCF, using Lam's own trailing cash flows and a conservative 11.8% WACC, requires the company to more than triple its own 10-year historical growth rate for the next decade to earn the current price.

9. Key risks & kill criteria

  1. Reported (GAAP or non-GAAP) revenue growth decelerates below 15% YoY for two consecutive quarters (roughly half the current run-rate).
  2. China revenue share stabilises or reverses its decline (i.e., a further adverse export-control tightening) and Taiwan/Korea demand fails to keep offsetting it, evidenced by a guidance cut.
  3. Non-GAAP gross margin falls back below 48% (below the FY26 average) for a full quarter.
  4. Book-to-bill (or qualitative order commentary) turns negative for two consecutive quarters — the sector's cleanest leading indicator of a WFE downturn.
  5. The MATCH Act or a further export-control tightening is enacted with a disclosed revenue impact beyond the ~$600M/year headwind already guided.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: ~2026-10-21 (est.), LRCX's fiscal Q1 2027 (quarter ending ~2026-09-27, essentially concurrent with this dossier's cutoff) — date sourced from third-party earnings calendars, not yet confirmed via an LRCX press release at the time of this pull. No lock-ups or index events identified in the data reviewed.

11. Red-flag scan

  • Litigation/SEC: no material litigation, SEC/DOJ investigation, restatement or going-concern language found in the sources reviewed for this pass.
  • Insider selling: several Form 4 sales in 2026 (Chief Legal Officer Ava Harter, $1.51M, 2026-08-31, under a 10b5-1 plan adopted 2026-04-28; directors/SVPs selling $6.1–20.0M across mid-2026) — these read as routine, plan-based diversification against a large stock-price run rather than a cluster of opportunistic, un-planned sales, but the magnitude (director sale of $20.0M) is worth monitoring next quarter.
  • Competitive: homegrown Chinese DUV lithography ramp (see §8) is an emerging, not yet financially material, competitive signal.

dossiers.LVS:
LVS — Las Vegas Sands Corp. — F20 diligence dossier

1. Verdict

INCLUDE — thesis horizon 12–36 months. This is the cheapest name in the F20 batch by a wide margin on a systematic reverse-DCF basis (the price implies FCF shrinking more than 11%/yr for a decade against a 5-year delivered CAGR of +27%), the business is genuinely improving (Macau mass-market share gains, a monopoly Singapore asset, an investment-grade upgrade), and management is returning capital aggressively and consistently. Named risks below (Macau concession renewal in 2032, a doubled Singapore expansion budget, family control) are real but are dated, sized and monitorable — none of them breaks the thesis today.

2. Business in plain English

Las Vegas Sands owns and operates large integrated resorts (casino, hotel, retail, convention/MICE space) — today essentially Macau (through ~70%-owned Sands China: The Venetian Macao, Londoner, Parisian, Plaza) and Singapore (Marina Bay Sands, 100%-owned). It sold its US Las Vegas properties in 2022 and is no longer a US casino operator in the traditional sense; earnings come almost entirely from Asian gaming and premium-mass tourism. It makes money on gaming win (mass-market table games and slots, plus VIP/junket-driven rolling chip volume), room/retail/MICE revenue, and — for Macau specifically — is subject to a government concession that sets the terms under which it may operate.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1_live_scores.csv ranks LVS moderately (composite percentile 56th, decile 6/quintile 3, live_rank 219 — not a top-70 name; it reached full diligence via the triage/quality-growth route after Q02 flagged it). The valuation gap the model is really responding to is in V1's own systematic reverse-DCF (see §7), not the factor composite. The underlying growth is durable, not a sugar-high: Sands China mass GGR +8% YoY in Q2-26 (vs the overall Macau market's +4%, i.e. genuine share gain, not just market recovery), and Marina Bay Sands mass gaming revenue +5% YoY in a quarter where overall visitation was depressed by the football World Cup — both are volume/share stories, not one-off VIP-hold luck.

4. Last 8 quarters — results table (GAAP, USD millions except EPS)

Source: SEC XBRL company facts (data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyfacts/CIK0001300514.json) — all eight quarters below are directly tagged as discrete 3-month periods (LVS's XBRL, unlike RDDT/EXPE, tags Q4 separately), cross-checked against the 8-K earnings-release exhibits for the two most recent quarters.

Mass-market metrics (the real underlying business) were strong in the same quarter (Sands China mass GGR +8% YoY; MBS mass +5% YoY).

5. Guidance track record

Las Vegas Sands, like most casino operators, does not issue formal quantitative revenue/EPS guidance. The closest analogue is management's informally stated Macau EBITDA aspiration of ~$700m/quarter, which the company missed in Q2-2026 ($430m actual, ~$517m hold-normalised) — disclosed above as a genuine, measurable shortfall against management's own stated bar, not glossed over. No formal guidance-track-record table applies; this absence itself is stated rather than treated as a pass (per the addendum's "missing evidence is not a pass" instruction).

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • OCF (TTM through Q2-26, sum of last 4 quarters): 567+... — quarterly OCF only reliably available at Q1-tagged (~90-day) contexts in this dataset for several years plus the two most recent 10-Qs; FY2025 OCF was strong and full-year metrics (below) are the more reliable read.
  • FY2025: net revenue $13.02bn, operating income $2.82bn (21.7% margin), net income (consolidated) $1.63bn, diluted EPS $2.35, adjusted property EBITDA $5.23bn (vs $4.38bn FY2024, +19.4%).
  • Net debt (30-Jun-2026): long-term debt & capital leases $13,694m + current portion $1,568m − cash $3,376m = $11,886m (matches V1's independently sourced figure to the dollar). Against TTM EBITDA of roughly $4.4–4.9bn, net debt/EBITDA is approximately 2.4–2.7x — S&P's own stated expectation is leverage sustained "around 2.5x" through the Singapore expansion, with a 3.0x downgrade threshold; S&P upgraded LVS/Sands China from BBB- to BBB in 2026 on disciplined financial policy, and LVS raised $1bn of bonds at the improved rating. This is a genuinely improving credit story, not a deteriorating one.
  • Capital return is aggressive and shrinking the equity base: $740m of buybacks in Q1-2026 and $787m in Q2-2026 (H1-2026 total $1,542m) plus $400m of dividends YTD; diluted share count fell from 675m (Q4-25) to 648m (Q2-26), a ~4% reduction in two quarters. Stockholders' equity attributable to LVS fell from $1,198m (Q1-26) to $581m (Q2-26) — this looks alarming in isolation but is mechanically explained by buybacks retiring equity faster than retained earnings accrete it, not by asset impairment or losses; still worth monitoring since it leaves a thin common-equity cushion on a historical-cost balance sheet that materially understates the properties' market value.
  • SBC is small (~$13–24m/quarter, under 1% of revenue) — not a distortive factor here.
  • Governance/control: the Adelson family (Dr. Miriam Adelson, Irwin Chafetz and related trusts) beneficially owns/controls ~59.7% of voting power — LVS is a controlled company. This concentrates capital-allocation authority in one family (a genuine governance risk for minority holders) but that family has run the business consistently and, on the evidence above, is currently allocating capital toward buybacks at a statistically cheap multiple — a reasonable use of control, not an obvious expropriation risk, but disclosed as a structural fact.

7. Valuation snapshot — V1 says attractive (near-maximum score); I agree

v4/outputs/v1_valuation.json / v1_valuation_table.csv (as of 2026-09-25, price $38.99): NTM P/E 11.5x, own-history percentile 1.9th (essentially LVS's cheapest valuation point in 156 months), peer median (Casinos & Gaming, n=3: LVS/MGM/WYNN) 16.9x. FCF yield 8.8% (SBC-adjusted 10.3%). WACC 7.10% (beta only 0.89 Blume-adjusted — surprisingly low for a name often perceived as high-beta/cyclical). Reverse DCF: the price implies FCF declining ~11.3%/yr for 10 years — against a trailing 5-year delivered FCF CAGR of +27.3% and sell-side consensus FY1 growth of +5.5%. Street 12-month target range $47–71.5 (mean $59.07): V1's own base-case fair value ($97 in 3 years) already exceeds the Street's 12-month high target of $71.5 — flagged by V1 itself as a "street_flag" worth independent scrutiny, not silently accepted. V1 verdict: attractive (score 0.988, near the maximum of the scale), base-case 3-year annualised return +37.5%, bear −7.7%, bull +78.7%.

My view: cheap, and I agree with V1, with two named caveats V1's own price-only model cannot see: (1) the Macau concession expires 31-Dec-2032 — six years inside V1's 10-year DCF horizon — carrying real (if currently low-probability, given the 2023 industry-wide 10-year renewal cycle just completed) renewal-terms risk that a naive perpetuity-style reverse DCF does not explicitly price; (2) the Singapore Marina Bay Sands expansion cost has already doubled to ~$8bn, a real execution/cost-overrun risk on top of the ~2.5x leverage plan. Neither changes the direction of the call — an implied decade of shrinking cash flow is not a plausible base case even after discounting for concession-renewal uncertainty and a capex overrun — but both are why this dossier flags them as explicit, named risks rather than accepting V1's "attractive" score uncritically. implied_vs_base = below.

8. Bull case

  1. Genuine, share-gaining mass-market recovery in both Macau (Sands China mass GGR +8% vs market +4%) and Singapore (MBS mass +5% in a soft-visitation quarter) — the durable part of the business is accelerating, while the volatile part (VIP hold) is what is currently depressing headline EBITDA.
  2. Credit quality is improving, not deteriorating: S&P upgrade to BBB, leverage target ~2.5x, and a successful $1bn bond raise at the better rating — the balance-sheet risk the market may be pricing (via the thin post-buyback common-equity base) is not corroborated by the rating agencies actually holding the debt.
  3. Marina Bay Sands is a structurally scarce, effectively monopoly asset (Singapore issues a small, fixed number of casino licences) now being expanded at scale ($8bn), and the concession renewal cycle for Macau just completed in 2023 with a full 10-year grant, i.e. the closest major renewal risk (2032) is still six years away.

9. Bear case

  1. The 2032 Macau concession renewal sits inside any decade-long valuation horizon and is a real, if not immediate, source of uncertainty on operating terms, tax/gaming-levy rates, and required non-gaming capex commitments (VML has already committed ≥35.84bn patacas / ~$4.47bn under the current concession).
  2. Singapore capex has already doubled from original estimates to ~$8bn — a live execution-risk pattern (cost overruns on large gaming-resort construction projects are common in the industry) that could pressure free cash flow and the capital-return program if it recurs.
  3. VIP-hold volatility (the Q2-2026 Macau EBITDA miss) demonstrates that quarterly headline numbers can swing by ~20% on pure statistical variance in a business line management does not fully control — a reminder that near-term print risk is real even if the multi-quarter trend (mass-market share gains) is sound; combined with majority family control (59.7% voting power), minority shareholders have limited recourse if capital-allocation priorities were ever to shift away from buybacks.

10. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Sands China mass-market GGR growth falls below the overall Macau market's growth rate for two consecutive quarters (loses the share-gain thesis).
  2. Consolidated net debt/EBITDA rises above 3.0x (S&P's own stated downgrade threshold) for two consecutive quarters.
  3. Marina Bay Sands expansion capex guidance is revised upward again beyond the current ~$8bn, or the 2031 opening date slips by more than two quarters.
  4. Any formal notice or public commentary from the Macau government casting doubt on standard renewal terms ahead of the December-2032 concession expiry.
  5. Quarterly dividend or buyback pace is cut (a reversal of the current aggressive capital-return program) absent a stated, value-accretive reinvestment alternative.

INCLUDE (24–36 month horizon). A duopoly card network with structural double-digit revenue growth, 46%+ operating margins and very low leverage, priced (25.6x NTM P/E, per d4_live_snapshot.parquet) for roughly 7%/yr long-run FCF-per-share growth in a reverse DCF — well below both consensus (+15.5% FY1 EPS growth) and the company's own recent run-rate (mid-teens revenue growth, high-teens EPS growth). Mastercard runs the payment "rails" that connect banks, merchants and consumers — it authorizes, clears and settles card transactions and takes a small fee on the dollar volume and transaction count that flows across its network (Payment network segment), plus a fast-growing Value-Added Services and Solutions (VAS) segment (cyber/fraud, data & insights, loyalty, open banking).
