1. Verdict

WATCH — 12–24 month horizon. Reasonable, business-appropriate balance sheet and a valuation sitting at the cheap end of both its own history and the Street's own 12-month target range, but two straight years of declining operating cash flow and a Q2 2026 guidance raise that is substantially a one-off tariff-refund story, not a volume recovery. Condition to upgrade to INCLUDE-SMALL: two consecutive quarters of organic (ex-tariff, ex-FX) revenue growth, or TTM operating cash flow inflecting positive year-over-year.

2. Business in plain English

Masco makes and sells branded home-improvement products — faucets and fixtures (Delta, Hansgrohe), paints and coatings (Behr), and cabinetry/other decorative building products — sold mainly through home-improvement retailers (Home Depot, Lowe's) and wholesale plumbing distributors to contractors and remodelers. It makes money on unit volume and price/mix across two reporting segments, Plumbing Products (~67% of Q2 2026 revenue) and Decorative Architectural (~33%). Its competitive position is strong (leading share in faucets and paint in North America, high brand recognition), but demand is tied to discretionary U.S. home-repair-and-remodel spending, which is cyclical and currently soft.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

B1 ranks MAS #52 (composite percentile ~89.6th) driven almost entirely by Value (earnings yield, FCF yield, EBIT/EV and book/price all in the 79th–87th percentile) and Quality (gross-profit/assets 90.6th percentile, OCF/assets 72.0th percentile), with weak Momentum (38.2nd percentile — the stock has lagged over the trailing 12-1 month window) and middling Earnings-momentum/SUE (70.1st percentile). This is partly an artefact: the "cheap and high quality" read is flattered by a shrinking denominator — MAS has been shrinking its own balance sheet and share count via buybacks (share count down from 233M in mid-2022 to 201.7M at Q1 2026, ‑13.4%) while GAAP net income has fallen in each of the last two fiscal years (FY2023 $908M → FY2024 $822M → FY2025 $810M, source: DEF 14A summary compensation table figures, filed 2026-04-21). Gross-profit/assets and OCF/assets ratios can stay statistically "high quality" even as the underlying earnings power softens, if assets shrink in step. MCD (McDonald's Corporation) — Diligence Dossier

Agent: F36 · Standard depth · Prepared 2026-09-26 · Prices/market data as of 2026-09-25 close ($236.50; mkt cap ≈$167.4B)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — 24–36 month horizon; named reservation: US comparable-sales/traffic momentum has decelerated for three straight quarters and the balance sheet carries high, buyback-driven leverage (negative book equity), so this is a lower-conviction "half-weight" holding rather than a full-conviction one despite a clearly favourable reverse-DCF read. No V1 systematic valuation row exists for MCD; v1_verdict = null.

2. Business in plain English

McDonald's is the world's largest quick-service-restaurant franchisor by system sales: ~95% of its ~43,000+ restaurants are owned and run by independent franchisees who pay McDonald's rent (McDonald's owns or leases much of the underlying real estate) plus a royalty on sales. McDonald's own P&L is therefore mostly a real-estate/ royalty annuity on other operators' sales, not a direct food-service P&L — which is why its operating margins (mid-to-high 40s%) look nothing like a typical restaurant operator's. It competes on value, speed and brand ubiquity, currently leaning on "McValue" promotions to defend US traffic.

Sector routing note: GICS "Restaurants" maps to aviation-hotels.md under the stock-analysis skill router, with an explicit cross-read to fmcg-consumer.md for the asset-light franchisor/royalty angle — the skill's own mapping table flags this exact distinction ("Lodging... Distinguish the owner... from the asset-light franchisor or manager, which is a royalty on system-wide RevPAR" — the restaurant analogue is systemwide sales). This dossier reads MCD primarily as a brand-royalty annuity (fmcg-consumer lens: same-store/systemwide sales, franchisee health) with same-store sales and franchisee economics as the operative KPIs, not restaurant-level unit economics.

data/b1_live_scores.csv live_rank 369; triage (Q09) scored quality 5 / growth 3 / price_vs_growth 4, citing "31.7% margins," franchise moat and international growth against a backdrop of US traffic softness. This analyst's base case (Section 8) assumes ~7%/yr EPS growth (mid-single-digit systemwide sales growth plus margin recovery toward the guided high-40s% range plus buybacks) over the next three years — well above the ~2.8%/yr the reverse DCF says is priced in. 8. Bull case / bear case

Bull (3): 1. Systemwide sales (+5%, +4% cc) and loyalty engagement (+13% 90-day actives to ~220M) are still compounding even while US in-restaurant traffic is soft — the platform is bigger than the comp-sales headline. 2. Operating margin has already recovered from a Q1 2026 trough (45.3%) back to 47.0% in Q2 2026, suggesting the value-menu-driven margin pressure is moderating, not structural. 3. At ~2.8%/yr implied growth, the reverse DCF gives a wide margin of safety versus a business with a multi-decade record of mid-single-digit systemwide growth even through prior soft-traffic cycles.

Bear (3): 1. US comparable sales have now decelerated for three consecutive quarters (to +0.8% in Q2 2026), and management's own explanation ("inconsistent restaurant execution," "lower consumer awareness" of value offerings) describes an execution problem the company itself has not yet fixed — this could persist. 2. Net debt/EBITDA ≈2.8x on a negative-equity balance sheet leaves little room for a real downturn in systemwide sales without credit-metric pressure; MCD's capital-return policy has structurally prioritised buybacks/dividends over deleveraging. 3. Franchise-system litigation (Section 11) — while mostly narrowed in McDonald's favour — signals ongoing friction in the franchisee relationship that is a second-order but real operating risk for a business entirely dependent on franchisee execution and goodwill.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. US comparable sales negative (turning from decelerating-positive to outright negative) for two consecutive quarters.
  2. Full-year operating-margin guidance (currently "mid-to-high 40% range") formally cut at any quarterly release.

  4. A credit-rating downgrade by S&P/Moody's/Fitch below the current investment-grade tier.

Moody's Corporation (MCO) — Diligence Dossier

Agent: F54 | As of: 2026-09-25 close ($468.70) | Depth: Standard

Note on naming: Moody's Corporation (ticker MCO) has two operating segments that it labels "MIS" (Moody's Investors Service — credit ratings) and "MA" (Moody's Analytics — data/research/software). This dossier always writes "MA segment" for Moody's Analytics to avoid confusion with Mastercard's ticker MA, which is a separate company covered in a separate dossier.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (24–36 month horizon), reservation: the price already assumes MCO keeps delivering mid-teens adjusted EPS growth and margin expansion every quarter — my reverse DCF implied growth (≈12%/yr) is essentially in line with, not below, a realistic base case, so there is limited valuation cushion if rated-debt issuance (structurally procyclical) turns down. Near-duopoly ratings franchise (with S&P Global) plus a fast-growing analytics/software arm, with an excellent and improving guidance track record, but a thin (and recently shrinking) equity base funded mostly by debt against a buyback program.

2. Business in plain English

Moody's has two businesses under one roof: MIS, which rates bonds and loans for issuers (governments, corporates, structured finance) and earns a fee — largely a toll on global debt-capital-markets issuance volume, in a global duopoly with S&P Global; and the MA segment, which sells data, analytics, research, risk-management software and now AI-enabled decision tools to banks, insurers and corporates on a subscription/ARR basis. MIS is highly cyclical with issuance volumes but very high-margin; the MA segment is recurring-revenue and growing faster, diversifying MCO away from bond-market cyclicality over time.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Triage (Q05) called out 76.9% ROE and a "near-regulatory moat," with the 25.5x multiple looking fair for 20% EPS growth. Confirmed and refined: b1_live_scores.csv (2026-09-25) shows gross-profit/assets in the 99th percentile and OCF/assets in the 99th percentile — genuinely best-in-class capital efficiency, not an accounting artefact, because MIS requires almost no incremental capital to rate an additional bond. The "76.9% ROE" figure is itself partly an artefact of a small, buyback-shrunk equity base (Total Moody's shareholders' equity fell from $4.054bn to $3.025bn in just six months — see §6) rather than pure operating economics; this dossier relies on operating cash flow, adjusted operating margin and the guidance track record (§5) rather than ROE as the primary quality evidence.

That is close to, i.e. roughly in line with, the company's own guided/realized trajectory (FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance implies ~13% growth off FY2025's $14.94 at the midpoint; medium-term algorithm is high-single-digit revenue plus buyback-assisted double-digit EPS growth). This is priced in line with, not below, the base case — a fine business, but not one offering a demonstrable margin of safety at the current price.

Bull: (1) the MA segment (Moody's Analytics) grew ARR +9% YoY in 1Q26 and margins expanded 250bps, diversifying MCO's earnings away from bond-issuance cyclicality over time; (2) MIS delivered record quarterly revenue ($1.26bn, 2Q26, +25% YoY) on record global rated issuance, showing the ratings franchise still has significant operating leverage in a strong issuance environment; (3) four consecutive guidance raises/narrowings-upward (§5) show real forecasting discipline and execution, not promotional guidance. dossiers.META:
META — Meta Platforms, Inc.

1. Verdict

WATCH. Horizon 12–36 months. Meta's ad engine is genuinely benefiting from AI (Advantage+ at a $20bn+ annual run-rate) and the FTC's monopoly case ended in Meta's favor at trial, but Q2 2026 delivered the company's first year-over-year profit decline of the AI era, operating margin compressed from 43% to 31%, free cash flow fell to $784m for the quarter, and the model's own factor scores are the weakest of the four names (bottom quintile). At the 25-Sep-2026 close ($751.66), a 10-year reverse DCF implies ~17.5% constant revenue growth versus an evidence-based base case of ~11.2% — the largest gap of the four mega-caps reviewed.

2. Business in plain English

Meta sells advertising across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Messenger, using AI to target ads and (increasingly) to automate ad creation and campaign optimization for advertisers (the "Advantage+" suite). It also runs Reality Labs, a large, persistently loss-making bet on VR/AR hardware and the metaverse, and develops the open-weight Llama model family, which it does not directly charge for but uses to build the same ad-serving AI.

3. Why the model likes it — durability check

Gates: checked — no pending-deal or data-coverage exclusion applies to META in the v4 quant universe; it is included in this dossier only via the pre-committed "quality-growth lane" override (STATE.md, 2026-09-26), not because it cleared the model's own top-30 rank gate. b1 composite 0.200 (decile 2, quintile 1 — the bottom quintile of the entire program's universe, live_rank 398). This is the weakest score of the four names by a wide margin, and the model's own quant screen would have excluded META entirely under normal rules; it is only in this dossier because of the pre-committed "quality-growth lane" rule for the eight largest AI/cloud names (see program STATE.md, 2026-09-26 entry). Family breakdown: Quality is actually the highest of the four (fam_Q 0.854) — reflecting Meta's historically strong ROE, gross-profit/assets and balance sheet — but this is a backward-looking (largely TTM) measure that has not yet fully absorbed the Q2 2026 margin compression described in §4; Value (0.159), Momentum (0.305) and especially earnings momentum (fam_S 0.195) are all weak, directly reflecting the first YoY profit decline and a stock that has underperformed on a beat/miss basis (7/8 beats, one miss, lower average surprise of +11% vs. +50% for AMZN/GOOGL). The composite score is telling a coherent, current story: strong balance-sheet quality, but weakening near-term earnings trend and a rich price.

4. Last two years of results (quarterly highlights, $bn GAAP unless noted)

Quarter Revenue YoY Op. income Op. margin FCF
Q1 2026 ~$58 (implied) — — — $12.39bn
Q2 2026 $60.8 +28% $18.775 31% (down from 38–43%) $0.784bn

Q2 2026 operating income of $18.775bn was down 8% YoY from $20.441bn — total expenses surged 55% to $42.0bn, driven by AI infrastructure/data-center costs, $2.4bn of legal-related charges and $1.18bn of severance tied to May-2026 layoffs [Meta Q2 2026 press release; Beancount.io]. Family of Apps (the profitable ad business) operating income was $23.394bn, down 6% YoY even before Reality Labs losses. Reality Labs posted a $4.619bn operating loss in Q2 2026 (vs. $4.530bn a year earlier) on just $431m of revenue (+16% YoY) — an enduring, ~$18bn/year drag against a company generating ~$240bn of annual revenue. Advertising revenue: $59.4bn, +27% YoY (26% cc), with impressions +14% and price-per-ad +12% — both growing, a healthy underlying ad-auction dynamic. Ad revenue growth is currently outrunning operating-income growth, i.e., the AI-driven ad improvements are real but are being outspent by AI infrastructure and one-off costs. TTM revenue (d4): $228.2bn. NTM consensus EPS $33.28 (d4); trailing EPS $26.52.

5. Guidance track record

2026 AI capex guidance was raised twice, most recently narrowing to $135–145bn (up from $72.2bn spent in 2025) [valueaddvc, 2026]. Quarterly capex hit $31.1bn in Q2 2026 — 98% of operating cash flow for the quarter, which mechanically explains the FCF collapse to $784m. This is a guidance-raised-on-spend pattern (like Alphabet's), not a revenue miss, but it is the most severe capex-to-cash-flow ratio of the four names reviewed.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • SBC: $13.69bn for H1 2026 (on H1 revenue of roughly $118–119bn implied), a materially higher SBC/revenue ratio (~11–12%) than any of the other three names in this batch — a real, disclosed cost, not a modeling assumption.
  • D&A: $12.35bn for H1 2026, rising with the capex ramp; capex (property/equipment purchases) was $49.11bn in H1 2026 alone.
  • Free cash flow collapsed from a healthy Q1 2026 print ($12.39bn) to $0.784bn in Q2 2026 — a single-quarter data point, but directionally consistent with the capex guidance trajectory (98% of OCF consumed by capex in Q2).
  • The $2.4bn of Q2 2026 legal-related charges should be treated as at least partly non-recurring when assessing the trend in operating margin, but they are real cash/GAAP costs, not adjustments to wave away entirely — flagged, not excluded, in this dossier's figures.

7. Valuation — reverse DCF (no V1 row exists for this ticker; valuation performed directly here)

10-year reverse DCF: 13% discount rate (highest of the four, reflecting the Reality Labs drag, capex-to-cash-flow intensity and open EU regulatory exposure), 34% terminal operating margin (below the pre-2026 peak of 43%, reflecting a structural Reality Labs drag and permanently higher AI infrastructure D&A), 18% tax, ~2.548bn diluted shares (from market cap/price), 20x terminal P/E. The $751.66 close requires a constant 10-year revenue CAGR of ~17.5% — the highest requirement of the four names.

My base case: ad revenue growth decelerating from 27–28% today toward the high-teens by year 3 as AI-driven ad-improvement gains (impression/price growth) mature, and toward high-single-digits by year 10 as the ad-auction business matures globally, with Reality Labs remaining a persistent drag throughout. Explicit path (19%/17%/14%/12%/11%/10%/9%/8%/7%/6%) gives a 10-year compound-equivalent of ~11.2% and a base-case fair value of ~$443 — ~70% below the current $751.66, the largest gap of the four names reviewed. implied_vs_base: above.

3-year scenario returns (IRR from $751.66): | Scenario | Yr3 revenue | Op. margin | P/E | Yr3 price | 3-yr IRR | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Bear | $287.5bn | 28% | 15x | $389 | −19.4% | | Base | $365.6bn | 34% | 20x | $800 | +2.4% | | Bull | $435.2bn | 39% | 26x | $1,420 | +23.9% |

Even the base case is barely above a breakeven 3-year return at this entry price — the stock needs the bull case (sustained margin recovery toward pre-2026 levels plus multiple expansion) to deliver a return that would justify a full-weight position today.

8. Bull case

  1. Meta won the FTC's monopoly trial outright in November 2025 (Judge Boasberg found no monopoly in social networking given TikTok competition) — the single largest structural risk (forced divestiture of Instagram/WhatsApp) is resolved in Meta's favor at the trial-court level, even though the FTC has now appealed (Jan-2026).
  2. Advantage+ (AI-automated ad buying/creative) is at a $20bn+ annualized run-rate — the clearest, largest, currently-monetizing AI product disclosed by any of the four companies in this program, not a future promise.
  3. Core ad metrics (impressions +14%, price/ad +12%, both YoY) show the auction is still healthy and growing on both volume and price — a two-lever growth engine, not reliant on one variable.

Bear case

  1. Q2 2026 was the first YoY profit decline of the AI era for Meta — operating margin fell 12 points (43%→31%) in one year, and the model's own factor scores (bottom quintile) are flagging this in real time, not lagging it.
  2. Reality Labs remains a ~$18bn/year structural loss with no disclosed path to profitability, and this capital is not going toward the core ad business's own AI infrastructure.
  3. Despite winning the FTC trial, Meta was fined €200m (April 2025) for its "pay or consent" advertising model under the EU DMA, and the European Commission has opened a further non-compliance investigation into that same pay-or-consent model — an unresolved, recurring regulatory cost center specific to Meta's ad-targeting business model, distinct from and in addition to the FTC appeal.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (thesis-invalidation triggers — signposts to watch)

  1. Operating margin remains below 35% for two consecutive quarters (confirms the Q2 2026 compression is structural, not one-off legal/severance noise).
  2. Quarterly free cash flow remains below $5bn for two consecutive quarters (confirms the capex-to-cash-flow ratio is not easing as capacity comes online).
  3. 2026 AI capex guidance is raised a third time beyond $145bn.
  4. The EU Commission issues a further fine or mandated product change on the "pay or consent" model (beyond the existing €200m April-2025 fine).
  5. Reality Labs operating loss exceeds $20bn on a trailing-12-month basis without a disclosed monetization roadmap.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 2026-10-28 (per d4 snapshot). FTC appeal of the November-2025 trial-court ruling: notice of appeal filed 20-Jan-2026; no briefing schedule/decision date identified in this window. EU DMA "pay or consent" non-compliance investigation: ongoing, no decision date identified.

11. Red-flag scan

No auditor changes, restatements or going-concern language identified. Legal-related charges of $2.4bn and severance of $1.18bn in Q2 2026 are disclosed, real cash items — not adjusted away in this dossier's operating-margin figures. EU DMA fine (€200m, April 2025) for the pay-or-consent model is a closed enforcement action but the underlying business practice remains under further non-compliance investigation, i.e., this is not fully resolved. No SEC/DOJ accounting investigation or short-seller report identified specific to Meta in this window.

Data basis, recency and disclaimer

All figures are consolidated (Meta Platforms, Inc. group-wide; no standalone parent-only statements are relevant here). Most recent period incorporated: Q2 2026 10-Q (quarter ended 30 June 2026, filed ~July/August 2026) and the Q2 2026 earnings release/call. Events checked to 2026-09-25 close. GAAP figures are labeled GAAP throughout this dossier; no company non-GAAP adjusted EPS is used or implied. Research, not personalized investment advice; not a recommendation to buy or sell.

MGM Resorts International (NYSE: MGM) — Diligence Dossier

Agent f10 | As of 2026-09-25 close ($32.58) | Most recent period incorporated: Q2 FY2026 (period ended 2026-06-30), 10-Q filed 2026-07-29; checked for events to 2026-09-25 (includes the confirmed 2026-09-24 withdrawal of the People Incorporated proposal).

1. Verdict

WATCH. Thesis horizon 12–24 months. The stock round-tripped a takeover premium (+16% on the bid, -11% on its withdrawal) that nets out close to zero, so the real story is operating, not deal-driven: Las Vegas Strip Resorts is genuinely improving (2nd straight quarter of YoY growth) but Regional Operations and MGM China are both shrinking on a profit basis, Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA has fallen YoY for two consecutive quarters even as GAAP net income has been flattered by one-off gains, and the balance sheet's ~1.5x conventional net-debt/EBITDA hides a much heavier ~$23.8bn triple-net lease obligation to VICI/other landlords. Move to INCLUDE-SMALL only once Adjusted EBITDA stabilizes.

2. Business

MGM Resorts owns/operates casino resorts on the Las Vegas Strip (its largest, highest-margin segment: Bellagio, MGM Grand, Aria, Cosmopolitan, etc.), a Regional Operations portfolio of US regional casinos, MGM China (Macau, via ~56%-owned MGM China Holdings), plus MGM Digital (LeoVegas and other consolidated European/international iGaming) and a 50/50 unconsolidated JV, BetMGM (US sports betting/iGaming). Most domestic real estate is monetized via triple-net sale-leaseback master leases, principally with VICI Properties — MGM operates the casinos but does not own most of the underlying real estate. Routing: primary playbook aviation-hotels.md (Resorts & Casinos — yield×occupancy, perishable capacity); the lease structure is read through a REIT-tenant/rent-coverage lens (cf. realestate-reit.md logic) because conventional leverage metrics understate the fixed obligation; BetMGM (equity-method, ~4% of consolidated Adjusted EBITDA) is a minor secondary item, not large enough to warrant a full exchanges-payments.md overlay.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1 composite 95.9th percentile (live_rank 24), driven by Value (83rd pct — genuinely cheap post-selloff) and high Momentum/SUE inputs that are now likely stale: the b1 snapshot's as_of is 2026-09-25 but factor construction typically uses data through the last rebalance, and the 11% single-day drop on the 2026-09-24 deal withdrawal plus the Macau EBITDAR miss (see §6) will not be reflected until the next rebalance — treat the Momentum leg as about to roll over, not as a current green light. Quality is flagged as incomplete: gp_a (gross-profit/assets) is blank in b1_live_scores.csv for MGM and n_Q = 6 vs. 7 for SWK/HAS — the Quality family score rests on one fewer input, plausibly because MGM's lease-heavy balance sheet does not map cleanly onto a gross-profit/assets construct. 5. "Guidance": none issued; qualitative outlook only

MGM gives no point or range guidance for revenue, EBITDA or EPS in any of the last five earnings releases (Q2 FY26 through Q2 FY25). Management commentary is directional only: continued Las Vegas Strip growth investment, MGM Osaka (Japan integrated resort) "on track for 2030 opening," and capital-return priorities (buybacks over dividend — MGM pays no regular dividend). Per the dossier template's instruction, this is stated rather than inferred.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • GAAP vs. Adjusted divergence is the central earnings-quality finding. Q2 FY26: GAAP net income $292.4m (EPS $1.11) vs. $49.0m (EPS $0.18) a year earlier — a huge GAAP improvement — while Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA fell 6% YoY ($610m vs. $648m) and Adjusted EPS fell 25% ($0.59 vs. $0.79). The GAAP headline is driven by one-off property/disposition gains (MGM Northfield Park was sold 2026-04-21) and other non-operating items excluded from Adjusted EPS; the underlying operating trend is negative for two straight quarters (Q1 FY26 Adjusted EBITDA -9% YoY; Q2 FY26 -6%). Q3 FY25's GAAP loss (-$1.05/share vs. Adjusted +$0.24) was itself driven by a goodwill impairment. A reader who quotes only the GAAP EPS trend would reach the opposite conclusion from the Adjusted-EBITDA trend.
  • Segment profit is narrowly led by one segment. Q2 FY26 Segment Adjusted EBITDAR: Las Vegas Strip Resorts $735m (+3% YoY, genuine growth); Regional Operations $280m (-9% YoY reported, flat same-store ex the Northfield disposition); MGM China $257m (-15% YoY) despite flat revenue and management's "market share gains" framing — margin compression from a $21m YoY increase in intercompany branding fees and (by inference from peer price action, see §9) broader Macau softness.
  • Lease-adjusted leverage is far higher than the conventional ratio. Balance sheet (Q2 FY26 10-Q/8-K Ex-99.2): cash $2,547.4m, long-term debt (net) $6,068.4m → conventional net debt $3,521.1m, matching the D3/V1 figure exactly (cross-check passed). Conventional net debt/TTM-EBITDA ≈ 1.4-1.6x looks comfortable. But operating lease liabilities are $23,778.5m — nearly 4x conventional debt — almost entirely the triple-net master leases with VICI Properties (plus Beau Rivage/MGM National Harbor ground subleases and MGM China land concessions). Triple-net lease rent expense was $552.2m in the quarter (~$2.2bn annualized). Rent coverage (Consol. Adj. EBITDA + rent) / rent ≈ (610+552)/552 ≈ 2.1x — a REIT-tenant credit metric, not a leverage ratio, and a more honest read of balance-sheet risk than net-debt/EBITDA alone. Lease-adjusted leverage ≈ (3,521 + 23,779) / (~4.6bn annualized EBITDAR) ≈ ~5.9x vs. the conventional ~1.5x — a roughly 4-turn gap.
  • BetMGM contribution is small relative to its narrative weight: equity income of $23.1m in Q2 FY26 (vs. $21.8m a year earlier) — modestly growing, profitable, but only ~4% of consolidated Adjusted EBITDA.
  • Capital return: $164m of buybacks in Q2 FY26 alone, $1.4bn remaining authorization; no regular dividend.

7. Valuation snapshot

NTM P/E 16.9x — 57th percentile of ~10 years of own history (mid-range, not a screaming discount despite the price decline, because forward estimates have also fallen). EV $11.92bn excludes the $23.8bn operating lease liability — the "cheap EV/EBIT" read embedded in the quant screen therefore overstates cheapness on a lease-adjusted basis. FCF yield 10.7%. WACC 8.02% (beta 1.19, elevated). Reverse DCF implied 10y growth -6.9% vs. consensus FY1 +1.2% and a delivered 10y CAGR of +7.1% (5y +22.1%, though this is flattered by the post-COVID low base) — a real "priced for shrinkage" setup, but note the segment-level EBITDAR deterioration in §6 gives that pessimism some grounding. Street targets ($40-57, mean $49.33, 19 analysts, "buy") sit entirely above the current $32.58 price and almost certainly predate the 2026-09-24 withdrawal and the Q2 Macau/regional EBITDAR softness — treat as stale, not as a live 23%+ implied margin of safety. Independent re-run of scripts/valuation.py reproduces V1's EV bridge exactly (EV $11,918.8m; net debt $3,521.1m, matching §6) and gives an FCF-anchored reverse-DCF implied growth of -9.2%/yr, slightly more bearish than V1's -6.9%.

8. Deal speculation vs. fundamentals (People Incorporated proposal) — quantified

D4's corporate-events file records a $48.30/share cash proposal from People Incorporated on 2026-06-01 and its withdrawal on 2026-09-24; both the proposal and the withdrawal are independently confirmed in MGM's own Q2 FY26 8-K (forward-looking-statements section names "any acquisition proposal from People Incorporated" explicitly). Using daily closes (v4/data/d2_close.parquet, Cboe/CNBC cross-checked): - Announcement day (2026-06-01): MGM +16.1% ($43.67→$50.69) vs. LVS +5.6%, WYNN +5.5%, CZR +0.3%, SPY +0.3% — an idiosyncratic, deal-driven gain of roughly +10-13pts. Note MGM traded above the $48.30 offer, implying the market priced a real chance of a bump or competing bid. - The stock then drifted from $50.69 down to ~$37-40 through the summer before the formal withdrawal — the market was already pricing out completion odds. - Withdrawal day (2026-09-24): MGM -11.0% ($37.85→$33.69) vs. LVS -1.4%, WYNN -1.5%, CZR ~flat, SPY ~flat — an idiosyncratic, deal-driven loss of roughly -10pts, an almost-exact round trip of the announcement-day gain. - Cumulative 2026-05-29→2026-09-25: MGM -25.4% vs. LVS -22.9%, WYNN -19.9%, CZR +1.9%, SPY +1.7%. Read-through: the deal itself is roughly a wash cumulatively (gained then gave back ~10-13pts). The bulk of MGM's four-month decline (~20-23pts) is shared with Macau-exposed peers LVS/WYNN, consistent with the MGM China EBITDAR miss in §6 — a sector/Macau re-rating, not an MGM-only story. Against CZR (Vegas/regional, no Macau exposure, up 1.9% over the same window), MGM's underperformance (~27pts) is stark and points to Macau as the dominant shared driver, with the withdrawn deal a secondary, largely self-cancelling contributor.

9. Bull case

  1. Las Vegas Strip Resorts — the largest, highest-quality segment — delivered a second consecutive quarter of YoY revenue and EBITDAR growth (+3%/+3%), with continued high-ROI luxury-room reinvestment.
  2. Valuation: reverse-DCF-implied shrinkage (-6.9%/10y) is more pessimistic than the 7-10y delivered track record; FCF yield ~10.7%; buybacks ($1.4bn remaining) are shrinking the float into weakness.
  3. BetMGM is durably profitable and MGM Osaka (2030) is a call option on a new, high-barrier Asian gaming market not yet in most near-term models.

10. Bear case

  1. The "modest" ~1.5x conventional net-debt/EBITDA is misleading: ~$23.8bn of triple-net lease liabilities against ~$2.4bn of annualized Adjusted EBITDA implies rent coverage of only ~2.1x, a REIT-tenant credit profile with a fixed obligation that does not flex down in a downturn.
  2. Two of three core segments are shrinking on a profit basis: MGM China Segment Adjusted EBITDAR -15% YoY despite flat revenue, and Regional Operations -9% reported; Vegas Strip alone is carrying the growth story.
  3. GAAP net income has been flattered by one-off gains for two of the last four quarters while Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA has now declined YoY for two straight quarters — the "record" GAAP headlines mask a shrinking operating base, and the failed takeover removes a speculative floor that had been supporting the stock.

11. Key risks & kill criteria

  1. Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA declines YoY for a third consecutive quarter (Q3 FY26).
  2. MGM China Segment Adjusted EBITDAR declines further or Macau GGR trends turn negative for two more quarters.
  3. Rent coverage (EBITDAR/triple-net rent) falls below ~1.8x.
  4. Las Vegas Strip YoY growth breaks (the one clearly improving segment rolls over).
  5. Any further goodwill/asset impairment in Regional Operations following the Northfield Park disposition precedent.

12. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings ~2026-10-28 (Q3 FY26, per D4 snapshot). Watch for: MGM China monthly Macau GGR data, any revived acquisition interest (from People Incorporated or another party) following the 2026-09-24 withdrawal, and MGM Osaka construction milestones.

13. Red-flag scan

No auditor change, restatement or going-concern language identified in the documents reviewed. Two GAAP-distorting one-offs in the last five quarters (Q3 FY25 goodwill impairment driving a GAAP loss; Q2 FY26 disposition gain flattering GAAP net income against a declining Adjusted EBITDA) — both disclosed, not concealed, but material to interpretation (§6). Unsolicited-proposal handling: MGM does not appear to have filed a standalone 8-K on either the receipt or the withdrawal of the People Incorporated proposal (only referenced inside the routine Q2 FY26 earnings 8-K's boilerplate) — consistent with a non-binding, board-rejected approach that did not trigger Item 8.01/14D-9 disclosure obligations, but it also means there is no primary document detailing the board's rationale. Insider Form 4 pattern and litigation docket not reviewed in this pass (time-boxed) — flagged as open, not asserted clean.

(1) b1's Quality family score for MGM rests on incomplete inputs (gp_a blank, n_Q=6) — logged as a data gap, not a clean read. (2) V1's EV/valuation snapshot excludes ~$23.8bn of operating lease liabilities, overstating cheapness on a lease-adjusted basis. (3) V1's "attractive vs. Street" framing (target range $40-57) is very likely stale — pre-dating the 2026-09-24 deal withdrawal and the Q2 FY26 Macau/regional EBITDAR miss — and should not be read as a live margin of safety. Data quality note

dossiers.MPC:
Marathon Petroleum Corporation (NYSE: MPC) — Diligence Dossier

Agent f7 | Prepared 2026-09-26 | Most recent period incorporated: Q2 2026 (10-Q filed 2026-08-04, period ended 2026-06-30); checked for events to 2026-09-25. Sector routing: GICS Energy / Oil & Gas Refining & Marketing → oil-gas.md playbook, segment-split explicitly between the cyclical Refining & Marketing (R&M) business and the majority-owned (~64%), more contracted MPLX midstream business, with the Deep Cyclicals overlay (13-situations.md §2 — "refining and petrochemical spreads" is explicitly named there) as the governing lens for the R&M segment.

Data quality note: GAAP/adjusted EPS, segment Adjusted EBITDA, refining margin $/bbl and guidance figures below are sourced from SEC filings and 8-K earnings-release exhibits with citations. The ratios.py run in §7 uses an estimated interest expense (~$1.5B/yr — MPC does not tag InterestExpense in a form this pass could extract) and does not separately model MPLX non-controlling-interest (~36% of MPLX belongs to public unitholders); as a result its derived EPS/P-E are directionally useful for trend but less precise than the directly-sourced GAAP/adjusted EPS figures used everywhere else in this dossier — flagged explicitly rather than presented as equally precise. This is research, not personalised investment advice, and not a solicitation to buy or sell; the reader is responsible for their own decisions.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight), thesis horizon 12–24 months, revisit sizing after Q3 2026 results confirm whether the margin spike is fading toward the ~$15–18/bbl 2024–2025 range as external forecasters expect.

One-sentence reason: Q2 2026's refining margin ($36.33/bbl, more than double the Q1 2026 and full-2025 run-rate) is a real, materially-elevated spike that coincides with the same Iran-conflict/Strait-of-Hormuz shock inflating CF's nitrogen margins — genuinely cyclical and likely to fade — but MPC differs from a pure cyclical in one important, evidenced way: ~64%-owned MPLX contributed a comparatively stable $1.6–1.8B of quarterly Adjusted EBITDA through both the 2024–25 refining trough and the 2026 spike, which is real, non-cyclical ballast a pure refiner (or CF) does not have — hence half-weight rather than an outright reject.

2. Business in plain English

Marathon Petroleum is the largest petroleum refiner in the US by throughput (~2.9m barrels/day crude capacity across Gulf Coast, Mid-Continent and West Coast refineries), selling gasoline, diesel and other refined products through its own Marathon-brand retail/wholesale network. It makes money on the "crack spread" — the difference between crude oil cost and refined product prices, which is set by global refining supply/demand, not by MPC. Layered on top, MPC owns the general partner and ~64% of the common units of MPLX LP, a separately-traded midstream MLP that gathers, processes, stores and transports crude/refined products/NGLs for fee-based income under longer contracts — a materially less cyclical business that MPC consolidates. Competitive position: scale, a geographically diversified refining footprint, and a captive midstream system that lowers its own logistics costs while also throwing off public-market-valued cash flow.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Preliminary QVM percentiles (sector-neutral within Energy, lead_prelim_rank.csv): Q = 0.769 (77th pctile), V = 0.673 (67th), M = 0.942 (94th pctile — the strongest momentum score of the three tickers in this batch), preliminary composite = 0.794. Momentum is real and price-confirmed (crack spreads and the stock have both re-rated sharply since Q1 2026). Value is more moderate than CF's, which is appropriate — MPC does not screen as extremely "cheap" on the model. Two artefacts to flag: (1) the pipeline's raw factor inputs for MPC contain a material data error — TTM revenue is shown as $77.4B against COGS of $134.4B (implying a negative $57B gross profit), which is not a real business fact (see §6/data conflicts); GPA (-0.604) is contaminated by the same error and should not be trusted at face value. (2) ROE (44.8% raw) is flattered by continuous, large buybacks that have shrunk book equity from $27.7B (FY2022) to $17.3B (FY2025) even as the business delevered its earnings — some of the "quality" signal is capital-structure engineering, not only operating improvement (ratios.py: equity multiplier rose from 3.24x to 4.64x over the same window). The durable part of the quality case is MPLX: its segment Adjusted EBITDA was $1,720M (Q1'25) → $1,641M (Q2'25) → $1,598M (Q1'26) → $1,778M (Q2'26) — a ~9% range across a period when R&M Adjusted EBITDA swung from $489M to $6,655M (13.6x) — genuine, evidenced non-cyclical ballast.

Unlike CF's Yazoo-City-driven slip, no negative guidance revision was identified for MPC in this window — operational guidance has been met or modestly improved each quarter, which is itself a data point in the bull case (execution has been good; the risk here is priced-in margin, not execution).

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

Data conflict (report explicitly): the v4 quant pipeline's TTM figures for MPC show revenue $77.4B against COGS $134.4B (implying a negative $57B gross profit) — this is not a real business fact; FY2025 actual revenue was $132.7B and FY2024 was $138.9B per the 10-K/XBRL (RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax), and this dossier's own TTM estimate is ≈$153.6B. A second, more subtle conflict: the pipeline's "yago"/actual EPS fields for MPC (FY2025 = $10.70, and the quarterly eps_q0_yago/eps_q1_yago fields) are MPC's adjusted (non-GAAP) EPS, not GAAP — GAAP FY2025 was $13.22. This is exactly the "adjusted numbers mixed with GAAP, unlabelled" failure the prior audit (lead_v3_audit.md) flagged; anyone using the pipeline's "EPS" field as GAAP without checking would be wrong by ~24% on this name. Third: the pipeline shows consolidated LT+ST debt of only ~$5.4B; actual consolidated debt (MPC + MPLX) was $32.8–32.9B as of Q2 2026 (MPC standalone $7.2B + MPLX $25.6B) — cash of $7.768B, however, does match the pipeline exactly, so the error is specific to the debt/revenue/COGS fields, not systemic to every field.

FCF conversion: FY2025 FCF (CFO $8,253M − capex $3,486M) = $4,767M; FCF/NI ≈ 1.18x (own-calc PAT). ratios.py flags capex below 90% of depreciation in FY2022–2024 (0.57x–0.76x), flipping to 1.07x in FY2025 as MPLX growth capex (Northwind Midstream acquisition, $2.4B, Aug 2025; BANGL acquisition, $703M, Jul 2025) and MPC's own high-return refinery projects ramp. SBC: immaterial as a % of revenue (not separately broken out in this pass). GAAP-vs-adjusted gap: material and volatile quarter to quarter (Q3 2025: GAAP $4.51 vs adjusted $3.01; Q4 2025: GAAP $5.12 vs adjusted $4.07) — always driven by asset-sale gains, legal settlements and LIFO, not a stable non-operating item; use adjusted EPS as the comparable series. Leverage: consolidated net debt/EBITDA on ratios.py's (approximate) FY2025 basis is 2.5x, versus 0.7x in FY2022 — leverage has genuinely risen as the trough years (2024–2025) compressed EBITDA while gross debt held roughly flat to slightly up; this is a real, if not alarming, trend, though it is sensitive to the flat-debt estimate used here (precise annual debt was not independently extracted this pass — verify against the 10-K debt note before final sizing). Importantly, ~78% of consolidated debt ($25.6B of $32.8B) sits at MPLX, a fee-based entity with its own investment-grade capital structure, not at MPC standalone. Debt maturities: MPC/MPLX have staggered senior notes into the 2030s–2050s and a revolver due 2027 and a new $5.0B (MPC) + $2.5B (MPLX) revolver due April 2031 (refinanced 2026-04-07, replacing 2022 facilities; no borrowings outstanding). M&A: MPLX Northwind Midstream ($2.4B, Aug 2025) and BANGL ($703M + contingent, Jul 2025) acquisitions; Rockies operations divested ($980M proceeds, Nov 2025); 49.9% stake in The Andersons Marathon Holdings sold ($427M, Jul 2025). Share count: extremely aggressive and sustained — diluted shares fell from 664M (2019) to 306M (2025), a 54% reduction in six years; buybacks were $11.9B (2022), $11.6B (2023), $9.2B (2024), then slowed sharply to $3.5B in 2025 (the trough year) before re-accelerating to >$1.0B (Q1'26) and a combined $2.8B buybacks+dividends (Q2'26) alongside a fresh $5B incremental authorization (total $8.6B available as of Q1'26, $6.1B remaining as of Q2'26) — i.e. management pulled back capital return exactly when the stock/margins were weak (2025) and re-accelerated exactly as margins spiked (2026), the same "buy more at the top" pattern flagged for CF's dividend increase.

7. Valuation snapshot

Basis P/E EV/EBITDA FCF yield

FY2025 GAAP actual (EPS $13.22) 29.8x — —
FY2025 Adjusted actual (EPS $10.70) 36.8x — —
FY2025 ratios.py own-calc (EPS $18.48, unadjusted for NCI — see data-quality note) 20.3x 12.5x 4.1% (mkt cap)
NTM consensus (d4, EPS≈$49.42, calendarised) 7.96x — —

The NTM consensus multiple is the headline reason this stock screens as "cheap," and this dossier finds real grounds for caution on that number. H1 2026 actual GAAP EPS (Q1 $1.73 + Q2 $17.73) was already $19.46 — for the FY2026 consensus of $55.73 to be realized, H2 2026 would need to deliver a combined ~$36/share, i.e. an acceleration beyond even Q2's blowout print, sustained for two more quarters. That is not impossible (if the Iran-related disruption persists or worsens) but should not be underwritten as a base case; the 90-day estimate-revision history (FY2026 consensus $29.70→$50.23→$55.73) shows analysts chasing the print upward in real time rather than a stable, converged view — the pipeline's own ntm_flags field independently notes "extreme dispersion." Mid-cycle framing (using $/bbl, the more appropriate unit for a refiner than %-of-revenue margin, since revenue is dominated by pass-through crude cost): the 2024–2025 (non-spike) refining margin ran $13–19/bbl, with FY2025 averaging $16.87/bbl — call this the mid-cycle band. Q2 2026's $36.33/bbl is roughly 2.0–2.5x that band. Cross-check via the %-of-revenue method (ratios.py, 2018–2025 EBIT margins: -17.6%, 4.0%, 3.6%, 12.1%, 9.8%, 4.9%, 6.2%, plus 5.4% for 2018 — median ≈5.2%, or ≈5.4% excluding the COVID-2020 outlier) points to the same conclusion: TTM/Q2-26 profitability sits well above MPC's own normal range, and the market multiple that makes the stock look "cheap" is being applied to an earnings base that recent history says is unlikely to persist at this level. A more conservative NTM P/E built off a normalized ~$17–20/bbl margin (i.e., closer to the FY2025 run-rate than the Q2'26 spike) would likely sit in the mid-teens to ~20x, not 8x. Peers for cross-check (not independently re-underwritten this pass): Valero (VLO), Phillips 66 (PSX), PBF Energy (PBF), HF Sinclair (DINO).

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull (3): 1. MPLX is real, evidenced, non-cyclical ballast, not a hoped-for diversification story — its Adjusted EBITDA held inside a ~9% band through the worst refining quarter (Q1'26, $489M R&M EBITDA) and the best (Q2'26, $6.655B R&M EBITDA) in this dataset, and MPLX's own growth capex (Northwind, BANGL) is expanding that base further; management states MPLX's growing distribution is "expected to more than fund MPC's 2026 dividend and standalone capital." 2. Execution and guidance discipline have been good — no guidance cut identified across the four releases reviewed (§5), opex/bbl guidance has trended down (better) each quarter, and refinery utilization has run 94–95%. 3. Capital return is large and structurally supported — a fresh $8.6B buyback authorization (post the Q1'26 $5B increase) backed by MPLX's stable distribution stream, on top of a 54%-since-2019 reduction in share count.

Bear (3): 1. The Q2 2026 print is a sharp, sudden, broad-based (all three regions) margin spike that coincides with the same Iran-conflict/Strait-of-Hormuz shock inflating CF's nitrogen margins — buying both CF and MPC in the same portfolio is a correlated bet on the same transient geopolitical driver persisting, not two independent theses; if the conflict de-escalates, both would likely reprice together. 2. The consensus FY2026 EPS ($55.73) that makes this stock look cheap on an NTM basis requires H2 2026 to out-run even Q2's blowout quarter — this dossier's own primary-source math (H1 2026 actual EPS $19.46) suggests the "8x NTM P/E" headline may be resting on an estimate base that has not yet converged and could prove too high, in which case the multiple re-rates upward on flat or falling estimates rather than the price falling. 3. Leverage has genuinely risen through the 2024–2025 trough (net debt/EBITDA ~2.5x on this dossier's estimate, up from 0.7x in 2022) even before the current spike reverses, and capital return was cut hardest exactly when the stock was cheapest (2025) and is being re-accelerated exactly as it is most expensive on a normalized basis (2026) — the opposite of disciplined counter-cyclical buying.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (thesis-invalidation triggers)

Any of the following would invalidate the "MPLX ballast justifies a small position despite a cyclical spike" thesis:

  1. Refining margin reverts toward the $13–19/bbl 2024–2025 band within 1–2 quarters (the base case per external nitrogen/energy-market commentary on the Iran conflict fading) — expected, and the trigger to re-underwrite the position size, not necessarily to exit.
  2. FY2026 actual EPS materially misses the $55.73 consensus (e.g., prints below ~$35–40) — would confirm the estimate-chasing pattern flagged in §7 and likely trigger a valuation re-rating.
  3. Net debt/EBITDA (consolidated) exceeds ~3.5x on a normalized (non-spike) EBITDA base — would elevate this from a cyclical-earnings question to a genuine balance-sheet question; verify the exact figure from the 10-K debt note before relying on this dossier's approximate leverage figures.
  4. MPLX distribution growth is cut or its own Adjusted EBITDA becomes meaningfully more volatile — would remove the specific evidenced reason (§3, §8) this name is INCLUDE-SMALL rather than REJECT.
  5. A second consecutive quarter of guidance cuts (opex/bbl rising or throughput guided down without a stated turnaround reason) — would break the "good execution" bull point.

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: ~2026-11-03 (Q3 2026, aggregator estimate — verify via IR calendar closer to the date).
  • Any Iran-conflict ceasefire/de-escalation or Strait-of-Hormuz normalization news — highest-frequency catalyst, shared with CF (see bear point 1).
  • CFO transition: John Quaid → Maria Khoury as EVP & CFO, effective 2026-01-19 (8-K, 2025-12-18) — appears an orderly, planned transition (Quaid remains in a non-executive transition role); worth a name-check in Q3 commentary.
  • MPLX Northwind/BANGL integration progress and any further bolt-on midstream M&A.
  • Senior notes due March 2026 — near-term maturity to confirm was refinanced in the ordinary course (small relative to total debt).

11. Red-flag scan

  • Auditor/controls: no Item 4.01 (auditor change) 8-K identified in the filing history window reviewed (2022–2026); no going-concern or material-weakness language identified in the sections of the FY2025 10-K/10-Q reviewed. Full CAM list and auditor tenure were not independently extracted in this pass — verify directly before final sizing.
  • Litigation/contingencies: 10-Q references "Note 22, Commitments and Contingencies" without a detailed dollar breakdown in the excerpt reviewed; MPC guarantees certain LOOP LLC/LOCAP LLC indebtedness (routine for a pipeline/terminal joint-venture structure). The $253M "legal settlement" gain referenced in the FY2025 earnings release was not identified to a named counterparty/matter in this pass — a gap to close before relying on it as fully understood.
  • Related-party transactions: $976M sales / $1,341M purchases with equity-method affiliates in H1 2026 (utilities, transportation, renewable diesel feedstock) — disclosed and appears to be ordinary-course JV commercial activity, not a governance concern on the evidence reviewed.
  • Management turnover: roughly a dozen Item 5.02 (officer/director change) 8-Ks were filed between 2022 and 2026, including the CFO transition above — this is a higher cadence than CF's single officer-retirement filing in the same universe, though nothing reviewed suggests a disorderly departure or a dispute; flagged for awareness rather than as a confirmed red flag.
  • Insider trading (Form 4) pattern: not independently pulled in this pass due to a repeated SEC-access issue with the ownership-filing feed — flagged as a data gap, not a finding, and should be closed out before relying on "no unusual insider selling" as clean, particularly around the Q2 2026 print.
  • Short-seller reports: none identified via search in this pass.

dossiers.MPWR:
MPWR — Monolithic Power Systems, Inc. (diligence agent F29, standard depth)

1. Verdict

WATCH (12–36 month thesis horizon). MPWR is executing exceptionally well operationally (record, accelerating revenue and margins on AI data-center power delivery), but the stock is priced for that acceleration to continue for a decade, the company has an unremediated material weakness, a live, partially-surviving securities-fraud suit centred on the exact customer-concentration risk the triage flagged, and V4's own quant model ranks it in the bottom quintile of the entire coverage universe. This is not a "no v1 row so skip" situation — the combination of valuation, litigation and governance overhang means it does not clear the bar for inclusion today.

2. Business in plain English

Monolithic Power Systems designs high-performance, mixed-signal power-management and voltage-regulation semiconductors — chips that convert and regulate electrical power for GPUs, servers, storage, industrial and automotive systems. It is fabless (it designs chips and outsources manufacturing). Its fastest-growing segment is voltage-regulator modules and power stages for AI-GPU/data-center racks, where its largest disclosed customer relationship is with Nvidia-class AI accelerator platforms.

3. Why the model likes it (triage) vs why the quant model does not (b1) — a direct data conflict

Triage (v4/outputs/Q12_triage.json) advanced MPWR on "+48% revenue growth and +112% EPS growth against a 42x NTM P/E" — sub-1 PEG optics. But V4's own systematic quant score (v4/data/b1_live_scores.csv, 2026-09-25) ranks MPWR composite 0.104, decile 2, quintile 1, live_rank 445 of ~500 — i.e., in the bottom fifth of the entire coverage universe, not a top name. Note on naming: the SEC registrant remains "Marsh & McLennan Companies, Inc." (ticker recently changed from MMC to MRSH); the company brands itself "Marsh" in current press releases. This dossier uses "MRSH" or "the Company" throughout. One of its four operating segments is also internally called "Marsh," distinct from the parent brand — this dossier always says "Risk and Insurance Services segment" for that unit to keep segment-level figures separate from consolidated ones (the wave-3 entity-scope requirement).

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (24–36 month horizon), reservation: a real, unresolved legal exposure (Credit Suisse's ~$2bn Greensill-related claim against two subsidiaries) could add materially to the $425M already charged, and GAAP diluted EPS actually fell 5% YoY in H1 2026 on that one-off — this is a genuine adverse fact, not merely a headline scare, so this is a half-weight position pending the next 1–2 quarters of clarity. Underneath that, the underlying franchise (world's largest insurance broker, plus Mercer and Oliver Wyman) is high-quality, growing, and — on a reverse DCF — priced for very little forward growth, i.e. cheap if the litigation resolves within the reserved range.

2. Business in plain English

MRSH is the world's largest insurance broker and professional-services group, organized in two segments: Risk and Insurance Services (Marsh — commercial insurance broking; Guy Carpenter — reinsurance broking) and Consulting (Mercer — retirement, health and workforce consulting; Oliver Wyman — management consulting). It earns commissions and fees for placing insurance/reinsurance and advising clients, plus fee income on consulting engagements — an asset-light, recurring-revenue model with high client-retention economics, growing both organically and through bolt-on and larger (e.g., McGriff) acquisitions.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Triage (Q05) cited 25.9% ROE, "durable recurring commissions," and 39% EPS growth, calling 15.3x forward P/E fair. Confirmed with primary data and refined: b1_live_scores.csv (2026-09-25) shows ROE (pct_roe) in the 86th percentile and gross-profit/assets in the 91st percentile — genuinely strong, durable broker economics, not an artefact. However, the "39% EPS growth" and the 15.3x forward P/E in d4_live_snapshot.parquet carry an explicit ntm_quality="caution" flag from the vendor data itself — this dossier does not rely on that NTM P/E; it is very likely distorted by the $425M Greensill charge booked in Q1 2026 depressing the trailing GAAP EPS base that a naive forward-growth calculation would use. Own reverse DCF (two-stage FCF/share basis, $10.03 TTM FCF/share from d4 FCF $4.785bn ÷ ~477.2M shares; cost of equity 7.1% from CAPM, beta 0.577 — a genuinely low beta for the sector, consistent with insurance broking's non-cyclical, recurring-commission model; 10-year explicit growth then an 18x terminal FCF multiple, below MRSH's own ~20x historical average) implies the market is pricing in ≈0.8%/yr FCF-per-share growth for 10 years — a very low bar, well below both MRSH's realized organic growth (mid-single-digit underlying, high-single-digit reported revenue growth even in the softer 2H25/1H26 quarters, §4) and its historical ~8–10%/yr adjusted-EPS growth. This is priced below a reasonable base case — the market appears to be discounting for the Greensill overhang and the GAAP-EPS optics, which is exactly the risk this dossier flags rather than dismisses. Sensitivity check: this result is highly sensitive to the WACC/terminal-growth spread in a pure Gordon-growth form (flipping to negative implied growth for WACC below ~7.5% with a 3% terminal rate) — the exit-multiple form used here is more stable and is the basis for the "below" call, but the honest range spans roughly 0–3%/yr across reasonable assumption sets, all still below the ~8% base case.

Bull: (1) the Board's 10% dividend increase alongside the Greensill charge signals management does not see the residual Credit Suisse exposure as solvency-relevant; (2) organic growth, while decelerating YoY (underlying growth ~3–5% in recent quarters vs high-single-digit two years ago), remains positive across a diversified four-brand (Marsh/Guy Carpenter/Mercer/Oliver Wyman) platform through a softening commercial- insurance pricing cycle — a resilience test many pure-play brokers do not face as well; (3) at a reverse-DCF implied growth near zero, almost any resolution of the Credit Suisse claim inside the currently-implied range should not re-rate the stock lower purely on that basis — the bad news looks largely priced. 1. Verdict

My own reverse-DCF read: starting from NTM consensus EPS ≈$5.86, a base case of ~15%/yr EPS growth for 3 years with the multiple normalizing from 44.7x toward a still-generous 25x by year 3 implies a price near $417 — only ~1.5%/yr price appreciation (plus a token dividend), i.e. the current price already assumes results close to or better than this base case. This is a genuinely strong business priced for continued strong execution, not for a margin of safety.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) AI data-center bookings are "exceptionally robust" and management is guiding accelerating growth each quarter through FY27 (quotes above); (2) the NVIDIA strategic-investment/partnership both funds and validates the custom-XPU/scale-up-networking roadmap; (3) Custom-silicon revenue is explicitly flagged to "significantly accelerate" in 2H FY27, a second growth leg beyond networking. 9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Data Center segment revenue growth below 20% YoY for two consecutive quarters (vs. +46% YoY in Q2 FY27).
  2. Public disclosure that a top-3 hyperscaler custom-silicon program (>10% of revenue) has been re-bid, cancelled, or is being in-sourced by the customer.
  3. Non-GAAP gross margin below 57% (below the low end of the current 57.5–58.5% Q3 guide) for two consecutive quarters.
  4. Consolidated net debt/EBITDA (per the 10-Q balance sheet, run-rate annualized EBITDA) rising above 2.0x (currently roughly 0.3–0.5x).
  5. NTM P/E above 55x with no corresponding upward revision to FY28 revenue guidance (a pure re-rating with no new fundamental support).

  • Series A Preferred Stock conversion terms and any regulatory/waiting-period conditions tied to the NVIDIA investment are a structural item to monitor (10-Q risk factors).

11. Red-flag scan

No restatement, auditor-change, going-concern, or SEC/DOJ-investigation language found in the reviewed 10-Q (2026-08-01) or the last three earnings press releases. No material named litigation. Two real, disclosed items to track: (a) customer/program concentration risk (qualitative, in risk factors); (b) the NVIDIA Series A Preferred Stock gives NVIDIA contractual consent/dividend rights "that differ from the rights of holders of our common stock" (10-Q risk factor) — a governance item, not a red flag today, but worth re-reading if NVIDIA's stake or influence grows. Agent: F45 · Standard depth · Prepared 2026-09-26 · Price/market data as of 2026-09-25 close ($196.31; mkt cap ≈$308.3B)

1. Verdict

WATCH — 12–24 month horizon. A genuinely stronger, more fee-based franchise than five years ago (Wealth Management now the largest single revenue segment, $10T in client assets), but the current record profitability is priced as if it is the new steady state rather than partly a cyclical trading/IB peak. 2. Business in plain English

Morgan Stanley is a global investment bank and wealth manager. Institutional Securities does M&A advisory, equity/debt underwriting, and trading (equities and fixed income) for corporations and institutions. Wealth Management advises individuals ($10T combined client/AUM assets across Wealth + Investment Management) and earns recurring fee-based revenue plus net interest income on client cash/lending. Investment Management runs asset-management strategies. It makes money on fees, spreads, trading margins and net interest income; its competitive position is top-3 in US equity trading/wealth management scale following the 2020 E*TRADE and Eaton Vance acquisitions.

3. Why the model likes it / durability

data/b1_live_scores.csv: live_rank 168, composite driven by Value (pct_fcfp/pct_ebit_ev high) and Momentum (pct_mom_12_1 0.90) — i.e. the model likes MS on cheapness-on-trailing-earnings plus strong recent price momentum. TTM P/E: $196.31 / $12.37 TTM diluted EPS ≈ 15.9x. Price/tangible book value: $196.31 / $53.18 ≈ 3.69x TBV — historically rich for MS (which traded 1–2x tangible book for most of the post-2008 decade and re-rated only as the wealth-management mix shift matured). Triage (Q05) separately cited a ~14.6x forward multiple on consensus estimates.

Reverse valuation (Gordon growth on ROTCE, the standard bank/broker method — no generic FCFF DCF, per sector convention): P/TBV = (ROTCE − g) / (COE − g). Solving for the ROTCE the market needs Morgan Stanley to sustain in perpetuity, at an assumed cost of equity ≈10% and terminal growth g≈4%: implied sustainable ROTCE ≈ 3.69 × (10%−4%) + 4% ≈ 26.1% — almost exactly the 26.6% ROTCE MS just posted this quarter, a quarter the company itself attributed largely to unusually favorable trading conditions. In other words, the price is already assuming the current cyclical-peak ROTCE is the new normal, not a cyclical high to fade. That is a materially more demanding ask than a normalized through-cycle ROTCE (management's own medium-term target has historically been discussed around ~20%, not 26%+) — implied growth/return is above my base case.

3-year scenario returns (annualised, price+dividends, exit-P/E method off TTM EPS $12.37): bear −9.4% (EPS reverts to ~$11, P/E to 12x) · base +3.3% (EPS ~$13.5, P/E ~15x) · bull +13.5% (EPS ~$16, P/E re-rates to 17x).

Bull: (1) Wealth Management has structurally re-mixed the firm toward recurring, less capital-intensive fee revenue ($10T client assets, record $148B net new assets in one quarter) — less cyclical than the old trading-led Morgan Stanley. (2) $20B new buyback authorization plus a 15% dividend raise show management conviction and shrink the share count into strength. (3) CET1 14.8% and Tier 1 leverage 6.0% leave ample room to keep returning capital even if credit costs tick up.

Bear: (1) Institutional Securities—especially Equity trading (+69% YoY)—is the swing factor behind the "record" quarter; a normalization of trading/IB activity (which the company's own release attributes to favorable market conditions, not a structural share gain) would pull ROTCE back toward the high teens/low 20s. (2) CET1 and Tier 1 leverage ratios are both declining YoY even as buybacks accelerate — a squeeze if credit costs or a market shock arrive together. (3) Recency of regulatory settlements ($249.4M DOJ/SEC block-trading settlement, Jan-2024; $15M SEC fine for failing to monitor advisor account transfers, Dec-2024) shows a pattern of compliance-control gaps that predates but overlaps the current management team's tenure.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Standardized CET1 ratio falls below 13.0% (currently 14.8%, down 20bps YoY already).
  2. ROTCE falls below 18% for 2 consecutive quarters (evidence the 26%+ level was cyclical, not structural).
  3. Wealth Management net new assets fall below $50B/quarter for 2 consecutive quarters (vs the $148.1B Q2 2026 record) — a sign the "structural re-mix" story is stalling.
  4. A new SEC/DOJ/FINRA enforcement action or fine >$100M is announced (given the 2024 pattern above).
  5. Provision for credit losses in Institutional Securities exceeds $300M in a single quarter (vs $71M in Q2 2026) without a matching one-off disclosed cause — a credit-quality deterioration signal.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next scheduled release: Q3 2026 earnings, estimated ~14-Oct-2026 (Q3 2025 was reported 15-Oct-2025 via 8-K; date not yet confirmed — flagged as an estimate). Watch for: whether Equity/Investment Banking revenue holds near Q2 2026 levels (durability test) and whether CET1 stabilizes as the new $20B buyback program starts to draw down capital in Q3 2026.

11. Red-flag scan

  • Regulatory settlements (2024, resolved but recent): $249.4M DOJ/SEC settlement (Jan-2024) over historical block-trading practices; $15M SEC fine (Dec-2024) for failing to monitor wire/ACH transfers that let four former advisors misappropriate >$1.7M from client accounts over 7 years; FINRA granted a waiver from statutory disqualification in early 2026 tied to the same matter. No new charges identified in 2026 to date.
  • Capital ratio drift: CET1 (Standardized) down 20bps YoY, Tier 1 leverage down 80bps YoY, while quarterly buybacks rose from $1.0B to $1.5B — capital return is running ahead of capital build, worth monitoring but not yet at a level that trips regulatory buffers.

dossiers.MSCI:
MSCI — MSCI Inc.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE — thesis horizon 24–36 months. A high-margin (56%+ operating margin), high-retention (95.3% Retention Rate) index/data/analytics compounder whose Q2 2026 release raised both expense and free-cash-flow guidance on genuine business momentum (Index Run Rate +17.4%), not one-offs. A reverse DCF on the 25-Sep-2026 close implies roughly 9.7% ten-year FCF growth — at or slightly below an evidence-based ~10–11% base case — so the stock is not priced for more than the business plausibly delivers. Main watch-items are share-count-funded buybacks partly on debt and a real, if modest, sensitivity to global AUM/market levels (asset-based fees are ~1/3 of Run Rate).

2. Business in plain English

MSCI sells subscriptions and asset-linked licenses for equity/fixed-income indexes (used as benchmarks and as the basis for trillions of dollars in ETFs and index funds), portfolio and risk analytics tools, ESG/climate data, and private-assets data — mainly to asset managers, asset owners, banks, hedge funds and insurers. It earns recurring subscription fees (the majority of revenue) plus fees that scale with the assets under management (AUM) benchmarked or linked to MSCI indexes (asset-based fees, the fastest-growing and most market-sensitive piece). Its moat is extreme switching cost: index methodologies are embedded in client mandates, benchmarks, fund names and regulatory/ compliance workflows, so clients rarely switch once an index is adopted, and MSCI's own analytics and ESG data reinforce the same client relationships.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

dossiers.MSFT:
MSFT — Microsoft Corporation

1. Verdict

WATCH. Horizon 12–36 months. Best-in-class enterprise AI/cloud franchise with real, accelerating evidence behind the growth story, but at the 25-Sep-2026 close ($516.17) the price already requires ~12.7% constant 10-year revenue growth (vs. an evidence-based base case of ~10.9%) — the smallest overshoot of the four mega-caps in this batch, and one that could close on a normal pullback rather than a broken thesis.

2. Business in plain English

Microsoft sells productivity and collaboration software (Office/365, Teams, LinkedIn), enterprise cloud infrastructure and platform services (Azure), and consumer/gaming products (Windows, Xbox, Search/advertising via Bing/Copilot). It makes money mostly through recurring commercial subscriptions and cloud consumption contracts with large enterprises and governments, monetizing its entrenched position inside corporate IT stacks and increasingly reselling AI compute and Copilot seats on top of that base.

3. Why the model likes it — durability check

b1 composite 0.697 (decile 7, live_rank 152 — outside the quant top-30, which is why it was never diligenced under the original rank gate). Driven almost entirely by Quality (fam_Q 0.784: high gross-profit/assets, ROE, operating-cash generation, low leverage) and Earnings momentum (fam_S 0.674). Value (0.512) and Momentum (0.317) are unremarkable — the stock is not cheap and has not been a recent price leader. This is durable, not an artefact: Microsoft's quality metrics reflect a genuine, multi-decade recurring-revenue moat, not a one-off. The earnings-momentum score is corroborated by 8/8 EPS beats over the last 8 quarters (avg surprise +7.5%).

4. Last two years of results (annual segments, FY ends 30 June; $bn, GAAP unless noted)

FY Revenue YoY Op. income Op. margin Productivity Intelligent Cloud More Personal Computing
FY2026 (10-K, filed ~Jul-2026) 331.8 — 155.2 46.8% 140.0 137.8 54.1
FY2025 (prior 10-K) ~282 ~14% ~128 ~45% ~125 ~114 ~43

Quarterly Azure growth (constant currency, company-reported): Q2 FY26 ~33–34%, Q3 FY26 40%, Q4 FY26 43% — accelerating, not decelerating, over the last four quarters [Microsoft FY26 Q3/Q4 press releases; TIKR/Webull summaries]. Microsoft's "AI business" (Azure AI consumption + Copilot) crossed a $37bn annualized revenue run-rate in Q3 FY26, up 123% YoY [GeekWire, 2026-04]. Microsoft 365 Copilot paid seats: 15m (Jan-2026) → 20m (Q3 FY26) → 30m by Q4 FY26, against a ~464m commercial M365 seat base (~6.5% penetration) [UCToday; Stackmatix]. NTM consensus EPS $20.70 (d4), trailing EPS $17.97.

5. Guidance track record

Guided Azure growth has been beaten each of the last two quarters shown (guide ~40% cc for Q4, delivered 43%). FY2027 guidance (from the Q4 FY26 call, not yet independently verified against outturn since Q1 FY27 has not reported by this cutoff) points to continued Cloud acceleration and further capex increases. Treat as guided, not yet delivered.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • FCF conversion / cash-flow challenge (Codex's independently verified figures, adopted here — see §7): FY26 CFO − cash capex − finance-lease principal = $63.886bn. SBC = $12.405bn (≈3.7% of revenue) — a real economic cost, not added back. Treating SBC as a cost gives a conservative cash diagnostic of $51.481bn (~1.34% of equity value at $516) [MSFT FY26 10-K, cash-flow statement and Notes 13/17].
  • Diluted share count essentially flat FY25→FY26 despite ongoing buybacks — do not assume a large repurchase tailwind.
  • Capex/finance-lease intensity has stepped up materially; a useful-life extension (buildings 15→25 years) has reduced reported depreciation and moved future leases off the capex line — a falling capex line alone does not prove improving economics [MSFT CFO commentary, Q4 FY26 call].
  • Net debt position is modest relative to EBITDA (d4: total debt $128.8bn vs total cash $76.8bn vs EBITDA $194.2bn) — balance sheet is not a constraint.

7. Valuation — reverse DCF and reconciliation with Codex v005

Codex (release v005, versions/v005_2026-09-26_codex/reports/review/ready/technology.md): BUY BELOW $500 against a $516.05 reference close; hurdle 12%; base case FY29 revenue $517.54bn (46% terminal margin, 20% tax, 7.453bn diluted shares, terminal EPS $25.55, 28x terminal multiple) → Sept-2029 price $715.51, 3-yr IRR 12.23% at $516.05 / 13.42% at a $500 entry. Bear −10.09%/−9.13%; Bull 25.39%/26.72%. Codex's own ceiling at the 12% hurdle is $519.15 — i.e., the market close is already almost exactly at the point where the base case just clears the required return, offering minimal margin of safety.

My independent check (10-year reverse DCF, same discipline: SBC as expense, nonoperating income normalized to zero): using Codex's own base-case terminal assumptions (46% margin, 28x terminal multiple, 12% discount rate) but solved over 10 years instead of 3, the $516.17 close requires a constant 10-year revenue CAGR of ~12.7% to be justified. My own base case — Cloud decelerating from today's 40%+ to high-teens by year 3 and to high-single-digits by year 10 as it scales past $500bn revenue, Productivity high-single-digit, PC flat-to-down — produces an explicit decelerating path (18%/15%/14%/12%/11%/10%/9%/8%/7%/6%) whose 10-year compound-equivalent growth is ~10.9%, and which produces a base-case fair value of ~$444 — about 16% below the current $516.17. implied_vs_base: above. This is the smallest overshoot of the four names reviewed under this program (GOOGL/AMZN/META all show larger gaps — see their dossiers). I agree with Codex's qualitative conclusion (limit-buy, not a market order) and adopt their $500 ceiling as a sensible near-term entry discipline; my own decelerating-growth base case is somewhat more conservative on the 10-year horizon, which is why my fair value ($444) sits below Codex's implied ceiling ($519) — the difference is entirely the growth-persistence assumption (Codex's explicit model is only 3 years; mine forces a view on years 4–10, where Azure/AI growth must structurally decelerate as the base compounds).

3-year scenario returns (bear/base/bull, IRR from $516.17): | Scenario | Yr3 revenue | Terminal margin | P/E | Yr3 price | 3-yr IRR | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Bear | $408.5bn | 39% | 22x | $376 | −9.2% | | Base | $517.5bn | 46% | 28x | $716 | +12.2% | | Bull | $583.3bn | 49% | 32x | $982 | +24.6% |

8. Bull case

  1. Azure is accelerating (33%→40%→43% cc over the last three quarters), not decelerating, against an already-large ($137.8bn) Intelligent Cloud base — the opposite of typical large-base deceleration.
  2. The Copilot attach motion is real and growing fast (15m→30m seats in ~9 months) inside a 464m-seat installed base — huge unmonetized runway even at modest penetration gains.
  3. Diversified moat: no single regulatory or competitive shock (search remedies, ad-tech fines, FTC social-media suits) hits Microsoft's core businesses the way it hits Alphabet/Meta/Amazon.

Bear case

  1. Capex and finance-lease intensity are rising faster than the depreciation shows (useful-life extension flatters reported margins); the $51.5bn SBC-adjusted cash figure is barely growing relative to the capex commitment.
  2. At $516, the stock is priced almost exactly at both Codex's and my own base-case ceiling — there is very little room for a growth disappointment before downside dominates (bear case is −9%/yr).
  3. The EU Commission's preliminary view (25-Jun-2026) is that Azure should be designated a DMA "gatekeeper" service, with the investigation due to conclude by November 2026 and six months to comply if designated — a genuine, dated regulatory catalyst that could force interoperability/licensing changes to Azure's most profitable enterprise contracts [Concurrences, DataCenterDynamics, 2026-06/09].

9. Key risks & kill criteria (thesis-invalidation triggers — signposts to watch)

  1. Azure constant-currency growth falls below 30% for two consecutive quarters while capex commitments keep growing (Codex's own trigger, adopted).
  2. Annual operating margin falls below 43% without a demonstrably attractive incremental-return explanation.
  3. SBC-adjusted cash generation (CFO − capex − finance leases − SBC) fails to cover dividends plus dilution-offsetting buybacks for two consecutive annual periods.
  4. EU DMA gatekeeper designation of Azure (expected by November 2026) is finalized with material interoperability/pricing remedies attached.
  5. Entry discipline: do not add fresh capital above $500 (Codex ceiling) / $444 (my base-case fair value); reassess on any pullback toward those levels.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 2026-10-28 (Q1 FY2027, first quarter to show whether the 43% cc Azure growth held). EU DMA Azure gatekeeper decision expected by November 2026. Ongoing OpenAI-relationship disclosures (Microsoft holds a large equity stake whose fair-value marks flow through non-operating income — normalized to zero in this valuation, consistent with Codex).

11. Red-flag scan

No auditor changes, material weaknesses, restatements or going-concern language identified in the FY26 10-K search. No SEC/DOJ investigation specific to Microsoft's core businesses identified beyond the EU DMA Azure gatekeeper inquiry (a regulatory-designation process, not an enforcement action for wrongdoing). No short-seller report identified. Metadata note (carried from the program's data audit): none specific to MSFT.

Data basis, recency and disclaimer

All figures are consolidated (Microsoft has no separately reported standalone/parent-only statements relevant here). Most recent period incorporated: FY2026 10-K (fiscal year ended 30 June 2026, filed ~July 2026) and Q3/Q4 FY26 earnings materials. Events checked to 2026-09-25 close. GAAP figures are labeled GAAP; "core"/normalized EPS in the valuation section strips non-operating gains to zero and treats SBC as an expense (Codex's convention, adopted for comparability) — this is not the company's own non-GAAP adjusted EPS. Research, not personalized investment advice; not a recommendation to buy or sell.

dossiers.MTB:
MTB — M&T Bank Corporation — Fundamental Diligence Dossier

1. Verdict: INCLUDE. Thesis horizon 12–36 months. The best risk/reward of the three names reviewed in this batch: expanding NIM, falling deposit costs, improving credit quality (nonaccrual ratio at its lowest since 2007), the only net-positive sell-side FY1 estimate-revision trend of the three (11 up / 2 down), fair (not rich) valuation, and disciplined, guided capital return. Real but manageable risks: CRE is growing again with no office-specific disclosure in the materials reviewed, expenses are guided to the high end of the FY2026 range, and management's own FY2026 net-charge-off guidance (~37bps) is above the actual run-rate of the last four quarters (23–31bps), implying they expect some credit normalization.

2. Business in plain English

M&T Bank is a ~$210bn-asset super-regional commercial bank headquartered in Buffalo, NY, operating retail and commercial banking across the Northeast/Mid-Atlantic (NY, PA, MD, NJ, CT, VA, DC, WV, DE, MA, ME), plus a sizeable wealth-management and institutional-services business built up via the 2022 People's United acquisition. It earns money primarily from net interest margin — the spread between what it earns on commercial & industrial, commercial real estate, residential and consumer loans, and what it pays on deposits and other funding — plus fee income from wealth/trust, mortgage banking and institutional services.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1 composite 0.930 (decile 10) — the highest of the three names — yet live_rank is 35 (live_top30 = False), a rank/composite inconsistency the dossier notes but cannot resolve (same caveat as CINF; flagged for the quant team, not the fundamental read below). Fundamentals support the high quality score and look durable, not artefactual: NIM has expanded for four straight quarters (3.62%→3.66%→3.68%→3.70%→3.70%/3.71%) on falling funding costs, credit metrics are improving on an absolute basis (not just YoY comps against a worse prior year), and the earnings-surprise history (beats 7 of 8, avg +5.9%) is corroborated by a positive, not negative, forward-estimate trend (FY1 EPS: 11 up / 2 down in 30 days) — the opposite pattern to HIG and CINF, which is itself informative.
