5. Guidance Track Record

  • Q3 2025 (2025-10-15): Narrowed FY2025 net-revenue guidance to $15.00–15.10B and NCO guidance to 5.6–5.7% [14]. Actual: FY2025 net revenue $14.981B — essentially in line, ~0.1% below the low end; FY2025 NCO 5.65% [2], inside the guided band.
  • Q4 2025 (2026-01-27): Initial FY2026 guidance: diluted EPS $9.10–9.50, NCO "approximately 5.5–6.0%" [14], plus macro assumptions (unemployment 4.8%, GDP +2.0%, Fed funds 3.25%, deposit beta ~65%) [14]. New $6.5B buyback authorization; dividend +13% to $0.34/share from Q3 2026 [14].
  • Q1 2026 (2026-04-21): EPS maintained at $9.10–9.50; NCO improved to "below 5.5%" for the year (down from 5.5–6.0%) — a favorable revision — with mid-single-digit receivables growth and RSA "within 4.0–4.5%" [14].
  • Q2 2026 (2026-07-21): EPS narrowed/raised to $9.25–9.50 (from $9.10–9.50, low end up) [14]; NCO maintained below 5.5%; RSA maintained within 4.0–4.5%; receivables growth maintained mid-single-digit, "expected to accelerate in the second half" [14]. No expense/efficiency-ratio guidance is given in any of the four releases — disclosed here, not assumed passing.

6. Earnings Quality & Balance Sheet

FCF/OCF metrics (FCF conversion, FCF yield) are not meaningful here — loan growth and deposit inflows dominate operating cash flow, so a fast-growing and a shrinking SYF would show opposite "FCF" signs with no read-through to franchise health [nbfc.md, banks.md]; the pipeline's ~40.8% "fcfp" field is disregarded accordingly. SBC expense is not separately XBRL-tagged (embedded in "Employee costs" [9]); as a proxy, quarterly share issuance from equity comp (0.2–2.0M shares) was dwarfed by repurchases (6.6–12.1M shares/quarter) [7,4] — dilution is a rounding error against the buyback. GAAP vs. adjusted: SYF reports two reconciled non-GAAP figures (tangible book value/share, ROTCE) [4] and no adjusted-EPS series, so no GAAP-vs-adjusted EPS gap exists. Capital: holding-company CET1 ran 13.7% (Q3 2025) → 12.6% (Q4 2025) → 12.7% (Q1 2026) → 13.2% (Q2 2026) [4,7] — a modest buyback-driven downtrend, cushioned by the Q2 2026 $500M preferred issue, still well above the ~7% regulatory minimum-plus-buffer; Synchrony Bank's own stand-alone CET1 was higher, 13.7% at FY2025-end [2] (a different, less-levered perimeter — see Data Quality Note). Funding: 83–84% deposits, 93% direct/retail within deposits [2,4]; total borrowings (securitized debt + senior/sub notes) $16,432M [4] — a maturity ladder was not pulled (n/a, out of budget). ACL coverage fell from 10.87% (Q1 2025) to 10.09% (Q2 2026) [4,7] on an unchanged 12-month CECL forecast period [2]. Buybacks: common shares fell from 389.2M (Q3 2024) to 325.4M (as of 2026-07-17, per the Q2 2026 10-Q cover [3]), ~16% in under two years; the current $6.5B authorization has no expiration [14].

7. Valuation Snapshot

Suppressed and why: EV/EBITDA, EV/Sales, generic FCF yield, D/E, ROCE and current ratio are all undefined or inverted for a deposit-funded lender — debt (deposits/borrowings) is raw material, not financing, and CFO is dominated by loan/deposit balance-sheet churn [nbfc.md, banks.md]. Primary method — P/TBV vs sustainable ROTE, P/B = (ROE − g)/(COE − g): at price $72.94 and disclosed tangible book value/share $42.01 [4], SYF trades at 1.74x P/TBV. Using COE 11% (above the DM-bank 9–11% range given SYF's 1.308 beta [18] and monoline card-cycle concentration) and g 4% (management's own mid-single-digit receivables growth guidance [14]): raw FY2025 ROE (21.3%, still credit-cost-flattered) implies a justified 2.47x; a through-cycle-normalized ROE — migrating NCO from ~5.4% to the mid-point of management's own 5.5–6.0% band, roughly a 1.5–2 point ROE haircut — implies 1.86x–2.00x. Current 1.74x sits at or slightly below even this more conservative normalized band, i.e. the market is already pricing in most of the credit-normalization risk, not ignoring it. Secondary — P/E on normalized credit cost: TTM diluted EPS ≈ $9.76 (sum of last four quarters [4,7]) at today's below-target NCO; normalizing to the 5.5–6.0% band cuts net income by an estimated 8–13%, giving normalized EPS of roughly $8.5–9.0 and a normalized P/E of ~8.1–8.6x vs. a raw trailing ~7.5x [17,18] — still not statistically demanding. Peers (secondary cross-check, Tier 2/4): Bread Financial (BFH), the closest pure private-label peer, trades at 1.54x P/TBV with 22.6% ROTCE [19]; Capital One (COF) at 2.05x P/TBV / 13.2x trailing P/E [20], though COF's ROE is currently distorted by Discover-integration charges and it is now a much larger, more diversified franchise. Discover (DFS) is excluded as a peer: Capital One completed its ~$35B acquisition of Discover on 2025-05-18 [13], so DFS is no longer an independently listed comparable.

Valuation reconciliation with V1 (added 2026-09-26): V1 rates SYF "attractive" (score 0.81) with a base-case 3-year annualized return of +31.2%, built on ROE settling at the 50th percentile of its own history (19.1%, versus 20.8% actual TTM) combined with aggressive buyback-driven per-share book-value growth and a P/B re-rating from 1.44x to an exit 1.61x — a 3-year price (~$160.83) that V1's own street-flag notes "exceeds Street 12m high target" ($104; mean $89.43, low $78). This dossier's own valuation read above is that SYF's 1.74x P/TBV already sits at or slightly below its own normalized band (1.86x–2.00x, using COE 11%/g 4%) and its normalized P/E (~8.1–8.6x) is "still not statistically demanding" but not a bargain either — i.e., "the market is already pricing in most of the credit-normalization risk, not ignoring it." This dossier's more measured "fair" read is better supported: NCO has plateaued at 5.37–5.43% for three straight quarters — just below, not deep inside, management's own 5.5–6.0% through-cycle target — and allowance coverage has fallen every quarter for over a year as reserve releases shrink (§3/§6/§9). That is exactly the mechanism that would prevent the further ROE improvement and re-rating V1's base case requires, and it is why this dossier sizes the position small (INCLUDE-SMALL) rather than at full conviction despite agreeing the shares are not expensive.

8. Bull Case and Bear Case

Bull case

  1. Genuinely low-cost, retail-funded balance sheet (93% direct deposits [2]) with expanding NIM (+30bp YoY to 15.08% [4]) and a management team giving, and largely meeting or beating, explicit forward NCO/RSA/EPS ranges every quarter [14] — a real transparency edge the v3 process's own audit flagged as often missing elsewhere.
  2. Valuation already screens as reasonable even after normalizing credit cost to management's own stated through-cycle range (Section 7), with a large, ongoing, uncapped buyback (16% share-count reduction in under two years [3,7]) compounding per-share value.
  3. The CFPB late-fee rule that would have cut fee income was vacated in April 2025 [2,11,12], removing a previously live overhang; no new rule is currently in effect.

Bear case

  1. Credit-cycle timing. NCO improvement has stalled — three straight quarters at 5.37–5.43% [4] — right near the low end of management's own 5.5–6.0% "entry of cycle" target [14], and ACL coverage has fallen every quarter for over a year (10.87%→10.09% [4,7]) as reserve releases shrink; the next leg for NCO is more likely up than down, and FY26 guidance already assumes normalization.
  2. Partner concentration. Five programs are 54% of interest-and-fee income, three of them (Lowe's, PayPal/Venmo, Sam's Club) individually above 10% [2]; loss or repricing of any one is a single-event risk with no comparable offset disclosed.
  3. Muted organic growth. Total net revenue has been range-bound at $3.65–3.82B/quarter for two years (Section 4); most of the FY2025 EPS growth came from a falling provision line, not core spread income, and RSA is running near the top of its 4.0–4.5% target range [14], structurally capping how much of any credit outperformance SYF keeps versus its partners. Sell-side Q3 2026 EPS estimates have been cut roughly 9% over the trailing 90 days (consensus $2.362 vs. $2.603 ninety days earlier) [17,18], consistent with [15], despite the Q2 2026 beat, consistent with the market pricing in this normalization.

9. Key Risks & Kill Criteria — What Would Invalidate This Thesis

  1. NCO rate exceeds 6.00% (top of management's own through-cycle band) for two consecutive quarters [4,14].
  2. Holding-company CET1 falls below 11.5% for two consecutive quarters (vs. 12.6–13.7% over the last four quarters) [4,7].
  3. Non-renewal or material repricing of any of the five largest partner programs (54% of interest-and-fee income) [2].
  4. RSA exceeds 4.5% of average receivables for two consecutive quarters with no offsetting NIM gain [14].
  5. CFPB finalizes and implements a new late-fee rule that SYF discloses as expected to materially reduce late-fee income [2,11].

10. Catalysts & Calendar

Q3 2026 earnings: 2026-10-20, confirmed [17,18]. CFPB late-fee matter: rule vacated 2025-04-15 via settlement; CFPB signaled 2026-07-08 it may revisit the issue [11] — watch for a new proposed rule. Dividend step-up to $0.34/share (+13%) begins Q3 2026 [14]. $6.5B buyback authorization (no expiration) ongoing since Q2 2026 [14]. No investor day identified within budget (n/a — not found). No index-event catalyst identified.

11. Red-Flag Scan

Auditor: KPMG LLP, unqualified opinion, no material weakness disclosed in the FY2025 10-K [2]. No restatement or going-concern language found. Regulatory: the Bank's two legacy CFPB consent orders (2013, 2014, from the GE Capital Retail Bank era — $259M total consumer redress plus a $3.5M penalty) were both terminated, most recently on 2025-05-12 [2,10] — a closed legacy matter, not a new action; two smaller 2026 consumer class actions (a TCPA debt-collection-calls suit and an FCRA credit-reporting suit) were found via WebSearch but are unverified beyond docket-level secondary reporting and look consistent with routine, industry-standard consumer litigation, not a systemic issue. A 2018-vintage securities class action (disclosure of retailer "pushback" on underwriting changes) settled for $34M in 2023 [16] — closed, pre-dates this window. Insider selling: checked a bounded sample of the 12 most recent Form 4 filings (all dated 2026-08-19, transactions dated 2026-08-17) — all were routine dividend-equivalent-unit accruals on outstanding RSU/PSU awards (Code A, small share counts), not open-market sales; a comprehensive multi-year Form 4/144 tally (719 Form 4s and 71 Form 144s on file since 2022 [1]) was not performed and is out of scope for this pass. No short-seller report was found via WebSearch. SYF has crossed the $100B total-assets threshold (assets $121.9B at Q2 2026 [4]), triggering enhanced Dodd-Frank/CFPB prudential and supervisory requirements the company itself flags as a forward risk factor [4].

INCLUDE-SMALL — 24-36 month horizon; reservation stated below. Stryker makes orthopaedic implants (hips, knees — increasingly via the Mako robotic-arm platform), MedSurg/neurotech equipment, and trauma/extremities products, sold to hospitals and surgery centers globally. TransDigm Group Incorporated (TDG) — Diligence Dossier

Agent: F57 (wave 3) | As of: 2026-09-25 close (px $1,116.20, mktcap ≈$62.43bn, per d4_live_snapshot.parquet 2026-09-25)

1. Verdict

WATCH. Not held at the current price. Condition to revisit: consolidated net leverage declines meaningfully (toward <5.0x net debt/EBITDA As Defined) and/or organic (ex-acquisition) growth demonstrates it can sustain high-single-digits on its own for several quarters. This overturns the triage's ADVANCE call: TDG is an exceptional, sole-source aftermarket-parts monopoly with real pricing power, but the reverse DCF — done properly, accounting for the debt-service drag that is already visible in the reported numbers — implies more per-share cash-flow growth for a decade than a defensible base case can deliver, at an already very high (~5.5–6.0x) and still-rising leverage level.

2. Business in plain English

TransDigm designs and manufactures highly engineered, proprietary aircraft components (cockpit security, actuators, ignition systems, specialty pumps and more) that are often the sole FAA-approved source for a given aircraft platform. It sells to commercial OEMs, the commercial aftermarket (repair/replacement parts — its highest-margin, most durable revenue) and defense customers, and its core strategy is to acquire and then re-price such sole-source niches under a highly leveraged capital structure (source: TDG FY2025 10-K, Item 1 Business, filed 2025-11-12).

3. Why the model likes it / is this durable

Q08_triage.json: quality 5/5, growth 4/5, price_vs_growth 3/5. This dossier confirms the 22–23% headline growth (FQ3 FY2026 net sales +23% YoY, company's own release, 2026-08-04) but finds it is materially M&A-driven, not organic: organic sales growth was only 13% of the 23% in FQ3 FY2026 (company's own disclosure), with the remainder coming from the Simmonds, Jet Parts Engineering (JPE) and Victor Sierra (VSA) acquisitions closed in FY2026. The moat (sole-source aftermarket pricing power) is real and durable; the growth rate, and the leverage used to fund it, are the parts this dossier finds less durable than the triage implied.

universe). Reverse DCF (2-stage: 10-yr explicit constant growth + Gordon terminal; terminal growth 3.0%; cost of equity tested at 9.5–10.5% given the elevated leverage): solving for the FCF-to-equity CAGR that reconciles today's ~$62.4bn market cap to the DCF value, using the TTM FCF-to-equity of $1.927bn from §6: - At ke = 9.5%: implied growth ≈12.5%/yr - At ke = 10.0%: implied growth ≈13.6%/yr - At ke = 10.5%: implied growth ≈14.75%/yr My own base case for a 10-yr FCF-to-equity CAGR — blending the company's own guided EBITDA As Defined growth (~15–20% YoY currently, heavily acquisition-assisted) with the demonstrated debt-service drag (FQ1 FY2026 net income fell even as operating income rose, §4) and the practical limit to how long a ~6x-levered acquisition pace can continue — is ≈9–12%/yr, i.e. below the entire implied range (12.5–14.75%) across every cost-of-equity tested. implied_vs_base = above.   1. Genuine sole-source aftermarket pricing power: FQ3 FY2026 commercial-aftermarket growth of 17% YoY, EBITDA As Defined margin of 52.8% — best-in-class economics, unmatched in industrials.
  2. Proven, repeatable M&A playbook (Simmonds, JPE, VSA closed in FY2026; Prince & Izant agreed 2026-07-27) with a disciplined "value-driven operating strategy" that has compounded EBITDA for two decades.
  3. $1.8bn of buybacks YTD FY2026 (39 weeks) plus a large ($5.0bn, authorized November 2025) remaining repurchase capacity show continued aggressive capital return even while leverage is elevated.

9. Bear case

Reported "22–23%" headline growth is materially M&A-driven (organic only 13% of the 23% total in the latest quarter) — a growth rate that depends on continuing to find and finance accretive sole-source targets, which by definition become scarcer and more expensive as TDG (and imitators) bid them up.
  3. The recurring DoD Inspector General scrutiny of TransDigm's aftermarket parts pricing (2019–2022 findings that the company's business model is "specifically designed to raise prices on defense contracts" after acquiring sole-source suppliers) is a persistent reputational/political tail risk even though no new enforcement action was found in the reviewed FY2025 10-K or the FQ3 FY2026 10-Q (both state "no material changes" to legal proceedings and risk factors vs. the FY2025 10-K).

  1. Net debt/EBITDA As Defined (consolidated, per the company's own quarterly reconciliation table) exceeds 6.5x.

  3. Organic sales growth (company's own disclosed figure, ex-acquisitions) falls below 7% for two consecutive fiscal quarters (vs. 7.4%/11.0%/13% in the last three quarters).
  4. FY guidance is cut (not raised or maintained) at any subsequent quarterly release, versus the current $10,470–10,550M sales / $35.38–36.21 GAAP EPS range.
  5. A new DoD Inspector General report or a congressional/DoD enforcement action (refund demand, mandatory cost-data-disclosure order) is issued against TransDigm specifically (vs. the historical 2019–2022 pattern with no new action found as of this dossier).

dossiers.TER:
TER — Teradyne, Inc.

1. Verdict

WATCH — a genuinely excellent, net-cash business riding a real AI/HBM-driven semiconductor-test upcycle, but the stock trades at a cycle-high multiple (36x NTM P/E) on what look like cycle-elevated earnings, and the company's own Q3 guidance is a sequential step-down from Q2's record — the first sign the market's implied growth path is ahead of what management itself is currently promising. Horizon if it re-enters: 12–24 months, on a valuation reset or on confirmation that the "growth in 2027 and beyond" management flagged is actually materializing quarter by quarter.

2. Business in plain English

Teradyne makes the automated test equipment chipmakers use to verify semiconductors work before shipping them (Semiconductor Test — its largest segment, especially memory and compute chips used in AI), plus test gear for other electronics (Product Test) and collaborative/mobile industrial robots (Robotics, via Universal Robots and MiR). It sells to chipmakers and their subcontractors; demand is tied to how much new silicon capacity the industry is building (a cyclical, capex-driven market), and it is currently benefiting from an AI-driven memory and compute testing supercycle.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1 factor scores: composite percentile 0.83 (top ~17%), live_rank 86, quintile 5, decile 9 — a genuinely strong quant score. Quality family (fam_Q) is strong (pct_gp_a 0.87, pct_roe 0.69, pct_ocf_a 0.76 — real profitability and cash generation, not an accounting artefact) and Momentum is extreme (pct_mom_12_1 0.98, stock +77% trailing volatility-scaled 12-1 month return per b1). Value factors are weak-to-middling (pct_ep 0.29, pct_fcfp 0.17, pct_bp 0.25) — i.e., the model likes Teradyne for quality and momentum, not because it is cheap; the FCF-yield weakness is real (FCF yield 0.7% per d4), not an artefact, and reflects that today's earnings are being capitalized at a rich multiple. No data conflict between the quant score and the qualitative growth story — both agree the business is strong; the open question the quant score cannot answer is how much of current earnings is cycle-peak.

  • Guide given 2026-02-02 (Q4/FY25 release): Q1 2026 revenue "$1,150 million to $1,250 million," GAAP EPS "$1.82 to $2.19." Actual Q1 2026 (2026-04-28 release): $1,282M / $2.53 — beat above the high end of both ranges ("Record revenue and earnings both above the high end of our Q1 Guidance").
  • Guide given 2026-04-28 (Q1 2026 release): Q2 2026 revenue "$1,150 million to $1,250 million," GAAP EPS "$1.83 to $2.12" — an unchanged revenue range versus the prior quarter's guide despite the Q1 beat. Actual Q2 2026 (2026-07-28 release): $1,329M / $2.38 — beat above the high end again ("Second consecutive quarter of record revenue, exceeding the high end of our Q2 Guidance").
  • Guide given 2026-07-28 (Q2 2026 release): Q3 2026 revenue "$1,200 million to $1,300 million" (midpoint $1,250M), GAAP EPS "$1.79 to $2.09." This is a raise versus the two prior quarters' $1,150–1,250M range (low end up $50M) but its midpoint ($1,250M) and EPS high end ($2.09) sit below Q2's actual print ($1,329M / $2.38) — i.e., management is guiding a sequential pull-back from the just-reported record, even while raising the range versus its own prior guides. CEO framing: "our Q3 guidance reflects robust AI-related demand. Looking further ahead, rapid increase in wafer fab equipment investment sets the stage for continued growth in 2027 and beyond" — a bet on 2027+, with Q3 2026 itself flagged as a breather. Pending; next report ~2026-10-21 per d4 snapshot.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet (Teradyne, Inc. — single consolidated reporting entity)

  • FCF conversion: OCF for the six months ended 2026-06-28 was $734.3M (10-Q XBRL) against GAAP net income of $773.4M for the same period — FCF/NI (after ~$155.4M of six-month capex) ≈ 75%, solid.
  • SBC: $42.0M for the six months ended 2026-06-28 vs. six-month revenue $2,611.5M ≈ 1.6% of revenue — low, a genuine quality signal versus many AI-adjacent semis names.
  • Balance sheet (consolidated, 10-Q, 2026-06-28): cash and equivalents $349.5M; long-term debt = $0 (has been zero since FY2013 per XBRL history) — Teradyne carries essentially no funded debt. Net cash position, not net debt. Buybacks resumed modestly ($74.2M in H1 2026, versus $702M for all of FY2025) and dividends ($40.7M H1 2026).
  • Hidden asset not marked to fair value on the balance sheet: Teradyne holds a 10% equity stake in Technoprobe S.p.A. (an Italian, publicly listed probe-card maker), accounted for under the equity method at a carrying value of $537.1M (2026-06-28); the 10-Q separately discloses the fair value of the publicly traded shares was $2,457.9 million at that date — i.e., roughly $1.9B of unrecognized mark-to-market value (about 3% of Teradyne's own market cap) sits off the income statement/balance-sheet fair-value line, a real but easily overlooked NAV item.
  • Litigation: the 10-Q's ordinary-course litigation language (patent, employment, commercial, environmental) is boilerplate; management states it believes potential losses are unlikely to be material. No restatement, going-concern, or investigation disclosure found.

7. Valuation snapshot

NTM P/E 36.3x (d4, 2026-09-25 close $398.38); FCF yield 0.7%; EV/Sales (NTM) 10.1x. No V1 systematic valuation row exists for TER → v1_verdict = null. Consensus: 15 analysts, mean target $446.47 (+12.1% upside), rating "buy." My own reverse-DCF read, starting from NTM consensus EPS ≈$10.97: a base case assuming EPS growth moderates from the current 100%+ pace to ~15%/yr over 3 years (a large deceleration, consistent with a cyclical capex-driven business normalizing) with the multiple compressing from 36.3x to a still-generous 25x by year 3 implies a price near $417 — only ~1.5%/yr, i.e. essentially fully priced for a soft landing. A bear case (growth reverses to a WFE-cycle downturn, EPS to ~$8 by year 3, multiple compresses to a trough 15x) implies roughly -33%/yr; a bull case (the "2027 and beyond" AI-capex supercycle materializes, 30%/yr EPS growth, multiple holds near 35x) implies roughly +28%/yr. The wide dispersion reflects genuine cyclicality at a multi-year-high multiple on multi-year-high earnings — the definition of low margin of safety even for a high-quality franchise.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) two consecutive quarters of beating guidance at the high end on real AI/HBM/DRAM/NAND test demand, not one-off; (2) management explicitly frames 2027+ as a continued growth runway on rising wafer-fab-equipment investment; (3) essentially debt-free balance sheet plus a ~$2.46B mark-to-market Technoprobe stake provide real downside cushion in a cyclical downturn. Bear: (1) Q3 2026 guidance is a sequential step-down in both revenue midpoint and EPS high end versus the just-reported Q2 record — the company's own numbers, not a bear-case assumption; (2) semiconductor test-equipment demand is structurally tied to chipmaker capex cycles, which have historically reversed sharply after AI-style demand spikes; (3) at 36x NTM P/E, the stock is priced closer to the bull case than the base case, leaving little room for the normalization most capital-equipment cycles eventually deliver.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. A quarterly revenue guidance midpoint sequentially below the prior quarter's actual revenue for two consecutive quarters (one instance already present in the Q3 2026 guide; a second would confirm a real turn).
  2. Semiconductor Test segment revenue growth turns negative YoY (vs. +100%+ currently).
  3. Consolidated GAAP operating margin below 20% for two consecutive quarters (Q1 2026 ≈37%, Q2 2026 ≈33%, per OperatingIncomeLoss/Revenues from the 10-Q income statement).
  4. NTM P/E stays above 30x while quarterly guidance shows sequential deceleration for two straight quarters.
  5. Management's own commentary on "2027 and beyond" WFE/AI-test capex (in the next two quarters' MD&A) turns cautious or is walked back.

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: 2026-10-21 (Q3 2026 results; d4 snapshot estimate; guided range above).
  • An 8-K dated 2026-08-07/filed 2026-08-10 (Exhibit 10.1, an agreement) was identified in the filing index but not opened this pass — flagged as an open item, not asserted immaterial (limitation).
  • Technoprobe's own share-price moves are a secondary, off-balance-sheet catalyst/risk given the $2.46B stake.

11. Red-flag scan

No restatement, auditor-change, going-concern, or SEC/DOJ-investigation language found in the reviewed 10-Q (2026-06-28) or the last three earnings releases. No material named litigation beyond ordinary-course boilerplate. Insider Form-4 pattern and the 2026-08-10 8-K exhibit were not independently checked this pass — flagged as further-diligence items.

dossiers.TGT:
Target Corporation (NYSE: TGT) — Fundamental Diligence Dossier

Recency: most recent reported period incorporated: Q2 FY2026 (13 weeks ended 2026-08-01), published 2026-08-19 (8-K earnings release) / 10-Q filed 2026-08-28; checked for events to 2026-09-25. Reporting basis: consolidated, USD millions unless stated per-share. Fiscal year ends the Saturday closest to January 31 (52/53-week year); "FY2025" = the year ended 2026-01-31.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Target's comparable-sales and margin trend has genuinely inflected positive after four straight negative quarters, the balance sheet and dividend are solidly covered, and the reverse-DCF shows the market isn't pricing in heroics — but the headline stock momentum (+86.6% raw, 99th percentile) is significantly flattered by a beaten-down 2025 base and a one-time $994M tariff-refund windfall in the most recent quarter, leadership has been in place only 8 months, and a live securities-litigation overhang and an already-normalized trailing multiple argue against a full-weight position. Thesis horizon: 12–24 months (through 2–3 more quarterly prints to confirm the comp/margin inflection survives the lap of easier prior-year comparisons).

2. Business in plain English

Target is a general-merchandise discount retailer operating 1,995 stores (~250.5 million sq ft, all 50 US states) plus a large digital/same-day business (Drive Up, Shipt, same-day delivery), selling apparel, home goods, food & beverage, beauty, electronics and toys mainly to middle-income US households. It competes most directly with Walmart, Costco, Amazon and Kroger, but differentiates on design-led owned/exclusive brands (~30% of merchandise sales) and store experience rather than lowest price. It earns money on merchandise gross margin (~28–30%) plus a growing slice of higher-margin non-merchandise revenue (Roundel retail-media advertising, the Target Plus third-party marketplace, and credit-card profit-sharing with TD Bank). Stores double as fulfillment hubs: they filled more than 97% of total merchandise sales, including digital orders, in each of the last three years — a structurally low-capex fulfillment model versus pure e-commerce peers. (Source: 10-K filed 2026-03-11, Items 1–2.)

3. Why the model likes it — and is the momentum earned?

Quant inputs: Quality (Q) = 0.732, Value (V) = 0.816, Momentum (M) = 0.99 (≈99th percentile of ~500 names), preliminary composite = 0.846.

  • Quality (0.732) — largely durable. TTM ROIC 15.3%, ROE 26.0%, interest coverage 13.5x, and FCF conversion (FCF/NI) ~101% TTM are real, filing-sourced numbers (see §6), not accounting artefacts. ROE is elevated partly by high leverage (equity multiplier ~3.6x) typical of mature retail, not a one-off.
  • Value (0.816) — genuine, not extreme. 9.3x TTM EV/EBITDA and a 6.2% FCF yield are reasonable but not deep-value versus peers (§7); the score reflects Target being cheaper than WMT/COST, not "cheap" in absolute terms.
  • Momentum (0.99) — this is the number to interrogate, per the lead's instruction. Three things are blended into the raw +86.6% (12-1 month) figure:
  • A genuine operating inflection. Comparable sales swung from -2.5% in Q4 FY2025 to +5.6% in Q1 FY2026 and +3.8% in Q2 FY2026 — a real, primary-sourced reversal, and traffic (not just ticket) is driving it (+4.4% and +3.6% respectively). This part is earned.
  • A severely depressed starting base. The stock's 52-week low of $83.44 was hit on 2025-11-20, the day after a disappointing Q3 FY2025 report (comp -2.7%) — the trough of a four-quarter run of negative comps tied to the 2025 DEI-related boycott. Even after the rally to ~$157–171, TGT remains ~31% below its November 2021 all-time high of $228.72. A large share of "+86.6%" is mean-reversion off a crisis low, not a move to new highs.
  • A one-time tariff-refund windfall inside the momentum window. Q2 FY2026 (reported 2026-08-19, the quarter that anchors the "1-month-ago" end of the window) included a $994M pretax / $752M net-income / $1.65-per-share benefit from IEEPA tariff refunds, following the Feb 20, 2026 Supreme Court ruling that those tariffs were unauthorized. Reported diluted EPS "doubled" YoY ($4.11 vs $2.05); excluding the refund, EPS growth was +20% YoY — still good, but a fraction of the headline. This is not repeatable: management's own guidance "excludes any potential future tariff refunds," and the FY2025 10-K states the timing/amount of any further recovery "remain uncertain."

Bottom line: the momentum is partially earned. The direction (comp reacceleration, margin/shrink improvement) is real and corroborated across multiple primary filings; the magnitude of both the EPS beat and the stock move is materially inflated by base effects and a non-recurring legal-ruling windfall. Extrapolating the +86.6%/+100% headline figures forward would be a mistake.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • FCF conversion (FCF/NI): FY2022 -54% (inventory-glut year — heavy markdowns, capex $5,528M vs depreciation $2,700M), FY2023 92%, FY2024 109%, FY2025 77%, TTM 101% ($4,456M FCF / $4,393M NI). Healthy in 4 of the last 5 periods.
  • SBC as % of revenue: 0.20–0.29% across FY2022–FY2025 (FY2025: $281M / $104,780M = 0.27%) — low, stable, not a dilution concern.
  • GAAP vs Adjusted gap: FY2025 GAAP EPS ($8.13) was above Adjusted ($7.57) because a Q1 litigation-settlement gain ($441M after-tax) exceeded Q3–Q4 severance/business-transformation charges. Caveat on non-GAAP quality: in Q2 FY2026, Target's own "Adjusted EPS" did not exclude the $994M one-time tariff refund — the single largest one-off item of the year sits inside both GAAP and "Adjusted" figures. Treat Target's current "Adjusted EPS" as a GAAP-adjacent, not a clean run-rate, number until the refund lapses.
  • One-offs/working capital: ratios.py flagged receivables growing faster than sales (11.5% CAGR vs -0.3% revenue CAGR, FY2022→TTM) and rising DSO (4→6 days). In absolute terms this is immaterial (~$1.8B, ~6 days) for a retailer that sells almost entirely for cash/card at point of sale; it more likely reflects growth in Roundel advertising and Target Plus marketplace receivables than consumer credit risk, but is noted as a data-quality flag rather than dismissed.
  • Leverage: Net debt/EBITDA (TTM, debt inclusive of finance and operating lease liabilities) = 1.44x (net debt $13,278M / EBITDA $9,196M, per ratios.py). Lease-adjusted per the sector convention — (net debt+leases)/(EBITDA+rent) — is ~1.34x ($13,658M / $9,896M). Explicit note per the retail playbook: under US GAAP (ASC 842), operating-lease expense stays a single opex line, so Target's EBITDA was not mechanically inflated the way an IFRS 16 filer's would be; the ~$3.3–3.7B of lease liabilities are correctly added to debt above. Interest coverage is strong (EBIT/interest 13.5x TTM). $2.0B of long-term debt matures within twelve months of the FY2025 10-K date, easily covered by $5.4B cash and $8.7B TTM operating cash flow.
  • M&A/financing: no acquisitions in FY2022–FY2025; $341M net new long-term debt issued in FY2025; no unusual financing activity.
  • Share count: diluted shares fell from 464.7M (FY2022) to 454.1M (TTM), a modest ~2.3% reduction. Buybacks were minimal through the downturn ($408M FY2025, ~$3M in Q2 FY2026) — capital priority was the dividend and reinvestment, not opportunistic buybacks even near the $83 low.
  • Dividend: quarterly dividend raised to $1.16/share in June 2026 (+1.8% from $1.14), the 55th consecutive year of annual increases (Dividend King status; 236th consecutive quarterly dividend since October 1967). Annualized $4.64/share against TTM GAAP diluted EPS $9.63 = 48% payout; against the more representative ex-tariff-refund TTM EPS (~$7.98) = ~58% payout — comfortably covered either way.

8. Bull case and bear case

Bull case: 1. Comp sales have inflected positive for two straight quarters (+5.6%, +3.8%) after four negative ones, led by traffic, not just ticket (+4.4%, +3.6%) — a healthier growth-quality signal than a price-led recovery. 2. Balance sheet and cash generation are solid: ~1.4x lease-adjusted net debt/EBITDA, $4.46B TTM FCF, a 55-year dividend-growth streak covered at ~50–60% of earnings, funding a ~$5B FY2026 capex plan and ~30 new stores without financial strain. 3. Shrink — a multi-year, widely-cited margin headwind — has genuinely reversed to a tailwind ("shrink rates reaching pre-pandemic levels," FY2025 10-K), corroborated across six-plus consecutive quarterly releases independent of the tariff-refund noise.

Bear case: 1. The single biggest print of the "momentum" window was inflated by a non-recurring $994M pretax tariff refund; strip it out and YoY EPS growth was +20%, not the headline +100%, and part of the 12-1 month momentum score is a rebound from a crisis-driven 52-week low rather than a move to new highs (TGT is still ~31% below its 2021 all-time high). 2. Leadership is unproven: CEO Michael Fiddelke has held the role only since 2026-02-01 (~8 months), promoted internally after four quarters of negative comps under his predecessor; two consolidated federal securities class actions (transferred to D. Minnesota, Nov 2025) tied to the 2023 Pride-merchandise/DEI-disclosure saga remain unresolved. 3. On a 2-year-stack basis the "reacceleration" is far more modest than the headline: Q1 FY2026's +5.6% stacks with Q1 FY2025's -3.8% for a ~+1.8% 2-year comp; Q2 FY2026's +3.8% stacks with Q2 FY2025's -1.9% for a ~+1.9% 2-year comp. Meanwhile the ~16–18x P/E is already at the upper end of TGT's own 4-year trailing range, and a probability-weighted scenario model puts fair value modestly (~8%) below today's price.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (thesis-invalidation triggers)

  1. Comp sales turn negative for two consecutive quarters again — would indicate the Q1–Q2 FY2026 reacceleration was a temporary base-effect bounce, not a durable inflection.
  2. Ex-tariff-refund gross margin falls back below ~28% (>150bps below the current ~29–30% ex-refund run-rate) without a clear offsetting driver — would signal shrink/tariff/markdown pressure re-intensifying.
  3. FY2026 guidance is cut at either of the next two releases (Nov 18, 2026 or Q4/FY2026) from the current $9.90–$10.90 GAAP (≈$8.25–$9.25 ex-refund) range — would break the current two-release raise streak.
  4. Lease-adjusted net debt/EBITDA rises above ~2.5x (from ~1.3–1.4x currently) — e.g., from debt-funded buybacks or a margin collapse.
  5. A materially adverse ruling/settlement in the consolidated D. Minnesota securities class actions, or a renewed, similarly-themed boycott that drives traffic growth (currently +3.6% to +4.4%) negative again.

Data Quality Note

CRITICAL DATA FLAG — resolved. The quant pipeline's TTM revenue figure of $72,618.0M is wrong by roughly $35 billion (real TTM revenue as of the Q2 FY2026 10-Q, period ended 2026-08-01, is $107,705M, and the most recent full fiscal year, FY2025 ended 2026-01-31, was $104,780M per the 10-K filed 2026-03-11, Item 8). Root cause, traced precisely via SEC XBRL companyfacts (CIK 0000027419):

  • Revenue ($72,618M): this is an exact match to Target's fiscal-year-2014 annual revenue (year ended 2015-01-31, filed 2015-03-13), tagged under the legacy XBRL concept Revenues. Target switched to the concept RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax around ASC 606 adoption (~fiscal 2018) and has not tagged Revenues since. The pipeline appears to query a fixed/hardcoded concept name and silently returns the last-ever value under that name — 11 years stale — with no error, rather than following the filer's tag migration or flagging missing data.
  • Gross profit ($20,754M): likewise an exact match, but to a different stale period — fiscal-year-2017 (year ended 2018-02-03, filed 2018-03-14), under the legacy concept GrossProfit, which Target also stopped tagging after that filing. Revenue and gross profit in the flagged snapshot are therefore not even from the same stale year as each other (2014 vs 2017).
  • COGS ($76,144M): this line was actually correct — it exactly matches this review's independently-derived current TTM COGS (ended 2026-08-01) computed from the still-current concept CostOfGoodsAndServicesSold. This is why the snapshot looked internally inconsistent (COGS > "revenue"): three unrelated points in time (2014, 2017, 2026 TTM) were being displayed together as if they were one coherent period.
  • Two further, related errors of the same kind found in the same snapshot: cash of $2,680M is an exact match to Target's April 2017 quarter-end cash balance (concept CashAndCashEquivalentsAtCarryingValue, deprecated in favor of CashCashEquivalentsRestrictedCashAndRestrictedCashEquivalents; true current cash is $5,411M, ~2x higher). Short-term debt of $161M is an exact match to Target's fiscal-2019 year-end current portion of long-term debt (concept LongTermDebtCurrent, last tagged 2020-03-11, deprecated in favor of LongTermDebtAndCapitalLeaseObligationsCurrent; true current figure is $1,136M, ~7x higher). By contrast, total assets ($61,235M), stockholders' equity ($17,843M), operating cash flow ($8,723M) and capex ($4,267M) in the snapshot are all exact matches to the correct, current (Q2 FY2026) values, because those concepts have been tagged continuously under the same name for over a decade.
  • Implication for the broader v4 pipeline: this looks like a systemic bug pattern — any line item whose XBRL tag a filer renamed or deprecated (most commonly around the ASC 606 revenue-recognition transition, ~fiscal 2018, or the ASC 842 lease-accounting transition, ~fiscal 2019) will silently return a stale value from whenever that old tag was last used, with no error raised. This is more dangerous than a missing value because it looks plausible. Given ASC 606/842 affected essentially all US GAAP filers, this risk is not specific to Target and is worth flagging to the orchestrator for the other tickers in this program.

1. Verdict: INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — thesis horizon 12–36 months

T-Mobile is compounding Core Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted Free Cash Flow at double digits, has raised guidance (not just met it) at multiple releases in the trailing year, and is returning capital aggressively (share count down ~4% in two quarters). The named reservation: postpaid net-account growth has decelerated for essentially every recent quarter on a year-over-year basis (396k in Q3'25, +26% YoY → 261k Q4'25 → 217k Q1'26, +6% YoY → 277k Q2'26, −13% YoY) even as revenue and EBITDA keep growing, and net debt is large (~$80bn) and still being used to fund heavy buybacks. The core "best network, best value" moat is real and primary-source-evidenced, but the deceleration in the volume metric that most directly reflects new-customer competitiveness, plus the leverage load, argue for a smaller position rather than a full-conviction one.

2. Business in plain English

T-Mobile is the second-largest US wireless carrier, selling postpaid and prepaid mobile phone service, fixed-wireless home internet/broadband, and (via joint ventures) fiber broadband, to consumers and businesses. It makes money on monthly service revenue per account/line, and its competitive position rests on having built out the largest contiguous 5G network (using mid-band spectrum acquired via the Sprint merger) faster than AT&T or Verizon, which it has converted into genuine customer-growth and churn advantages ("best network, best value, best experiences," per every release reviewed) — now expanding into fixed-wireless and fiber (via the Metronet/Lumos joint ventures) and absorbing UScellular's spectrum and customer base via a 2025–26 acquisition.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

The Q2 2026 release is the one release in this sample independently verified against the company's own explicit "Previous / Current / Change" guidance table (source #4, §12) — a genuine, numbers-quoted raise on cash flow, with account and profitability guidance held flat rather than also raised, which is a more conservative and more credible signal than "raised across the board" would be. The Q3'25 and Q1'26 "raised" characterizations are taken from the releases' own headlines but the specific prior-vs-current numeric ranges were not re-extracted in this time-boxed pass (disclosed gap, not treated as fabricated evidence for the verdict).

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • GAAP vs adjusted gap is well-explained and shrinking: the Q1 2026 GAAP EPS decline (−12% YoY) and Q2 2026 near-flat GAAP net income growth (+1% YoY) are both directly attributed by the company to UScellular merger-related accelerated depreciation and integration costs ($476m and $146m net-of-tax respectively) — a real, quantified, disclosed item, not an unexplained gap. Core Adjusted EBITDA (+12%, +12% YoY in Q1/Q2 2026) is the cleaner read on underlying trading performance.
  • Legacy litigation cost still flowing through adjustments: the Q2 2026 release's non-GAAP reconciliation footnotes still exclude "the settlement of certain litigation and compliance costs associated with the August 2021 cyberattack, net of insurance recoveries" — i.e., five years on, data-breach litigation costs are still being adjusted out of Core Adjusted EBITDA. Not large enough to size, but a real, recurring red flag for the "adjusted" framing.
  • SBC is modest: ~$214m (Q2 2026 quarter) on ~$21bn quarterly revenue (service + equipment) ≈ ~1% of revenue.
  • Balance sheet and leverage: long-term debt was $86.28bn at FY2025 (XBRL LongTermDebt, includes current portion) against cash of $5.60bn (FY2025) — net debt ≈ $80.7bn. Against FY2025 Core Adjusted EBITDA of $33.9bn, that is ≈2.4x net debt/EBITDA (this dossier's own calculation from XBRL primary data; T-Mobile's own investor-materials leverage definition may differ slightly by including securitization/tower-related items not captured in the LongTermDebt XBRL tag, so this figure is presented as an estimate, not a company-reported number). Cash fell further to $2.83bn by Q2 2026 as buybacks accelerated.
  • Capital return is large and running ahead of the authorization pace: Q2 2026 alone: $2.2bn of buybacks + $1.1bn of dividends = $3.3bn of stockholder returns, against an $18.2bn authorization running through 31 December 2026; cumulative since program inception, $54.6bn ($44.2bn buybacks + $10.4bn dividends). Weighted-average diluted shares fell from 1,131m (FY2025) to 1,082m (Q2 2026 quarter), a ~4.3% reduction in two quarters — an aggressive pace that is drawing down cash (see above) rather than being funded entirely from the quarter's own FCF.
  • Governance: Srini Gopalan (former T-Mobile COO, ex-CEO of Deutsche Telekom's German unit) became CEO effective 1 November 2025, succeeding long-tenured CEO Mike Sievert, who moved to a newly created Vice Chairman advisory role through December 2026. This is a completed, orderly transition (not a live catalyst), but the current CEO has under one year of tenure as of this review — a modest key-person/strategy-continuity item to track, not a red flag.

7. Valuation snapshot (this dossier's own reverse read — no V1 row exists)

NTM P/E ≈12.6x and FCF yield ≈10.4% (per b1_live_scores.csv), against 47.6% cited "street upside" in the triage note (not independently re-verified against current analyst targets this pass). A simple reverse read using the company's own guidance: FY2026 Adjusted FCF guided at $18.4–18.8bn (midpoint $18.6bn) against a ~$177.5bn market cap (b1_live_scores.csv, 2026-09-25) is a ~10.5% FCF yield for a business still growing Core Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted FCF at high single-to-low-double digits and returning most of it to shareholders — a genuinely attractive combination if the net-account deceleration in §4 stabilizes rather than continues, and a much less attractive one if it does not (revenue growth would then depend increasingly on ARPA/price alone, a slower and more competitively contested lever). Dossier view: fair-to-cheap on the numbers as guided, with the net-account trend as the swing factor — this dossier does not have an independent DCF/reverse-DCF tool run against TMUS this pass (no V1 row; time-boxed), so this read is qualitative and should be treated as lower-confidence than the STLD/UBER valuation sections in this batch.

3-year annualised scenario returns (this dossier's own simple build — no V1 row): bear −7.1%/yr (net-add deceleration persists, FCF/share flat, exit P/FCF compresses to 7.0x from ~9.6x now), base +10.1%/yr (FCF/share +8%/yr, multiple flat), bull +19.0%/yr (deceleration reverses, FCF/share +12%/yr, multiple re-rates to 11.0x) — each includes a ~$4.08/share/yr run-rate dividend (Q2'26 dividend annualised), undiscounted.

8. Bull case and bear case

Bull (3 points): 1. Core Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted FCF are compounding at low-double-digit rates with guidance being raised (not just met) on cash flow at the most recent release, against numbers explicitly quoted in the company's own table (§5). 2. Aggressive, sustained capital return (share count down ~4.3% in two quarters, $54.6bn cumulative since program inception) directly benefits per-share metrics even if top-line account growth slows. 3. Fixed-wireless/fiber (Metronet, Lumos) and the UScellular spectrum/customer absorption are genuine incremental growth vectors beyond the core postpaid-phone business, not yet fully reflected in the net-account figures being watched here.

Bear (3 points): 1. Postpaid net-account growth has gone from +26% YoY (Q3'25) to −13% YoY (Q2'26) in three quarters — a real, filed deceleration in the metric that most directly measures competitive customer-acquisition strength, not adequately explained away by ARPA gains alone. 2. Net debt of ~$80bn (≈2.4x EBITDA by this dossier's estimate) is being drawn down further (cash fell from $5.6bn to $2.8bn in two quarters) to fund buybacks running ahead of quarterly FCF — a capital-allocation pace that has less room to continue if EBITDA growth itself decelerates. 3. UScellular merger-integration costs are still flowing through GAAP results (accelerated depreciation charges in both Q1 and Q2 2026) — full clean-quarter comparability has not yet been reached, and the true post-integration run-rate is not yet visible.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Postpaid net account additions turn negative (net losses) in any quarter.
  2. Full-year guidance is CUT (not just reiterated) on Core Adjusted EBITDA or Adjusted Free Cash Flow at any release.
  3. Net debt/Core Adjusted EBITDA (this dossier's estimate, currently ~2.4x) rises above 3.0x.
  4. Postpaid net-account YoY growth stays negative for two additional consecutive quarters beyond Q2 2026 (i.e., through Q4 2026), confirming a structural rather than transitory slowdown.
  5. The current $18.2bn buyback/dividend authorization (through 31 Dec 2026) is not renewed or is renewed at a materially smaller size while cash continues to draw down.

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: ~2026-10-22/23 (Q3 2026 results; estimated from the 2025-10-23 Q3 2025 reporting date, not yet confirmed by the company).
  • Buyback/dividend authorization ($18.2bn) runs through 31 December 2026 — a renewal/re-sizing decision is a near-term catalyst.
  • Metronet/Lumos fiber joint-venture build-out and UScellular integration are multi-quarter execution items with no single hard date identified in this pass.

11. Red-flag scan

No auditor changes, material weaknesses, restatements, or going-concern language identified in the sections reviewed. No SEC/DOJ investigation of TMUS itself identified in this pass (not exhaustively searched — disclosed limitation). The 2021 cyberattack litigation/settlement costs are still being excluded from Core Adjusted EBITDA as of the Q2 2026 release (§6) — a real, if not newly material, ongoing legal-cost item. Insider Form 4 pattern and short-seller reports were not independently checked in this pass (time-boxed; disclosed gap).

dossiers.TPR:
TPR — Tapestry, Inc. — Diligence Dossier

Agent: f4 (Fundamental diligence analyst) | As of: 2026-09-25 close | Most recent period incorporated: Q4/FY2026 (ended 2026-06-27), published 2026-08-13 (10-K same day). Checked for events to 2026-09-25 (latest: 8-K 2025-09-19 reporting a director not standing for re-election — routine, see §11). Sector playbook applied: retail-ecommerce.md (branded consumer, wholesale + DTC luxury accessories) — 1P principal model throughout. Reporting basis: Consolidated, GAAP, USD (single reporting entity; Stuart Weitzman divested 4-Aug-2025, so FY26 brand mix is Coach + Kate Spade only from that date forward). Data quality note: All income-statement, balance-sheet and guidance figures trace to SEC XBRL (data.sec.gov) or the company's own 8-K EX-99.1 press releases (Tier 1). Two items are explicitly Tier-4/secondary and flagged inline (the $45.1m Capri termination fee, and the securities-litigation dismissal status) because the primary 8-K for the Nov-2024 Capri termination returned persistent SEC EDGAR 503 errors this session. Three items are explicitly not available (exact Q4-FY25 8-K text; precise Greater-China % of revenue; insider-trading pattern). This dossier is not personalised investment advice — see disclaimer at the end.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE (full weight). Thesis horizon 12–24 months. Coach is executing at a level rarely seen in mature accessories brands (four straight quarters of 20%+ growth with margin expansion), guidance was raised at every one of the last four releases, and the balance sheet has been fully repaired since the failed Capri deal. The risks are real but bounded: Kate Spade remains a genuine drag, FY2027 guidance itself concedes a sharp deceleration to mid-single-digit growth, and the stock has already re-rated ~4.6x from its 2023 low — this is a "keep riding a proven winner, size for the deceleration already guided" call, not a deep-value entry.

2. Business in plain English

Tapestry is a "house of brands" in premium/accessible-luxury handbags and accessories: Coach (86% of FY26 revenue, the growth engine), Kate Spade (~13%, declining), and (until divested 4-Aug-2025) Stuart Weitzman footwear. It sells through its own stores/e-commerce (direct-to-consumer) and wholesale/department-store distribution, with Greater China and North America the two largest and fastest-growing geographies. Revenue is booked as principal (1P) — the company owns the inventory it sells even through department-store concessions — so standard margin and revenue metrics are directly comparable across periods without the marketplace-style distortions the sector playbook warns about.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Prelim rank: Q 0.936, V 0.683, M 0.628, composite 0.749. Independently verified: FY26 GAAP operating margin 23.9% (vs 5.9% in FY25 — see §6 for why FY25 was depressed), FY26 non-GAAP operating margin 23.4% (+340bps YoY on a clean basis), FY26 diluted EPS GAAP $7.27 / non-GAAP $7.05. The Quality read is durable at the Coach-brand level — mid-teens AUR (average unit retail) growth alongside mid-teens unit growth is genuine pricing power plus volume, not just price-led inflation, and it is broad-based (every FY26 quarter posted double-digit Coach growth, in every major region). It is not durable at the consolidated level in the sense that ~all of the growth and margin expansion is a single-brand (Coach) story riding on top of a still-shrinking Kate Spade (FY26 revenue −10%, following an $854.8m Kate Spade brand-intangible/goodwill impairment taken in FY2025). The Momentum score (0.628) is well earned — TPR has raised guidance in each of the last four quarters — but momentum factors are backward-looking by construction and the FY2027 initial guide explicitly signals the pace won't continue.

5. Guidance track record (last 4 releases, all figures quoted)

Net: raised at every single one of the last four releases, then beat the final raised number — as clean a "beat and raise" run as exists in this sector. The FY2027 guide is the tell: management itself is calling for the growth rate to fall by roughly two-thirds.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

FY26 OCF $1,978.5m vs capex $166.0m → FCF ≈$1,812.5m; FCF/NI ≈119% (FY26 NI $1,527.7m) — strong cash conversion. SBC $104.5m (~1.3% of revenue), unremarkable. GAAP-vs-adjusted gap is unusually structured (see §4 note) — driven by net favorable one-offs (IEEPA tariff refunds) rather than the more common pattern of GAAP being dragged down by charges; non-GAAP ($7.05) is the more conservative, recurring-earnings figure and is the one to use for a multiple. Balance sheet fully normalized post-Capri: long-term debt is $2,396.6m (Q4 FY26), down from $7,071.5–7,422.0m in the quarters when ~$6.3bn of escrowed acquisition notes (issued Feb-2024 to fund the never-completed Capri deal) sat on the balance sheet; cash fell correspondingly from a ~$6.9–7.0bn peak to $974.7m as those notes were redeemed after the deal's termination. Capri deal aftermath, quantified: Tapestry paid Capri a $45.1m expense-reimbursement fee under the Nov-13-2024 Termination Agreement (sourced from secondary legal/news coverage — Skadden, Clifford Chance, UPI — the primary termination 8-K returned persistent SEC EDGAR 503 errors this session and could not be independently re-verified; flagged Tier-4). Two related securities class actions (D. Del., filed Dec-2024/Jan-2025, alleging misrepresentation of the deal's approval prospects during Aug-2023–Oct-2024) were dismissed without prejudice in March 2026 (Judge Bibas) — a live overhang has become a much smaller one, though refiling remains theoretically possible. Tariffs are explicitly quantified every quarter (unlike DECK): gross-margin drag of 70bps (Q1), 190bps (Q2), 180bps (Q3), 60bps (Q4) — FY26 full-year ≈130bps, with FY27 guidance embedding "a mid-20% tariff rate on U.S. inventory receipts" for a "neutral net impact year-over-year" (i.e., management believes the headwind is now fully anniversarized). Buybacks: $1.35bn in FY26 (11.5m shares at ~$118 avg); dividend raised 16% to $1.85/share annualized for FY27. Share count down from 233.2m (FY24) to 210.2m (FY26) — meaningful.

7. Valuation snapshot

Price $113.88 (2026-09-25), well below its 1-year high of $164.16 but up ~4.6x from its 3-year low of $24.90 (set during the Capri-deal-uncertainty period in 2023). NTM P/E 13.9x — modest for a business posting >20% growth and expanding margins, but the FY2027 guide (mid-single-digit growth) means the multiple is really being paid on a much slower forward path; on FY27 guided EPS ($7.80–7.90) the multiple is ~14.4–14.6x, in line with pe_ntm. FCF yield ≈8.0% (prelim fcfp) vs d4's 6.2% — both in a reasonable range, no conflict of substance. Short interest is comparatively elevated at ~8.0% of shares outstanding (15.97m shares short / ~200m shares out) — worth watching as a sentiment gauge given how far the stock has already run. Peer set: Capri Holdings (CPRI, remains independent post-deal-break, direct Coach/Kate Spade competitor in accessible luxury) and Ralph Lauren (this program's own RL dossier) are the natural comps; exact current CPRI/PVH multiples were not pulled this session (FMP hit a rate limit mid-session) and are flagged not available rather than guessed.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) Coach's mid-teens AUR growth and mid-teens unit growth together, sustained for four straight quarters across every region, is a rare, high-quality signal that pricing power is real, not just inflation pass-through. (2) Balance sheet is fully repaired (net debt trivial relative to ~$1.8bn FCF) and capital returns are large and growing (dividend +16%, buyback >100% of FCF planned for FY27). (3) Guidance discipline has been excellent — four consecutive raises followed by a beat, with tariffs fully quantified and apparently anniversarized for FY27. Bear: (1) Kate Spade is not a "hold at breakeven" problem — it lost money in FY26 (non-GAAP Q4 operating loss $28.9m, FY $27.2m) after an $854.8m impairment the year before; if Coach ever slows, there is no second engine. (2) FY2027 guidance itself concedes the growth rate falls from >20% to mid-single-digits — the multiple re-rating this stock has enjoyed assumed continuation of a pace management says is ending. (3) The stock's own re-rating (4.6x off the 2023 low) plus 8% short interest suggests a crowded "already worked" trade with an asymmetric downside if Q1 FY27 (due ~Nov 5, 2026) merely meets rather than beats the newly modest guide.

9. Key risks & kill criteria

  1. Coach quarterly growth falls below 10% for two consecutive quarters (from the mid-20s/30s currently).
  2. Kate Spade revenue decline steepens past −15% YoY, or the brand posts a further impairment.
  3. Non-GAAP operating margin gives back more than 200bps YoY in any quarter (FY26 exit rate: 19.3% adj. Q4).
  4. FY2027 guidance is cut at any point during the year (would break the four-quarter raise streak).
  5. Refiling or revival of the Capri-related securities litigation, or any new SEC inquiry tied to the terminated merger's disclosures.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: ~Nov 5, 2026 (Q1 FY2027; both FMP-independent d4 snapshot and TPR's own historical early-November cadence agree). Annual meeting held Nov-13-2025 (director JP Bilbrey did not stand for re-election — routine, no disagreement stated). No investor day identified in the window reviewed.

11. Red-flag scan

Litigation: the Capri-related securities class actions (dismissed without prejudice, March 2026 — see §6) are the one substantive item; no other SEC/DOJ investigation, restatement, or going-concern language identified (WebSearch, 2025–2026). Governance: one director (Bilbrey) not standing for re-election Sep-2025, explicitly stated as not due to any disagreement — routine. Insider selling: not separately pulled this session (FMP insiderTrades tool is gated on the current plan tier); flagged not available rather than assumed clean. Data-quality finding on the quant inputs (important): v4/outputs/lead_prelim_rank.csv's own rev field for TPR ($5,972.3m) is internally inconsistent with its own cogs ($1,775.2m) and gp ($6,229.0m) fields in the same row — cogs+gp = $8,004.2m, which matches TPR's actual FY2026 GAAP revenue exactly (confirmed against SEC XBRL and the 8-K), while the standalone rev field does not. ni in the same row ($1,528.0m) is correctly current (matches FY26 actual of $1,527.7m almost exactly), so this looks like a field-level mapping bug isolated to rev, not a wholesale stale snapshot. This does not appear to corrupt TPR's Q/V/M scores — the pre-registered model's factors (gross-profit/assets, ROE, CFO/assets, accruals, leverage, asset growth, earnings yield, FCF yield, EBIT/EV, book/price, 12-1 month momentum) do not use raw revenue as an input — but the underlying D3/D4 pipeline should fix the rev field before any revenue-based screen or report is built on it. (For comparison, DECK's and RL's rev fields were independently verified to be correct, properly-computed TTM figures.)

1. Verdict

WATCH. T. Rowe Price is a well-capitalized, genuinely free-cash-flow-generative active manager trading close to fair value on a normalized P/B-vs-ROE framework, with a real (if decelerating) structural net-outflow problem in its core active-equity franchise and sell-side sentiment that has turned more negative in the last several weeks, including two price-target cuts (one below the current share price). Thesis horizon: 12–24 months — shorter than a typical multi-year compounder call, because the near-term question (does the Q4'25→Q2'26 outflow deceleration continue, or reverse) is resolvable within 2–3 quarters and should be watched before sizing a position.

2. The Business

T. Rowe Price is a pure-play active investment manager: it earns fees (predominantly a percentage of assets under management, "investment advisory fees," $1,744.8M of Q2 2026's $1,907.4M net revenues [Q2 2026 earnings release, 8-K Ex-99.1, 2026-07-31], plus smaller administrative/distribution/servicing fees) for managing money across equity, fixed income, multi-asset and alternatives strategies for retail investors (largely US retirement accounts, where it is a major target-date-fund manager) and institutions. Revenue is a direct function of average AUM × blended fee rate, so it moves with both markets (beta) and the firm's own net flows. Its competitive position is a large, diversified, historically strong-performing active shop increasingly squeezed by the decades-long structural shift toward passive and lower-fee vehicles — the single dominant theme in this dossier.

8. Bull Case and Bear Case

Bull case

  1. Net outflows have decelerated for three straight quarters (−$25.5B → −$13.7B → −$6.5B) [8-K Ex-99.1 releases]; if this continues toward flat/positive, the stock is priced for a permanent decline that may not materialize, and the reverse-DCF bar (~3.5%/yr FCF growth) is low.
  2. Genuinely clean balance sheet — no real corporate debt (Section 6), improving FCF conversion (72.6% of NI in FY2025), a dividend raised every year including through Q1 2026, and buybacks up 52.6% YoY, all self-funded from a business generating $1.48B of FY2025 FCF.
  3. On current-run-rate ROE (~20%), the stock trades close to its own justified P/B (2.1x model vs ~2.0x actual) — it is not obviously overpriced even before crediting any flow-stabilization upside, and the 4.99% dividend yield provides a real cash return while waiting.

Bear case

  1. Every single quarter in the 8-quarter table shows net outflows, concentrated in active equity (−$74.9B of the −$56.9B FY2025 total came from equity alone, more than offsetting positive fixed-income/multi-asset/alternatives flows) [Q4/FY2025 earnings release] — this is the industry's dominant secular trend (active-to-passive), not a cyclical dip, and TROW's own Item 1A risk factors name it as a top-three risk [FY2025 10-K].
  2. Sell-side sentiment has gotten more negative in the last several weeks, not less: Morgan Stanley cut its target to $97 (below the current $105.51 price) explicitly citing flow and NAV pressure, Barclays cut to $103 with an "underweight," and the broader analyst consensus was reported as "Reduce" in mid-September 2026 [MarketBeat 2026-08-03; TipRanks/"the Fly"; stockanalysis.com accessed 2026-09-26] — professional analysts covering the name see less upside than either the price or the quant composite implies.
  3. Reported GAAP earnings growth is partly a function of volatile non-operating investment/hedge marks (Section 6) that can reverse quarter to quarter (Q1 2026 was a $48.3M non-operating loss); a run of "ongoing" restructuring charges every quarter for a year raises the question of whether the cost base is durably reset or merely being trimmed reactively each quarter as flows disappoint.

Strongest counter to the bear case: the outflow-deceleration trend is real and three-quarters-long, not a one-off, and it is happening while the stock already prices in only very modest (~3.5%/yr) forward growth — so the bear thesis is largely already reflected in the valuation, which is why this is a WATCH, not a REJECT.

Outflow re-acceleration: net outflows exceed $20B in any single quarter, or the three-quarter deceleration trend reverses for two consecutive quarters — observable in each quarterly earnings release (8-K Ex-99.1). By: next two quarterly releases (est. 2026-10-30 and Q4 2026 release, early Feb 2027).
  2. Dividend increase streak breaks or the quarterly dividend is cut/frozen at a Q1 reset date — observable in the Q1 2027 10-Q/dividend declaration (expected ~April 2027).

  5. A major sell-side price target moves below the DCF bear case (~$76.50), or two or more of the covering banks currently at Reduce/Underweight downgrade further — would indicate the professional consensus sees a worse outcome than modeled here.

1. Verdict: INCLUDE — thesis horizon 12–24 months

Well-run, disciplined P&C underwriter trading at a reasonable multiple of a currently cycle-elevated earnings base; include at full weight but size and monitor with the explicit assumption that 2026 combined-ratio/ROE levels will not persist into 2027–28.

2. Business in plain English

Travelers is the third-largest U.S. property-casualty insurer, organized in three segments: Business Insurance (commercial P&C for companies of all sizes), Bond & Specialty Insurance (surety bonds, management/professional liability), and Personal Insurance (auto and homeowners for individuals). It sells almost entirely through independent agents and brokers, and makes money two ways: underwriting profit (premiums minus claims and expenses) and investment income earned on the "float" (reserves held before claims are paid). Competitive position: top-3 scale in commercial lines with a long underwriting track record; mid-pack but improving scale in personal auto/home.

3. Why the model likes it — and whether that's durable

b1-family prelim scores (source: internal lead_prelim_rank.csv): Q 0.858, V 0.438, M 0.938 (12-1m return +32.6%), composite 0.878. Adversarial read: a meaningful share of this is an artefact, not a moat. Reverse-DCF sense: at 2.2x book against a currently-elevated ~20-25% core ROE, the market is not extrapolating peak profitability indefinitely — it is roughly consistent with core ROE settling in the mid-teens, which is a reasonable, not aggressive, assumption given the underlying-ratio evidence in §4.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) Underlying combined ratio is stable-to-improving even after stripping cat/reserve noise — real pricing discipline, not just luck. (2) Aggressive, well-covered capital return ($3.9B buyback authorization, rising dividend, book value compounding at 5-6%/yr ex the cyclicality). (3) Diversified three-segment model with only one segment (Bond & Specialty) showing underlying deterioration. Bear: (1) ~$2B of the 1H26 pre-tax earnings improvement vs 1H25 is a catastrophe base effect (LA wildfires) that will not repeat — 2027 comps get harder. (2) Reserve releases ($991M pre-tax 1H26) are running above historical norms across multiple segments; a reversal to flat/adverse development would remove a real chunk of "beat" (avg EPS surprise +57.9% over the last 8 quarters per d4 — a magnitude that itself signals estimates/base-effects are unusually distorted, not stable outperformance). (3) Hard-market commercial pricing cycles historically compress once capital rebuilds (which is exactly what's happening industry-wide); Bond & Specialty's underlying ratio is already worsening.

  2. Net favorable prior-year reserve development flips to net adverse in Business Insurance or Bond & Specialty for two consecutive quarters.
  3. Core ROE < 12% for two consecutive quarters (vs ~19-25% now).
  4. Personal Insurance underlying combined ratio rises back above ~90%.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — 24–36 month horizon. Dominant public-sector (courts, property tax/appraisal, ERP, courts recording) software vendor with 22 consecutive quarters of 20%+ SaaS growth and 86.7% recurring revenue; the reverse DCF shows the market pricing in only ~1.9%/yr FCF growth for 10 years, far below the growth actually being delivered. Tyler sells mission-critical software to US state and local governments: court case management (Odyssey/Enterprise Justice), property tax and appraisal systems, municipal/county ERP and financial systems, public-safety records management, and (since April 2026) digital court recording (For The Record). It earns subscription/SaaS fees, maintenance on legacy on-premise licenses being migrated to the cloud, and services revenue from implementation. The moat is multi-decade government contracts and extreme switching costs — a county does not re-platform its court system or property-tax rolls lightly — reinforced by data-residency and public-record requirements that favor an incumbent with an existing certified footprint in most US counties.

TTM operating income (Q3'25–Q2'26) is $4.87bn on TTM revenue $62.9bn (7.7% margin) — independently re-derived from XBRL and matches V1's D3 TTM figures exactly (cross-check passed).

5. Guidance track record (last 3 full-year guides, company 8-K exhibits)

  • Jan-2026 (Q4 2025 release): FY2026 adjusted diluted EPS guided $12–$14.
  • Apr-2026 (Q1 2026 release): guidance cut to $7–$11, explicitly attributed to a jet-fuel cost spike driven by the Middle East war, not to weaker demand (Q1 2026 results themselves beat estimates: adjusted EPS $1.19 vs. ~$1.07 consensus, revenue $14.6bn vs. ~$14.37bn consensus).
  • Jul-2026 (Q2 2026 release): guidance raised to $9.00–$11.00 (bottom of range lifted from $7 to $9; top held at $11) — a genuine, evidenced partial recovery from the fuel shock, not a return to the original $12–$14 range.
  • Management stated it expects to recover 80–90% of the incremental fuel cost in Q3 2026 and 100% by Q4 2026 (assuming current oil prices), and reiterated confidence in double-digit pre-tax margins in 2027.

Assessment: this is a credible, evidence-based "cut-then-partial-raise" pattern driven by an external, dated shock (war-driven oil spike — the same macro driver flagged for EOG in this program's earlier diligence, F15), with the underlying demand/RASM trend actually improving throughout. It is a mark in favor of management credibility, but the level of guidance ($9–$11) is still below the original $12–$14, i.e., the fuel shock has not been fully offset yet.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • TTM net leverage 2.2x (company-reported, Q2 2026 release) — down from higher levels, with $3.7bn of new liquidity raised and ~$1bn of higher-cost debt prepaid since the start of Q2 2026. Available liquidity $19.6bn. Management explicitly targets an investment-grade rating in 2026.
  • Total debt & financial liabilities (company-reported) $26.5bn; XBRL long-term debt + capital leases $24.29bn (30-Jun-2026), down from $21.68bn+$2.97bn≈$24.65bn combined LT+current at year-end 2024 and a further step-down from $17.17bn+$4.10bn LT+current at year-end 2025 under a different tag split — the debt-reduction trend across 2024→2026 is directionally clear and corroborated by two independent XBRL tag families.
  • TTM (Q3'25–Q2'26) FCF ≈ $2.54bn (CFO $8.91bn − capex $6.37bn), independently re-derived and matching V1's D3 TTM figure to the dollar (cross-check passed). FCF yield ≈ 6.9% on today's market cap, in line with V1's 6.4% SBC-adjusted figure.
  • No dividend; buybacks are modest and inconsistent ($82mn in 9M 2024, $610mn in 9M 2025, only $27mn in H1 2026) — capital return is secondary to debt paydown right now, consistent with the stated investment-grade target.
  • No litigation, DOJ action, restatement or auditor issue specific to United was identified in this search window (Boeing-related 737 MAX litigation involves Boeing and crash victims' representatives, not United as a defendant). United's 2024 pilot contract (35.1% raise over 4 years) appears to be the source of the Q2 2026 $184mn "labor contract ratification bonus" special item — an already-known, disclosed labor cost, not a new surprise.

7. Valuation — reconciled against V1 (v1_valuation_table.csv / v1_valuation.json)

V1 verdict: fair (score 0.06/1.00, near-neutral). V1's reverse FCFF DCF (WACC 7.72%, 10-year fade to 3% terminal, EV $47.06bn) finds the price implies FCF growing at 12.8%/year for 10 years — well above the 5.2% consensus FY1 growth and the 5.5% delivered 10-year CAGR, though well below the (likely cycle-flattered) 33.9% delivered 5-year CAGR. V1's scenarios: base case revenue growth 3.4%/yr, margin 5.2%, exit multiple 9.3x → annualised 3-yr return of −3.4%/yr; bull case (12.3%/yr revenue, 6.1% margin, 12.0x exit) → +29.6%/yr; bear case is a degenerate negative-price result (a −1.8%/yr revenue, −1.8% margin scenario combined with a 6.25x exit multiple on negative EPS), which should be read as an approximate "floor near −100%" rather than a literal number (a known modeling artefact this program has already documented for other cyclical/loss-making names).

I agree with V1's verdict and reasoning. United's own Q2 2026 guidance ($9–$11 adjusted EPS, i.e., a partial recovery from a fuel shock) and its own long-run delivered growth (5.5%/10yr) both sit far below the 12.8%/year the current price requires for a full decade. Airlines are structurally cyclical, capital-intensive and exposed to fuel/labor cost inflation that historically prevents sustained double-digit FCF compounding; the current strong quarter (16% revenue growth, raised guidance) is encouraging execution, not evidence that the business can compound at that rate for 10 years. implied_vs_base = above — this is the specific case the wave-1 brief calls out: good business, priced for more than the evidence supports.

8. Bull case

  1. Deleveraging is real and evidenced (TTM net leverage 2.2x, new liquidity raised, high-cost debt prepaid), with an explicit, credible path to investment-grade in 2026 — a re-rating catalyst if achieved.
  2. Revenue growth accelerated to 16% yoy in Q2 2026 despite a $2.3bn fuel headwind, with management guiding 80–90% fuel-cost recovery by Q3 and 100% by Q4 2026 — near-term margin recovery is plausible and management-guided, not speculative.
  3. The Polaris/international premium-cabin franchise is a genuine structural differentiator versus lower-cost domestic-focused peers, supporting a durable revenue-per-seat premium.

Bear case

  1. The price requires 12.8%/year FCF growth for a full decade from a cyclical, capital-intensive, fuel- and labor-cost-exposed business that has delivered 5.5%/year over the last 10 years — a gap this large has historically closed through price decline, not sustained outperformance.
  2. FY2026 guidance was cut by more than half at the low end (from $12–$14 to $7–$11) within a single year due to an external fuel shock, illustrating how quickly the earnings base can move against the company; the subsequent partial raise ($9–$11) still leaves guidance below where the year started.
  3. Trailing 5-year ROE (33.9%) is likely flattered by post-pandemic pricing power and capacity discipline across the industry; if competitive capacity additions or a demand slowdown normalize yields, the "quality" score the model rewards today may prove cycle-dependent rather than structural.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (thesis-invalidation triggers)

  1. Full-year adjusted EPS guidance is cut again from the current $9.00–$11.00 range (a second cut within the same fiscal year).
  2. TTM net leverage rises back above 3.0x (from 2.2x currently).
  3. Quarterly RASM growth turns negative for two consecutive quarters.
  4. Full fuel-cost recovery (100% guided by Q4 2026) fails to materialize and adjusted operating margin falls below 4% for two consecutive quarters.
  5. Net debt/EBITDA-equivalent leverage metrics prevent United from reaching an investment-grade rating by end of 2027 (management's own stated 2026 target slipping by a year or more).

1. Verdict: INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — thesis horizon 12–36 months

Uber's underlying operating business is genuinely strong and improving on primary-source numbers: Gross Bookings +22–24% YoY, Adjusted EBITDA margin expanding from 4.1% to 4.9% of Gross Bookings over the trailing eight quarters, guidance beaten in every quarter sampled, trailing-twelve-month free cash flow exceeding $10bn for the first time in company history, and a shrinking share count. The named reservation, and the reason this is sized small rather than full: GAAP net income is dominated by large, volatile, non-operating items (a $4.9bn one-off tax-valuation-allowance release in Q3 2025; $1.5–1.6bn swings each quarter since from mark-to-market revaluations of minority equity stakes in Aurora, Didi and Delivery Hero) that must not be read as operating profit, and legal/regulatory/safety exposure is real and currently expanding, not just legacy: a ~$966m Dutch data-protection fine (under appeal, announced after the 10-Q), a June 2026 shareholder derivative suit alleging the board is a "serial compliance offender," and a federal sexual-assault multidistrict litigation whose pending-case count grew from "over 3,000" (as of 1 June 2026) to 4,588 (as reported in September 2026) in three months, against a next trial date of 7 October 2026.

2. Business in plain English

Uber runs a two-sided marketplace connecting riders/consumers with independent drivers (Mobility) and connecting consumers with restaurants/retailers via couriers (Delivery), plus a freight-brokerage business (Uber Freight) and a growing advertising business layered on top. It earns a "take rate" — the difference between what riders/consumers pay and what it pays out to drivers/couriers/merchants — on Gross Bookings, at large and improving scale (208 million Monthly Active Platform Consumers in Q2 2026, up 16% YoY). Its competitive position is as the largest global rideshare/delivery platform by Gross Bookings, now also positioning itself as an aggregation layer for third-party autonomous-vehicle (AV) fleets (Waymo, Nvidia-backed partners, WeRide) rather than only building its own AV technology.
