8. Bull case and bear case

Bull (3 points): 1. Guidance beaten in all four quarters sampled, with Adjusted EBITDA margin expanding every year-over-year comparison shown (4.1%→4.9% of Gross Bookings) — durable, filed operating improvement, not a one-off. 2. Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow exceeded $10bn for the first time in company history (Q2 2026 release), funding continued buybacks (share count down ~3.4% in two quarters) without balance-sheet strain (liquid assets roughly cover total debt). 3. The AV strategy is explicitly a "capital-efficient" aggregation/partnership model (Waymo, Nvidia-linked partners, WeRide) rather than a capital-intensive proprietary build — a genuine hedge against the single biggest bear-case risk (robotaxi disintermediation) rather than a denial of it.

Bear (3 points): 1. Legal/regulatory/safety exposure is expanding, not just a legacy overhang: a ~$966m Dutch privacy fine (appealing, announced 23 Aug 2026, after the last 10-Q), a June 2026 shareholder derivative suit calling Uber a "serial compliance offender," and a sexual-assault MDL whose case count grew from 3,000+ to 4,588 in three months (next trial 7 Oct 2026) — none of this is yet reflected in the $1.8bn accrued liability on the balance sheet. 2. GAAP net income is not a usable trend metric on its own: every one of the last four quarters shown carried a $1.5–4.9bn non-operating swing (tax valuation release, or equity-stake mark-to-market), meaning headline "GAAP EPS growth" figures reported in the press (e.g., +77% YoY in Q2 2026) substantially overstate underlying operating improvement. 3. SBC (~3.5% of revenue) is a real, larger dilution drag than peers in this batch, and driver-classification litigation (California AG suit, Swiss Federal Tribunal rulings classifying drivers/couriers as employees in Geneva) remains open and could, in an adverse outcome in a major market, force a structural change to the cost model.

  4. A major AV/robotaxi partner (Waymo, an Nvidia-linked platform partner, or WeRide) terminates or materially narrows its Uber platform agreement.
  5. A court or regulator in a top-5-revenue market (US federal, California, or a major EU member state) legally mandates employee (not independent-contractor) classification for drivers, forcing a structural change to the cost model.

UDR, Inc. (NYSE: UDR) — Fundamental Diligence Dossier

Agent: F14 | As of: 2026-09-25 close (price $33.84) | Classification: Multi-Family Residential REIT

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — thesis horizon 12–36 months. UDR is a statistically cheap, well-capitalized apartment REIT buying back its own stock, but this is a valuation-repair/capital-allocation thesis, not a near-term growth story: FFO-as-Adjusted per share has been range-bound ($0.61–$0.65) for eight straight quarters, the company's own FY2026 guidance implies roughly flat per-share cash flow versus FY2025, same-store NOI is outright declining in the Southeast and Southwest, and leverage (5.6x net debt/EBITDAre) is on the high side of the multifamily peer group. Reservation: hold at reduced weight until same-store NOI reaccelerates broadly (not just in the West/Northeast) or leverage comes down.

2. Business in plain English

UDR owns and operates ~60,000 apartment homes (as of Q2 2026) concentrated in coastal gateway markets (Boston–DC corridor, California, Seattle) and Sunbelt growth markets (Florida, Texas, Southeast). It makes money from rent, minus operating costs, property taxes and depreciation; it also runs a "Debt and Preferred Equity" program that lends to other apartment owners/JVs and recycles capital via property sales into new development and buybacks. Competitive position: a top-10 U.S. apartment REIT by scale, S&P 500 member, geographically diversified (no single region is more than a third of same-store NOI), competing with AvalonBay, Equity Residential, Camden, Mid-America and Essex Property Trust for both tenants and capital.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Gates: the formal Stage-1 intake-gate script was not re-run for this dossier within the time box; no disqualifying findings (auditor change, going-concern language, restatement) surfaced during the manual primary-source review in §11. B1 composite score 0.859 (decile 9, live_rank 58). Driven mainly by Value (fam_V 0.883 — high earnings-yield percentile 79th, reflecting a stock price that looks cheap against reported metrics) and Quality (fam_Q 0.665 — high gross-profitability percentile 75th, and favourable low-net-issuance/low-asset-growth percentiles that mechanically reward the ongoing buyback), reinforced by decent 12-month momentum (74th pctile) and a strong earnings-surprise score (SUE, 86th pctile). Assessment: the Value and buyback-driven Quality components are durable and verified in primary filings (real repurchases, real balance-sheet discipline). The SUE (earnings-surprise) driver is partly an artefact: UDR's GAAP EPS has been repeatedly boosted by lumpy gains on property sales (see §6), which flow through the "surprise" statistic even though they say nothing about the operating business. Treat the momentum/SUE legs of the score with more suspicion than the value/quality legs.

The FY2026 FFOA guidance midpoint ($2.53) is essentially flat versus FY2025's actual FFOA ($2.54) — i.e., the company's own current guidance does not point to per-share growth this year.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • FCF conversion / cash-flow quality: 1H26 operating cash flow was $390.9M, down 3.8% YoY ($406.5M in 1H25) — even as GAAP net income more than doubled (1H26 net income $276.6M vs $114.4M 1H25). The gap is explained by a $193.1M gain on sale of real estate in 1H26 vs $47.9M in 1H25 — a non-cash, non-recurring item that inflates GAAP net income and EPS (Q2'26 diluted EPS $0.21 vs $0.11, +91% YoY) without a matching cash or FFO improvement (FFO per share actually fell -1.6% YoY in Q2).
  • Capex: 1H26 "capital expenditures and other major improvements — real estate assets" were $104.2M, plus $53.0M of development spend (~$314M combined annualized, ~18% of TTM revenue). This is materially higher than the $7.8M TTM figure in the firm's own D3/V1 dataset (see §7 — a data conflict).

  • Net debt/EBITDAre (adjusted, company-reported): 5.6x at Q2'26, up from 5.5x a year ago (5.6x also at Q1'26, 5.5x at Q4'25, 5.5x at Q3'25) — a mild but persistent creep, and on the higher side of the multifamily REIT peer set (EQR/AVB/CPT/MAA/ESS have typically run mid-4x to low-5x in recent years; not independently re-verified this cycle within the time box).
  • Debt maturities: total debt $5.81B, weighted-average rate 3.4%, weighted-average years-to-maturity 3.9. Only $808M (14%) matures through 2026 (includes the revolving $480M commercial-paper balance, which rolls); no maturity wall before 2029 ($966M). $1.3B revolver fully undrawn; ~$885M total liquidity. In compliance with all covenants.
  • Share count / buybacks: repurchased 8.2M shares in 1H26 (avg $36.43, $300.3M) — note this average price is above the current $33.84 quote, so recent buybacks were not at today's cheaper level (still net share-count accretive: 328.3M→321.3M shares outstanding since YE2025, -2.1%). Board expanded authorization to ~30M shares; 25.5M remain. ATM program: 14.0M shares available, unused YTD (no dilution from that channel).
  • M&A: none pending. Routine portfolio recycling (sold a 1977-vintage Nashville asset for $41.5M in Q2; $252.5M more under contract).
  • Dividend: switched from quarterly to monthly dividends starting July 2026 ($0.145/month, $1.74/yr annualized, +1.2% YoY) — the first residential REIT to do so; ~69% of FY26 guided FFOA, a sustainable payout.

7. Valuation snapshot — reconciliation with V1

V1's verdict: "attractive," score 0.874, base 3-yr annualised return +21.9%/yr (bear -7.4%, bull +57.4%). V1's method: P/FFO(proxy) 13.3x vs the stock's own 177-month history's 10.2nd percentile (i.e., statistically cheap vs its own past); reverse-DCF implied 10-year growth of -5.2% (vs consensus FY1 +2.7%, delivered 5y CAGR +6.97%); WACC 6.54%.

I partly agree, partly disagree — and V1's own inputs contain a real, quantified error. V1's reverse-DCF used TTM capex of just $7.76M for UDR (0.45% of revenue). The Q2'26 10-Q cash-flow statement shows $104.2M of "capital expenditures and other major improvements" plus $53.0M of development spend in 1H26 alone (~$314M annualized, ~18% of revenue) — roughly 20–40x the figure V1 used. Understated capex inflates V1's computed FCFF, which mechanically makes the reverse-DCF's implied growth look more negative than it should be (i.e., V1 overstates how "underpriced for growth" UDR is). Correcting this would likely bring implied growth up from -5.2% toward something closer to 0%, still comfortably below the 5–7% growth UDR has actually delivered — so the stock still screens as reasonably priced, just not as dramatically as V1's score (0.874, near the top of the scale) implies. Separately, V1's peer_median (44.6x) is NTM GAAP P/E of peers (CPT, ESS, MAA, and an unrecognised "VMRK" ticker), not true P/FFO — flagged by V1 itself as unreliable, and I did not have time to independently rebuild real peer P/FFO multiples. Note also that two of UDR's closest peers, AvalonBay and Equity Residential, announced an all-stock merger in 2026 (~$52B combined equity value, ~$69B enterprise value) and have suspended their own FFO guidance pending closing — reshaping the multifamily peer set and adding a sector-consolidation/re-rating theme that V1's static peer snapshot cannot capture.

valuation_view_vs_v1: dossier view = cheap; consistent = false. I agree UDR is statistically cheap vs its own history, but I do not endorse V1's degree of conviction: the capex-input error means the "achievable minus implied growth" gap driving most of V1's 0.874 score is overstated, and V1 does not see that FY2026 guided FFOA is flat YoY or that leverage has crept up — both of which argue for a smaller position than V1's score alone would suggest. Net: cheap-but-slow-growing, hence INCLUDE-SMALL, not full INCLUDE.

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull: (1) Trades at the bottom decile of its own 15-year P/FFO range with an active, board-expanded buyback shrinking the share count ~4%/yr annualized; (2) same-store fundamentals are healthy in West/Northeast/Mid-Atlantic (+3–4% NOI) as new supply moderates nationally into 2027; (3) monthly dividend and 217 consecutive quarterly-equivalent payouts signal capital-return discipline, covered at ~69% of FFOA.

Bear: (1) FFOA per share has not grown in two years and FY2026 guidance implies another flat year; (2) Southeast (-2.0%) and Southwest (-2.2%) same-store NOI are still contracting on new supply (23% of the same-store book) — the cited "waning supply" thesis is not yet visible in the numbers there; (3) leverage (5.6x net debt/EBITDAre) has crept up, not down, over the last year, reducing balance-sheet flexibility just as buybacks and development ($167M remaining commitment on 2 wholly-owned projects, plus $200M remaining JV commitments) compete for capital.

9. Key risks & measurable kill criteria

The specific, observable, time-bound conditions that would invalidate this thesis:

  1. Same-store NOI growth negative for two consecutive quarters (FY26 guide is barely positive at +0.625% midpoint).
  2. Consolidated Net Debt-to-EBITDAre (adjusted) rises above 6.0x (from 5.6x now).
  3. FFO-as-Adjusted per-share guidance is cut (not just plain FFO) at either of the next two quarterly updates.
  4. Southeast or Southwest same-store NOI decline exceeds -4% YoY in any quarter (supply absorption failing, not just slowing).
  5. Share buyback program paused or reduced to a token level for two consecutive quarters (loss of the primary capital-return signal underpinning the thesis).

UPS reports both GAAP and non-GAAP "adjusted" figures every quarter with a large and growing gap between them — every number below is explicitly labeled.

1. Verdict

WATCH. Thesis horizon: 12–24 months. UPS is executing a real, now-largely-complete restructuring (the "Amazon glide-down" is done, management says, as of Q2'26) that is genuinely improving the business's unit economics — but the GAAP results are currently ugly (Q2'26 GAAP operating margin 4.1% vs adjusted 9.2%; GAAP EPS $0.71 vs adjusted $1.76), the dividend is frozen and paid out of a thin FCF margin, buybacks have been suspended entirely in 2026, and the company is now in active litigation with the Teamsters over the very buyout program driving the "adjusted" earnings story. This is a legitimate turnaround candidate, not yet a demonstrated one — WATCH until GAAP and adjusted results converge and at least one full guided quarter is delivered cleanly.

2. Business in plain English

UPS moves and delivers packages and freight through three segments: U.S. Domestic Package (ground and air parcel delivery within the US, the largest segment), International Package (parcel delivery outside the US, structurally the highest-margin segment), and Supply Chain Solutions (freight forwarding, contract logistics, and healthcare logistics — including the recently acquired Andlauer Healthcare Group). It earns money on a per-package basis (yield), competing against FedEx, national postal services, regional carriers, and — as both customer and increasingly competitor — Amazon's own logistics network.

3. Why the model likes it

From the preliminary quant screen (lead_prelim_rank.csv, families Q/V/M): UPS ranks #16 of ~500, prelim composite 0.790, with the Value family strongest (0.876) — consistent with a stock trading near multi-year lows on a depressed earnings base — and Quality (0.751) and Momentum (0.742) more middling. This is a coherent, explainable combination: the stock is cheap in absolute terms (trailing P/E 17.5x looks unremarkable, but on adjusted TTM earnings the multiple is materially lower, and NTM P/E is 12.0x per the calendarized d4 snapshot) precisely because GAAP earnings are currently depressed by restructuring charges that management says are largely one-time. Whether the Value signal is durable depends entirely on whether the "adjusted" story becomes the GAAP story within the thesis horizon — this is not yet proven (see §4, §6).

2026-01-27 (Q4'25/FY25) Revenue ~$89.7B, adjusted operating margin ~9.6% Initial FY2026 guide

Sources: [4], [5], [6], [8]. No prior-report claim of "guidance raised" should be taken at face value without this table — this is exactly the failure mode the program's own v3 audit flagged.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

FCF conversion: FY2025 FCF/NI (GAAP) ≈ $4.77B/$5.572B = 86%; the GAAP-vs-adjusted gap is the dominant earnings-quality issue this quarter (§4) — treat adjusted EPS as management's estimate of run-rate earning power, not as a substitute for GAAP cash economics. SBC: not independently broken out in this session — flagged as a gap for the quant/valuation team. Leverage: gross debt $24.2B, cash $4.65B, net debt ≈ $19.6–24.2B depending on treatment; net debt/EBITDA ≈ 1.8–2.2x (via ratios.py, FY2025 GAAP EBITDA ~$10.9B) — moderate, not alarming, but up from UPS's historical low-1x range, and ROE of ~37% is substantially leverage-driven (equity multiplier 4.7x per the DuPont decomposition), not purely an operating-quality signal. Interest coverage ~11x on FY2025 GAAP EBIT — adequate. M&A: completed the ~$1.6B (CAD $2.2B) acquisition of Andlauer Healthcare Group on 2025-11-05 (healthcare/cold-chain logistics, adds debt-funded growth capital intensity); separately, UPS sold Coyote Logistics (freight brokerage) to RXO for $1.025B, closed 2024-09-16 — both add real complexity to any YoY comparison of the Supply Chain Solutions segment. Share count / capital return — a genuine adverse fact: UPS repurchased $1.0B of stock in 2025 but has repurchased zero shares in H1 2026 (confirmed via XBRL: PaymentsForRepurchaseOfCommonStock = $0 in both Q1 and Q2 2026 10-Qs), while continuing to pay $5.398B of dividends in FY2025 ($6.56/share annualized, 7.1% trailing yield) — the quarterly dividend has been held flat for seven consecutive quarters and the payout ratio is ~80–90% of GAAP net income, well above UPS's own long-stated 50–60% target. This is not a dividend cut, but it is real, current strain, not a hypothetical risk, and the buyback suspension is the clearest evidence management is prioritizing balance sheet and the dividend over total shareholder return via repurchases.

7. Valuation snapshot

NTM P/E (calendarized, per d4_live_snapshot.parquet) 12.0x; trailing P/E on GAAP EPS 17.5x (valuation.py EV bridge: EV $99.5B on FY2025 GAAP EBITDA ~$10.9B → EV/EBITDA 9.2x, EV/EBIT 12.6x); FCF yield ~6.0–7.0%. Versus its closest listed peer, FedEx trades at a similar forward P/E (~15–16x both names) but a higher EV/EBITDA (~10.6x FedEx vs ~9.1–9.2x UPS) — i.e. UPS is not obviously cheaper than FedEx once capital structure is normalized, despite the much lower headline P/E some sources quote. [Aggregator cross-check only, not a source of record: stockanalysis.com and GuruFocus, accessed 2026-09-26, source 11 — dated differently than the program's own d4 snapshot; treat this specific peer comparison as directional, not primary-sourced.] Reverse-DCF (WACC 8.0%, terminal growth 2.5%): the current EV implies only ~4% per-year FCF growth for a decade — a low, easily-clearable bar if the transformation savings ($3B targeted for 2026, $1.2B delivered in H1) show up in free cash flow rather than being reinvested or absorbed by restructuring cash costs. A probability-weighted bear/base/bull scenario (bear $5.50 EPS/12x, base $7.22 adjusted-EPS guide/14x, bull $8.50/17x) centers on ~$101/share, roughly 8% above the current price — i.e., unlike JBHT, this dossier's own scenario math does not find UPS obviously overpriced; the risk here is much more about whether the adjusted-EPS trajectory is real than about paying too much for a proven number.

8. Bull case

  1. The Amazon glide-down is complete, not still unfolding — management says Amazon is now ~9% of UPS's business (down from a much larger, lower-yield share), and US Domestic revenue-per-piece rose 8.3% in FY2025 as low-yield volume was deliberately shed. If the "leaner, more automated, more agile network" the CEO describes is real, incremental volume from here should carry materially better margin.
  2. International segment remains a genuinely high-margin, resilient business (17.5% GAAP / 18.0% adjusted operating margin in FY2025, +2.5% revenue with +7.1% RPP) that is under-appreciated when the narrative is dominated by the US Domestic/Amazon story.
  3. Valuation already reflects a depressed earnings base: at 12x NTM P/E and a reverse-DCF hurdle of only ~4%/year FCF growth, this is priced for a company in distress, not for the "return to consolidated revenue and operating profit growth" management guided to starting Q2'26.

9. Bear case

  1. The GAAP results, not the adjusted ones, are what the balance sheet and dividend actually run on, and Q2'26 GAAP operating margin of 4.1% (vs. 9.2% adjusted) is the worst GAAP print in the two-year window reviewed here. A thesis that requires "trust the adjustments" is exactly the pattern this research program's own prior audit flagged as a repeat mistake — this dossier does not resolve that tension, it surfaces it.
  2. The dividend is under real, current strain: flat for seven quarters, 80–90% GAAP payout ratio vs. a 50–60% target, and buybacks fully suspended in 2026. A dividend cut — while not our base case — is a plausible tail outcome if transformation cash costs run longer than the "largely complete" framing suggests, and would likely trigger a sharp de-rating given the stock is partly held for yield.
  3. Active Teamsters litigation directly tied to the restructuring (the union sued in Q1 2026 alleging that UPS's buyout program breaches the 2023 National Master Agreement, which runs through July 2028 and covers roughly 80% of UPS's US workforce) is a concrete, current legal risk that could constrain management's ability to execute the very cost program the bull case depends on, and is a cost/distraction regardless of outcome.

10. Key risks & kill criteria

These are the specific, observable, time-bound conditions that would invalidate the WATCH-to-INCLUDE upgrade path: - GAAP operating margin fails to close materially toward the adjusted figure by Q4 2026 (i.e., the gap is still >300bps a year from now) — would indicate "one-time" charges are recurring. - The Teamsters litigation results in an injunction or settlement that reverses or materially slows the network-restructuring program. - The board cuts the dividend, or the payout ratio (GAAP basis) exceeds 100% for two consecutive quarters. - Full-year 2026 guidance is cut (not just "raised by less than expected") at the Q3'26 or Q4'26 release. - Buybacks remain at zero through year-end 2026 with no board commentary on resumption — would confirm capital-return capacity is more impaired than management's framing suggests.

11. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 2026-10-27 (Q3 2026; per company snapshot data, confirm closer to date). An 8-K with items 5.02/7.01/9.01 was filed 2026-08-31 (leadership/regulation-FD/exhibits) — not examined in depth in this session; recommend a follow-up read before the position is sized, since 5.02 items indicate an officer or director change. Watch for Q3'26 commentary on whether the GAAP/adjusted gap narrows and any update on buyback resumption.

12. Red-flag scan

Auditor: Deloitte & Touche LLP; no change identified. Litigation — material and current: the Teamsters sued UPS in early 2026 alleging the pending buyout program breaches the September 2023 National Master Agreement (ratified through July 2028); UPS is contesting the suit. This is the single most important red flag in this dossier and is discussed in §9 and §10 — do not treat it as boilerplate litigation. Pension: UPS carries a legacy multiemployer pension withdrawal liability related to the New England Teamsters and Trucking Industry (NETTI) Fund — $813M non-current + $9M current as of the most recent figure located (FY2023 10-K; not re-confirmed for FY2025 in this session, flagged for follow-up) — a real, if legacy and apparently stable, quasi-debt obligation. Union exposure: ~80% of the US workforce (out of ~460,000 employees total) is union-represented, primarily Teamsters plus separate pilot and mechanic unions; the current National Master Agreement runs through July 31, 2028, so there is no near-term full-contract renegotiation risk, but the buyout litigation above shows contract disputes can still arise mid-term. Material weakness/restatement/going concern: none identified in the sources reviewed. Insider ownership: negligible per the quant snapshot (0.02%) — this is a widely-held, dispersed-ownership company; no unusual Form 4 pattern was identified in this session, but a dedicated insider-trade pull was not completed due to a third-party data vendor rate limit during this session and should be done as a follow-up. Short-seller reports: none identified in this session's research.

Data-quality note for the lead (D3/B1 pipeline)

lead_prelim_rank.csv's rev field for UPS ($75.656B) is wrong — verified FY2025 GAAP revenue (10-K, filed 2026-02-17) is $88,661M, and TTM-through-Q2'26 is ~$89,930M ($13–14B, or ~15–16%, understated). Working hypothesis (unconfirmed, worth ~30 minutes for the D3/B1 owner to check): $75.656B is close to US Domestic + International Package segment revenue combined and excludes Supply Chain Solutions (~$88.661B − $75.656B ≈ $13.0B, in the right range for the SCS segment) — suggesting a dimensional/segment-member XBRL selection error rather than a wrong concept entirely. Also separately verified: the Q/V/M/prelim percentile scores do not appear to depend on the broken rev column (they reconcile from ni/ocf/assets/equity/mcap/capex instead).

dossiers.V:
Visa Inc. (V) — Fundamental Diligence Dossier

Verdict: INCLUDE — 24–48 month thesis horizon. One-sentence reason: the highest-quality payments network in the batch (51% net margin, net-cash-like leverage, mid-teens EPS growth reaffirmed and raised twice this fiscal year) trades at a price that a reverse DCF says requires only ~9% 10-year FCF growth — below this analyst's 13% base case — even after netting out a large, real, recurring interchange-litigation drag.

1. Business in plain English

Visa operates the world's largest card-payment network (VisaNet), connecting banks, merchants and consumers; it does not lend or take credit risk itself (that sits with issuing banks). Revenue is a small, growing take-rate on global consumer/commercial spend (service and data-processing fees) plus incentive-netted assessments, so nominal GDP + card-share-of-spend + cross-border travel/e-commerce are the underlying volume drivers. The moat is network effects (merchants accept Visa because consumers carry it; consumers carry it because merchants accept it) plus decades of processing-security infrastructure that is expensive to replicate.

2. Why the model likes it / is it durable

b1_live_scores.csv shows V with an incomplete live-scoring row (composite, decile, live_rank all blank; mktcap blank) — a data conflict: Visa is unambiguously a >$650B mega-cap and should be scored. fam_Q 0.868 (very high quality percentile) and roe 0.624 are populated and consistent with a durable, high-return network business; mom_12_1 0.120 is unpopulated for value/earnings-momentum families. This looks like a pipeline gap for this name rather than a real quality signal — flagged for the quant team rather than treated as a fundamental red flag. The durability case (network effects, non-lending model, 51%+ net margin) is independently verifiable in filings below and does not depend on the model score.

TTM (FQ4 FY25–FQ3 FY26): revenue $44.4B, GAAP net income $22.6B, non-GAAP diluted EPS $12.78, GAAP diluted EPS $11.76*. [1][2][3][4]

4. Guidance track record

Visa's 8-K earnings-release exhibits carry no numerical guidance; forward ranges are given verbally on the earnings call (secondary transcript sources, clearly marked as such below — never treated as filed facts). - FQ1 FY26 call (29-Jan-2026): no FY2026 range disclosed in the release itself. - FQ2 FY26 call (28-Apr-2026): management raised full-year FY2026 guidance to net revenue growth "low double-digit to low teens" and non-GAAP EPS growth "low teens" (per Motley Fool/Investing.com transcripts of the call) — this was itself a raise from the prior (FQ1) commentary, per secondary reporting. - FQ3 FY26 call (28-Jul-2026): management raised again to net revenue growth "low end of low teens", non-GAAP EPS growth "low end of mid-teens", opex growth "low end of low teens", tax rate 18.0–18.25% (Investing.com transcript quoting the CFO). CEO Ryan McInerney said results "exceeded the company's expectations." Two consecutive raises in the fiscal year, consistent with the acceleration seen in the filed quarterly numbers above. [5][6]

5. Moat, competitive position and secular drivers

  • Non-lending network model: Visa carries no consumer credit risk, so credit-cycle stress hits issuer banks, not Visa's income statement directly (though it can slow volume growth in a downturn).
  • Cross-border volume (ex.-intra-Europe) grew 11–12% in each of the last three quarters — a higher-take-rate segment than domestic, and the main reason margin has stayed >50%.
  • New growth vectors disclosed in filings/calls: Visa Stablecoin Platform (stablecoin minting/movement/management), an "Open Standard" partnership for OpenUSD issuance, tokenized-deposit work with Pismo, and an OpenAI partnership to enable Visa payments inside agentic-commerce flows. These are optionality, not yet revenue lines — treated as bull-case items, not base-case drivers.
  • Competitive risk: Mastercard is the direct scaled competitor; real-time/account-to-account rails (FedNow, Pix-style schemes, stablecoins) and large-merchant surcharging (post-MDL settlement, see §6) are the structural threats to take-rate over a 10-year horizon.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

Entity scope: all figures below are consolidated Visa Inc. (there is no separately reported bank/subsidiary segment balance sheet for Visa — unlike banks/insurers in this batch). - FY2025 (10-K for fiscal year ended 30-Sep-2025, filed 06-Nov-2025): operating cash flow $23,059M − capex (PaymentsToAcquireProductiveAssets) $1,482M = FCF $21,577M, FCF/GAAP-NI = 108% (favorable, no working-capital red flag). - TTM-through-31-Mar-2026 (derived: FY2025 10-K annual − six-month YTD ended 31-Mar-2025 [10-Q filed 30-Apr-2025] + six-month YTD ended 31-Mar-2026 [10-Q filed 29-Apr-2026]): OCF $22,756M, capex $1,571M, FCF ≈ $21.2B. This slightly understates the true trailing-twelve-month figure because the FQ3 FY26 quarter (Apr–Jun 2026) is not yet in the SEC bulk XBRL companyfacts feed as of this write-up (see §13 limitation) — GAAP net income for that quarter ($5.6B, per the earnings release) suggests TTM FCF is closer to $22–23B on the same conversion ratio. - Balance sheet, Condensed Consolidated Balance Sheet, Form 10-Q for the quarterly period ended 31-Mar-2026 (filed 29-Apr-2026), consolidated: cash and cash equivalents $12,404M; current maturities of long-term debt $1,559M; long-term debt (noncurrent) $22,417M; total debt $23,976M; total stockholders' equity (incl. non-controlling interest) $35,661M. Net debt ≈ $11.6B, against TTM EBITDA of roughly $32–33B — net leverage under 0.4x, a fortress balance sheet by any standard. - Share count: FQ1 FY26 buybacks $3.8B (11.0M shares @ $342.13); FQ2 FY26 $7.9B (~25M shares), plus a new $20B authorization; FQ3 FY26 $4.9B (14.5M shares @ $330.71), $28.4B authorization remaining. FY2025 full year: ~54M shares for $18.2B. Buybacks are a structural, multi-billion-dollar-per-quarter EPS tailwind. Dividend $0.670/quarter (~0.7% yield). - SBC not separately broken out in the release exhibits reviewed; not flagged as material based on Visa's historically low SBC/revenue ratio (<2%).

7. Valuation — reverse DCF (no V1 systematic valuation row for V)

v4/outputs/v1_valuation_table.csv and v1_valuation.json were checked: no row exists for V. v1_verdict is therefore set to null in the summary JSON, per instructions. Inputs: EV ≈ market cap $689,703M (d4 snapshot, 25-Sep-2026 close, price $367.38) + net debt $11,572M (31-Mar-2026) = $701.3B; FCF₀ $21.2B (TTM through 31-Mar-2026, §6); WACC 8.3% (CAPM: rf 4.2%, ERP 5.0%, beta 0.76 per d4); terminal growth 3.5%; 10-year horizon. Solving for the constant FCF growth rate that justifies the price: ≈8.9%/year for 10 years. - Bear case (EPS/FCF growth ≈6%/yr): cross-border/travel volume growth normalizes to low-single-digit, real-time-rail and stablecoin disintermediation start taking measurable share, litigation costs stay elevated (see §11), multiple compresses to ~22x. - Base case (≈13%/yr): continuation of management's own "low-teens revenue / mid-teens EPS" FY2026 guide moderating slightly over the decade as cross-border normalizes, buybacks continue at the current $15–20B/yr pace, multiple holds near 27x. - Bull case (≈17%/yr): stablecoin/agentic-commerce initiatives add a genuine new volume vector on top of the base network, opex leverage continues, multiple re-rates to 30x. Implied vs. base: BELOW. The reverse-DCF-implied 8.9% sits meaningfully below the 13% base case — the market is pricing Visa for something closer to its bear/base blend, not crediting it with sustaining its own guided mid-teens EPS growth for a decade. This is the basis for the INCLUDE verdict.

8. Bull case

  1. Two consecutive guidance raises within FY2026 (Apr and Jul 2026 calls) on real, filed acceleration in quarterly revenue growth (12%→17%).
  2. Reverse-DCF implied growth (8.9%) sits below both management's own guide and this analyst's base case (13%) — the stock is not priced for its own guidance to hold.
  3. Net-debt/EBITDA under 0.4x with $28.4B of buyback authorization remaining — capital return is a durable, self-funded EPS tailwind independent of volume growth.

9. Bear case

  1. Interchange MDL litigation costs have been large and recurring: $2.5B provisioned in FY2025 alone, plus $707M (FQ1 FY26), $311M (FQ2 FY26) and $237M (FQ3 FY26) — over $3.7B added across the last five reported quarters, a real and growing (not one-off) drag on reported margins.
  2. Real-time account-to-account rails and stablecoin payment rails are a genuine long-run disintermediation threat to card interchange economics — the same secular risk the company itself is now hedging via its own Stablecoin Platform.
  3. FQ3 FY26 revenue growth (14%) decelerated from FQ2's 17% — a single data point, but worth watching for whether the FQ2 print (aided by FIFA World Cup-related value-added-services demand per management) was a temporary pull-forward.

10. Key risks & kill criteria

  1. Net revenue growth falls below 8% YoY (constant-currency) for two consecutive fiscal quarters.
  2. Quarterly interchange-litigation provisions exceed $500M in any single quarter (vs. $237–707M range seen FQ1–FQ3 FY26), signalling the MDL settlement is deteriorating rather than resolving.
  3. Net debt/EBITDA rises above 1.5x (from ~0.4x today) without a offsetting acquisition-driven earnings step-up.
  4. Non-GAAP diluted EPS growth guidance is cut (vs. today's "low end of mid-teens" for FY2026) at any of the next two quarterly calls.
  5. Cross-border volume growth (ex.-intra-Europe) falls below 6% YoY for two consecutive quarters (from 11–12% today) — the highest-margin volume line decelerating structurally.

11. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: fiscal Q4/full-year FY2026, estimated late October 2026 (not yet confirmed as of this cutoff) — FY2025's equivalent release was 28-Oct-2025.
  • Interchange MDL: the district court granted preliminary approval of the amended/superseding settlement agreement in June 2026 (the agreement itself is dated 10-Nov-2025); final approval and the 90-day implementation window for merchant-surcharging changes are the next milestones to watch — a real catalyst/risk date, not yet reached as of 25-Sep-2026.

12. Red-flag scan

  • Litigation (the primary red flag): the interchange multidistrict litigation (In re Payment Card Interchange Fee and Merchant Discount Antitrust Litigation, E.D.N.Y.) is decades-old; Visa entered a superseding amended settlement agreement dated 10-Nov-2025, which received preliminary court approval in June 2026 (10bps reduction in the US combined average effective credit interchange rate for five years, expanded merchant surcharging rights). This is disclosed and provisioned for in the earnings releases cited in §9 — a known, sized, recurring cost, not a surprise, but large enough (>$3.7B across five quarters) to matter to margin trend.
  • No auditor changes, restatements, going-concern language, or SEC/DOJ investigations beyond the above found in sources reviewed.
  • Insider-selling pattern not independently re-checked at Form-4 level this pass (time-boxed); flagged as unverified rather than asserted clean.
  • Data conflict: b1_live_scores.csv shows V with a blank mktcap/composite/live_rank despite being a >$650B constituent — a data-pipeline gap, reported to the quant team, not evidence of any fundamental issue.

dossiers.VEEV:
Veeva Systems Inc. (VEEV) — Fundamental Diligence Dossier

Verdict: INCLUDE — 24–48 month thesis horizon. One-sentence reason: dominant, sticky, net-cash life-sciences cloud software (CRM/Vault) with four consecutive quarterly guidance raises and 16–18% revenue growth at 44–45% non-GAAP operating margin — a reverse DCF says the price requires only ~7% 10-year FCF growth, well below this analyst's 16% base case, with the company's one real legal overhang (the eight-year IQVIA dispute) already settled with no damages exchanged.

1. Business in plain English

Veeva sells cloud software to pharmaceutical and biotech companies: Vault CRM (managing interactions with doctors), Vault Clinical/Regulatory/Quality (managing drug development and compliance paperwork), and adjacent data/analytics products. Customers are pharma/biotech commercial and R&D organizations; revenue is subscription-based (84–87% of total) with the balance in professional services (implementation). The moat is high switching costs (life-sciences workflows are validated/regulated, so ripping out the system of record is expensive and risky) plus a purpose-built, life-sciences-specific product set that horizontal CRM/ERP vendors have not successfully replicated.

2. Why the model likes it / is it durable

b1_live_scores.csv: composite percentile 0.752 (decile 8, quintile 4 — the strongest score among this batch's three names), live_rank 124. Every family is populated and strong: fam_S (earnings momentum/SUE) 0.916 is the standout (raw SUE 5.98 — a large, consistent positive earnings-surprise trend); fam_Q 0.619 (gp_a percentile 0.286 is middling but roe 0.137/accruals/leverage components are clean); fam_V 0.573 (fcfp percentile driven by a genuinely large FCF base relative to price); fam_M only 0.281 (mom_12_1 raw −0.041, i.e., trailing 12-month price return is roughly flat-to-down) — a data point worth noting: the stock has not re-rated with its earnings beats over the past year, which is consistent with (and supportive of) the reverse-DCF finding in §7 that the market is not yet pricing in the demonstrated growth. This is a durable signal set (real earnings beats, weak price momentum), not an artefact.

3. Last 8 quarters (fiscal quarters; fiscal year ends 31 Jan; $M except EPS; GAAP unless marked)

4. Guidance track record (last 4 releases; full-year total-revenue and non-GAAP EPS guidance) — a clean four-for-four raise streak

Four consecutive releases, four raises, zero cuts or holds — the cleanest guidance track record in this batch. [1][2][5][6]

5. Moat, competition and secular drivers

  • Vault CRM migration: Veeva is mid-way through migrating its own legacy Salesforce-hosted CRM product onto its own Vault platform; management cited "five top-20 biopharmas" and "12 global top-20 commitments" to Vault CRM in the FQ2 FY27 release — a genuine internal-platform-transition catalyst (higher-margin, Veeva-owned infrastructure replacing a Salesforce-hosted layer) rather than new-market share-taking, but it is real, filed evidence of continued enterprise-customer commitment.
  • Competitive position: no other vendor offers a comparably complete, purpose-built, validated life-sciences CRM+Vault suite; Salesforce itself was historically Veeva's infrastructure landlord for the CRM product (now being exited via the Vault CRM migration above), which removes a structural dependency rather than adding a new competitive threat.
  • AI: management commentary ("AI is opening up the next big chapter") is directionally bullish but not yet quantified in filed revenue — treated as bull-case optionality, not base case.
  • Customer concentration: 1,500+ customers; no single-customer concentration disclosed in the releases reviewed — a positive, diversified base for a company serving a concentrated end-industry (large pharma).

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

Entity scope: all figures below are consolidated Veeva Systems Inc. - TTM FCF (derived, period ended 31-Jul-2026: FY2026 10-K annual OCF $1,415.225M − H1 FY2026 YTD OCF $1,115.591M + H1 FY2027 YTD OCF $1,365.825M = OCF ≈ $1,665.5M; capex is not separately broken out under a stable XBRL tag in the period reviewed — historically <1.5% of revenue for this asset-light SaaS business — so FCF ≈ $1.64–1.65B, i.e., FCF/non-GAAP-NI conversion well above 100%, consistent with a high-margin subscription model with negative working capital (deferred revenue is a source of cash, not a use)). Source: Form 10-K for FY2026 (filed 20-Mar-2026), Form 10-Q for FQ2 FY26 (filed 27-Aug-2025) and Form 10-Q for FQ2 FY27 (filed 27-Aug-2026), consolidated statements of cash flows. - Balance sheet, Condensed Consolidated Balance Sheet, Form 10-Q for the quarterly period ended 31-Jul-2026 (filed 27-Aug-2026), consolidated: cash and cash equivalents $1,812.0M; short-term investments $5,430.9M (total liquid assets $7,242.9M); stockholders' equity $7,431.4M; no debt reported at any point in the two-year lookback — a genuinely debt-free balance sheet, the cleanest of the three names in this batch. - SBC: stock-based compensation $136.8M in FQ2 FY27 (≈14.7% of revenue) is the primary GAAP-to-non-GAAP reconciling item, alongside a small amount of purchased-intangible amortization ($4.1M) — SBC is meaningful but has been declining as a share of revenue over time and is fully disclosed, not hidden. - One-off/litigation: $30.6M in litigation-settlement charges in FY2026 (see §12) — a real GAAP cost, now resolved and non-recurring, correctly excluded from non-GAAP in the release.

7. Valuation — reverse DCF (no V1 systematic valuation row for VEEV)

v4/outputs/v1_valuation_table.csv and v1_valuation.json were checked: no row exists for VEEV. v1_verdict is therefore set to null in the summary JSON. Inputs: EV = market cap $45,444.6M (d4 snapshot, 25-Sep-2026 close, price $280.68) minus net cash $7,242.9M (31-Jul-2026, §6) = EV ≈ $38.2B; FCF₀ $1.64B (TTM, §6); WACC 9.2% (CAPM: rf 4.2%, ERP 5.0%, beta 0.974 per d4; no debt so WACC = cost of equity); terminal growth 3.5%; 10-year horizon. Solving for the constant FCF growth rate that justifies the price: ≈6.7%/year for 10 years. - Bear case (≈10%/yr): Vault CRM migration stalls, large-pharma R&D budget cuts (a real industry risk given ongoing biopharma cost discipline) slow new-seat growth, professional-services growth (a leading indicator) reverses; exit multiple compresses to 24x. - Base case (≈16%/yr): continuation of the demonstrated 16–18% revenue growth for several more years, moderating gradually as the company scales past ~$4–5B revenue, non-GAAP margin holds in the mid-40s%; exit multiple ~30x (below today's ~32x trailing multiple, i.e., some mean reversion assumed). - Bull case (≈22%/yr): AI-driven product expansion (Vault CRM + new AI-native modules) adds a genuine second growth wave on top of the core migration, international/biotech-segment penetration accelerates; exit multiple 34x. Implied vs. base: BELOW — materially so. The reverse-DCF-implied 6.7% sits far below the 16% base case (and below even the bear case), despite four consecutive quarters of guidance raises and no deceleration in the filed numbers. This is the strongest valuation-support finding in the batch and the basis for the INCLUDE verdict; it is also consistent with the b1 momentum signal in §2 (earnings beating consistently while the stock re-rates only modestly).

3-year scenario returns (annualised total return from $280.68; no dividend)

Scenario EPS growth (yrs 1–3) Exit non-GAAP P/E Annualised return
Bear 10%/yr 24x ≈ −0.4%/yr

8. Bull case

  1. Four consecutive quarterly releases (Nov-2025 through Aug-2026), four consecutive full-year guidance raises, zero cuts — the cleanest execution track record in this batch, on both revenue and non-GAAP EPS.
  2. Reverse-DCF-implied growth (6.7%) is roughly half this analyst's base case (16%) and below even the bear case (10%) — a large apparent margin of safety if the demonstrated growth trajectory merely continues, let alone accelerates on AI/Vault CRM.
  3. Debt-free, $7.2B in liquid assets against a business generating ~$1.6B of FCF/year — no financing risk, full optionality for further R&D investment or opportunistic M&A/buybacks.

9. Bear case

  1. Trailing 12-month price momentum is flat-to-negative (mom_12_1 raw −4.1%) despite the earnings beats — either the market has already priced in mean reversion of pharma-sector software spend, or there is a real, not-yet-visible-in-filings concern (e.g., large-pharma budget tightening) that the quantitative screen and this dossier have not fully captured; worth treating the DCF "cheapness" with some humility rather than certainty.
  2. Revenue growth is now running almost entirely on subscription re-signs/expansion within an already-large, concentrated pharma customer base; a slowdown in large-pharma R&D/commercial IT budgets (a live industry theme given drug-pricing and tariff pressure discussed by other names in this program) would show up here with a lag.
  3. High SBC (≈15% of revenue) means the non-GAAP EPS figures driving the guidance-raise narrative overstate cash economics to shareholders relative to the FCF figure in §6 — real, but standard for enterprise SaaS and already disclosed.

10. Key risks & kill criteria

  1. Total revenue growth falls below 12% YoY for two consecutive quarters (from the current steady 16–18%).
  2. A full-year guidance range is cut (not just held or raised more slowly) at any of the next two quarterly releases (FQ3 FY27, ~Nov-2026, or FQ4/FY2027, ~Mar-2027) — would end the current four-release raise streak.
  3. Non-GAAP operating margin falls below 40% for two consecutive quarters (from the current 44–45%).
  4. Professional-services revenue growth turns negative YoY (a leading indicator for future subscription bookings) for two consecutive quarters.
  5. Net cash position declines by more than $1B in a single quarter outside of a disclosed buyback/M&A program (would signal an unexplained cash-burn event in an otherwise FCF-generative business).

11. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: FQ3 FY2027 (quarter ending 31-Oct-2026), estimated ~19-Nov-2026 (pattern-based: FQ3 FY26 was reported 20-Nov-2025) — not yet confirmed via a company press release as of this cutoff.
  • Vault CRM migration progress (customer-commitment counts) is a recurring, filed-each-quarter data point worth tracking for signs of stalling.

12. Red-flag scan

  • IQVIA litigation — resolved, not a live overhang. Veeva and IQVIA settled all outstanding litigation (an eight-year dispute; IQVIA alleged trade-secret misappropriation, Veeva asserted antitrust counterclaims) via a Settlement Agreement dated 13-Aug-2025: no damages were paid by either party, both sides dismissed all claims with prejudice, and the companies entered mutual data-access agreements. The $30.6M GAAP charge in FY2026 represents Veeva's own contingency-fee legal costs, not a payment to IQVIA. This is now closed and is disclosed here for completeness, not as an ongoing risk.

Schwenger: 5,000 shares/$1.0M on 16-Jul-2026; 1,000 shares/$265,200 on 14-Sep-2026) were the only insider activity found in a light check; the CEO (Peter Gassner) has made no reported open-market sale since Feb-2023. No unusual insider-selling pattern identified, though this was a light (not Form-4-database-exhaustive) check.
  • No auditor changes, restatements or going-concern language found in sources reviewed.

dossiers.VICI:
VICI Properties Inc. (VICI) — Diligence Dossier (F34, standard depth)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Thesis horizon 12–36 months. One-sentence reason: as of the 2026-09-25 close, an 8x-forward-AFFO, ~7.7%-yielding, investment-grade-adjacent triple-net gaming REIT with a clean four-release guidance-raise streak (2025–2026) is priced for AFFO/share to shrink forever, which its own results and pipeline contradict — but two tenants still supply ~70% of rent per the Q2 2026 10-Q, which is why this is a starter, not a full, position.

Thesis (≤25 words): Owns irreplaceable Las Vegas Strip and regional casino real estate on long, CPI-linked leases, priced far below what its own steady growth and diversification deals justify.

2. Business in plain English

VICI Properties is a triple-net-lease REIT that owns the real estate under casino-resorts (Caesars Palace, MGM Grand, The Venetian, Mandalay Bay and dozens of regional properties) and leases it back to operators on long-term, CPI-linked leases, plus a growing book of experiential and leisure assets (bowling via Bowlero, golf via Cabot, and now a first Club Med Caribbean resort). It makes money on the spread between its cost of capital (debt + equity) and the yield it earns funding new acquisitions and mortgage/financing-receivable deals, so growth comes from rent escalators plus accretive external deal-making, not from operating the casinos itself. Competitive position: the largest gaming-focused net-lease REIT, with essentially no direct competitor of similar scale in single-purpose casino real estate.

3. Why the model likes it / durability

Triage (Q14_triage.json, as_of 2026-09-25) scored VICI quality 4, growth 3, price_vs_growth 5, no red flags, reasoning "8x NTM P/E with a 7.7% yield and high-teens revenue growth is a rare combination for an investment-grade landlord; main risk is tenant concentration (Caesars/MGM) rather than the real estate itself." The pre-registered quant composite (b1_live_scores.csv) is far less enthusiastic: live_rank 441/503, composite 0.113, driven by a very strong value percentile (fam_V 0.997 — cheapest-in-market on book/price and EBIT/EV) but a weak quality percentile (fam_Q 0.204, because REIT accruals/leverage/asset-growth inputs are largely NaN or penalize balance-sheet growth funded by debt) and near-bottom momentum/earnings-momentum (fam_M 0.088, fam_S 0.014). This is explainable, not a fundamental red flag: the composite's quality and momentum families are built for operating companies, not net-lease REITs whose "growth" is intentionally debt/equity-funded acquisition, and whose stock has simply been unloved (rate-sensitive sector) rather than fundamentally weak — the durable driver is the value/income combination triage flagged, which primary-source results below confirm is real and growing, not an artefact.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

Data-quality note: Yahoo/d4's generic freeCashflow field for VICI (as_of 2026-09-25 snapshot) implies only a ~1% FCF yield on price, which is not usable for a net-lease REIT (capex there is "PaymentsToAcquireRealEstate," i.e. growth investment, not maintenance capex); this dossier uses AFFO, which the company itself reports and guides to in its 8-K releases, consistent with the program's known REIT-metric flaw disclosed in STATE.md for HST/FRT. Balance sheet: total debt $17.2bn at the Q2 2026 8-K (filed 2026-07-29), leverage ~4.9x annualized adjusted EBITDA, liquidity $2.5bn (cash $288M + $2.2bn revolver capacity), remaining below VICI's own target leverage range. Per the Q2 2026 10-Q, stockholders' equity was $29.17bn, up from $26.6bn a year earlier (Q2 2025 10-Q). Shares outstanding rose modestly from ~1.057bn (Q2 2025 10-Q) to ~1.101bn (Q2 2026 10-Q), consistent with ATM equity issuance funding accretive acquisitions rather than dilutive stock-based comp. Dividend: quarterly $0.4525+ (raised ~4% YoY per the Q3 2025 8-K declaration), trailing yield ~7.7–7.8% at the 2026-09-25 price; AFFO payout ratio ~73–75%, leaving a modest retained-cash cushion. Tenant concentration is the central balance-sheet-adjacent risk: per the Q1 2026 and Q2 2026 10-Qs, Caesars represented ~36–37% and MGM ~34–36% of total contractual rent in the most recent quarters (Q1 2026: MGM 36%/Caesars 37%, ~73% combined; Q2 2026: Caesars 36%/MGM 34%, ~70% combined) — a real, undiversified two-tenant credit exposure, though the trend is modestly improving as new deals (Golden Entertainment, Gamehost, Club Med) add other operators.

7. Valuation snapshot & reverse DCF

Price (2026-09-25 close) $23.51; NTM P/E ~8.0x (d4, calendarised); dividend yield ~7.7–7.8%; FY2026 P/AFFO on the guided midpoint ($2.46/sh) ≈9.6x. No V1 row exists for VICI (checked v1_valuation_table.csv — no row; VICI appears only as a peer-comparison sample inside FRT's V1 detail JSON, not as its own valuation) → v1_verdict = null; no systematic reconciliation is possible, so this dossier's valuation view is independently derived using a REIT-appropriate framework (AFFO yield / required-total-return), not a generic FCF DCF.

Reverse DCF (Gordon-growth on AFFO/share): Price = AFFO₁×(1+g)/(r−g). Using AFFO/share $2.46 (2026 guide midpoint) and a required total return r of 8.5–9.5% (a net-lease-REIT risk premium appropriate for VICI's leverage and two-tenant concentration — a pure CAPM beta-based WACC (β≈0.68) would imply an unrealistically low ~6–7% and is not used here because beta understates single-name lease-concentration risk), the price of $23.51 implies perpetual AFFO/share growth of roughly −0.9% to −1.8% across that discount-rate range — i.e. the market is pricing VICI as if AFFO per share will shrink indefinitely. My evidence-based base case is +3–4%/yr (embedded CPI-linked escalators, most capped at 2–3%/yr on the largest leases, plus the demonstrated pace of accretive third-party acquisitions — Golden Entertainment $1.16bn, Gamehost C$200.6M, Club Med $20.3M+$55.2M redevelopment — funded at a spread to VICI's cost of capital, consistent with the guided +3.4% for 2026 and the 4.6–5.7%/quarter AFFO/share growth actually delivered over the past two years). Implied growth is clearly below base case: the stock is priced more cheaply than a no-growth, in-perpetuity REIT. Bear case (AFFO/share growth slows to +1%/yr on tenant stress, exit multiple compresses to 7x from ~9.6x): 3-yr annualized total return ≈ +4%. Base case (+3.5%/yr growth, multiple stable): ≈ +11%/yr. Bull case (+5%/yr growth on continued accretive/diversifying deal flow, multiple re-rates to ~9.5x as rate fears ease): ≈ +18–19%/yr.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) Rent escalators (CPI-linked, several uncapped in early lease years) plus an active, accretive acquisition pipeline (Golden Entertainment, Gamehost, Club Med) funded at a spread to cost of capital keep compounding AFFO/share even with zero cap-rate compression; (2) management is visibly diversifying away from the Caesars/MGM duopoly — combined concentration fell from ~73% (Q1'26) to ~70% (Q2'26) in one quarter, and the Club Med and Gamehost deals open entirely new verticals (leisure resorts, Canadian gaming); (3) at ~9.6x forward AFFO and a 7.7–7.8% yield, VICI is near the cheapest it has traded relative to its own multi-year history for a business generating long-duration, largely investment-grade-adjacent contracted cash flows. Bear: (1) Caesars + MGM still supply ~70% of contractual rent — an unusually concentrated exposure for a REIT this size; a material deterioration at either operator (regional gaming softness, a leveraged refinancing squeeze, new-supply competition) leaves VICI with limited ability to quickly re-lease single-purpose casino real estate; (2) higher-for-longer interest rates raise VICI's own refinancing cost on $17.2bn of debt faster than escalators grow rent, compressing the spread that funds accretive growth; (3) GAAP net income is highly volatile quarter to quarter (−39% YoY in Q2'26) on non-cash fair-value items in VICI's financing-receivable and preferred-equity book, which creates real headline/print-day risk (the Q2'26 print was reported as an "EPS miss" despite AFFO growth) even though the underlying cash-flow metric is steady.

9. Key risks & measurable kill criteria

Any of the following would break the thesis; each is a specific, observable, time-bound signpost to monitor at each earnings release, not a vague worry: 1. Combined Caesars + MGM share of total contractual rent stops declining and rises back above 75% for two consecutive quarters (from ~70% currently), signalling the diversification trend has reversed. 2. AFFO/share guidance is cut (any reduction to the low end of the then-current full-year range) at a subsequent release — track record is currently four-for-four raises/holds. 3. Net debt/adjusted EBITDA rises above 5.5x (from ~4.9x currently) without a stated deleveraging plan. 4. A monetary default, lease restructuring, or sub-investment-grade credit-rating downgrade (below B1/B+) at either Caesars or MGM. 5. Realized rent growth trails CPI by more than 100bps for two consecutive years, i.e. the escalator caps bind and erode real rental income (VICI's own disclosed risk).

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 2026-10-29 (Q3'26, per d4 next_earnings_date). Watch for further tenant-diversification deal flow (following Golden Entertainment/Gamehost/Club Med) and any update on the Caesars/MGM concentration trend.

11. Red-flag scan

No auditor change, restatement, or going-concern language found in the filings reviewed. No SEC/DOJ investigation or short-seller report found in this cycle's search. Insider activity: routine Form 4 activity (RSU vesting/settlement and associated tax-related sales), no unusual pattern; short interest ~3.0% of float as of end-April 2026, up ~22% from the prior count but still a low absolute level. The only real, open item is the tenant concentration discussed throughout (§6, §8, §9) — it is disclosed, quantified, and the trend is (modestly) improving, not a hidden risk.

VLTO (Veralto Corporation) — Diligence Dossier

Agent: F37 · Standard depth · Prepared 2026-09-26 · Prices/market data as of 2026-09-25 close ($97.14; mkt cap ≈$23.68B)

Data quality note: all figures are consolidated (Veralto has no separately-reported standalone entity), in US dollars ($ = USD; m/mn = millions, bn = billions unless a per-share $ figure), sourced primarily from SEC EDGAR XBRL and company earnings releases as cited in Section 13; GAAP vs. non-GAAP/adjusted figures are labelled throughout; approximated (derived) figures are flagged where used.

1. Verdict

WATCH — not now; would revisit on a pullback toward the mid-$80s or on two consecutive quarters of Product Quality & Innovation (PQI) core growth back above ~4%. Veralto is a genuinely high-quality, Danaher-heritage compounder (34% ROE, 17.3% net margin, low leverage, recurring consumables/service revenue), but the reverse DCF shows the price already assumes roughly the growth rate the company can plausibly deliver given a soft PQI segment — this is the "great business priced for more than it can comfortably deliver" case the mandate explicitly asks to be honest about, not an INCLUDE. No V1 row exists for VLTO, so v1_verdict is null.

2. Business in plain English

Veralto (spun off from Danaher in September 2023) operates two segments: Water Quality (~57% of revenue — instruments, chemistries and services for testing/treating municipal and industrial water, brands including Hach and ChemTreat) and Product Quality & Innovation (~43% — marking/coding equipment (Videojet), and packaging/color-management software and hardware (X-Rite, Pantone, and the newly acquired GlobalVision packaging-compliance software)). Revenue is heavily recurring: consumables, service contracts and software subscriptions tied to installed equipment, inherited from Danaher's playbook of pricing the instrument to sell the annuity. The moat is regulatory-driven demand (water-quality testing is often legally mandated) plus high switching costs once an instrument/workflow is validated into a regulated process.

Sector routing note: none of the stock-analysis skill's sector playbooks fit cleanly. waste-environmental.md is explicitly about waste collection/disposal and landfill permits, which does not describe Veralto's analytical- instrumentation and marking/software business at all; Veralto is closer to a diversified, high-margin instrumentation/consumables business (the Danaher/Roper archetype). This dossier therefore uses the generic core-factor/DuPont framework rather than forcing an ill-fitting sector playbook, and says so explicitly per the skill's own instruction for when no playbook applies.

3. Why the model likes it / durability

data/b1_live_scores.csv: live_rank 294, composite 0.409 (decile 5) — a more middling composite than PAYX/TYL, driven by decent but not exceptional Quality (fam_Q 0.424: ROE 32.2%, gp/assets 0.437) and good Value (fam_V 0.773), offset by weak Momentum (fam_M 0.255, mom_12_1 -0.071 — a flat-to-slightly-down year) and average earnings momentum (fam_S 0.455, though SUE is actually strong at 1.153 — recent quarters have beaten). The quality (34% ROE, 17.3% margin, 1.1x leverage per the original triage) is real and durable — Danaher-system pricing discipline and consumables mix do not disappear on spin-off — but growth is genuinely modest: Water Quality core growth has been accelerating (3.8% Q1 2026 → 5.7% Q2 2026) while PQI has been soft (-1.0% Q1 2026 → +2.0% Q2 2026), and a $0.05/share Q2 EPS benefit came from one-off IEEPA tariff refunds, not operations.

No V1 row exists for VLTO; v1_verdict = null. Analyst-derived reverse DCF (stock-analysis/scripts/valuation.py, 10-year fade to 4% terminal growth):

That sits close to — arguably slightly below, but not comfortably below — a plausible base case: Water Quality mid-single-digit-and-accelerating core growth, PQI low-single-digit-and-recovering core growth, modest margin expansion, and a buyback program, blending to roughly a 4–5%/yr FCF growth base case. Trailing P/E 24.0x, EV/EBITDA 18.1x and FCF yield 4.4% are all "fair-quality-business" numbers, not "cheap" ones. Because the margin of safety is thin, valuation_view_vs_v1.implied_vs_base = "in_line" (the analyst's judgment call: implied growth is close enough to the base case that this is priced fairly for the quality on offer, not priced for distress or for excess optimism) — and per the mandate's explicit instruction, a great business priced roughly for what it can deliver is a WATCH, not an INCLUDE.

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull (3): 1. Water Quality core growth is genuinely accelerating (3.8% → 5.7% over two quarters) and is regulation-backed, recurring-revenue demand, not a cyclical bounce. 2. SBC at 1.3% of revenue and net debt/EBITDA of ~1.1x show real capital discipline — a Danaher-system business that compounds through bolt-on M&A (GlobalVision) and buybacks without diluting shareholders. 3. If PQI's Q1→Q2 2026 improvement (-1.0% → +2.0% core growth) continues into H2, the "soft segment" bear case weakens and the stock could re-rate off a currently fair, not cheap, multiple.

Bear (3): 1. The reverse DCF shows the price already assuming close to the growth rate a sober base case would forecast — there is little valuation cushion if PQI's recovery stalls or Water Quality decelerates. 2. Part of the FY2026 guidance raise is explicitly a one-off tariff refund ($0.05/share in Q2), not organic reacceleration; stripping it, the "raise" is smaller than headline. 3. A newly-issued $725M senior notes offering, even if framed as refinancing, modestly increases fixed obligations at a company whose PQI segment has been growing below the rate needed to comfortably grow into more leverage.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. PQI segment core sales growth falls back below 0% for two consecutive quarters (it was -1.0% in Q1 2026, +2.0% in Q2 2026 — the recovery is one data point, not yet a trend).

VRSN — Verisign, Inc. — Fundamental Diligence Dossier

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — 24–36 month horizon. A durable, contractually-protected monopoly on .com/.net domain registry with real, exercised pricing power and an aggressive buyback program, but the current 27.3x NTM P/E is pricing in roughly 14.5%/yr growth for a decade against a delivered 5-year CAGR of just 5.8% — even generous credit for the newly-resumed price increases doesn't fully close that gap. Named reservation: hold at reduced weight versus a full-conviction name; do not size this as if the bull case (25.8%/yr) were the base case.

2. Business in plain English

Verisign operates the authoritative registry for the .com and .net top-level internet domains under an exclusive agreement with ICANN (renewed in November 2024 through November 30, 2030) and a related Cooperative Agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce. It sells wholesale registrations and renewals to domain registrars (GoDaddy, Namecheap, etc.), who in turn sell to end customers; Verisign itself does not sell to consumers. Because the marginal cost of adding or renewing a domain in an existing registry database is close to zero, incremental revenue converts to profit at very high margins (68.2% GAAP operating margin, Q2 2026). Its competitive position is not "market share" in the normal sense — it is a government-linked, contractually exclusive registry operator, with pricing capped by that same contract.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

B1 ranks VRSN #53 (composite 89.4th percentile), driven by exceptionally strong Quality (gross-profit/assets 98.8th percentile — reflecting the registry's near-zero marginal cost — OCF/assets 96.9th percentile) and strong Value (FCF yield 79.4th percentile, EBIT/EV 64.8th percentile), with average Momentum and Earnings-momentum. This is durable, not an artefact — the underlying economics (near-100% incremental margin, contractual multi-year pricing rights, sole-source registry) are structural, not accounting-driven, and are directly confirmed in this review by the actual Q2 2026 operating margin (68.2%) and the just-announced Nov 2026 price increase. Data conflict flagged and resolved: V1's own valuation model flagged a conflict — "D3 TTM revenue implies an implausible EBIT margin (67.9%)" and substituted a Yahoo revenue figure to compute the DCF. Having independently confirmed the 67.9–68.2% operating margin directly from Verisign's own SEC filings and Q2 2026 earnings release, this is not a data error — it is a real, structural feature of the registry business and V1's "implausible" flag was a false positive that should not have triggered a data substitution. 7. Valuation snapshot — reconciliation with V1

V1 verdict: fair (score −0.084). NTM P/E 27.3x — 39.5th percentile of its own ~14.75-year history (i.e. somewhat cheaper than its own historical average) but well above the peer median of 16.7x (peer set: AKAM, GDDY — only 2 true comparables, and neither is a close business-model match: AKAM is a CDN/security vendor, GDDY is a retail registrar, not a sole-source wholesale registry — peer-set quality is a real limitation on this comparison). WACC 8.85%. Implied 10-year growth from the current price: +14.5%/yr, vs. consensus FY1 growth +9.7%, delivered 5-year CAGR +5.8%, delivered 10-year CAGR +4.4%. Bear/base/bull 3-year annualised returns: −10.2% / +7.8% / +25.8%. The model's own base-case fair value ($359.70) already exceeds the single highest Wall Street 12-month price target ($355). My view: the "fair" verdict is right, and I would not push back on the base case (+7.8%/yr) — but the "implied 14.5%/yr growth" framing overstates how aggressive the pricing really is. VRSN can raise .com prices up to 7%/yr in years 3–6 of each 6-year ICANN term (no increases allowed in years 1–2) — it just exercised this, raising the wholesale price from $10.26 to $10.97 (+6.9%) effective November 1, 2026 — and domain-base growth guidance has just been raised to 5.2–6.0%. Price (~+7%) × base (~+5.5%) is a plausible ~12%/yr revenue tailwind in peak-pricing years, before the buyback-driven EPS uplift (~4%/yr from share-count reduction) — i.e., something in the low-to-mid-teens EPS growth is achievable in good years, which is close to, but still below, the 14.5%/yr the reverse-DCF requires every year for ten years. The bull case (25.8%/yr, requiring 34.9x exit multiple) is the scenario that needs the most scepticism, not the base case. dossier_view: fair; consistent with V1: yes (I agree with the verdict and the base case; I flag the "implied growth" framing and the thin peer set as nuances, not disagreements with the number itself).

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: 1. Contractually exclusive registry through Nov 2030 with demonstrated, exercised pricing power (7% max annual increase, just taken) flowing through at near-100% incremental margin. 2. Domain-base growth reaccelerating and guided up twice in 2026 (3.1–4.3% → 5.2–6.0%), with record new registrations, management attributing part of the strength to AI-related tailwinds rather than headwinds. 3. Extremely capital-light (capex <2% of revenue), funding a large, sustained buyback program (14.9% share-count reduction in ~4 years) against only ~1.1x net debt/EBITDA.

Bear: 1. The reverse-DCF's implied 14.5%/yr decade-long growth rate is well above anything VRSN has ever delivered (5-year CAGR 5.8%, 10-year CAGR 4.4%), and rests on a thin, imperfect 2-name peer comparison; the model's own base-case value already exceeds the Street's most bullish 12-month target. 2. Pricing power is not unlimited: no increases are allowed in years 1–2 of each 6-year ICANN cycle, and the whole framework is a negotiated, government-linked agreement (ICANN / U.S. Dept. of Commerce) that is renewed, not permanent. 3. Negative and deepening equity (−$2,254.1M, worsening ~$277M in 15 months) now funded partly by debt refinanced at a higher coupon (5.10% vs. 4.75%) — a modest but real increase in the cost of capital.

9. Key risks & measurable kill criteria

  1. ICANN/.com pricing authority is capped, revoked or renegotiated below the current "7%/yr in years 3–6" framework before the Nov 2030 expiry.
  2. Domain-base growth falls back below 3% YoY for two consecutive quarters (current guide 5.2–6.0%).
  3. Net debt/EBITDA rises above 2.0x (currently ≈1.1x).
  4. Quarterly revenue growth decelerates below 4% YoY for two consecutive quarters (currently +6.0% Q2'26, +6.6% Q1'26).
  5. A materially adverse outcome in any future .com/.net registry-agreement renewal or a DOJ/ICANN antitrust or regulatory action against the arrangement.

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • November 1, 2026: .com wholesale price increase to $10.97 takes effect (already announced).
  • .web gTLD launch flagged by management as expected "later this year" (2026) — a new, currently non-material registry line.
  • Next earnings: ~late October 2026 (estimated from cadence: 2025-10-23, 2024-10-24; not yet officially confirmed).

11. Red-flag scan

An October 2025 short-seller report raised concerns about the impact of "AdSense for Domains" on VRSN's economics; per a follow-up trade-press piece (Domain Name Wire, Dec 2025), the subsequent registration data did not bear out the bearish thesis, and record H1 2026 new-registration growth is at least directionally inconsistent with it — presented here even-handedly as a single secondary source, not independently re-verified against the original short report. No 8-K Item 4.01/4.02 (auditor change / restatement) filings found in the submissions history reviewed. Scope limitation: no MAS/VRSN-specific Form 4 insider-trading pattern was surfaced in this pass (search returned no results); this should be read as "not found," not "confirmed clean."

dossiers.VRT:
VRT — Vertiv Holdings Co

1. Verdict

WATCH — thesis horizon 12–36 months. Vertiv is a genuinely excellent business right now: the pure-play leader in power and liquid-cooling infrastructure for AI/hyperscaler data centers, growing net sales 24–30% YoY with margins expanding ~400+bps and free cash flow up 150–240% YoY, now sitting in a net-cash position with a record $15bn backlog. But the 25 September 2026 close (already down from a post-Q2-selloff level, after the stock fell as much as 26% on 29 July 2026 when reported net sales missed consensus by ~3%) still prices in continued strong growth on a reverse DCF (~14.3%/year for ten years) that is at or slightly above this dossier's own evidence-based base case (~11–12%/year, reflecting an expected deceleration from today's 30%+ organic growth as the current 2.9x book-to-bill normalizes). This is exactly the triage's own caution: "significant re-rating already happened; a hyperscaler capex pause is the key risk." A genuinely strong operating story, priced for more strength than a conservative base case can defend — WATCH, not INCLUDE, pending either a better entry price or firmer evidence that the current order/backlog surge is durable rather than a pull-forward.

2. Business in plain English

Vertiv makes the power and thermal-management ("cooling") equipment that keeps data centers running — uninterruptible power supplies, power distribution, switchgear, and (increasingly, as AI chips get hotter) liquid-cooling systems for the racks that house GPUs. It sells almost entirely to data-center owners and operators: hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta and others building AI infrastructure), colocation providers, and enterprises. It does not own or operate any data centers itself — it is a picks-and-shovels equipment and services supplier to the AI buildout, competing with Schneider Electric and Eaton. Its revenue is driven by (a) new data-center construction and retrofits tied directly to hyperscaler capital-expenditure cycles, and (b) a growing recurring services/parts business on its large installed base. The backlog ($15bn, +109% YoY) and book-to-bill (2.9x as of the most recent quarter reviewed) reflect orders placed well ahead of installation — a genuine demand signal, but also a source of potential volatility if that order pace normalizes or hyperscalers pause spending.

3. Why the model likes it — and is it durable?

B1 composite is upper-mid (live_rank 177/~2,300, decile 7, quintile 4; composite 0.646). Family drivers: Momentum (fam_M ≈0.76, high) — the stock has rallied hard (12-month price return ≈+72%, mom_12_1 0.716); Quality (fam_Q ≈0.64, good) — strong gross-profit/assets and ROE (36.4%), though leverage/asset-growth metrics are elevated by the scale of the AI-infrastructure buildout; Earnings momentum (fam_S ≈0.59, above average); Value (fam_V ≈0.21, weak) — VRT screens expensive on every value sub-metric, the honest counterweight the triage itself flagged (57x trailing P/E).

Durability check: the underlying demand is real and evidenced in primary filings — revenue, backlog and margin all corroborate the AI-infrastructure narrative, and management's FY2026 guidance has been raised at every release this year (see §5). But two specific, dated facts temper the "durable" read: (1) Q2 2026 (reported 29 July 2026) missed analyst revenue estimates ($3.27bn vs. ~$3.38bn consensus) despite the guidance raise and EPS beat, with management attributing the shortfall to "minor timing shifts, primarily due to temporary supply chain congestion and multi-phased project execution" — a plausible but unverified explanation for a real, market-moving miss (the stock fell as much as 26% that day); (2) a 2.9x book-to-bill ratio is, by the company's own historical standards, extreme, and even a modest normalization toward a more typical 1.2–1.5x ratio (as seen as recently as Q3 2025) would mechanically slow reported backlog growth even if underlying demand stays strong.
